title: No token expiration check allows indefinitely-valid stale sessions
description: LoginGuard.canActivate() (line 17-24) only checks whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage — it never decodes or validates the token's 'exp' claim before granting access. tokenDecode() (line 33-44) similarly decodes the payload but performs no check against the current time or any expiration claim. AdminGuard/AccountingGuard build their role decision entirely on top of this expiration-blind decode. As a result, once a token is placed in localStorage, the guards treat it as perpetually valid regardless of whether the token has actually expired server-side, extending the window during which a leaked or stale token can be used to access guarded client routes.

title: Authentication token persisted in localStorage

Unlike an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, this storage mechanism provides no built-in protection against script-based theft.

title: Notification-repeat action gated only by client-held challenge state, with no visible re-authorization check
description: The component's repeatNotification() method (exercised at lines 75, 83, 92 and invoked via a button click at line 131) is called directly against whatever `component.challenge` object is currently set on the client, with the 'solved' flag and challenge name taken entirely from client-side component state (see line 73, 81, 89, 105, 113, 121 where tests set `challenge = { name, solved }` freely). The tests show the UI conditionally renders the clickable 'solved' badge based on `challenge.solved`, and the ability to trigger the call is additionally gated only by another client-held boolean (`allowRepeatNotifications`, set at line 72), with no indication anywhere in this spec that the method re-validates solved status or authorization server-side before calling challengeService.repeatNotification(encodeURIComponent(name)). Because Angular component instances and their bound data/flags are inspectable/mutable from browser devtools, and because the method can be invoked directly (as tests do at line 75/83/92 without going through the rendered button), an attacker with access to the page could set `component.allowRepeatNotifications = true` and `component.challenge = { name: <any>, solved: true }` for an arbitrary challenge and directly invoke `component.repeatNotification()`, triggering repeatNotification against the backend for a challenge that was never actually solved — a classic trust-the-client design gap if the backend does not independently re-verify solved status (which cannot be confirmed from this file, but no such control is exercised or asserted anywhere in this spec).

title: Security-relevant API failures are only logged to the browser console, never reported to any monitoring/alerting channel

Both tests assert only `console.log` was invoked with the raw error value — there is no call to any remote logging/telemetry service, no error-tracking SDK, and no user-visible alert. Failures of the continue-code endpoint are security-relevant: they can indicate tampering with progress state, malformed/forged socket 'challenge solved' events, or backend authorization failures on the progress-saving flow, none of which would ever surface anywhere except a single client's local devtools console (which the affected user, not a defender, controls and can simply ignore or clear). Because this is confirmed only through the component's externally observable behavior in the test file (the actual console.log call sites live in the untested component.ts), there is no server-side or centralized monitoring signal produced for these failure conditions, meaning repeated/automated attempts to abuse the continue-code or country-mapping endpoints would never trigger any detection or alerting.

title: Continue-code progress cookie test only validates the 'expires' attribute, suggesting missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite hardening on a sensitive persistence cookie
description: The test 'should store retrieved continue code as cookie for 1 year' asserts that cookieService.put is called with the cookie name 'continueCode', the raw code value, and an options object matched only via `expect.objectContaining({ expires: expect.any(Date) })`. Tracing the full path: the backend continue-code value is mocked (146); the test independently computes a reference `expires` Date before invoking the component (148); component.saveProgress() is called, which internally invokes cookieService.put with the code and an options object (149); the test then advances its own reference date by one year to compute the expected expiry for later comparison (150); the assertion checks the call using `objectContaining`, a partial match that only inspects the `expires` field and never inspects `secure` or `sameSite` (152). Because objectContaining performs a partial match, this test would pass regardless of whether the options object also sets secure or sameSite restrictions. The suite never exercises or asserts on these attributes anywhere in the test, so there is no verification that this progress-tracking cookie (used to restore challenge completion state for a year) is transmitted only over HTTPS or protected against cross-site sending. This is inferred from the absence of any positive test coverage for these flags in the spec, not from direct visibility into the cookie-writing implementation, so it is reported with reduced confidence.

title: Password-change failures are only surfaced via console.log, not sent to any security monitoring channel

Because this behavior is locked in by a passing unit test, it represents an intentional design choice in the shipped component, not an oversight caught later. The full call sequence — mocking the failing service, spying on the reset/log hooks, driving the three form controls, invoking changePassword(), and then asserting the resulting state (confirmation left unset, error populated, console.log invoked, resetPasswords invoked) — shows the component's entire error-handling pipeline collapses to a console.log call with no monitoring integration at any point along the way.

title: Sensitive financial/order routes lack authentication guard (canActivate)
description: Several Angular routes that expose financial or per-user order data are registered without any canActivate guard, while comparable routes in the same file (e.g. address/select, address/saved, address/create, deluxe-membership) are protected with LoginGuard. Walking the routes array from 'saved-payment-methods' onward shows the same unguarded pattern repeats across every finance/order-related entry: 'basket' (125), 'order-completion/:id' (129, order id supplied via URL param), 'order-summary' (145), 'order-history' (150, a user's full order history) and 'wallet' (158, financial balance) are all declared with no canActivate array — none of these route objects contain a canActivate property between their path/component declaration and the closing brace. Since Angular route guards are the only client-side authorization control visible in this file, an unauthenticated visitor (or a script driving the router directly) can navigate straight to any of these routes and have the corresponding components activated and begin fetching/displaying account-specific financial data, unless every downstream service call independently re-checks authentication (not visible here). The inconsistency with sibling routes that do apply LoginGuard strongly suggests this is a missing check rather than an intentional design choice.

title: Account-security child routes (change-password, 2FA, data-export, last-login-ip) missing LoginGuard
description: The 'privacy-security' parent route and all of its children — privacy-policy, change-password, two-factor-authentication, data-export and last-login-ip — are declared without any canActivate guard. Tracing the object from the parent path/component declaration through the children array confirms no guard property is introduced at any level: the parent (204-205) has no canActivate, the children array (206) opens directly into unguarded child route objects, starting with 'privacy-policy' (208) and continuing through 'change-password' (212-213) and 'two-factor-authentication' (216-217) before reaching 'data-export' (220). change-password, two-factor-authentication and data-export are highly sensitive account-management operations (password change, MFA enrollment, export of personal data) that should require an authenticated session at minimum before the component is even activated client-side, matching the pattern used elsewhere in this same file for less sensitive routes (address/*, deluxe-membership use LoginGuard). Because no guard is present anywhere in this subtree, any visitor can directly navigate to '/privacy-security/change-password' or '/privacy-security/data-export' and have the corresponding Angular component instantiate and attempt to load/submit sensitive account data, relying entirely on whatever server-side session checks exist elsewhere (not visible in this file) rather than on the routing layer that this file is responsible for.

title: Obfuscated hardcoded token used as sole access gate for token-sale route
description: The 'tokenMatcher' function gates the TokenSaleComponent route using a regular expression assembled at runtime from two helper functions (token1/token2) that reverse-engineer a string via simple character-code subtraction from hardcoded numeric literals. Tracing the function body: it first guards against an empty url array (291), then takes the first path segment as the candidate string (294), builds the match pattern by concatenating token1(...) and token2(...) output with hardcoded literals and tests it against that path (296), and on a match returns { consumed: url }, which is the control decision that grants the router permission to activate the token-sale route (297). Both token1 (302-308) and token2 (310-316) implement the same trivial 'char-code minus constant' deobfuscation, meaning the 'secret' path segment that unlocks the token-sale feature is embedded directly in the shipped client bundle and can be trivially recovered by anyone who runs these exported functions with the same arguments in devtools, defeating the intended obfuscation. Because this is the only gating logic for reaching the token-sale route (no LoginGuard/AdminGuard is applied), it demonstrates a design that substitutes obscurity for real authorization.

title: OAuth access_token propagated from URL fragment into route data (implicit-flow token exposure)
description: oauthMatcher activates the OAuth route whenever the current URL fragment contains '#access_token=' (283), and the corresponding route definition then extracts the entire fragment into route data. Tracing the flow: window.location.href is first captured into the local 'path' variable (282), tested for the '#access_token=' marker (283), and on success the matcher returns { consumed: url } (284), which is the control decision causing the Router to select the route object that wires this matcher (matcher: oauthMatcher, 254). That route object's static data.params re-reads window.location.href and slices out everything from the '#' onward — including the raw access token — via substr() (255), and hands it to OAuthComponent (256), making the bearer token available to any Angular services/interceptors observing route data (e.g. analytics, error trackers, route-change loggers). Storing/propagating the bearer token via the URL fragment is the classic OAuth 'implicit flow' weakness: the token can persist in browser history, be leaked through browser extensions, or be captured by any script that reads window.location or ActivatedRoute.data.

title: Authorization enforced only via client-side Angular route guards
description: The only visible access-control mechanism for privileged sections (administration, accounting) in this file is a client-side canActivate guard (AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, LoginGuard imported from ./app.guard at 40). Tracing where these guards are actually applied: the routes array begins at 76, and the very first two entries are the privileged sections — 'administration' (78) with component AdministrationComponent (79) gated by canActivate: [AdminGuard] (80), immediately followed by the closing brace (81) and the 'accounting' entry (83) with component AccountingComponent (84) gated by canActivate: [AccountingGuard] (85). Route guards run entirely in the browser and only prevent the Angular component from being instantiated in the SPA UI; they do not, and cannot, prevent a client from calling the underlying REST endpoints directly (e.g. via fetch/XHR) or from manipulating the SPA's in-memory router state. This file shows no indication that navigation is backed by an equivalent server-side authorization check for the same resources — a trust assumption where the design relies on the client to decide who may reach 'administration' or 'accounting', which is bypassable if the corresponding APIs do not independently re-verify the caller's role.

title: Client blindly trusts unauthenticated 'challenge solved' socket events to display and acknowledge flags
description: The component's WebSocket handler treats any 'challenge solved' payload received over the socket.io channel as ground truth for a real challenge completion. There is no signature, token, or server-issued nonce verification tying the event to an actual authorized completion on the server side — the handler only checks that `data?.challenge` is truthy (line 66) and that `data.hidden` is falsy (line 67) before showing a notification containing the (attacker/server-supplied) flag value, and — gated only by the same top-level `data?.challenge` check — immediately echoes the received flag back to the server via `emit('notification received', data.flag)` (line 78), regardless of whether the notification was even displayed. Because the client only reacts to whatever arrives on this channel with no origin/authenticity validation, if an attacker can get any message onto this socket event (e.g. via a compromised dependency, malicious extension, a permissive/broadcast socket.io configuration, or another client able to push events), forged 'solved' notifications and flags can be displayed to the victim and immediately acknowledged back to the server, potentially being used to mark challenges as noticed/solved without a legitimate completion. This is a design gap: the client is the trust boundary for a security-relevant achievement/flag value instead of the server independently re-validating on each render.

title: Unbounded growth of notifications array from repeated socket events
description: Every 'challenge solved' socket event that is not hidden results in an unconditional push into `this.notifications` (line 128) inside showNotification(), reached via the translate.get promise resolution. A client (or a compromised/misbehaving server-side emitter, or any actor able to trigger repeated socket events as described in the sibling finding) that fires the 'challenge solved' event many times in a loop will cause the notifications array — and the corresponding DOM elements once rendered — to grow without bound, degrading or crashing the browser tab (client-side resource exhaustion/DoS).

title: Long-lived progress-restoration cookie set without Secure/SameSite hardening
description: saveProgress() persists the `continueCode` — a credential-like value that can be used to restore a user's entire challenge-solving progress — in a cookie with a 1-year expiration (lines 146-148), but the only option passed to `cookieService.put` is `expires`. title: Sensitive user chat content passed via URL query parameter
description: onMessageSent obtains a new conversation identifier entirely from a client-side service call (this.conversationStorage.generateId()) and immediately uses it to construct the route/resource address for a new conversation, with no indication that the server independently allocates or validates this ID. Design-wise, the application never establishes that the server is the source of truth for conversation identity; instead the client asserts an ID and the app navigates/operates as if that ID is valid and uniquely owned. If the ID generation is predictable, non-server-verified, or not checked for collision/ownership server-side (unknown from this file, since ConversationStorageService is defined elsewhere), an attacker can craft or predict IDs for conversations they should not access, or create ID collisions that overwrite/merge another party's conversation state. Because this component treats the client-produced ID as immediately authoritative for navigation without any server round-trip or confirmation step, it embodies a trust-boundary violation: a value the server should mint and validate is instead accepted from client logic.

title: Privileged-account password policy check is decorative — never blocks weak passwords
description: The component contains logic intended to enforce a stronger password-complexity policy for privileged 'support@*' accounts (uppercase, lowercase, digit, special char, 12-30 length). However, when the check fails, the code only writes a console.error message — it does not return, does not set this.error, does not disable the submit action, and does not prevent the subsequent call to userService.changePassword(). The weak/non-compliant password is submitted to the backend exactly as if the check had never run. In addition, the decision of whether the account is 'privileged' is derived from localStorage.getItem('email'), a client-controlled value that an attacker can trivially read or spoof in the browser without affecting server-side authorization — the server is never asked to re-derive or re-validate this fact. This is a design flaw: the control that should gate a security-sensitive workflow step (rejecting weak passwords for privileged/support accounts) exists syntactically but performs no enforcement, so the workflow can never actually be stopped by it. An attacker (or a support account holder) can set a trivially weak new password (e.g. 'abcde', which only needs to satisfy the generic Validators.minLength(5)/maxLength(40) on line 57-61) and it will be accepted end-to-end through this component regardless of the console.error branch.

title: Unbounded, unvalidated chat message content forwarded to backend without any client-side constraint
description: The component accepts arbitrary-length, arbitrary-content user input via the two-way bound `message` model (populated from a textarea in the associated template, outside this file) and, in `send()`, performs only a `.trim()` before emitting the raw content through the `messageSent` output to the parent component / eventual chatbot backend. There is no maximum length check, no character/content filtering, and no rate limiting beyond the caller-supplied `disabled` flag. In a chatbot context, this design establishes no bound on what a user can submit as a prompt to the backend LLM/service: a user (or automated script driving the DOM) can submit extremely large payloads or content crafted for prompt injection / resource-exhaustion attacks against the downstream chatbot service, and this file's design never re-derives or caps the content before treating it as safe to dispatch. Because the only gating condition is a client-supplied boolean (`disabled`) and a trim, the design assumes the parent/backend will fully re-validate — if that assumption is not held on the server side, this is the point where unbounded trust in client input is baked into the design.

title: Auto-sent LLM prompt from unauthenticated URL query parameter (link-based prompt injection / CSRF-like agency trigger)
description: The component reads an `initialMessage` value directly from the route's query parameters and immediately feeds it to the LLM chat pipeline via sendMessage() with no user confirmation, no origin check, and no content validation. Because Angular query parameters are fully attacker-controlled (any link like `/chatbot/<id>?initialMessage=...` a victim clicks while authenticated will trigger this), an attacker can craft a URL that, the instant a logged-in victim opens it, causes the victim's session to silently submit an attacker-chosen prompt to the chatbot backend. If the chatbot's tool-calling capability (streamed via chatService.streamMessages, tool_calls handled at lines 156-165) can perform account-affecting actions, this becomes a CSRF-like vector that leverages the victim's authenticated identity to trigger LLM tool actions the victim never consciously requested — an agency boundary crossed without user awareness or confirmation.

trace.description: initialMessage is read straight from the URL query string, fully attacker-controlled via a crafted link.
Query param is cleared from the URL but the value has already been captured for use.
The truthiness check on initialMessage is the only gate before the value is used; there is no confirmation, origin check, or content validation applied here.
sendMessage(initialMessage) is invoked automatically with no user confirmation, immediately submitting attacker-supplied content to the LLM as if typed by the victim.

title: Unbounded conversation history sent to LLM on every message (no truncation, no cap)
description: Every call to sendMessage() rebuilds the entire message history (apiMessages) from the full messages() signal and sends it whole to the backend LLM streaming endpoint. There is no maximum message count, no truncation window, and no size cap applied client-side before the request is issued. A user (or an automated script/bot driving this UI) can keep appending messages indefinitely, causing the payload sent per request to grow without bound. This is an OWASP LLM10 Unbounded Consumption pattern: each subsequent request re-sends the ever-growing transcript, multiplying token/API cost and network payload size per turn, with no client-side control to cap it before dispatch.

trace.description: sendMessage(content) can be invoked repeatedly by the user (or programmatically) with no limit on call frequency or resulting history size.
apiMessages is derived from the entire messages() array with no slicing/window limit beyond dropping the last placeholder entry.
The new user message is appended to the persistent messages() array, growing it by one entry with no cap check.
An assistant placeholder message is also appended to messages(), further growing the array that will be re-sent on every future turn.
.slice(0, -1) only removes the trailing empty assistant placeholder; it applies no windowing or maximum-length truncation to the growing history.
.filter(m => !m.error) removes only error entries, leaving the full unbounded set of prior turns intact.
.map(m => ({ role: m.role, content: m.content })) repackages every remaining message but still carries the entire unbounded history forward with no size cap applied.
chatService.streamMessages(apiMessages) sends the full, unbounded conversation history to the backend/LLM on every turn.

title: Conversation lookup by route-supplied ID with no visible ownership check
description: The component takes the conversation identifier directly from the route path parameter and uses it to fetch a stored conversation via conversationStorage.getById(), then renders its messages with no check confirming the conversation belongs to the current user/session. If ConversationStorageService is (or later becomes) backed by anything beyond a strictly per-browser, non-enumerable store — e.g. a shared or server-synced store, or IDs that are sequential/guessable — a user who supplies another party's conversation ID in the URL would receive that conversation's full message content. This file provides no per-resource authorization check between the ID and the lookup call; authentication of the app is not the same as verifying the caller owns this specific `id`.

conversationStorage.getById(conversationId) performs the lookup with no ownership/session-scoping check visible in this file.
The only gate before use is an existence check (if (existing)); no ownership or authorization predicate is evaluated here, so any resolvable ID passes through.
existing.messages is loaded into the component and rendered without verifying the conversation belongs to the current user.

title: Unsanitized LLM-streamed and user content persisted for later rendering (potential stored XSS via prompt injection)
description: Assistant message content is built directly from streamed deltaContent chunks (attacker-influenceable via prompt injection against the LLM, since the model's output is not filtered here) and user content is taken verbatim from input. Both are stored into the messages signal and then persisted verbatim via persistConversation()/conversationStorage.save() with no sanitization or encoding applied in this file. The actual DOM rendering happens in the associated template (chat-conversation.component.html), which is outside this file, so it cannot be confirmed here whether Angular's default auto-escaping is bypassed (e.g. via [innerHTML] to render markdown/HTML from the bot). If the template renders message.content as raw HTML anywhere (a common pattern for chatbots that want to show formatted/markdown bot replies), a successfully prompt-injected LLM response containing HTML/script would execute as stored XSS when the conversation is reloaded.

title: Raw error objects logged to browser console on configuration load failure
description: The test at lines 335-343 confirms that when configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() errors out, the component's ngOnInit error handler calls console.log(err) with the raw Error object. This is executed in the end-user's browser (client-side code), meaning any internal error detail (stack traces, backend error messages, potentially API endpoint paths or other diagnostic information bundled into the Error object) is exposed directly in the browser devtools console for every user, including in production builds. There is no scrubbing, redaction, or use of a controlled logging abstraction — the raw exception is passed straight to console.log. This is both a logging/monitoring hygiene failure (sensitive/internal diagnostic data surfacing in an uncontrolled sink) and a client-observable information disclosure path if the underlying HTTP client attaches response bodies/headers to the Error object.

The Error('boom') instance that will travel through the whole chain is constructed here as the exact object later asserted to reach console.log unmodified.

Test asserts console.log has been called with the raw error object (expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith(err)), confirming the component logs the unfiltered Error to the browser console rather than a controlled/redacted logger.

title: Conversation retrieval keyed solely by a client-supplied, low-entropy ID with no ownership verification
description: The route parameter 'id' (e.g. '1234567890_abcdefgh', which looks like a timestamp concatenated with a short lowercase-alphanumeric suffix) is passed straight through to conversationStorage.getById(id) in ngOnInit to retrieve and render a full prior conversation (messages, title, timestamps). None of the tests exercise or assert any check that the retrieved conversation belongs to the currently authenticated user (UserService.whoAmI and LoginGuard.tokenDecode are wired up as providers but never asserted against the loaded conversation in any test), and getById is mocked as a pure ID-to-record lookup both by default and in the override. If the underlying storage is anything beyond strictly per-browser localStorage (e.g., a shared/service-backed store, which the DI-wired UserService/LoginGuard hints at), any actor who can guess or enumerate another user's conversation ID (low entropy, partially time-based) could load and render someone else's chat history — a classic BOLA pattern combined with a weak/guessable resource identifier standing in as the entire access-control boundary.

The global beforeEach sets a default getById.mockReturnValue(undefined), establishing the baseline lookup behavior used by most tests: a bare id-to-record (or id-to-undefined) mapping with no ownership/ACL logic modeled anywhere.

The ActivatedRoute provider is wired with the snapshot object containing that id, showing exactly how the id value is injected into the component under test with no accompanying identity/session claim alongside it.

title: Client-side-only guard against concurrent/repeated LLM streaming calls
description: The only control preventing repeated invocation of chatService.streamMessages (which drives an LLM backend call per message) is the in-memory isLoading signal, checked and set entirely within the Angular component. This is a UI-level safeguard, not a server-enforced rate limit: it can be trivially bypassed by calling the component method directly (as tests do), by using multiple browser tabs/windows, or by any client that talks to the underlying chat API directly rather than through this component. Once the stream finishes, the flag resets with no cooldown, backoff, or invocation counter, so nothing in the traced logic prevents an actor from immediately re-invoking sendMessage in a tight loop. If the backend chat endpoint imposes no independent throttling, a user can trigger unbounded concurrent/rapid LLM invocations, leading to excessive compute/API cost and potential denial-of-service on the LLM backend.

sendMessage sets isLoading during the stream and only clears it after the async generator completes (lines 137-141) — this state exists only in the client and is not tied to any server-side session/request token or rate limiter visible in this file.

component.sendMessage('Hello') is invoked while the flag is true; this is the same external entrypoint an attacker-controlled or scripted caller would use to submit chat content.
Assertion confirms the message list is unchanged, proving the block is enforced purely by reading the in-memory isLoading signal at call time, with no external throttle involved.

In the streaming-call test, chatService.streamMessages is mocked to supply the async generator that sendMessage awaits, illustrating the direct, unthrottled call path from a user action straight into the LLM streaming service.

Immediately after the call returns (synchronously, before any await completes), isLoading() already reads true, confirming the flag is set in-process with no external token, lock, or server round-trip acquired.

title: Irreversible bulk/individual conversation deletion exercised without any confirmation control
description: The test suite directly invokes component.deleteConversation(event, 'conv_1') and component.deleteAllConversations() and asserts only that the underlying storage service's delete/deleteAll methods were called and that the in-memory conversations() signal was updated. There is no test anywhere in this spec that exercises or asserts a confirmation dialog, an 'are you sure?' prompt, an undo window, or any other compensating control prior to the irreversible deletion of a single conversation or of all of a user's chat history. Walking the full path: the single-item deletion test seeds state (150-152), renders the DOM so the delete control exists (153), synthesizes a bare click Event (155) and calls deleteConversation directly (156), then asserts the storage delete call happened and the list shrank (158-159) — at no point is a confirmation step invoked or asserted. The bulk-deletion test follows the identical shape: seed two conversations (163-166), render (167), call deleteAllConversations directly (169), and assert the entire list is wiped (171) with, again, no confirmation gate anywhere in the chain. Since this spec is the behavioral contract for the component, the complete absence of any confirmation-related assertion across both destructive paths strongly implies the production click handlers wire straight from click to permanent deletion with no intermediate confirmation/undo step. A single stray click, a misclick, or a scripted click (e.g. via clickjacking or a malicious script calling .click() on '.history-item' or the delete-all control) can therefore permanently destroy a user's entire conversation history with no compensating control — a design gap in the interaction model itself, not merely a missing validation.

title: StoredConversation data model lacks an owner/user-scoping field
description: This file defines the client-side data model for AI chatbot conversations (StoredConversation) that is persisted and presumably later retrieved by id (StoredConversation.id: string). The interface carries no userId/ownerId field, and ChatMessage/StoredConversation carry no access-control metadata at all. If any persistence or retrieval layer built on top of this model (not visible in this file) looks up a conversation purely by its id — a common pattern for chat history / load-conversation features — there is no structural field here to bind a conversation to the authenticated user, and no type-level enforcement that would force callers to filter by owner. This is a design gap rather than an implementation bug: the model, as designed, gives the caller nothing to check ownership against, so a correct implementation of every individual read/write operation using only this model could still allow one user's conversation id to be used to fetch another user's stored chat (including any tool_calls / assistant content, which may contain sensitive info surfaced by the AI agent). Because the consuming service/route is outside this file, this is reported as a design-level concern with the caveat that exploitability depends on how StoredConversation is persisted and looked up elsewhere in the app.

The id field is the only identifier; any external service that loads/saves a StoredConversation by this id (outside this file) has no model-level owner field to check against the current user.

title: Irreversible bulk deletion of conversation history with no confirmation or compensating control
description: deleteAllConversations() immediately and irreversibly wipes all stored conversations by calling conversationStorage.deleteAll() and resetting the local signal to an empty array, with no confirmation step, undo mechanism, or any server-side/audit trail visible in this component. Similarly deleteConversation() permanently removes a single conversation record by id with no safeguard beyond stopping event propagation. Because the component itself performs the destructive action synchronously on invocation, any caller (e.g., a mis-clicked button, a scripted UI interaction, or a component reused in another context) triggers permanent data loss for the user with no recoverable path. This is a design gap: the component establishes no requirement (e.g., a confirmation dialog, soft-delete, or restore window) before performing an irreversible, cascading action, and nothing in this file enforces one.

conversationStorage.deleteAll() is called unconditionally, performing the irreversible deletion immediately.

title: Server-supplied configuration value used to construct asset path without validation
description: The chat bot avatar path is built by directly concatenating an attacker/administrator-influenced configuration field (config.application.chatBot.avatar) onto a fixed prefix, with no validation of its contents (e.g., no check against path traversal sequences like '../', no allow-list of filenames, no encoding). The resulting string is stored in a signal that is presumably bound to an image src in the companion template. The design trusts the external configuration payload wholesale rather than validating or sanitizing the avatar field before using it to build a resource path, which is a trust-boundary violation: data originating from a network response is used unchecked to construct a path used by the rendering layer.

title: Configuration fetch failures are only logged to browser console with no structured error handling or monitoring
description: When the call to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() fails, the only handling is console.log(err), which dumps the raw error object to the browser devtools console. There is no structured/security logging, no reporting to an application monitoring or error-tracking service, and no user-facing indication of failure. If the error object contains internal details (stack traces, request/response metadata, endpoint URLs), these are exposed only in the client console with no server-side record, meaning failures of a security-relevant configuration fetch (which determines bot identity/behavior surfaced to the user) are neither monitored nor alertable, and any anomalous or repeated failures (e.g., indicating tampering or an unavailable/misconfigured backend) go undetected.

trace.description: Subscription to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration(), an external network call outside this file's control.

title: Coding-challenge result/answer types suggest client-trusted correctness state
description: This file defines the shared type contract for the coding-challenge feature: a ResultState enum with explicit Right/Wrong/Undecided values (lines 6-10) and a RandomFixes interface that pairs a candidate 'fix' string with its 'index' (lines 12-15). These types are the data contract between the coding-challenge UI and whatever supplies challenge data/results (a component or service outside this file). If, as the naming strongly implies, a RandomFixes[] array containing the position/identity of the correct fix is delivered to the client before the user submits an answer, or if ResultState is set/trusted based on client-side comparison rather than an authoritative server-side check, then the challenge's core business rule ('the user must correctly identify the fix without being told which one it is') can be bypassed by simply inspecting the client-side data/state (e.g., via browser devtools or the network response) rather than solving the challenge. This is a design-level trust-boundary issue: the type shape does not separate 'what the client needs to render a multiple-choice UI' from 'what would reveal the answer', and there is no visible mechanism in this file (or attributable to it) preventing the correct index from being shipped to the client. Because the actual consuming component/service is outside this file, this cannot be fully confirmed here, but the exposed shape (fix + index bundled together, with a client-visible Right/Wrong result state) is exactly the pattern that leads to answer-key leakage in guess-the-vulnerable-line style challenges.

The 'index' field on RandomFixes ties a fix candidate to its position; if this array (including the correct entry's index) is sent to the client to render the challenge UI, the correct answer becomes discoverable client-side before submission.
ResultState.Undecided = 0 establishes the default/no-answer-yet state that a consumer would initialize before the user responds.

ResultState.Right = 1 is the value a consumer would set to indicate a correct answer; nothing in this file ties that transition to a server-verified check rather than a client-side comparison against the RandomFixes data above.
ResultState.Wrong = 2 is the paired negative outcome value, completing the client-visible result-state contract used to represent challenge pass/fail.

The 'fix' string field holds the actual candidate code-fix text; this is the content that, together with its index, forms the answer-key data the client would need to render (and potentially inspect) all candidate fixes.
Interface closes here and is exported as the full RandomFixes shape (fix + index bundled together) available to any consumer of this module, including client-side rendering code.

ResultState enum (Undecided/Right/Wrong) is the shape used to represent challenge outcome; if this state is derived or trusted on the client rather than being an authoritative server verdict, the workflow's correctness check can be spoofed or bypassed.

title: Client-side formatting of coding-challenge answer with no visible server-side re-validation boundary
description: This utility takes an array of line numbers (presumably the lines the user selected as containing the vulnerability in a 'Find It' coding challenge) and renders them into a compact range string (e.g. '3-5 & 9'). The function itself performs no validation of the input and produces a value that, by its name and context (coding-challenge-find-it component), is very likely used to determine or display whether the user's selection matches the expected vulnerable-line answer. Because this file contains no server round-trip or cryptographic/verification step, the correctness check for the challenge — if it is done by comparing this client-computed string in the browser rather than being re-derived/verified authoritatively on the server — would allow an attacker to mark the challenge solved by manipulating the `lines` array passed in (e.g., via devtools calling the exported function directly, or monkey-patching the component state) without actually identifying the real vulnerable lines. This file only shows where such caller-supplied data is received and formatted; the actual verification/submission logic is outside this file and could not be inspected, so this is reported as a design-boundary concern rather than a confirmed bypass.

Only a trivial empty-array short-circuit is applied; no other validation of the caller-controlled values (range, duplicates, ordering) is performed before proceeding.
The range end is initialised to the same unchecked value (`end = start`).
The loop walks the remaining caller-controlled entries one by one, each iteration deciding how the selection is grouped into ranges with no re-validation against the actual challenge answer.
Conditional check assumes ascending, contiguous ordering (`lines[i] === end + 1`); this decision silently merges or splits the caller-controlled values with no bound/order enforcement.
When contiguous, `end` is extended to the unchecked value, growing the range that will later be rendered as the user's 'answer' text.
Otherwise the accumulated (unchecked) range is pushed into the `ranges` output array that ultimately becomes the displayed/compared answer string.
A new range is started from the next caller-controlled value (`start = lines[i]`) with no validation.
`end` is reset to the same unchecked value, continuing propagation of unvalidated caller input through the range-building state machine.
After the loop, the final accumulated (still unvalidated) range is pushed to `ranges`, completing the transformation of raw caller input into the answer representation.

A conditional selects the short-form join of `ranges` when there are two or fewer segments — this is the last decision point before the value is handed back to whatever caller uses it to judge/display challenge completion.

The formatted range string is returned to the caller, presumably for display and/or comparison against the expected solution; if that comparison happens purely client-side elsewhere, the challenge outcome is trust-the-client rather than server-verified.

title: Fix-It challenge answers fetched and held client-side before Find-It prerequisite is verified, with unlock gated only by a local boolean
description: The test suite shows that CodeFixesService.get() (which returns the 'fixes' — effectively the answers/solution hints for the Fix-It stage of a coding challenge) is invoked and its result stored on the component (component.fixes) unconditionally on load, regardless of whether the prerequisite Find-It challenge has been solved (codingChallengeStatus: 0 in the default beforeEach at line 71, yet 'should load fixes from service' at line 116-119 still expects the fixes array to be populated). The only thing gating visibility of the Fix-It section is a client-side boolean (findItSolved) that is flipped by onFindItSolved(), a plain synchronous method with no server round-trip or re-validation (see tests at lines 121-125 and 217-231, which call component.onFindItSolved() directly and observe only local state changes). The wiring in TestBed (lines 76-98) shows these mocked services are provided directly into the component under test, i.e. this is exactly the data path the real component uses to fetch and store challenge content on init. The locked-section test (178-183) confirms the gate is a purely visual/DOM element, not a withholding of data, and the fix-it-rendered test (185-191) confirms that once the local flag flips, the already-resident answer data is displayed. Because the sensitive answer data is already resident in the component/DOM data model (just hidden by *ngIf-style conditional rendering behind '.locked-section'), an attacker can bypass the intended step-gating by manipulating client-side state (e.g., via browser devtools calling the component instance's onFindItSolved(), or by inspecting the already-completed HTTP response from CodeFixesService in the Network tab) to view the Fix-It solution without ever completing the Find-It step. This is a workflow-bypass / trust-assumption violation: the server hands the client data that should only be released after step completion, and step completion itself is enforced only by client-side rendering logic, not by withholding the data until the prerequisite is verified server-side.

title: Error handling paths for failed snippet/fix loads show no security event logging
description: The tests 'should handle snippet load error' (line 133-137) and 'should handle fixes load error' (line 139-143) demonstrate that when the backend calls (codeSnippetService.get / codeFixesService.get) fail, the component under test simply swallows the error and substitutes a fallback display value (e.g. { snippet: 'Error' } or null) with no assertion anywhere in the suite that the failure is logged, reported, or surfaced to any monitoring mechanism. Repeated failures of these calls (which could indicate tampering with challengeKey route params, probing of the coding-challenge API, or backend failures) would go unnoticed since nothing in the observable behavior indicates an audit/log call. This is inferred from the test file's behavior-only assertions; the actual component implementation is outside this file, so this is reported with lower confidence as a gap suggested by the test surface rather than a directly observed missing log statement.

title: Server error payload trusted and rendered as valid code snippet without sanitization or logging
description: When the code-snippet fetch fails, the component's catchError handler (line 53) does not log the failure or treat it as an error condition. Instead it repackages the raw error body (`err.error`) as if it were a legitimate `CodeSnippet` object. This fake snippet observable is combined inside the forkJoin (lines 50-58) alongside the challenges and fixes observables, then delivered into the subscribe callback (line 61) where it is destructured as `snippet` with no re-validation, and finally assigned directly to `this.snippet` (line 68), which is presumably rendered in the challenge UI as source code. Any information the backend put into the error body (stack traces, internal messages, validation details) is silently forwarded straight to the browser and displayed as if it were valid snippet content, with no server-side or client-side logging of the failure occurring anywhere along this path.

title: Silent swallowing of fetch errors with no logging or monitoring signal
description: Both the code-snippet fetch (line 53) and the code-fixes fetch (line 56) use catchError operators that discard the original error entirely — one is masked as a fake snippet, the other is discarded to `of(null)` — with no console logging, telemetry, or error reporting of any kind. The challengeKey driving both fetches comes straight from the route (line 48) and is used to trigger the fetch pipeline via switchMap (line 47) and the fixes-specific call (line 55); the two independently-erroring observables are then merged by forkJoin (line 58) and delivered into the subscribe callback (line 61), which processes the combined, error-swallowed results with no logging path anywhere in the chain. There is no way to distinguish a benign missing-fixes scenario from a genuine backend failure, a malformed/malicious challengeKey probe, or a server error caused by an attack attempt, and repeated failed lookups leave no trace for detection or incident response.

title: Solved-status flags not reset when challenge lookup fails, causing stale cross-challenge state
description: After a route parameter change, the component re-fetches the challenge list and looks up the current challenge by key (line 62), using the challengeKey that was captured from route params (line 48). The subscribe callback (line 61) receives the freshly-fetched `challenges` array before performing this lookup. If a matching challenge is not found, the `if (challenge)` block (line 63) is skipped entirely — but `challengeName`, `findItSolved`, and `fixItSolved` are never reset to their default/false values in an else branch. This means the solved-state flags from a previously viewed challenge persist and are displayed against the new (unmatched) challenge context, since these are instance fields that survive across route-parameter-triggered re-subscriptions. A user rapidly switching between challenge routes (some of which momentarily fail lookup, e.g. due to load ordering or an invalid key) could see a challenge falsely marked as solved (or not solved) based on unrelated prior navigation state — a workflow/state-consistency defect the design never accounts for.

title: Client-callable UI methods flip 'solved' state without any server round-trip confirmation in this component
description: onFindItSolved() (line 74) and onFixItSolved() (line 83) unconditionally set this.findItSolved / this.fixItSolved to true whenever invoked. These are presumably invoked by child components (CodingChallengeFindItComponent / CodingChallengeFixItComponent) upon detecting a correct answer, but from this file's perspective they are plain public methods on the component instance with no re-verification against `challengeService`/server truth before updating the authoritative-looking UI flags. The subsequent gate at line 76 only checks `this.fixes !== null`, a value that was itself populated earlier from an unauthenticated-looking, error-tolerant fetch (line 69) rather than from any confirmation that findItSolved was legitimately earned. When the condition passes, a setTimeout (line 77) fires a real DOM side effect — scrolling the fix-it section into view (line 78) — purely on the basis of the unverified client-set flag. Because the actual challenge-completion truth is only refreshed from the server on the next route change (via challenge.codingChallengeStatus, lines 65-66), this design creates a trust boundary where the UI's notion of 'solved' and the workflow progression it drives can be triggered purely by a client-side call.

title: Coding-challenge answer key (vulnLines) delivered to client before verification
description: The 'snippet' input bound to CodingChallengeFindItComponent carries both the code text and the array of correct vulnerable line numbers (vulnLines) as a single object that is set on the component before any check is performed (see beforeEach setup). The actual pass/fail decision is only later delegated to VulnLinesService.check() (mocked in this spec), but the correct-answer data is already resident in the component's client-side state from initialization. If, as this test demonstrates, the parent supplies the full answer key up front rather than only line content, a user can trivially read the correct vulnerable line indices via browser devtools/Angular component inspection instead of actually locating the vulnerability, completely bypassing the intended verification workflow enforced by checkLines()/vulnLinesService.check(). This is a trust-boundary violation: the server (or parent component, the actual entrypoint of this data is outside this file) sends a secret grading value to an untrusted client before the client has earned it, and the server-side check afterward provides no protection against a user who simply reads the already-present client-side value.

A later test reuses this same pre-initialized component (with vulnLines already resident from the shared beforeEach) to exercise the verification flow, showing the answer persists across the component's lifecycle up to the point of checking.

component.checkLines() is the only gating mechanism the design relies on to determine correctness, but since the answer key is already present client-side at line 68, this check can be bypassed by simply reading the pre-existing state instead of relying on the outcome of vulnLinesService.check().

title: No verification of security-relevant challenge-attempt events (success/failure) in the tested component behavior
description: The component's verdict handling (right/wrong answer, hint display, already-solved short-circuit) is fully exercised in this spec, but at no point does any test assert that a security/audit-relevant event, such as a wrong verdict, a correct verdict, or an already-solved bypass, is logged, sent to a monitoring endpoint, or otherwise recorded beyond updating local UI state (component.result/hint/shaking). Given the surrounding code only calls challengeService.continueCodeFindIt() and vulnLinesService.check() with no logging call captured or asserted anywhere in this spec, there is no visible mechanism ensuring repeated failed attempts, or the alreadySolved bypass path (ngOnInit setting result to Right without a check call, line 82-86), are observable for anomaly detection (e.g., brute-forcing hints or spoofing the 'alreadySolved' state).

title: Unrestricted repeated challenge-check requests enable brute-force guessing of correct line selection
description: The checkLines() method sends the currently marked line numbers to the backend verification service (vulnLinesService.check) every time it is invoked, with no client-side throttling, debounce, or attempt counter. The selection itself is built by toggleLine(), which lets the user add or remove any line to markedLines an unlimited number of times, and selectedLines is recomputed fresh from that set on every toggle, so there is no cap on how many distinct guesses can be assembled and submitted. The only guard present (line 328, inside setVerdict) short-circuits once the challenge is already solved, but places no limit on the number of incorrect attempts, and nothing disables the check button or backs off after a wrong verdict. Because the 'Find It' challenge's security property depends on the user actually identifying the correct vulnerable lines rather than discovering them by trial, an attacker (or a simple automated script driving toggleLine/checkLines) can repeatedly toggle different line combinations and call checkLines() in rapid succession until the verdict comes back true, defeating the intended design of the challenge and potentially generating excessive load against the verification endpoint if it performs any non-trivial server-side work per request.

setVerdict() only blocks further processing once the result is already ResultState.Right; incorrect attempts are never counted, rate-limited, or capped.

toggleLine() mutates the markedLinesField on every click/keypress with no maximum count or attempt budget enforced, so the guess space (which lines are selected) can be freely reshaped before each check.

vulnLinesService.check(this.challengeKey(), this.selectedLines) is called with no throttling; each invocation is a fresh, unrestricted network request/verification attempt.

title: Challenge-solved state delegated to a cookie-based helper without visible integrity enforcement
description: setVerdict() hands off the server-reported verdict, along with a reference to CookieService and ChallengeService, to an external helper (handleVerdict, imported from '../../helpers/handle-verdict') to decide and persist solved state and emit the solved event. Because CookieService is passed directly into this helper, solved/progress state for this challenge appears to be tracked via a client-readable/writable cookie rather than purely server-side session state validated on every request. The helper is additionally handed direct setter callbacks that mutate this.result and this.shaking, meaning it has full authority to flip the component into ResultState.Right. This file cannot show whether handleVerdict cryptographically signs or server-validates the cookie value before trusting it, but passing a mutable client-side cookie store and the raw result-setter into the function that decides ResultState.Right (and triggers the solved output which downstream code may treat as authoritative) is a pattern that is exploitable if the cookie is not integrity-protected: a user could forge/replay the cookie to mark a challenge as solved without ever submitting a correct verdict. The concrete verification logic lives outside this file, so this is reported as the point where an unvalidated/externally-influenced trust decision is initiated.

cookieService is injected as a private field on the component; this is the same mutable, client-accessible cookie store instance that will later be threaded into the external helper.

The subscribe callback immediately forwards the server-supplied boolean into this.setVerdict(verdict.verdict), starting the trust-decision path with unmodified server data but no independent integrity check at this layer.

title: Client-supplied 'alreadySolved' flag directly marks a coding challenge as correctly solved without server re-verification
description: The spec exercises a code path where the component's `alreadySolved` @Input, when set to true, causes `ngOnInit()` to set `component.result` to 1 (the 'Right'/success state) with no call to `codeFixesService.check()` or any other server round-trip to confirm the claim. The shared `beforeEach` (lines 55-63) first establishes a baseline component instance whose `alreadySolved` Input defaults to `false` (line 61) and runs an initial lifecycle pass via `fixture.detectChanges()`. The specific test (lines 76-80) then overrides that Input to `true` and re-invokes `ngOnInit()` directly, which is enough to flip `component.result` to 1 — the same success state the correct-verdict test (lines 98-105) only reaches by actually calling `codeFixesService.check()` and receiving `verdict: true`. Comparing the two paths shows that `codeFixesService.check` (mocked at line 26) is never invoked when `alreadySolved` is true: the component trusts whatever boolean value is handed to it via the externally supplied Input rather than deriving 'solved' status from an authoritative, freshly obtained server check. Because `alreadySolved` is populated from outside this file (presumably a parent component or route resolver reading challenge-progress data), if that upstream value can be influenced by stale caches, manipulated component composition, or attacker-controlled state, the fix-it UI can be forced into a 'solved/correct' verdict without the underlying verification service ever being called — a trust-boundary violation in the component's own design, independent of any implementation bug.

ngOnInit() is invoked and, per the test's own assertion, consumes the alreadySolved input directly rather than calling codeFixesService.check to obtain a server-verified verdict.

codeFixesService.check is the only mocked verification mechanism in this suite; it is defined here but, as this test's assertions confirm, is never called or asserted against on the alreadySolved=true path, showing the server-side check function is completely bypassed when the client-controlled flag is true.

Shared beforeEach establishes the baseline value of the same Input as false for every test, showing that the component treats 'alreadySolved' as an ordinary externally-set flag whose value at ngOnInit time is what drives the result state — the override at line 77 simply supplies a different value into the exact same unguarded path.

title: Unlimited fix-check attempts allow brute-forcing the correct answer / unthrottled backend calls
description: The 'Fix It' challenge is meant to be solved by the user analyzing a code diff and picking the correct fix. The actual correctness decision is made server-side (via codeFixesService.check), and the client only receives a boolean verdict plus an explanation. checkFix() can be invoked repeatedly with any of the available fix indices (this.randomFixes[this.selectedFix].index) with no client-side throttling, no attempt counter, and no back-off. setVerdict() only short-circuits once the result is already 'Right' (line 136); it does not limit how many times a wrong guess can be resubmitted, nor does it prevent the user from calling setFix()+checkFix() in a tight loop to enumerate every fix index until the server returns verdict:true. Because the server acts as a pure oracle returning correct/incorrect for a caller-supplied index, and there is no rate limiting, debounce, or attempt cap in this component (or any disabling of the check action while a request is in flight), an attacker can script repeated calls to brute-force the correct index in a fraction of the time the challenge is meant to take, and can also flood the underlying (potentially expensive, e.g. AI-graded) verification endpoint with unbounded concurrent requests. This is both a design flaw (the workflow never establishes a limit on verification attempts, defeating the challenge's intended skill-based resolution) and a resource-consumption issue (no cap on how many expensive verification calls a single client can trigger).

setVerdict only blocks further state changes once the result is already ResultState.Right; it places no limit on repeated wrong guesses or on how often checkFix can be invoked with a different selectedFix.
setFix() lets the caller freely change this.selectedFix to any index in randomFixes before each check, with no tracking of how many distinct indices have already been tried.
The subscription callback receives the verdict object and immediately forwards verdict.verdict into setVerdict() for processing on every single call, with no aggregation or limiting across calls.

The verdict, along with challengeService and cookieService, is forwarded whole to the external handleVerdict helper, which is the only place a solved-state side effect (e.g. persisting completion) occurs; nothing here throttles how often this hand-off can happen.

The setResult callback updates this.result based on the external handler's decision; because this is the only state gate, a wrong guess simply leaves the component ready to accept another unrestricted checkFix() call.

Unbounded repeated invocation of codeFixesService.check(...) — an external verification call (server-side sink, outside this file) — acting as a correctness oracle that can be brute-forced and that can be spammed without any client-side throttle.

title: Server-supplied explanation text stored without sanitization before later rendering
description: The verdict response's explanation field is taken verbatim from the backend (verdict.explanation) and assigned directly to the public `explanation` property with no validation, encoding, or allow-listing. This property is presumably rendered in the component's template (coding-challenge-fix-it.component.html, not visible in this file). If that template renders `explanation` via an unsafe binding (e.g. [innerHTML] or a bypassSecurityTrust call) rather than plain interpolation, any HTML/script content embedded in a server- or LLM-generated explanation would execute in the victim's browser as stored/reflected XSS. Even if Angular's default interpolation auto-escapes the value (which would neutralize this), the persistence point here accepts arbitrary free-form text with no sanitization hook, so the safety of this data flow depends entirely on a rendering choice outside this file.

title: Reward/continue-code issuance trusts a client-supplied correctness verdict
description: handleVerdict() receives a boolean `verdict` from its caller (an Angular component outside this file) and uses it, without any further server-side proof of correctness, to decide whether to request and persist a 'continue code' that unlocks progression in the coding challenge (FindIt/FixIt). The correctness check for these coding challenges is evaluated client-side and simply passed in as `config.verdict`. When true, the function updates UI state, selects the appropriate continuation call based on the client-supplied `variant`, subscribes to it, and on success immediately persists the returned code in a long-lived (1 year) cookie via `config.cookieService.put`. At no point does the code re-derive or verify on the server side which challenge/answer was actually solved — the call to `continueCodeFindIt()`/`continueCodeFixIt()` takes no parameters proving correctness. Because the decision of 'did the user answer correctly' is made and reported entirely by client code the user controls (e.g., via browser devtools, by monkey-patching the component, or by invoking `handleVerdict` directly with `verdict: true`), an attacker can force this function down the 'right answer' path for any challenge without ever solving it, obtaining the same continuation code, cookie persistence, confetti and solved-emit behavior as a legitimate solve. This is a trust-assumption violation: the server-facing call that hands out the reward token doesn't require any evidence of correctness, only that the client asserts it, so the server's own progression-gating logic is effectively delegated to and controlled by the client.

The expiry is set one year forward, making the eventual reward cookie long-lived.
The reward continue code returned by the server call is persisted in a year-long cookie, granting progression/credit based solely on the client-asserted verdict.

title: Sensitive continuation-code cookie set without Secure/SameSite protections
description: When a correct verdict is recorded, the server-issued continue code (a token that lets the user skip/continue a challenge) is written to a cookie using `config.cookieService.put(...)` with only an `expires` option set roughly a year in the future. No `secure`, `sameSite`, or `path` restriction options are passed, meaning (depending on the ngy-cookie defaults) the cookie may be sent over plain HTTP and/or attached to cross-site requests. Since this cookie encodes progression/reward state for the coding challenge feature and is long-lived, failing to scope it with Secure/SameSite attributes is an avoidable weakening of its confidentiality and integrity guarantees, especially given the file already demonstrates awareness of cookie configuration (it sets `expires`) yet omits the security-relevant flags.

title: Silent, unstructured error handling for failed continue-code retrieval
description: When the server-side call to retrieve a continue code fails, the only handling is `error: (err) => { console.log(err) }`. This dumps the raw error object to the browser console with no correlation ID, no structured reporting to any monitoring/telemetry backend, and no user-facing or server-side signal that a challenge-completion/reward request failed. A failed or repeatedly failing continue-code request (e.g., from automated tampering attempts exploiting the client-trust issue described above, or from replay/abuse of the challenge-completion flow) would go completely unnoticed by any monitoring system, since it never leaves the user's own browser console.

title: Security-relevant failures only logged to browser console, not to any monitoring backend
description: The spec at lines 140-155 proves that handle-verdict.ts, when the server call to retrieve a continue code fails (network error, tampered/invalid response, etc.), only calls console.log(...) to report the failure. Because handle-verdict.ts is a browser-side helper, console.log output is visible only in the individual user's own browser DevTools console and is never transmitted to any server-side logging/monitoring/alerting system. A failure of this kind could indicate an attacker tampering with challenge verification traffic, a broken/blocked backend, or repeated probing of the continue-code endpoint, yet none of this is ever recorded anywhere the operations/security team can see it. There is no structured logging, no correlation ID, and no alerting threshold — the event is functionally unmonitored from the server's perspective, satisfying the A09 'absence of logging for security-relevant events' pattern.

title: Client-supplied 'verdict' boolean is trusted to mark a coding challenge solved and request the reward continue-code
description: handleVerdict() (exercised via this spec) receives a `verdict: boolean` parameter and, when it is true, calls challengeService.continueCodeFindIt/FixIt, stores the resulting continue code as a cookie, and (per the assertions distinguishing verdict=true vs false) drives the 'solved' state of the challenge. This spec file shows no evidence that handleVerdict re-derives or re-validates the verdict from a trustworthy source — it is simply handed a boolean and acts on it as ground truth for whether the user solved the challenge. If the caller of handleVerdict (outside this file, e.g. the component that evaluates the user's submitted code) computes this verdict client-side, or if this boolean can be influenced by the caller, an attacker could invoke handleVerdict with verdict=true directly (e.g., from the browser console or by manipulating the calling component) to obtain a valid continue-code/reward cookie and have the challenge marked solved without the server independently confirming success. This is a classic 'trust assumption violation' — the server-issued continue code is only requested because the client already believes the challenge was solved, rather than the continue-code endpoint independently verifying solved status.

title: Continue-code cookie set without verified secure/sameSite attributes
description: The test at line 110 verifies that cookieService.put is called with only the key, value, and an object containing an 'expires' Date, using expect.objectContaining. This confirms the implementation sets an expiration but the test suite provides no assertion (and thus no regression protection) that the cookie is written with 'secure' or 'sameSite' attributes. Given that this cookie carries a 'continueCode' — a token that lets the holder skip/resume a scored challenge — failing to pin down secure/sameSite behavior in tests suggests these protections may not be configured in the underlying implementation, which would allow the cookie to be sent over plaintext HTTP or attached to cross-site requests.

title: Coding-challenge submission gate enforced only by client-side UI state, with no in-component safeguard against direct event emission
description: This component receives `solved`, `result`, and `submitDisabled` as plain boolean/enum inputs (lines 24-27) that are presumably populated by a parent component from some upstream (possibly server-derived) state, and exposes a `submitClicked` output (line 29) that a parent presumably wires to the actual answer-submission logic for a coding challenge. Nowhere in this file is there any check, before allowing/emitting the submit action, that re-validates `submitDisabled` or `solved` — the disabling of the submit control is delegated entirely to whatever template binding uses `submitDisabled()`/`solved()` (not visible in this .ts file, and not enforced here). Tracing the class's own internal logic shows the only guard flag it actually implements is `destroyed` (line 20), set via `DestroyRef.onDestroy` in the constructor (line 33), and it is used exclusively to protect `shakingDone` emission in `onShakingDone()` (line 36) — a purely cosmetic animation-completion event. No analogous guard exists for `submitClicked`: the output declared at line 29 is emitted (from the template, outside this file) with the `submitDisabled` value at line 27 never consulted anywhere in this class's TypeScript logic before that emission. Angular's `[disabled]` binding is a UI convenience only: it does not prevent a script (browser console, extension, or automated tooling) from directly invoking the component's `submitClicked.emit()`, since the guard exists only as a rendering property, not as a code path check inside the emitting logic itself. If the actual code-challenge-correctness determination reflected via `result`/`solved` is not independently re-derived and re-checked server-side at submission time, an attacker can submit challenge answers (or repeat submissions) irrespective of the `submitDisabled`/`solved` flags this component exposes, because this component performs no server-authoritative or even client-side re-check before signalling `submitClicked` — unlike the `destroyed`-guarded `shakingDone` path, which shows the class is capable of guarding emissions but chose not to apply that pattern to the security-relevant one.

`submitDisabled` is a purely presentational input with no corresponding code-level check preventing `submitClicked` from being emitted/handled when it is true, allowing bypass of the intended submission gate if the click can be triggered by any means other than the disabled button (e.g., programmatic emit).

title: No logging of coding-challenge submission attempts or results in the component that handles the submit action
description: This component is the UI touchpoint for submitting a coding-challenge answer (`submitClicked` output, line 29) and for displaying whether the submission was right or wrong (`resultIcon()`, lines 44-53, driven by `result` input, line 25). Tracing the verdict from entry to render: the `solved` flag (line 24) and `result` enum (line 25) arrive as inputs, are exposed to the template via the `ResultState` getter (line 42), and are branched on inside `resultIcon()` (line 45), including the specific `ResultState.Wrong` case (line 48) that represents a failed challenge attempt. At no point along this path — from the user's `submitClicked` action through to the rendering of a 'wrong answer' icon — does the code emit any log entry, counter increment, or telemetry event. While client-side logging is not the primary control point, the absence of any correlation/tracing hook (e.g., an event id or timestamp passed along with `submitClicked`, or a recorded count of consecutive `ResultState.Wrong` results) in this component means the frontend contributes nothing towards reconstructing a timeline of repeated failed challenge-submission attempts, which — combined with an assumed lack of visibility into the backend from this file — could hinder detection of automated brute-forcing of coding-challenge answers. This is a secondary/coverage-gap style finding rather than a total absence of logging infrastructure, since the actual security-relevant event (a submission and its verdict) is only observable through this component's inputs/outputs and is never surfaced anywhere in the code for auditing or alerting.

`resultIcon()` consumes the right/wrong verdict only to pick a Material icon name; no log entry, counter, or event is recorded for repeated wrong attempts, which are a security-relevant signal for potential automated challenge-answer guessing.

title: Complaint message length/content enforced only via client-side Angular validator, no evidence of server-side re-validation
description: The spec exercises the message field's validity purely through Angular's ReactiveFormsModule validators (required, maxLength 4096) and never demonstrates that ComplaintService.save() or the backend independently enforces these constraints. Client-side form validation is a UX control, not a security boundary — an attacker can call the underlying /api/Complaints endpoint directly (bypassing the Angular form entirely) and submit a message of arbitrary length or empty content. Tracing the value's path: the maxLength/required checks (lines 90-94) only gate the FormControl's `valid` flag; the same control's raw `.value` is what later gets read when the save flow runs. The save() invocation (line 129) and its underlying saveComplaint/complaintService.save() call (lines 125-130) never re-check the control's validity or length before forwarding the message — they simply mock/expect a successful save regardless of content, meaning nothing in the traced path re-derives or re-bounds the message server-side. Because complaintService.save() is mocked in these tests, there is no evidence in this file (or reachable from it) that the server independently caps message size, meaning a design assumption ('the client already validated this') may be the only control in place. This is a trust-assumption / missing-bound design gap that also enables resource consumption (large payload flooding) if the backend has no independent cap.

title: No test coverage or visible control for file upload size/count limits in complaint attachment flow
description: The spec verifies mime-type filtering behavior (onWhenAddingFileFailed rejecting a bad mimeType) and successful upload flow, but at no point does it test or reference any maximum file size or maximum number of queued files for the complaint attachment uploader (ng2-file-upload). Tracing the path: a FileItem is constructed directly from an arbitrary File object (line 134) and its upload() method is spied on and invoked (lines 135-137) with no size assertion anywhere in the surrounding test. The only rejection path exercised anywhere in the suite is the mimeType-based one (lines 141-144), and even that test only checks the file's `name`/type field, never its size. Combined with the architecture context showing a dedicated file-upload-capable POST route for complaints, the absence of any size-limit assertion in this spec suggests the component/service pairing tested here may not enforce an upper bound on uploaded attachment size, which could allow a single request to consume excessive server memory/disk if unconstrained elsewhere.

title: Identity-retrieval failure logged only to client console with no security event trail
description: The test at line 105-110 mocks console.log specifically to suppress output when userService.whoAmI() fails, which reveals that the underlying component logs the error via console.log(...) purely to the browser console when it cannot determine the current logged-in user. Tracing the flow: the mock is configured to throw (line 107) immediately before ngOnInit() is invoked (line 108), and the assertion only checks that component.complaint ends up undefined (line 109) — there is no assertion, callback, or side effect anywhere in the test verifying that this failure is reported to any server-side logging/monitoring/alerting mechanism. This is not a security-relevant audit trail: browser console output is local, ephemeral, not correlated with a request ID, and invisible to any server-side monitoring or alerting system. A failure to resolve identity (which could indicate an authentication/session problem being probed) leaves no server-side record for detection or investigation.
