title: Silent failure of system-wide notification polling with no logging
description: The component polls an external notification endpoint on an interval and any error from the fetch (network failure, non-2xx response, malformed payload, blocked/hijacked endpoint, etc.) is caught and converted to `of(null)` with zero logging or telemetry. There is no console/log/monitoring call anywhere in the error path, so if the notification endpoint starts failing, is taken down, is redirected, or begins returning malicious/garbage data that fails downstream validation, the application has no record of it. Because this channel is meant to broadcast security-relevant, system-wide messages (a CTF/administrative broadcast mechanism), silently swallowing failures removes the only signal an operator would have that the broadcast channel is being tampered with or is unreachable, defeating incident detection for this feature.

title: System-wide broadcast content trusted from a configuration-supplied URL with no origin or integrity validation
description: The component derives the notification source URL entirely from remote application configuration (config?.ctf?.systemWideNotifications?.url) and then polls that URL indefinitely, feeding whatever JSON payload it returns directly into `this.notification`, which is rendered to every user of the application (a system-wide broadcast). There is no validation that the URL is same-origin, uses HTTPS, or belongs to an allow-listed host, and no verification of payload authenticity (e.g., no signature, no expected-origin check on the response) before trusting `data.enabled`, `data.message`, and `data.updatedAt`. The design assumes the configuration value and the remote endpoint's response are inherently trustworthy and pushes their content to every connected client without any server-side re-validation visible in this component. If the configured URL can be pointed at (or is already) an attacker-influenced or third-party endpoint — via a compromised/misconfigured config value — this becomes a trust-boundary violation: the client fully trusts externally-sourced, unauthenticated content for a global broadcast surface. This is a design gap (no integrity/authenticity check is ever established for broadcast content) rather than a single missing validation, and it is compounded by the absence of any origin allow-list on the fetch target, which is itself a misconfiguration.

title: Stored XSS via unsanitized feedback comment persisted to backend
description: The user-entered feedback text (feedbackControl.value, bound to a free-form textarea with only a client-side maxLength validator) is concatenated into a comment string and sent verbatim to the backend via feedbackService.save(). No HTML/script sanitization or encoding is applied to the value before it is persisted. Juice Shop's admin/feedback review views later render stored feedback comments; if that render path does not apply context-appropriate output encoding (a defect that would live outside this file), a comment such as '<script>...</script>' becomes stored XSS that executes in the browser of anyone who views the feedback list (e.g., an administrator). Validators.maxLength(160) is a length constraint, not a sanitizer, and does not prevent markup/script characters from being included.

title: Client-supplied UserId trusted for feedback attribution (BOLA / mass assignment risk)
description: userIdControl (line 42) is created without a disabled flag, unlike authorControl (line 39) which is explicitly disabled after being populated from the authenticated whoAmI() response. At save time (line 83) the feedback payload's UserId is re-read from userIdControl.value rather than being fixed/derived once from the session. Because this is client-side state, an attacker can trivially modify the FormControl value via devtools/console or simply edit the outgoing HTTP request body to submit feedback attributed to an arbitrary user id (e.g., another customer or an admin), regardless of what the form displayed. If the backend feedback-creation endpoint trusts this client-supplied UserId field instead of deriving the owner from the authenticated session (server-side enforcement not visible from this file), this is a Broken Object Level Authorization / mass-assignment condition allowing feedback to be falsely attributed to, or associated with, another account.

title: Raw server error text displayed without encoding in feedback error snackbar
description: When feedback submission fails, the raw err.error value from the HTTP error response is passed directly to snackBarHelperService.open() for display to the user, with no sanitization or type/content validation. If the backend ever returns attacker-influenced or HTML-containing error text (e.g., reflected validation messages) and the snackbar helper renders content via innerHTML or an unescaped binding (not visible in this file), this could result in reflected script execution in the victim's browser.

title: No verification that notification fetch failures are logged for monitoring
description: The spec simulates a failed fetch from the CTF system-wide notification service (a network/security-relevant error) and only asserts that the UI state (component.notification) remains null. There is no assertion anywhere in the suite that the underlying component logs, reports, or surfaces this failure (e.g., to a monitoring/error-tracking service). Since this notification channel is presumably used to broadcast security-relevant announcements (e.g., CTF status, incident notices), silent swallowing of fetch errors without any logged trace prevents operators from detecting when the notification pipeline is broken or being tampered with (e.g., an attacker blocking/altering the notification endpoint). Because the test suite does not exercise or require any logging call on this path, it strongly suggests the component itself performs no security-relevant logging on failure, which would hinder incident detection and response.

Only the resulting UI state (component.notification === null) is asserted; no assertion exists for any error/security logging call, indicating the failure path is handled silently with no monitoring hook exercised or required by the tests.

title: Notification re-display gated solely on unchanged updatedAt allows critical message updates to be silently suppressed after dismissal
description: The component's design (as verified by these tests) suppresses a previously-dismissed notification for as long as the server-provided updatedAt timestamp is unchanged, and only re-shows it when updatedAt changes (lines 154-179). This design trusts that any content change on the server side will always be accompanied by a timestamp bump. If an administrator edits or escalates a system-wide notification (e.g., updates a critical security/CTF announcement) without changing updatedAt, or if the backend fails to update the timestamp for any reason, users who previously dismissed the old notification will never see the updated content, because the client's suppression logic is keyed purely on a value the server-side workflow does not guarantee to change in lockstep with content. This is a business-logic/workflow gap: the design never establishes an invariant that updatedAt is authoritative proof of a distinct message, yet the client treats it as such.

title: No enforcement or test coverage that the system-wide notification endpoint must use HTTPS or a trusted origin
description: The configuration model used throughout the suite (BASE_CTF_CONFIG) allows ctf.systemWideNotifications.url to be an arbitrary, admin-supplied URL, exemplified here with a plain HTTP endpoint ('http://example.com/notify', line 24). None of the tests validate that the component enforces HTTPS, validates the URL's origin, or otherwise restricts where notification content may be fetched from. Since the fetched message is later displayed to all users of the application (a broadcast trust boundary), allowing an unauthenticated/plaintext HTTP source with no origin pinning is a design gap: the client implicitly trusts whatever content arrives from the configured URL, and an on-path attacker able to tamper with plaintext HTTP traffic to that endpoint could inject arbitrary notification content shown to every user, with no test or code path in this file demonstrating a guard against it.

title: Client-controlled UserId is trusted and forwarded when submitting feedback
description: The spec file demonstrates that ContactComponent.save() builds the feedback payload directly from component.userIdControl.value and forwards it verbatim to FeedbackService.save() as the 'UserId' property. In the test at line 184 the value is set programmatically to an arbitrary string ('2'), and the assertion at line 186 confirms this exact attacker-influenceable value is included in the outbound API call with no server-side re-derivation visible from the client. Unlike authorControl, which is explicitly asserted to be disabled (line 105-107) to prevent tampering, there is no equivalent assertion anywhere in this spec suite that userIdControl is disabled or otherwise protected from user manipulation in the rendered template. If the corresponding form field is not hard-disabled in the DOM (or if an attacker calls the underlying service directly, bypassing the UI entirely), a user could submit feedback attributed to an arbitrary UserId — i.e., impersonate another user's feedback record. This is a mass-assignment style trust issue: the client determines an identity-bearing field or the server is expected to accept it as-is, and the design here surfaces no compensating control for it. The actual persistence/authorization enforcement lives server-side outside this file, so this should be treated as evidence of the client-side trust boundary flaw and a design gap.

trace.description: Test sets component.userIdControl to an arbitrary caller-controlled value ('2'), simulating a value that originates from outside the component (form input or direct API/service call).
component.save() is invoked, which (per the component under test) assembles the feedback object including the raw userIdControl value with no re-validation against the authenticated session's own id.

For contrast: authorControl is explicitly tested to be disabled (component.authorControl.disabled toBe(true)), a control decision that hard-blocks caller tampering with that field. No equivalent disabled/allow-list check exists anywhere in this spec for userIdControl, so the value set at line 184 is not shown to be protected by any comparable control before it reaches save().

feedbackService.save is asserted to be called with UserId: '2' taken directly from the client-controlled control, confirming this value is forwarded to the backend feedback-creation call without narrowing to an authorized/allow-listed value.

title: Free-form feedback comment persisted without any client-side sanitization before submission
description: The feedbackControl accepts arbitrary free text (validated only for non-emptiness and a 160-character length cap, see lines 109-124) and this raw text is concatenated into the 'comment' field and sent to FeedbackService.save() unmodified (line 182, 186: comment: 'feedback (anonymous)'). No encoding, stripping, or content validation of the feedback text is performed anywhere in the component's tested behavior before it is persisted via the feedback API. Because length/type constraints are not equivalent to output encoding, if this stored comment is later rendered (e.g., in an admin feedback review view or public feedback carousel) without context-appropriate escaping, it becomes a stored XSS vector. The render sink is outside this file and was not observed, so this is reported at the persistence point as required by the playbook.

trace.description: component.feedbackControl.setValue('feedback') sets user-controlled free-text comment content; only length is constrained (see lines 114-124), no sanitization is applied at this layer.
component.save() is called, assembling the payload with the raw feedback text embedded in the 'comment' field.

The validator suite for feedbackControl (character-count loop building a 161-char string) shows the only enforced control on this field is a maximum length, established here and reasserted at line 120; no content/character sanitization or HTML-encoding rule is present.

component.feedbackControl.setValue(str) confirms the control accepts and holds arbitrary raw string content up to the length boundary, with no transformation applied to the stored value itself before it can later be submitted.

feedbackService.save is called with comment: 'feedback (anonymous)', persisting the unsanitized user text via the backend feedback API; the eventual rendering location of this stored comment is outside this file.

title: Client-side-only enforcement of file type, file size, and message length before submission
description: The FileUploader is configured with allowedMimeType and maxFileSize (lines 45-46), and the message field is constrained via Validators.maxLength (line 39). These are purely client-side/UI-layer restrictions implemented by ng2-file-upload and Angular's ReactiveForms — they run in the browser and can be trivially bypassed by an attacker who calls the backend '/file-upload' or '/api/Complaints' endpoints directly (e.g., via curl or a modified request), sending an oversized file, a disallowed MIME type, or an arbitrarily long message. Nothing in this file re-validates these constraints server-side, and this component treats client-side filtering as if it were a security boundary. The full path shows the limits are defined once at construction, only enforced through the onWhenAddingFileFailed handler (itself purely client-side), and then the save()/saveComplaint() flow forwards whatever passed that client filter straight to the backend with no re-check. If the backend endpoints (outside this file) do not independently enforce these limits, an attacker can submit oversized payloads (resource exhaustion) or unexpected file/content types (potential downstream processing risk).

title: User-controlled complaint message forwarded without sanitization (potential stored XSS carrier)
description: The complaint message is taken directly from free-form user input (messageControl) and assigned to this.complaint.message, then sent to the backend via complaintService.save() with no client-side sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing of content. Complaint messages are exactly the kind of free-text field (per stored-XSS patterns) that is often later rendered in an admin/support interface. Tracing the full path shows both the direct submission route (save() -> saveComplaint()) and the post-upload route (onSuccessItem -> saveComplaint()) converge on the same unsanitized assignment and transmission. This file is the origin point of the taint; the persistence and eventual rendering sink live outside this file (in the backend and any admin complaint-viewing UI), so this cannot be fully confirmed here, but no mitigating control is visible in this file's data path from user input to submission.

title: Auth token read from localStorage and embedded as a static Bearer header
description: The FileUploader's authToken is populated by reading the JWT directly from localStorage.getItem('token') at object construction time (line 44). Storing bearer tokens in localStorage (rather than an httpOnly cookie) makes them readable by any JavaScript running in the page context, so any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the application (including the potential stored XSS via the complaint message noted separately) can be used to exfiltrate this token and achieve full account takeover. Tracing the path shows the token is embedded once into the FileUploader configuration object alongside the destination URL, and is only ever actually dispatched when save() triggers queue[0].upload() — meaning a token captured at component construction time is reused for every subsequent upload during the component's lifetime, regardless of any token rotation in between.

trace.description: authToken is built directly from localStorage.getItem('token') and embedded as a static Bearer header for the FileUploader instance.
The token is embedded into the FileUploader configuration object literal, fixed at construction time and shared by every subsequent upload.
this.uploader.queue[0].upload(), reached via save(), is the point at which the stored token is actually dispatched with the HTTP request.

The token is sent as the Authorization header value to environment.hostServer + '/file-upload', an endpoint whose authorization decision now depends on a token exposed to any script running on the page.

title: Complaint save failures and lookup errors are silently discarded without logging or user notification
description: When saveComplaint() fails, the error handler at line 109 does nothing but return the error object — it is not logged, reported to any monitoring facility, or surfaced to the user in any actionable way. Similarly, initComplaint()'s error handler (lines 77-80) resets state and only writes the raw error to the browser console via console.log, which is neither a durable security log nor protected from exposure (it is visible to anyone with access to browser devtools, including any script achieving XSS). This means failed complaint submissions or failed identity lookups — which could indicate authorization failures, tampering attempts, or abuse — leave no actionable trace and the user receives no feedback that their action failed.

Error from whoAmI() is only written to console.log with no structured logging or reporting.
The error callback for whoAmI() is defined here.
On error, this.complaint is silently reset to undefined with no security-relevant record of why the identity lookup failed.

The subscribe block for complaintService.save() defines both success and error callbacks.

title: Unsanitized exported user data written via document.write into a new window
description: The test 'should show the confirmation and fetch user data and reset data export form on requesting data export' mocks `window.open()` to return an object whose `document.write` is a spy, then calls `component.save()` and asserts that `component.userData` equals the raw string returned by the (mocked) `DataSubjectService.dataExport()` call. This strongly indicates that the real `DataExportComponent.save()` implementation opens a new browser window and writes the server-returned `userData` field directly into that window's document (e.g. `window.open().document.write(this.userData)`), rather than rendering it through Angular's template binding (which auto-escapes) or an explicitly sanitized pipe. `document.write` interprets its argument as HTML/script, so if `userData` (a JSON/text blob representing exported personal data, which itself may contain user-supplied fields such as profile name, email, or other text fields previously stored without encoding) contains HTML or script-like content, it will be executed in the context of the application's origin when the export window is opened. This is a classic DOM-based XSS sink pattern. The actual component source (data-export.component.ts) is not visible in this file, but this spec file's mocking/assertion pattern is strong evidence of the vulnerable call shape being exercised and validated as expected behavior.

Test mocks window.open() to return an object exposing document.write as a spy, indicating the component under test opens a new window and calls document.write on it during save().
Test installs a spy on component.resetForm before invoking save(), part of the same call sequence that leads into the vulnerable write path but not itself transforming the userData value.
Test installs a spy on component.ngOnInit, completing the setup immediately preceding the save() call that triggers the document.write sink.

component.save() is invoked; the assertions that follow (line 107: component.userData toBe '{ user data }') confirm the raw server payload is passed through unmodified to the write path exercised by the mocked document.write, with no sanitization step visible in the test.

title: Raw backend error message surfaced directly to the user without sanitization or generic messaging
description: In the failure-path test, `dataSubjectService.dataExport` is mocked to throw `{ error: 'Error' }`, and the test asserts `component.error` is set to exactly `'Error'` — i.e., the component takes the `error` property from the caught HTTP error object and assigns it verbatim to a component field that is presumably bound in the template for display to the user. In a real deployment, the `error` property of an HTTP error response can contain verbose backend detail (validation messages, stack traces, internal identifiers) rather than a sanitized, generic user-facing message. Displaying this unfiltered value is a security-misconfiguration pattern (information disclosure through error handling) since the component performs no mapping to a safe, generic error string before exposing it to the DOM.

trace.description: Test simulates a backend/service error response object { error: 'Error' } being thrown by DataSubjectService.dataExport, standing in for whatever the real backend returns on failure.
component.save() is called, triggering the component's error-handling branch which is expected to extract and store the error content.

Assertion confirms component.error is set to the raw, unmodified 'Error' string from the backend response, implying this value is later rendered to the user without filtering or generic replacement.

title: No verification of security-relevant audit logging for GDPR data export requests
description: Data export is a sensitive, security-relevant operation (it produces a complete dump of a user's personal data). The spec file's tests for both the successful path (lines 100-111) and the failure path (lines 113-120) only assert on component state changes (confirmation, userData, error, resetForm/ngOnInit calls) — there is no assertion, mock, or spy anywhere in this file indicating that a data export request (success or failure) is logged, audited, or reported for monitoring purposes. Every intermediate line of the successful export flow (data mocking, window mocking, spy setup, the save() call itself, and every resulting assertion) is accounted for and none of them touch a logging, audit, or telemetry service. Given that this is the authoritative test suite for the export-triggering component, its complete silence on any audit/logging call is evidence that the underlying component performs no client-side security event logging for this sensitive action, which would normally be expected to allow later reconstruction of who exported what data and when (especially relevant for GDPR compliance and abuse detection e.g. repeated bulk exports).

title: Client-controlled delivery method ID trusted for downstream pricing/checkout without validation
description: The component lets the user select a delivery method id via selectMethod(id) and stores it directly into sessionStorage (a client-writable, attacker-modifiable store) with no verification that the id corresponds to an entry actually present in this.methods (the list fetched from the DeliveryService). The value is then used to drive navigation into the payment/checkout flow. Because sessionStorage can be trivially edited via browser devtools or a scripted request, an attacker can set 'deliveryMethodId' to any arbitrary value (including an id for a cheaper/free method, a non-existent id, or an id disallowed by business rules) before entering the payment step. Nothing in this file re-derives or validates the chosen method against the server-fetched list before persisting it, meaning the client is the sole authority over a value that likely influences shipping cost/ETA at checkout. This is a classic trust-boundary violation: a value the server should re-validate is instead accepted verbatim from client-controlled storage.

this.deliveryMethodId is set directly from the caller-supplied id without checking it exists in this.methods.

The gating condition only checks whether a selection already exists or id is truthy — it never checks that id matches an entry in the fetched this.methods array, so any truthy id value is allowed through.
chooseDeliveryMethod() is invoked and reads the still-unvalidated this.deliveryMethodId field set earlier.

The unvalidated deliveryMethodId is persisted to sessionStorage (client-writable) and immediately used to drive navigation to /payment/shop, trusting the client-controlled value for the rest of checkout.

title: Address lookup driven by client-controlled sessionStorage value with no visible ownership check
description: ngOnInit reads 'addressId' straight out of sessionStorage and passes it unmodified into addressService.getById(), then assigns the result directly to this.address for use in the delivery/checkout flow. sessionStorage is fully attacker-controllable client-side storage — a user can trivially change the stored addressId (e.g., via devtools) to another numeric id and have the client request that address record. This file performs no verification that the returned address belongs to the currently authenticated user before using it; the ownership check, if any, would have to occur inside AddressService/the backend, which is not visible from this file. This is the classic BOLA/IDOR sink shape: an identifier taken from an untrusted source is forwarded straight to a by-ID lookup and consumed without a subsequent ownership check in this component.

The returned address is assigned to this.address and used for the checkout flow with no ownership check performed in this component.

title: Unstructured console logging of backend error responses
description: Errors from both the address service and delivery service subscriptions are logged with a bare console.log(error) call. Depending on what the backend returns in error responses (stack traces, validation messages, internal details), this can leak sensitive diagnostic information into the browser console, and more importantly there is no structured/security-relevant logging pipeline here at all — failures fetching a user's address or delivery options are silently swallowed from a monitoring perspective (no telemetry, no correlation id, no alerting hook), making it impossible to detect or investigate abuse of this flow (e.g., repeated failed address lookups consistent with ID enumeration described in the other finding).

title: Error details logged via console.log instead of structured/security logging
description: The test at lines 122-126 asserts that when ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration fails, the component under test calls console.log(err) directly with the raw error value. This confirms the underlying DeluxeUserComponent implementation logs errors to the browser console rather than to any structured, security-aware logging/monitoring mechanism. Using console.log for error handling means: (1) no correlation ID or contextual metadata is attached to reconstruct an incident timeline, (2) whatever the backend returns as an error (which could include stack traces, internal messages, or other diagnostic detail depending on the real HTTP error shape) is exposed directly in the client browser console rather than being sanitized/aggregated server-side for monitoring, and (3) there is no server-side or centralized capture of this failure, so repeated configuration-fetch failures (which could indicate tampering, probing, or backend issues) are invisible to any monitoring/alerting system. This is a recurring anti-pattern in this codebase of relying on console.log as the error-handling/logging strategy for security-relevant failures such as failed configuration retrieval on an authenticated 'Deluxe User' account page.

title: No logging assertions for deluxe membership privilege upgrade action
description: The test suite mocks and exercises userService.upgradeToDeluxe (lines 47, 51) which represents a privilege-elevation action (a normal user becoming a paying 'deluxe' member with expanded application privileges). This mock is wired into the component under test via Angular's dependency injection and instantiated with the component, yet nowhere in this spec file is there any test verifying that a successful or failed privilege upgrade is logged or audited. While the actual component implementation is outside this file, the complete absence of any logging-related assertion around this security-relevant state transition (analogous to a role/privilege change event) is notable given that other outcomes in this same file (the configuration-fetch failure) are explicitly tested for console logging. This suggests the upgrade-to-deluxe flow, a financially and privilege-relevant transaction, has no equivalent observable audit/logging behavior being validated, which is a gap for incident detection and dispute resolution (e.g., a user claiming they never authorized the upgrade).

title: Raw backend/service errors logged verbatim to the browser console
description: The component under test (DeliveryMethodComponent) is verified by this spec to catch errors from AddressService.getById and DeliveryService.get and pass them, unmodified, straight into console.log(). The tests explicitly assert this behavior ('should log errors from address service directly to browser console' and 'should log errors from delivery service directly to browser console'), proving the production code contains an error handler of the form `.subscribe({ error: (err) => console.log(err) })` or similar with no sanitization, filtering, or environment gating. Any error payload returned by these HTTP-backed services (which could include internal exception messages, stack traces, or other backend implementation details in a real deployment) is written to the client-side console verbatim. This is a logging-monitoring anti-pattern: sensitive/internal error detail is exposed via an uncontrolled, non-security-reviewed sink (the end user's browser console) instead of being sanitized and sent to a proper monitoring/logging pipeline. Any browser extension, injected script (e.g., via an unrelated XSS elsewhere in the app), or a user opening devtools can observe internal error detail that should not be user-facing.

title: Delivery method selection persisted to sessionStorage without server-side re-validation
description: The test 'should store address id in session storage' confirms that chooseDeliveryMethod() writes the client-selected deliveryMethodId directly into window.sessionStorage via setItem('deliveryMethodId', '1') with no accompanying integrity protection (signature, server confirmation, or re-fetch). sessionStorage is fully attacker/user-controllable client-side state. If a later step in the checkout flow (outside this file, e.g. the payment or order-placement component) reads this value to determine the delivery price or ETA without the server independently re-deriving the selected delivery method's price from the deliveryMethodId, a user could tamper with sessionStorage (via devtools or a script) to select an ineligible or manipulated delivery option, causing a trust-boundary violation between client-declared state and server-enforced business rules. This file only shows the write step; the downstream consumer is outside this file's visibility, so the finding is a design observation rather than a fully confirmed exploit.

title: DOM XSS via document.write() of unsanitized exported user data
description: The save() handler receives the server's data-export response and writes the userData field directly into a newly opened browser window using document.write(), with no HTML sanitization or encoding. Angular's template auto-escaping does not protect this code path because the write happens outside the Angular template via a raw DOM API. If any field contained in the user's exported data (e.g. free-form text the user or another party previously entered elsewhere in the application, such as review/comment/memory-caption fields that end up bundled into the account data export) contains HTML/script markup, that markup is rendered and executed in the new window's document context. Because the export aggregates various previously-stored fields, this is effectively a stored-XSS sink: the injection point (wherever the original text was captured) lies outside this file, but this file is the render sink that turns stored markup into executed script with zero sanitization.

trace.description: save() submits the export request via dataSubjectService.dataExport(...) and subscribes to the server response; the server response content (including any user-supplied text aggregated into the export) is external/untrusted from this component's point of view.
this.userData = data.userData assigns the raw response field, with no HTML sanitization or encoding applied.
The 'next' callback receives the response object 'data' from the server; data.userData will be extracted from this object with no sanitization applied at any point in this callback.
window.open(...).document.write(this.userData) writes the unsanitized data directly into the DOM of a newly opened window, executing any embedded HTML/script.

title: Explicit Angular sanitizer bypass on captcha image markup
description: getNewCaptcha() takes data.image from the captcha service response and passes it through DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml before assigning it to this.captcha, which is presumably rendered with [innerHTML] in the template. bypassSecurityTrustHtml explicitly disables Angular's built-in HTML sanitization for this value. While the captcha image is typically server-generated SVG markup, using an explicit trust bypass on this content path means that if the captcha-generation service is ever compromised, misconfigured, or returns attacker-influenced content (e.g. via a dependency vulnerability), it would render as live HTML/script with no defense-in-depth from Angular's sanitizer. This is a real bypass reaching a render sink; the only mitigating factor is that the immediate data source is a trusted internal service rather than direct end-user input. The subscribe callback and the assignment/bypass call are adjacent statements with no intervening transformation, so the two-line path already reflects the complete flow of this value.

trace.description: imageCaptchaService.getCaptcha().subscribe receives data from the captcha backend service; content of data.image is external to this component.
this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(data.image) explicitly disables Angular's HTML sanitizer for this content before it is bound (presumably via innerHTML) in the template.

title: Anti-automation captcha requirement decided entirely client-side via forgeable localStorage value
description: needCaptcha() decides whether the user must solve a CAPTCHA before requesting a data export purely by comparing the current time against a timestamp read from localStorage ('lstdtxprt'). This value is fully controlled by the client (an attacker can clear it, edit it via devtools, or simply not run this component code and call the export API directly). The comparison result is stored in the presenceOfCaptcha flag, which is the sole gate later consulted in save() to decide whether to attach a captcha answer to the outgoing request; when the flag is false, dataRequest.answer is never set at all, yet the request (now only carrying dataRequest.format) is still submitted to the export endpoint. This treats an anti-automation/rate-limiting control as a client-side trust decision rather than something the server independently enforces and verifies; if the backend export endpoint trusts the absence/presence of an answer field as sufficient, an attacker can trivially bypass the intended rate limiting on this potentially expensive, data-disclosing operation by manipulating or clearing localStorage, enabling scripted repeated export requests.

trace.description: needCaptcha() reads the 'lstdtxprt' timestamp from localStorage, a value fully under client/attacker control, to decide whether an anti-automation captcha challenge should be presented.
save() only appends the captcha answer to dataRequest when presenceOfCaptcha (derived from the forgeable localStorage check) is true; otherwise no answer field is sent at all.
The if-condition compares nowTime against the forgeable timeOfCaptcha to decide whether a captcha is required for this export attempt.

presenceOfCaptcha is set to true only when the client-controlled comparison indicates a captcha is needed; otherwise it remains at its default false (line 39), and this flag becomes the sole control gate used later.

title: Client trusts raw URL query parameter to control asset path and triggers unauthenticated SVG-injection probe via WebSocket
description: The component reads a query-string parameter called `testDecal` directly from the URL (`this.route.snapshot.queryParams.testDecal`) and explicitly comments that it is a 'Forgotten' test parameter left over from development. This attacker-controlled value is used, with no validation, whitelisting, or sanitization, to build the image asset path (`this.logoSrc = \`assets/public/images/${decalParam || logo}\``) and is also emitted verbatim over the websocket connection as `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`. This is a design flaw: a debug/testing hook that was never removed and lets any caller influence which asset is requested (and probe a server-side SVG-injection verification channel) purely by adding `?testDecal=...` to the URL. There is no authentication, no server-side re-validation visible from this file, and no indication the parameter is restricted to non-production builds. An attacker can freely experiment with arbitrary path segments or payloads to (a) attempt path traversal / asset substitution on the logo image, and (b) probe the hidden 'verifySvgInjectionChallenge' socket event to test for SVG-injection vulnerabilities that the developers apparently know exist ('Forgotten' comment implies awareness this is a leftover debug channel).

title: Raw backend error details surfaced to end user without sanitization
description: When the deluxe status request fails, the component takes the raw error message straight from the HTTP error response (`err.error.error`) and assigns it to `this.error`, which is presumably rendered in the template. There is no filtering, generic-message substitution, or classification of the error before display. If the backend ever returns a verbose error (e.g., stack trace fragment, internal object property name, SQL/ORM error text), it will be surfaced directly to the end user, aiding reconnaissance for further attacks. This reflects a missing compensating control: the design never establishes a rule that backend error content must be sanitized/generalized before being shown to the user.

title: Unfiltered error objects written to browser console
description: In the configuration-fetch error handler, the full error object received from the HTTP call is passed straight to console.log with no filtering. Depending on what the ConfigurationService's underlying HTTP client attaches to error objects (e.g., request headers, response bodies, or other diagnostic data), this could log sensitive configuration or session-related details into the browser console. This is not classic server-side security logging, but it does illustrate a lack of controlled, structured logging: instead of a scrubbed, purpose-built security/diagnostic log entry, the raw error is dumped as-is, and there is no mechanism to redact potentially sensitive fields before they reach the console (which can be captured by browser extensions, error-tracking scripts, or shared screenshots).

title: Unvalidated Client-Controlled Query Parameter Used as Displayed Error Content (Content Spoofing)
description: The component reads the `error` query parameter directly from the URL (`route.snapshot.queryParams.error`) and uses it, without any validation, allow-listing, or sanitization, as a translation lookup key. Both the success path and the failure path of the translation call end up storing attacker-supplied content into the public `error` field, which is bound in the component's template and displayed to the user. Because the raw `translationId` (which equals the original client-controlled `errorKey`) is used verbatim when translation fails, an attacker can craft a URL such as `/error?error=<arbitrary text>` and the page will display that arbitrary text as if it were a legitimate application error message. There is no server-side or client-side derivation/validation restricting `errorKey` to a known, safe set of error codes (e.g. an enum of expected i18n keys) at any point along the path: the truthiness guard only checks for presence, the translate.get() call forwards the raw value to the i18n service, and both the success and failure subscription callbacks ultimately funnel content (either a resolved translation or the raw key itself) into the same public field that the template renders. This is a trust-assumption violation: the design lets the client fully dictate content that is presented as trusted, first-party application messaging, which can be used for phishing / social engineering or to spoof misleading system state to a victim who follows a crafted link.

errorKey is passed unvalidated into translate.get(errorKey) with no allow-list of accepted error codes.

On the success path, this.error is assigned the resolved errorMessage, an alternate route by which content driven by the attacker-chosen key reaches the displayed field.
The observable's error handler receives translationId, which for an unresolved key equals the original attacker-supplied errorKey, with no re-validation before use.

On translation failure, translationId (equal to the raw attacker-supplied errorKey) is assigned to the public 'error' field, which the component template renders to the user, resulting in fully attacker-controlled displayed content.

title: No Logging of Displayed Error Conditions Reaching the Error Page
description: This component serves as a generic landing page for application errors (likely reached after authorization failures, upstream exceptions, or blocked operations elsewhere in the app that redirect here with an `error` query parameter). At every stage of handling that error condition -- extracting the parameter, gating on its presence, requesting a translation, and handling both the success and failure outcomes of that request -- no logging, telemetry, or reporting call is made. The failure is only shown to the end user via the `error` field and never recorded or forwarded for monitoring. Combined with the fact that the `error` value can be arbitrary attacker-supplied text, there is no mechanism to detect abuse of this parameter (e.g., mass probing of translation keys, or repeated attempts to reach this page via forced errors) since no event is emitted at any point in the flow for correlation with server-side logs. This is a minor/secondary logging gap since the component is purely client-side presentational and primary logging should occur at the origin of the error server-side; it is reported here as the point where the security-relevant event is observed and silently discarded without any audit trail hook.

The failure callback fires with no logging of the failed translation lookup or the underlying error condition it represents.

title: Unvalidated, untyped trust of externally-injected dialog data (MAT_DIALOG_DATA)
description: The component receives its entire data model via Angular's dependency injection of MAT_DIALOG_DATA and assigns it directly to public, loosely-typed (`any`) fields without any runtime validation, shape checking, or sanitization: `this.feedback = this.dialogData.feedback` and `this.id = this.dialogData.id`. The component never verifies that `dialogData` actually contains the expected structure (e.g., that `feedback` is a well-formed feedback object rather than an arbitrary object or string), nor does it constrain what fields of the feedback object are exposed to the bound template. Because the `feedback`/`id` fields are declared and typed `any`, TypeScript's compile-time protections are bypassed entirely, and whatever object the caller (a component outside this file) passes through the Material dialog service is trusted implicitly at every step — from injection, through the field declarations, into the lifecycle hook that performs the assignment, to the final unchecked assignment — and rendered. This is a design-level trust-assumption gap: the component that displays data should be the last line of defense validating the shape/content of what it renders, but here no such validation exists at any point in the flow.

public id: any is likewise declared untyped, with no constraint on the value it will later receive.

title: No audit logging when sensitive feedback/user data is viewed
description: This component is responsible for displaying feedback details (potentially including user-submitted comments and an associated id, which in the Juice Shop data model can be tied to a specific user) inside a modal dialog, likely from an administrative feedback-management view. There is no logging call anywhere in ngOnInit or elsewhere in the file when this potentially sensitive data is displayed: the injected dialog data flows straight from injection through the lifecycle hook into the component's public fields with no observability at any of those points. If this dialog is used by administrators to inspect feedback that may contain PII or is associated with specific user accounts, the absence of any audit trail (who viewed which feedback, when) means there is no way to reconstruct who accessed what user data after the fact, which is a logging/monitoring gap for a data-viewing event.

title: Configuration fetch subscription has no error handling or logging
description: The module constructor subscribes to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() and only supplies a next-handler that mutates the DOM (adds a theme class). No error callback is provided, so if the configuration request fails (network error, malformed response, backend compromise, or an attacker manipulating the configuration endpoint) the failure is silently swallowed by RxJS with no logging, no user feedback, and no monitoring signal. Because this is the mechanism that also drives visual state (theming) and is the pattern used across the app for pulling security-relevant configuration, a failed or tampered fetch here would go completely undetected — there is no security event trail to investigate a configuration-service outage or manipulation.

title: CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA disables Angular's template safety checks
description: The module declares `schemas: [CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA]`, which instructs the Angular compiler to allow any unknown element and any unknown attribute/property binding on FaucetComponent's templates without validation or compile-time errors. This is a broad, permissive default that removes a layer of defense — normally Angular will reject unrecognized bindings, which helps catch mistakes such as inadvertently binding to a raw DOM property/attribute that could be an XSS vector (e.g., innerHTML-like attributes on custom/unknown tags) or template typos that silently become no-ops instead of build failures. Using this schema module-wide (rather than scoping it only where truly needed for a specific known custom element) is an unnecessarily permissive configuration that weakens template-level guardrails for this whole module.

title: Unvalidated server-supplied theme string inserted directly into DOM classList
description: The constructor takes `conf.application.theme` returned from the configuration service and concatenates it with the literal '-theme' before passing it straight to `classList.add()` on the global overlay container element, with no validation, allow-listing, or sanitization of the theme value. The design never establishes a constraint on what `theme` may contain — it is trusted implicitly as if it were always a safe, pre-vetted identifier. If the configuration source can ever be influenced (e.g., a compromised or misconfigured backend, a supply-chain issue in the config API, or a future code path that lets non-admin input reach this same service), an unexpected value (e.g. containing whitespace) would throw a DOMException breaking the whole overlay container's theming for all users, or could be used to inject an attacker-chosen literal CSS class name application-wide if any stylesheet matches attacker-controllable class names. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client renders configuration data into the DOM without the server (or client) ever validating/deriving a safe theme value from a known allow-list.

title: Password reset flow relies on guessable security question and leaks user-existence (enumeration), with no rate limiting or token verification exercised by tests
description: The spec file exercises ForgotPasswordComponent's password-reset workflow, which the tests show is designed as: (1) enter an email, (2) the component asynchronously queries SecurityQuestionService.findBy(email) to fetch that user's security question, (3) the caller answers the security question and supplies a new password, and (4) UserService.resetPassword() is invoked directly with the composed data to change the password — of({}) being returned indicates that presence of the security question response is enough to allow a full reset. Two design defects are visible from the test behavior: (a) the differing observable outcome of findSecurityQuestion() for a 'known@user.test' email (component.securityQuestion becomes the actual question, line 173) versus an 'unknown@user.test' email (securityQuestion stays undefined, line 181) demonstrates a user-enumeration oracle — an attacker can iterate emails and learn which ones are registered, and for registered accounts learn the exact security question to target for guessing/social-engineering; and (b) the overall reset flow, as exercised in 'should clear form and show confirmation after changing password' (lines 151-157), completes and calls resetForm() as soon as userService.resetPassword() succeeds, with nothing in the test suite indicating server-side proof of identity beyond the (guessable, low-entropy) security-question answer typed client-side — i.e., there is no token/email-confirmation step visible, and no evidence of throttling/lockout on repeated security-question guesses (findSecurityQuestion can be invoked repeatedly, see line 172, 180, 189, 196 with no attempt counter). The only guard visible in the tests is a purely client-side emptiness check (line 194-197, findBy not called for an empty email) — there is no accompanying test or control demonstrating rate-limiting on repeated non-empty guesses. This mirrors the classic OWASP-documented weakness of security-question-based password resets: low-entropy, often-public answers combined with no rate limiting enable account takeover. Because the actual component/service implementation lives outside this spec file, the concrete absence of server-side throttling and audit logging for repeated failed security-question lookups or reset attempts cannot be fully confirmed here, but nothing in the exercised test behavior indicates such protections exist, and no test asserts that failed/successful reset attempts are logged for monitoring.

title: Weak password policy enforced only by minimum length, no complexity or maximum-length bound
description: The tests explicitly document the password validation rule enforced by the forgot-password reset flow: passwordControl is invalid only when shorter than five characters ('should have a password length of at least five characters', lines 99-108) and is explicitly asserted valid for a 21-character all-'a' string with no complexity requirement (line 110-117: 'should allow password length of more than twenty characters'). This confirms the reset-password design accepts trivially weak passwords (e.g., 'aaaaa') as long as they meet a bare minimum length, with no enforcement of character-class diversity, denylisting of common passwords, or any additional strength requirement. Combined with the security-question-based identity check documented in the sibling finding, an attacker who determines or guesses the security question answer can reset an account to a weak, easily-remembered password without the system-level password-strength design objecting. This is a design gap (the rule the server enforces is simply 'len>=5') rather than an implementation bug in one field. The trace below follows the value from the length-boundary assertions through the additional all-repeated-character long-password assertion into the actual reset call that persists the accepted-but-weak password.

title: DOM-based/Stored XSS via unsanitized JWT-derived lastLoginIp rendered with bypassSecurityTrustHtml
description: The component reads the JWT stored in localStorage, decodes it client-side with jwt-decode (which performs NO signature verification — it merely base64-decodes the payload), and then takes the `lastLoginIp` claim from that decoded payload and interpolates it directly into an HTML string that is passed to Angular's `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml()`. This call explicitly disables Angular's built-in output-encoding/sanitization for the resulting value, which is then almost certainly bound via `[innerHTML]` in the companion template (last-login-ip.component.html) since it is stored on a property typed `any` used for HTML display. The `lastLoginIp` value ultimately originates from a request header (X-Forwarded-For / similar) that the server captures at login time and embeds into the JWT — a value historically attacker-controllable by spoofing the header on the login request. Because jwt-decode never validates the token's signature, any token payload — including one an attacker could tamper with directly if they can write to localStorage, or one issued by a server that trusted an attacker-controlled header — is accepted verbatim and rendered as raw HTML with no sanitization. An attacker who can influence the `lastLoginIp` field (e.g. by sending `X-Forwarded-For: ` at login, or via any other path that lets the server persist that string into the JWT claim) achieves script execution in the victim's browser session the next time this component renders, enabling session/token theft, account takeover, or further pivoting.

title: Silent console-only error handling on token parsing failure (no security event visibility)
description: ngOnInit wraps parseAuthToken() in a try/catch that, on any failure (e.g. malformed/tampered JWT, unexpected payload shape), only performs console.log(err) and otherwise silently continues. There is no structured logging, telemetry, or reporting of what could be a security-relevant event (a corrupted or forged auth token failing to parse). This is a minor, client-side-only logging gap; because this is purely local browser console output rather than a server-side/security log, its monitoring value is inherently limited, but it still represents an unmonitored failure path for a security-sensitive parsing operation.

title: DOM-based XSS via unsanitized JWT 'lastLoginIp' claim passed to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml
description: This spec file documents (and asserts) the behavior of LastLoginIpComponent: on ngOnInit() it reads the 'token' value from localStorage, decodes it as a JWT without any visible signature verification, extracts the 'data.lastLoginIp' claim, wraps it in a raw HTML string ('' + value + ''), and passes that string directly to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml — an explicit Angular sanitization bypass. The test at lines 71-75 proves the exact unescaped concatenation ('1.2.3.4') is what gets marked as trusted HTML, and the mock at lines 21-25 shows bypassSecurityTrustHtml is used verbatim (mockImplementation just returns the argument), meaning whatever HTML string is built from the claim is later bound via [innerHTML] (or similar) in the component template without further sanitization. Since the JWT token is read from localStorage — a value that is client-writable (via dev tools, an XSS elsewhere, or a maliciously issued token if the app does not verify JWT signature before using its claims) — an attacker who controls the 'lastLoginIp' claim value (e.g., setting it to '') can achieve script execution in the victim's browser once this data is rendered. This is a known OWASP Juice Shop challenge pattern (bypassSecurityTrustHtml + unsanitized claim). The vulnerable sink itself lives in last-login-ip.component.ts, which is not present in this file set, but this spec file's assertions make the vulnerable data flow and the explicit sanitizer bypass observable and confirmable.

Logging raw token parsing errors/content to the browser console can leak sensitive session/token material or internal error details to anyone with access to the browser devtools (e.g., shared machines, browser extensions with console access, or screen-recording tooling), and provides no structured security event logging (no correlation ID, no distinction between benign and malicious tampering attempts). This is a minor client-side information exposure / inadequate security event logging pattern rather than a server-side log leak.

Test asserts console.log was called, confirming the component writes JWT parsing error details to the browser console rather than handling the security-relevant event (a tampered/invalid auth token) via a controlled, non-sensitive reporting mechanism.

title: Unvalidated pass-through of external form value with no sanitization boundary
description: AbstractControlValueAccessor.writeValue() (used by mat-search-bar and any other component extending this class) accepts an arbitrary string and stores it directly in `this.value`, then immediately forwards it to the registered `onChange` callback via `updateChanges()` with zero validation, length limiting, or sanitization. Because this is a shared abstract base class intended to be reused by multiple form controls, the design never establishes a validation boundary for the value flowing from the DOM/model into application state and onward to whatever consumer registered via `registerOnChange`. If any downstream consumer (e.g., a search query built from this value, or a template that renders it) trusts this value as already-vetted because it passed through a 'form accessor', that trust assumption is misplaced — the class provides no validation hook at all. This is a design gap (no validation contract exists anywhere in the class), not merely a missing check on one field, since the class is explicitly the reusable data-entry boundary for its subclasses.

The raw value is assigned unchanged to this.value with no type/format/length validation or sanitization.

title: NFT mint eligibility enforced only in UI state, not in mintNFT() business logic
description: The mintNFT() method is the function that actually executes the privileged on-chain workflow: approving 1000 BEE tokens and calling the NFT contract's mintNFT(). The precondition for this action -- that the user holds at least 1000 BEE and that the 'Mint the Pot' challenge has not already been solved -- is computed in fetchMyBeeBalance() (lines 121-129) and only used to toggle the mintButtonDisabled/challengeSolved UI flags. mintNFT() itself (line 247) only checks this.session before proceeding through the approve call (264), its confirmation wait (269), NFT contract instantiation (274) and the final mint call (276); at no point in this path is this.myBEEBalance or this.challengeSolved consulted. Because Angular component methods are reachable directly from the browser console/devtools regardless of a disabled button, any connected wallet can invoke mintNFT() and walk this entire path to the mint call without ever satisfying the balance precondition that the UI implies is required. This is a workflow-bypass / trust-assumption insecure design flaw: the privileged action trusts a client-side UI flag computed in an unrelated method as the sole gate instead of re-validating the precondition inside the privileged function's own execution path.

The NFT contract instance is constructed immediately prior to the mint call, still without any balance/challenge validation in this path.

BeeTokenContract.approve(nftAddress, amountToApprove) and the subsequent contract.mintNFT() call at line 276 execute the privileged mint workflow without re-checking the 1000 BEE balance precondition.

title: Wallet identity self-reported to backend verification endpoint without cryptographic proof of ownership
description: metamaskAddress is populated directly from the wallet-connect response (provider.account) with no accompanying signature challenge (e.g. personal_sign/eth_sign) proving that the connected browser actually controls the private key for that address. The same unverified value is folded into the userData object as a trusted identity attribute, then later -- after the mint transaction completes -- passed into keysService.verifyNFTWallet(this.metamaskAddress) inside a setTimeout callback, and the server's response is trusted to flip successResponse and lock the mint button. Because the identity value that ultimately authorizes/records a completed action is taken from an unauthenticated client-supplied string rather than a value cryptographically bound to a signature, and it is carried unchanged through userData construction and the mint workflow before being submitted, an attacker able to influence the outbound request (e.g. via browser tooling) could supply an arbitrary address. This is an authentication-outcome defect: the code resolves 'whose wallet is this' from unverified client input and carries that unverified claim all the way to the point where it authorizes/records a privileged NFT-verification outcome.

mintNFT() runs the mint workflow that will eventually trigger wallet verification using the stored, still-unverified metamaskAddress.
setTimeout wraps the verification call so it fires after the mint transaction is confirmed, carrying this.metamaskAddress forward unchanged.
keysService.verifyNFTWallet(this.metamaskAddress) sends the unverified, self-reported address to the backend as the identity used to authorize the success/verified state at lines 292-295.

title: Unvalidated user-supplied withdrawal amount forwarded directly to faucet contract call
description: extractBEETokens() accepts amount (defaulting to this.withdrawAmount, which is bound to a user-editable form field in the template outside this file) and passes it directly into contract.withdraw(amount) with no bounds validation -- no minimum, maximum, integer, or sign check is performed on amount anywhere in this file. Between the entrypoint and the sink, the method only builds unrelated context (provider, signer, gas-balance check) and never inspects or transforms the `amount` value itself: the provider is created, the signer's address is fetched, the signer's ETH balance is retrieved and formatted purely to gate on gas availability (lines 226-229), and the faucet contract instance is instantiated -- but at no point is `amount` bounded before being handed to the contract. This is a trust-assumption violation: a value the client fully controls and that determines how many tokens are requested from the faucet is carried unmodified through the whole method to the sink with zero application-side validation, relying entirely on the smart contract (outside this file, unverifiable here) to enforce any limits.

Only the caller's ETH-for-gas balance is checked; the requested BEE amount value itself is never validated (range, sign, type).
A Web3Provider is constructed from window.ethereum; amount is not touched here but this sets up the call context.

title: Raw contract/provider error messages surfaced directly to end users
description: Caught exceptions from ethers.js contract and provider calls are assigned verbatim to this.errorMessage and presumably rendered in the UI. Provider/contract error objects can include internal details such as RPC endpoint responses, revert reasons, or stack-trace-like data. Displaying these unfiltered to the end user is an information-disclosure-flavored misconfiguration -- no sanitization or generic error mapping is applied before the raw error.message reaches the UI-bound property; the entire catch block consists of only a console log and a direct assignment, with no intervening transformation step where the message could have been sanitized.

console.error('Error extracting BEEs:', error.message) also writes the raw message to the browser console.

title: Unsanitized search-term forwarded to parent without validation or encoding (potential DOM XSS entrypoint)
description: MatSearchBarComponent captures raw user-typed text from its search input (bound in the associated template, not shown in this file) and forwards it verbatim via Angular @Output() events (onEnter, onBlur, onFocus) to whatever parent component consumes it. There is no validation, length limiting, or sanitization applied to `searchValue` anywhere in this file before it is emitted, through any of the three forwarding paths (onEnterring, onBlurring, onFocussing). In this application family (Juice Shop-derived UI), search terms are a well-known vector for DOM-based XSS when a downstream component highlights/renders the raw query string via `innerHTML`/`bypassSecurityTrustHtml` without escaping. Because this component is the first point in the client where free-form, attacker-controlled text enters the application, and it performs no defensive encoding or allow-listing before propagating the value onward through any of its emit paths, it is the origin of that unsanitized data flow. The actual rendering sink lives in a different file (the parent component subscribing to `onEnter`/`onBlur`/`onFocus`), which is not visible here, but the defect — accepting and forwarding arbitrary text with zero validation across every emission path — is fully present in this file. There is also no upper bound on the length of the search string, so an attacker can enter an arbitrarily long string that is forwarded unchecked through any of these paths, which could contribute to excessive processing/memory usage in whatever expensive matching/highlighting logic consumes it downstream.

The raw searchValue is emitted unchanged via this.onEnter.emit(searchValue) with no sanitization, encoding, or length capping applied.

onBlurring similarly receives and forwards the same unsanitized searchValue via this.onBlur.emit(searchValue) at line 82, and onFocussing does the same at line 90, showing the pattern is consistent across all emitted events in this component.

The conditional `if (!searchValue && !this.alwaysOpen())` branches on the truthiness of the raw value but performs no content sanitization or escaping; the tainted string continues unchanged regardless of which branch is taken.
this.searchVisible = false is a UI-visibility side effect triggered along the way; it does not touch or clean searchValue, which remains available for emission immediately after.
this.onBlur.emit(searchValue) forwards the still-unsanitized string out of the component via the onBlur output, identical in kind to the onEnter path.
onFocussing(searchValue: string) is a third parallel entry path receiving the same kind of untrusted raw string with no validation on the parameter.
this.onFocus.emit(searchValue) forwards the unsanitized string out of the component via the onFocus output, completing the third unguarded propagation path.

This is the boundary where this file hands off the unvalidated string to external code (a parent component's event handler) outside this file; the actual DOM-rendering sink that would turn this into exploitable XSS, and any downstream expensive-processing sink for resource consumption, is not visible in this file.

title: Open redirect: post-login navigation target taken directly from unvalidated query parameter
description: The test 'should redirect to the URL provided via the redirectUrl query parameter' demonstrates that LoginComponent.login() reads a 'redirectUrl' value from the route's queryParamMap and passes it directly to Angular Router's navigateByUrl() without any allow-list or same-origin validation. Because the query parameter is fully attacker-controlled (an attacker crafts a link like /login?redirectUrl=//evil.example.com or an internal-but-unauthorized route), a victim who logs in via a phishing link is silently redirected post-authentication to a destination the server/app never validated. This is a classic trust-assumption violation: the client/URL is trusted to specify where an authenticated session should be forwarded, and the design never re-derives or validates that target against a safe set of routes. Combined with the fact that this happens immediately after a successful authentication (component.login() success path), it can be leveraged for phishing or for redirecting a freshly authenticated session to an attacker-controlled page that mimics the real app to harvest the freshly issued token.

component.login() is invoked; internally it must read the queryParamMap value and use it as the post-login navigation target.

The component's injected router instance is obtained so the eventual navigation call can be observed/intercepted, confirming that the component itself holds a direct reference to the Router used for the redirect.
router.navigateByUrl is spied on and mocked, isolating the exact sink method the component calls internally once it decides where to send the user after login.

await fixture.whenStable() lets the asynchronous login/basket-merge pipeline resolve, which is the point at which the component actually invokes the navigation with the carried-over redirect value.

router.navigateByUrl is asserted to have been called with the exact, unvalidated value from the query parameter ('/profile'), confirming the component forwards caller-controlled input straight into the navigation sink with no allow-list check.

title: Authentication token persisted to localStorage, exposing it to XSS-based theft
description: The test 'stores the returned authentication token in localStorage' confirms that on successful login, LoginComponent takes the token returned by the login API response and writes it into localStorage (a JavaScript-readable, non-HttpOnly storage). Any XSS vulnerability anywhere in the application (or a malicious/compromised third-party script loaded on the same origin) can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token, enabling full session hijacking. This is a well-known anti-pattern versus storing session identifiers in a secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie which JavaScript cannot read. The design choice to keep the long-lived auth token in localStorage is a structural weakness in how the identity/session token is issued and stored on the client.

component.login() is called; it consumes the login response and is expected to persist the token client-side.

The default mock for userService.login (set up in beforeEach) returns an empty object, establishing the baseline observable that line 153 later overrides — confirming the token value flows solely through this mocked login() observable into the component.

The test asserts localStorage.getItem('token') equals the raw token value, confirming the auth token is stored in JS-accessible localStorage rather than a protected, HttpOnly cookie.

title: TOTP (2FA) temporary token stored in localStorage in plaintext
description: The test 'should redirect to 2FA page when login requires a TOTP token' shows that when the backend signals totp_token_required, the component takes the tmpToken from the error payload and stores it under localStorage key 'totp_tmp_token' before redirecting to the 2FA entry page. This intermediate authentication-state token — which represents 'first factor verified, second factor pending' — is placed in the same JS-readable storage as the main auth token, with no visible expiration handling in the client. If an attacker can run script on the origin (XSS) or otherwise access localStorage, they can steal this tmp token and potentially complete or replay the second-factor step themselves, effectively bypassing the MFA step's intended protection against credential-only compromise.

component.login() processes the error and is expected to persist the tmpToken and navigate to the 2FA entry route.
The component's injected router is obtained so the subsequent forced navigation to the 2FA entry page can be observed, confirming this is part of the same authentication-state handling branch.

The rejected error's data.tmpToken field carries the actual sensitive intermediate-auth value ('tmp') that the component must extract from the error object.

Assertion confirms localStorage.getItem('totp_tmp_token') equals the raw tmp token, showing the MFA intermediate token is stored in unprotected, script-readable client storage.

title: Security-relevant errors surfaced only via console.log with no structured security logging
description: Multiple tests show that failure conditions — OAuth configuration load failure, unauthorized OAuth redirect URI detection, and guest-basket merge failure after login — are handled purely by calling console.log with the raw error/string. There is no evidence in the tested behavior of any structured, correlate-able security event logging (e.g., recording failed OAuth configuration fetches, redirect URI mismatches, or basket-merge failures tied to a user/session/request id) that could be aggregated for detection of abuse or misconfiguration attempts. Relying on browser console output means these events are visible only to the local user/browser devtools and are not captured for server-side monitoring or alerting, so repeated anomalous events (e.g., many mismatched OAuth redirect attempts, which could indicate probing) would go undetected.

component.ngOnInit() runs and is expected to react to the mismatch by disabling OAuth and logging.

The only durable observable outcome is the oauthUnavailable flag being flipped to true — a UI-state change with no accompanying audit trail, correlation id, or alerting hook.

title: OAuth authorized-redirect configuration permits plain HTTP scheme
description: The 'google OAuth configuration' test suite configures authorizedRedirects entries using plain 'http://localhost:4200' (and windowRefService.nativeWindow.location.protocol is likewise mocked as 'http:'), and the component's authorization check is satisfied by this insecure-scheme URI. While this mirrors a local dev setup, it reflects that the component's redirect-URI matching logic does not enforce HTTPS for OAuth callbacks — an OAuth authorization code or token could be exposed to network-level interception if such an insecure URI were authorized in a real deployment. This is a configuration-acceptance weakness: the authorized-redirect list is trusted as-is with no scheme enforcement.

title: Security question disclosed to unauthenticated caller based solely on typed email address
description: findSecurityQuestion() fires an unauthenticated lookup against securityQuestionService.findBy() for any email string typed into the form, with no proof that the caller owns that email account. The response directly reveals whether an account exists for that email (user enumeration) and, if it does, reveals the security question text itself (securityQuestion.question), enabling an attacker to harvest security questions for arbitrary target emails ahead of a password-reset attack. This is a classic weak-password-recovery design flaw (CWE-640): the server should never disclose recovery metadata to an unauthenticated party. The client-side debounce (setTimeout, 1000ms) is not a security control - an attacker driving the same underlying API directly (bypassing this Angular component entirely) can query it as fast as the (unseen) server allows, with no application-level throttling visible from this file.

Email is sent unauthenticated to securityQuestionService.findBy(), debounced only 1000ms client-side (line 51/75), which is not an effective anti-enumeration control.
Security question text is returned and displayed (this.securityQuestion = securityQuestion.question), disclosing recovery metadata to any unauthenticated caller who can enumerate emails.

title: Password reset workflow relies solely on security-question answer with no out-of-band verification, and enforces only a 5-character password policy
description: resetPassword() completes an account password change using only email + security question answer + new password, gathered entirely from client-controlled form fields, with no server-issued reset token, one-time code, or email confirmation link involved in this flow. Since the security question itself can be harvested via the enumeration flaw above (or is often low-entropy / guessable, e.g. 'favorite color'), an attacker who can answer or brute-force the security question can take over any account by supplying only that account's email - the design never establishes a stronger identity-verification step. Compounding this, the new password is only required to be 5 characters long (Validators.minLength(5) on passwordControl, line 41), making the credential set at the end of this weak recovery flow itself weak and easier to guess/brute force post-takeover.

The response directly reveals whether an account exists for that email (user enumeration) and, if it does, reveals the security question text itself (securityQuestion.question), enabling an attacker to harvest security questions for arbitrary target emails ahead of a password-reset attack. This is a classic weak-password-recovery design flaw (CWE-640): the server should never disclose recovery metadata to an unauthenticated party. The client-side debounce (setTimeout, 1000ms) is not a security control - an attacker driving the same underlying API directly (bypassing this Angular component entirely) can query it as fast as the (unseen) server allows, with no application-level throttling visible from this file.

title: Failed/erroneous password reset attempts are not logged, only surfaced to the UI
description: In the resetPassword() error handler, a failed reset attempt (e.g., wrong security answer, invalid email) only sets this.error = error.error for display and resets the form; there is no client-side logging, telemetry, or audit event emitted for this security-relevant failure. Combined with the previous finding, an attacker brute-forcing security-question answers against this endpoint would generate a stream of failed attempts that this component makes no attempt to surface to any monitoring path, hampering detection/response to a credential-recovery attack in progress (assuming server-side logging is absent or cannot be confirmed from this file).
