title: Stored XSS via unsanitized caption/username concatenation rendered on Photo Wall
description: Memory captions are free-text values (see form control at line 42, which applies only a `required` validator and an async MIME-type validator — no output encoding or sanitization) that are submitted via `addMemory()` and later retrieved via `photoWallService.get()`. When memories are received in `ngOnInit`, the component builds a new caption string by concatenating the raw `memory.caption` value with `memory.User.username` using a template literal (line 65), with no HTML-encoding or sanitization applied to either field. The resulting string is pushed into `slideshowDataSource` (line 67), which is bound for display in the companion template (photo-wall.component.html), a file not visible here. Because neither `caption` nor `username` is sanitized at this construction point, if the rendering template does not apply context-appropriate escaping (e.g. if it uses `[innerHTML]` rather than plain interpolation), an attacker who controls either their own caption text or their own username can have arbitrary markup/script persist and execute in the browser of every user who views the Photo Wall — a classic stored XSS. The persistence/assembly point is in this file; the actual render sink is outside it, so exploitability there cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone.

title: Client-side authentication check trusts mere presence of a localStorage token
description: isLoggedIn() determines the user's authenticated state solely by checking whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage (line 126), without validating the token's signature, structure, or expiration. Any code in the surrounding template that gates UI functionality (e.g., showing the upload form) on this method's return value will treat a stale, expired, or manually-fabricated non-empty localStorage value as proof of a valid session. While actual authorization must ultimately be enforced server-side on the backend calls this component makes, this local trust decision is not itself an authentication check (it does not verify the token content), and using it as the sole gate for UI-level access to sensitive functionality is a weak identity-verification implementation.

title: Photo upload lacks any client-side size cap, and file-type enforcement relies solely on a bypassable client-side async validator
description: The upload form (line 40-43) validates the 'image' control only with `Validators.required` and the `mimeType` async validator; there is no maximum file size constraint anywhere in the component, and the MIME-type check is a client-side Angular validator that can be trivially bypassed by calling the underlying API directly (the entrypoint for this data is outside this file, in PhotoWallService.addMemory). The selected file flows from the raw DOM file input, through form state, through the only validation step present (an async MIME-type check with no size bound), and directly into the upload call with no intervening size cap. Because the design never establishes or enforces a bound on upload size before invoking `save()` → `addMemory()` (lines 111-112), a malicious or careless client is not prevented, at the level this file controls, from attempting arbitrarily large uploads, and the only file-type gate present is a soft client-side check offering no real security guarantee if the corresponding server endpoint does not independently re-validate.

title: Errors from configuration fetch are only console-logged with no security monitoring or structured logging
description: The subscription to getApplicationConfiguration() defines an error handler that does nothing but `console.log(err)`. There is no structured/centralized logging, no correlation ID, and no alerting mechanism tied to this failure path. If the configuration endpoint is unreachable, tampered with, or returns an error indicating backend compromise or a blocked/failed request (e.g., due to a proxy/CORS misconfiguration or an attacker intercepting the request), this security-relevant signal is silently dropped into the browser console where it is visible only to the end user and never reaches any monitoring/alerting system. Additionally, if the underlying HTTP client surfaces response bodies or headers inside the error object (common with Angular's HttpErrorResponse), those details are printed to the browser console, which is a plaintext log sink that could include internal implementation details useful to an attacker or accidentally exposed sensitive data.

title: Server configuration response consumed without any validation and trusted implicitly
description: The component types the configuration payload as `config: any` and directly assigns nested fields (config.application.name, config.application.privacyContactEmail) to component state without any schema validation, type checking, or sanitization. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client blindly trusts whatever shape/content the configuration service returns and propagates it into the UI-bound fields `applicationName` and `privacyContactEmail`. If the configuration source is ever compromised, proxied through an untrusted intermediary, or manipulated (e.g., via a misconfigured/insecure config endpoint elsewhere in the app), arbitrary attacker-controlled strings can be pushed into displayed identity fields (site name, contact email) with no server-side or client-side validation ever performed on this data before use.

Response is typed as `any` with no schema/shape validation applied before use.
Only an existence check (config?.application?.name) gates the assignment — the content/value of `name` itself is never validated or sanitized, only its presence.

title: Fallback privacy contact email derived from unvalidated client-side hostname
description: When the server-provided configuration lacks a privacyContactEmail, the component falls back to constructing one from `this._document.location.hostname` (the browser's current hostname) rather than a hardcoded, trusted organizational default. In deployments where the hostname can be influenced by the client's request (e.g., app served behind a misconfigured reverse proxy that reflects an arbitrary Host header, or via DNS rebinding / alternate domain binding), this design causes the application to synthesize and display a plausible-looking but attacker-influenced contact email address (e.g., donotreply@attacker-controlled-domain). This is a weak default that assumes the browser-observed hostname is always trustworthy for constructing security/contact-relevant content, without any allow-list or server-side canonical value being enforced.

title: Client-side authentication gate relies on mere presence of a localStorage token, not its validity
description: The test suite documents that PhotoWallComponent.isLoggedIn() simply returns the raw value of localStorage.getItem('token') (line 226-232, any string such as 'abc' is treated as a valid logged-in state). This value then gates rendering of the privileged 'share-a-memory' form and its submit button (lines 280-290). Because localStorage is fully attacker/script controllable (e.g. via XSS elsewhere, browser extensions, or simply manual devtools manipulation) and no signature/expiry/format validation of the token is performed before granting UI access to the memory-upload flow, this is a weak, forgeable authentication check pattern. While the backend addMemory endpoint presumably re-validates the token server-side (not visible in this file), the client-side authorization decision itself is based on an unauthenticated, unverified value, which is the core weak-session-token pattern (no signature check, no expiry check) combined with a broken function-level access decision made purely on the client.

title: API and configuration errors are only logged to the browser console with no security monitoring or user-facing handling
description: Across multiple tests (get() failure, addMemory() failure, getApplicationConfiguration() failure), the component's only observable error-handling behavior is `console.log(error)` (verified at lines 120, 128, 174). This means failures of authenticated actions (e.g., a failed memory submission, which could reflect an authorization failure or blocked request) are not reported to any centralized logging/monitoring/alerting mechanism, are not surfaced to the user in an actionable way, and are only visible transiently in the client browser console. Security-relevant failures (e.g., repeated denied uploads, malformed responses) would be undetectable to defenders, preventing incident detection and response for this feature.

description: The test at lines 177-181 shows that when a memory record contains a caption and an associated User.username (both attacker-influenced values coming from a stored memory / uploader profile), the component builds a new display string via concatenation: `caption + ' (© ' + username + ')'` (observed result 'Hi (© alice)'). This assembled string is then rendered into the photo grid tiles, as shown by the later template-rendering tests (lines 244-254) that assert one '.container' tile per memory. This spec file cannot show the actual template binding (interpolation vs. innerHTML) used to render `slideshowDataSource[*].caption`, so if the component or its template inserts this concatenated string via an unescaped HTML sink, it constitutes stored XSS carried through the caption/username fields. title: Client-side image upload handling has no observable file size restriction before reading into memory
description: The onImagePicked() handler (exercised at lines 200-224) reads a selected file entirely via FileReader.readAsDataURL with no test coverage or evidence of a maximum file size check before the read occurs. If the underlying component does not enforce a size cap (not shown to exist here), a user (or malicious script driving the file input) could select an extremely large file, causing the browser to attempt to load and base64-encode the entire file into memory as a data URL, potentially freezing or crashing the tab, and subsequently submitting a very large payload to the addMemory upload endpoint.

title: Component relies on client-side console.log for error handling instead of proper security logging/monitoring
description: The spec file explicitly tests and asserts that when the ProductReviewService.patch() call fails, the component under test (ProductReviewEditComponent) logs the raw error directly to the browser console via console.log(err), rather than reporting it to any server-side logging/monitoring facility or a structured error-handling service. This test (lines 88-96) locks in that behavior as expected/required. Because the failure path only writes to the browser's local console, there is no server-side record of the failed review-update attempt, no correlation ID, and no mechanism for security operations to detect repeated failures (which could indicate probing, tampering with review IDs, or abuse of the patch endpoint). Additionally, logging raw caught error objects to the console is a pattern that can leak internal error details (stack traces, backend messages) to anyone with access to the browser devtools, and the test does nothing to constrain what is logged, so if a future/backend error object contains sensitive data (e.g., validation details, IDs, tokens embedded in error responses) it would be exposed the same way. This is a genuine security logging/monitoring gap: failed mutation attempts against the review-edit API are only observable client-side and never reach a monitorable, auditable channel.

title: Stored XSS: unsanitized review text persisted without any output-encoding contract
description: addReview() takes the raw value of a native HTMLTextAreaElement (not even routed through the reviewControl validator declared on line 49) and sends it verbatim as the review 'message' field to productReviewService.create(). There is no sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing of the text before it is persisted. Juice Shop's review list renders review messages elsewhere (outside this file) typically via a template that may not always context-appropriately encode rich content, and this is the canonical Juice Shop 'Five-Star Feedback' / persisted XSS pattern. Even if the rendering sink is not visible in this file, the persistence point is here: a free-form text field accepted from the DOM with zero validation or encoding before being written to the backend is where the stored-XSS vulnerability is introduced. Any other client (or admin panel) that renders this review message without escaping will execute attacker-supplied markup/script in the victim's session.

title: Client-side authentication decision based solely on localStorage token presence
description: isLoggedIn() determines the user's authenticated state purely by checking whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage, with no validation of the token's structure, signature, or expiration, and no server round-trip. An attacker with access to the browser (or via any injected script, e.g. from the stored-XSS finding above) can set an arbitrary non-empty value under localStorage['token'] via devtools/console and cause isLoggedIn() to return truthy, flipping any UI logic in the associated template that gates review-authoring controls or other functionality on this method. This is a client-controlled identity signal being treated as an authentication/authorization decision; it establishes both a broken function-level check (UI elements gated by unverifiable client state) and an authentication weakness (identity/session state decided from unverified client storage rather than a verified token).

title: No client-side or design-level control preventing repeated/duplicate 'like' actions on a review
description: likeReview() fires productReviewService.like(review._id) every time it is invoked, with no check for whether the current user has already liked this review, no debouncing, and no rate limiting on repeated clicks. If the backend does not independently enforce one-like-per-user-per-review (which cannot be confirmed from this file), a user can call this repeatedly (e.g., by scripting rapid calls or holding down the UI action) to arbitrarily inflate a review's like count, an economic/reputation-integrity imbalance the design here does nothing to prevent. Even setting aside server-side enforcement, the design leaves the like operation entirely unthrottled from the client, and a scripted/automated caller reaching the like() sink could trigger unbounded repeated calls with no cool-down.

title: Security-relevant failures are only logged to the browser console, never reported to a backend monitoring system
description: The spec explicitly asserts that when UserService.whoAmI() fails (line 123-129) or ProductReviewService.create() fails (line 131-143), the component's error handling calls console.log(error) and nothing else. This confirms the production component's behavior: authentication/identity lookup failures and failed review-submission attempts (both security-relevant events — one is an auth-adjacent failure, the other a failed write operation) are surfaced only to the end user's local browser console. There is no call to any telemetry, error-reporting, or backend logging service visible from these tests. As a result, an operator/security team has no way to detect patterns of failure (e.g., repeated whoAmI failures indicating session/token issues, or repeated review-post failures potentially indicating abuse or backend errors) because the only record of the event exists in the individual user's browser, which the server-side team can never see. This is a textbook absence of security logging/monitoring for events that should be reported to a central system. The same console-only pattern is independently re-confirmed for the review-creation failure path (lines 133-141), showing this is the component's consistent, deliberate error-handling design rather than an isolated oversight.

title: Free-form review text is submitted verbatim with no client-side sanitization before persistence
description: Multiple tests (e.g. lines 99-106, 113-121, 137-141, 151-156) show that whatever raw string is placed into the review textarea's `.value` (user-controlled input) is passed unmodified as the `message` property of the object handed to `ProductReviewService.create()`. No encoding, stripping, or allow-listing of the textarea content is performed by the component before the request is dispatched — the test only checks that the exact string 'Great product!' is forwarded unchanged, and the assertions on the call's arguments (id and payload shape) confirm the value is passed through the submit handler with no intervening transformation step. Since this is a review 'message' field that will be persisted server-side and later re-rendered to other users viewing the product page (the review list, exercised elsewhere in this same spec via productReviewService.get), any HTML/script content typed here would flow through unsanitized at the point of submission. This file establishes the persistence-point half of a potential stored XSS: user text goes straight from the DOM input into the outbound create() call without any sanitizing transformation. The actual encoding (if any) occurs either in ProductReviewService, on the backend, or in whatever component renders review.message later — none of which are visible in this file, so this cannot be confirmed complete or ruled a false positive from here alone.

title: Review edit resource ID trusted from client-supplied dialog data with no ownership check
description: The component receives reviewData (including the review's _id) via Angular's MAT_DIALOG_DATA injection token, which is populated by whatever calling component opened this dialog. The editReview() method then submits a patch request using this._id id directly to the backend (productReviewService.patch) without this component performing, or being able to verify, any check that the currently authenticated user actually owns the review being edited. The component simply trusts that the ID it was handed corresponds to a review the current user is allowed to modify. If the parent component (or any code path that opens this dialog) can be induced to supply an arbitrary review _id — e.g., via manipulated UI state, a modified API response, or a compromised parent component — this component will happily submit an edit request for a review belonging to another user, relying entirely on an unseen server-side check to reject it. Because the authorization boundary the design depends on (server-side ownership validation on PUT/PATCH review-by-id) is not visible from this file, and this component performs zero defense-in-depth validation of its own, this is a trust-assumption violation typical of BOLA-enabling client design.

This value is taken directly from user input and sent verbatim to the backend via productReviewService.patch() in editReview(). Per standard guidance for persisted user text, the defect should be reported at the persistence point since the rendering sink lives in a different file/component not visible here. Length caps and required/minLength validators are input constraints, not sanitizers, and do not prevent HTML/script content from being submitted and stored.

This is an uncontrolled/verbose client-side logging of security-relevant failure data rather than a structured, minimized log entry. The two lines are directly consecutive in the error callback, so there is no intermediate transformation of the error value before it is logged.

title: Basket operations trust a client-controlled basket ID (bid) from sessionStorage, enabling BOLA on another user's basket
description: When a logged-in user adds a product to the basket, the component reads the target basket's identifier directly from `sessionStorage.getItem('bid')` and uses it both to look up the basket (line 71) and to construct the payload sent to the server when creating a new basket item (line 137, inside the `.save(...)` call at lines 134-139). sessionStorage is fully attacker/user controllable via browser devtools or a script, so a logged-in attacker can simply overwrite the 'bid' value with another user's basket ID. The subsequent `basketService.find(...)`, `basketService.get(...)`, `basketService.put(...)`, and `basketService.save(...)` calls all operate on whatever basket ID is supplied, with no ownership check performed in this file before the requests are issued (and, given the values are the sole identifiers sent for these operations, the server-side handler in Juice Shop's basket API is only prompted with this attacker-suppliable ID). This is the classic Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) pattern: the client is trusted to supply the resource identifier for a resource it does not necessarily own, and this component's design does not derive the basket ID from any server-verified session state, only client-stored data. An attacker who can view or guess another user's basket ID can view its contents (line 72-73), modify existing item quantities (line 84), or add products directly into someone else's basket (line 135-139).

title: Basket identity trusted from client-controlled sessionStorage ('bid') with no visible per-user ownership check
description: The spec repeatedly seeds sessionStorage with a basket id ('bid') immediately before invoking component.addToBasket(...), e.g. sessionStorage.setItem('bid', '4711') followed by component.addToBasket(1). This reveals that the production ProductComponent (not visible in this file) resolves which basket to read/mutate from a value stored in client-side sessionStorage rather than from a server-derived, session-bound identifier. The subsequent assertions confirm the full path: basketService.find is invoked (implicitly keyed on the sessionStorage-derived context) to look up the basket, productService.get is invoked to resolve the product being added, and basketService.save is invoked to persist a new basket item — all without any test ever exercising or requiring a check that the resolved basket id belongs to the currently authenticated user. If the actual component simply forwards this client-supplied 'bid' to the backend basket endpoints, an attacker can overwrite the sessionStorage value with another user's basket id and add/update items in someone else's basket (BOLA), and the design itself never establishes a rule that the server must re-derive the basket id from the authenticated session rather than accepting the client's value. Because the real sink (the component's addToBasket implementation and the BasketService HTTP calls) lies outside this file, this is reported at the boundary where the spec demonstrates the client-controlled input feeding basket lookup and mutation calls.

component.addToBasket(1) is invoked; the production implementation (not present in this file) is expected to use the sessionStorage 'bid' value to locate the basket via basketService.find, without any ownership verification visible in the test expectations.

basketService.save is asserted to have been called, confirming the basket mutation proceeds using the client-supplied 'bid' with no test coverage of an ownership/ownership-mismatch rejection path.

title: Failed basket/product operations are only surfaced via client-side console.log, with no server-side security audit trail
description: Multiple tests in this file assert that when basketService.find, basketService.get, basketService.put, basketService.save, or productService.get fail, the sole observable handling behavior is a call to console.log with the raw error (e.g. expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')). Tracing one representative case end to end: the failure is injected into basketService.find, a basket-id context is established via sessionStorage exactly as in the normal-path tests, the console.log spy is installed to observe the component's error handler, the component method is invoked to actually trigger that handler, and the resulting assertion shows the handler's only action is a console.log call. This confirms the production component's error-handling design: failures during basket operations — including failures that could indicate abuse such as repeated failed attempts to access/modify a basket a user does not own — are logged only to the end-user's local browser console and are never reported, forwarded, or logged to any backend/security-monitoring mechanism. There is no evidence in any of these test cases of a security event log, correlation id, or alerting path being exercised. Because browser console output is neither centrally collected nor monitored, an operator has no way to detect brute-forced basket ids, repeated authorization failures, or anomalous add-to-basket activity from this code path.

title: Security-relevant basket errors are logged only to the browser console, never surfaced to a monitoring/alerting system
description: The spec repeatedly confirms that when BasketService calls fail (find(), del(), get(), put()) the component's only response is a console.log(errorMessage) call — no server-side audit trail, no alerting, and no user-visible error state is asserted. Six separate tests (lines 122-127, 201-206, 225-230, 240-246, 248-255, 283-289, 291-298) mock console.log and assert it was called with the raw error, confirming this is the sole error-handling path implemented in the component under test. Failed basket loads, failed quantity mutations, and failed deletions are all security/business relevant events (e.g., could indicate broken authorization, tampering attempts, or backend rejection of an operation) but leave no trace anywhere the operations team could review, and repeated failures (e.g., automated probing of basket item IDs) would never trigger any alert.

Test asserts `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')` — confirming the component's error handling terminates at a client-side console.log with no server-side logging, alerting, or audit record.

title: Authentication state derived solely from presence of a client-readable localStorage token
description: The test harness establishes 'authenticated' behavior purely by writing a token value into localStorage (`localStorage.setItem('token', 'token')`) and 'unauthenticated/guest' behavior purely by removing that key (`localStorage.removeItem('token')`). The component under test (per lines 129-137) branches its entire behavior — whether to call userService.whoAmI at all, whether to use the authenticated basket vs. the guest basket — based only on whether this key exists in localStorage, not on any validation of the token's authenticity or expiry from within the component. This mirrors a known weak session-management pattern: bearer tokens held in localStorage are readable by any script (XSS-exploitable, unlike httpOnly cookies), and client-side code trusts mere key presence to decide the user's authentication tier for UI/data-fetching purposes.

A separate test removes the same localStorage key to simulate a guest; component.ngOnInit() is then called and its behavior changes based purely on key presence.
TestBed.createComponent constructs the component while the localStorage token is present, priming the component's construction-time state.

title: Basket item mutation methods accept caller-supplied numeric IDs with no visible ownership scoping
description: component.delete(id), component.inc(id) and component.dec(id) are exercised throughout the spec purely with arbitrary numeric literals (e.g., delete(1), inc(1), dec(1), delete(42)) and directly forward that ID to basketService.del/get/put without any assertion that the ID is checked against the current user's own basket contents before the mutating call is dispatched. If the backing BasketService/API does not itself re-verify basket-item ownership server-side (not visible from this file), a logged-in user could invoke inc()/dec()/delete() with another user's basket-item ID and have the request dispatched unconditionally by the client, which is the classic BOLA precondition (client performs no per-resource ownership check before calling the mutating operation).

component.inc(1) is shown forwarding the id straight into basketService.get(1) and basketService.put(1, {quantity}) with no intervening ownership check asserted anywhere in the surrounding test.
A second test seeds basketService.find so a BasketItem with id 1 is treated as the 'current' item, establishing the id that subsequent mutation calls will target.

Assertion confirms basketService.get was called with the raw id unchanged — the id flows straight through the component with no ownership check applied anywhere in the traced path.
basketService.put is called with (id, {quantity}) to perform the mutating write, completing the id-driven request dispatch with no ownership verification anywhere in the traced path.

Assertion confirms basketService.del was called with the raw id (1) directly, evidencing the component performs the mutating call without any client-side verification that the id belongs to the current user's basket.

title: Negative/tampered basket quantities are silently corrected client-side rather than rejected, indicating the invariant is not enforced upstream
description: Two tests (lines 308-315 and 317-324) show that when basketService.get() returns a BasketItem with a negative quantity (-100), component.dec()/inc() simply clamp the outgoing value to 1 and proceed with the update. This demonstrates the application's data model permits basket item quantities to reach invalid/negative states in the first place (otherwise there would be nothing to correct), and that the client component is the layer papering over that invariant violation rather than the value being validated/rejected at its source. Because the quantity used server-side ultimately comes from a client-controlled request (put(id, {quantity})), an attacker bypassing this UI path (e.g., calling the underlying API directly) could submit arbitrary negative or unbounded quantities without a corresponding invariant enforced by this component or, as far as can be seen here, elsewhere.

title: Basket identifier read from client-controlled sessionStorage enables BOLA on basket contents and mutations
description: The component determines which basket to load, and which basket item ids are subsequently deleted or quantity-modified, entirely from the client-controlled sessionStorage value 'bid'. load() calls basketService.find(parseInt(sessionStorage.getItem('bid'), 10)) with no server-side ownership re-derivation visible in this file, then populates dataSource with the returned basket's products. The row-level id values coming from that basket are then passed straight through to delete(id) and addToQuantity(id, value), which invoke basketService.del(id), basketService.get(id) and basketService.put(id, ...) i.e. mutating operations keyed purely by an id sourced from client state. Because sessionStorage is fully writable by the browser/user (e.g. via devtools or a script), an attacker can overwrite 'bid' with another user's basket id. If the backing API (outside this file) does not independently verify that the authenticated caller owns the requested basket id, this yields Broken Object Level Authorization: the victim's basket contents can be viewed, its items can be deleted, or quantities can be changed, all driven by values this file trusts without any ownership check. The authorization decision is delegated entirely to a value this file never validates.

The returned basket's Products (potentially belonging to another user if 'bid' was tampered with) are assigned directly to dataSource and rendered/operated on.

The subscribe next handler receives the basket object returned for the (possibly attacker-substituted) bid, beginning to process it as if it were the current user's own basket.

The guest-vs-authenticated branch check lets execution continue to the real deletion call for any authenticated session, regardless of whether the id actually belongs to that session's basket.

The guest-vs-authenticated branch check lets execution continue to the real quantity-update path for any authenticated session using the untrusted id.

The subscribe next handler receives the basketItem for the untrusted id and proceeds to compute an updated quantity for it.

title: Deluxe pricing entitlement determined and applied entirely on the client
description: Whether a basket item is charged at the discounted 'deluxePrice' versus the normal price is decided purely client-side by this.isDeluxe() (backed by DeluxeGuard, whose state ultimately derives from client-held token/claim data). In both load() and loadGuestBasket(), if isDeluxe() returns true the component overwrites product.price with product.deluxePrice before computing itemTotal and bonus, which are then emitted to the parent component via sendToParent()/emitTotal. The server-authoritative price is never re-derived here; the price used for the displayed (and potentially checkout-bound) total is a value this file itself substitutes based on a client-evaluated boolean. If the guard's deluxe determination can be influenced by client-held state (a token claim, local flag, or similar) without a corresponding server-side re-validation at the point of purchase, an attacker can obtain deluxe pricing without actually holding deluxe status - a trust-boundary violation where the client, not the server, decides an economically significant price outcome.

The client-computed itemTotal/bonus (derived from the client-decided price) is emitted to the parent component via emitTotal, presumably feeding downstream checkout/total display without independent server verification visible in this file.

title: Guest basket load issues unbounded parallel product requests driven by client-controlled storage
description: loadGuestBasket() maps every item in the guest basket (sourced from basketService.getGuestBasketItems(), which is backed by client-writable local storage) into an individual productService.get() HTTP call, then fires all of them concurrently via forkJoin. There is no cap on the number of guest basket items processed this way. Because the guest basket contents are entirely client-controlled, a user (or a script acting on their behalf) can inflate the guest basket with a very large number of distinct product ids, causing this component to issue a correspondingly large burst of concurrent requests to the backend product endpoint every time the basket view loads, with no batching, pagination, or throttling control in this file.

Every guest basket item is mapped to its own productService.get() call with no batching or cap on the number of items processed.
Each item triggers its own productService.get(item.ProductId) call, so the number of outbound requests scales linearly and unboundedly with the attacker-controlled guest basket size.
Each request's result is piped through map() to pair the product with its quantity, continuing to process every item regardless of how many there are.
catchError absorbs individual request failures without aborting or throttling the overall batch, allowing the full unbounded set of requests to proceed.
guestProductRequests is finalized as an array whose length is exactly the unbounded, client-controlled item count.
forkJoin fires all generated product requests concurrently with no throttling, so an inflated guest basket produces an unbounded burst of simultaneous outbound requests.

title: Full home address exposed in unredacted, shareable QR code
description: QrCodeComponent renders a QR code (via NgQrCodeComponent) directly from data injected through Angular's MAT_DIALOG_DATA token. The component copies dialogData.address (and dialogData.data/url/title) verbatim into this.address/this.data/this.url/this.title with no masking, truncation, or consent step before encoding it into a scannable QR image. In the Juice Shop application this dialog is used to let a user share/display their delivery address as a QR code. Because the design never establishes a rule that PII fields must be redacted or partially masked before being rendered into a machine-readable, easily-photographed/scanned artifact, any legitimate use of this feature (e.g. showing the code on a shared screen, in a screenshot, or on a printed receipt) trivially leaks the user's full street address, city, and other profile data to anyone who can view or scan the code. This is a design gap: the component that is supposed to let a user share a limited piece of information (e.g., an order reference) instead has no mechanism to prevent full PII disclosure, and no calling code visible here performs redaction either. The caller/opener of this dialog is outside this file, so the exact data source cannot be fully confirmed, but the component as designed places no compensating control on sensitive-data exposure at the point where it is rendered.

NgQrCodeComponent (imported and used in the component's template) renders the unredacted address/data as a scannable QR code image, exposing full PII to anyone who views, screenshots, or scans it.

title: Unvalidated trust in dialog-injected data used for rendering
description: The component blindly trusts whatever object is provided via MAT_DIALOG_DATA (title, url, address, data) with no runtime validation or sanitization before assigning to strongly-typed fields (declared with definite-assignment assertions '!'). The design never establishes that the caller must supply validated/sanitized content; any component or route that opens this dialog can pass arbitrary data (including sensitive fields or unexpected content) which is rendered without checks. While the immediate rendering sink is a third-party QR library rather than raw HTML, the lack of any contract or validation on dialogData is a trust-boundary violation: the component assumes the caller has already validated and scoped the data appropriately, which is not enforced anywhere in this file.

title, url, address, data fields are copied from dialogData without any validation, type-guarding, or sanitization in ngOnInit.
Unvalidated data field is stored and subsequently bound into the template for QR generation/display.

title: Global HTMLCanvasElement.prototype monkey-patch applied without teardown
description: At module load time (outside any beforeEach/afterEach lifecycle hook) this spec file permanently overwrites HTMLCanvasElement.prototype.getContext with a stub that returns fake 2D context methods for any '2d' request (lines 16-48). Because this mutation happens as a top-level side effect of importing the spec file rather than being scoped to this test suite and reverted afterward (no afterAll/afterEach restoring originalGetContext), it silently persists for the remainder of the test process. The patched getContext is then actively exercised when the fixture is created and change detection runs (lines 72-74), causing the ng-qrcode child component to render against fully faked canvas primitives. Because the describe block ends (line 85) with no afterAll call restoring HTMLCanvasElement.prototype.getContext = originalGetContext, the stub remains installed globally for any other spec file executed afterward in the same worker/process. Any such spec will transparently receive fake, no-op canvas operations (fillRect, drawImage, getImageData, etc. all become vi.fn() stubs) instead of real jsdom/canvas behavior. This is a design flaw in the test harness: a control meant to be local to one component's tests is installed globally with no scoping and no cleanup, which can mask real bugs or security-relevant rendering behavior (e.g., canvas-based fingerprinting/data leakage tests, or QR code content validation) in unrelated test suites, undermining the reliability of the test suite as a detection mechanism.

title: Dialog-supplied data (url/address/data) bound to component with no sanitization or validation exercised in tests
description: The test configures MAT_DIALOG_DATA as a provider with attacker-shaped fields ('data', 'url', 'address', 'title') and simply asserts that QrCodeComponent exposes these values verbatim after ngOnInit() (lines 65, 79-84). There is no test coverage validating that url/address values are checked for dangerous schemes (e.g., javascript:, data:) or otherwise sanitized before being used by the component (e.g., rendered as a clickable link, encoded into the QR image, or interpolated into the DOM). Since MAT_DIALOG_DATA in the real application flow originates from whichever caller opens this dialog (a boundary this spec file cannot see but which is outside this file), the tests establish that the component's contract is 'trust and pass through' rather than 'validate and constrain'. The data flows unchanged through component instantiation, an implicit Angular lifecycle pass triggered by detectChanges, and an explicit second ngOnInit() call, and is asserted field-by-field to be identical to the raw input at every step, with none of those assertions checking for encoding, escaping, or scheme restriction. If the underlying component (qr-code.component.ts) mirrors this test's assumption and does not itself validate the address/url fields, arbitrary values supplied by the dialog opener are surfaced without a re-derivation/validation step, which is the trust-boundary violation pattern this playbook flags as insecure design. This finding is speculative regarding the component implementation, which is not visible in this file.

title: Flat, unordered role constants provide no centralized privilege hierarchy
description: This file is the single source of truth for the application's role identifiers (customer, deluxe, accounting, admin), but it defines them as an unordered, flat map of string-to-itself with no notion of hierarchy, precedence, or numeric privilege level. Because the design never establishes an ordering between roles (e.g., admin > accounting > deluxe > customer), every consumer of this module is forced to independently implement its own ad-hoc authorization logic (typically string equality checks like `role === roles.admin`) rather than relying on a centrally enforced privilege comparison. This is a design gap rather than an implementation bug in any single call site: the file that is supposed to be the authoritative definition of the authorization model does not encode the relationships between roles that the rest of the application presumably depends on (e.g., 'admin can do everything a customer can', or 'accounting is a distinct, non-hierarchical role that should not inherit admin rights'). Without that central definition, it becomes easy for a downstream check to be written incorrectly (e.g., checking for the wrong exact string, forgetting to include a role in an allow-list, or accidentally treating unrelated roles as ordered) and there is no code in this file that would catch such a mistake. I cannot see the consumers of this constant from this file alone, so I cannot confirm a concrete bypass, but the absence of any enforced structure is a design-level gap in the file whose entire purpose is to define the authorization model.

The roles object is finalized and exported without any hierarchy, level, or centralized comparison helper, forcing all authorization decisions elsewhere in the codebase to be implemented ad hoc against these raw string constants.

title: Weak password policy validated by RegisterComponent allows trivially guessable credentials
description: The spec exercises RegisterComponent's password validators and confirms the only enforced rules are a minimum length of 5 and a maximum length of 20 characters — there is no requirement for character-class complexity (uppercase, digit, symbol). A 5-character all-lowercase string ('aaaaa') is accepted as valid (lines 112-113), and this exact class of weak, single-case value is then shown to be the live registration credential submitted end-to-end: the form is populated with the plaintext password 'password' (lines 151-152), assembled into the outgoing user object (line 155), submitted via component.save() (line 157), and finally asserted to have been forwarded verbatim, in plaintext, to userService.save() (line 159). This confirms the registration workflow's server-facing contract accepts low-entropy passwords by design and forwards them unmodified, which materially weakens resistance to credential stuffing / brute-force attacks against the resulting account (crypto-auth), and reflects a design that never establishes a stronger credential policy anywhere along this path (insecure-design).

title: Backend errors during registration flow are only logged to the client-side console, with no security event logging
description: Two tests confirm that RegisterComponent's error handling for failed operations — fetching security questions (ngOnInit) and saving a new user (save()) — routes the raw error value straight to console.log rather than to any structured security/audit logging mechanism. When securityQuestionService.find() throws 'Error', console.log is called with that raw value (lines 179-184); when userService.save() throws 'Error', the same pattern occurs (lines 186-191). This means failed registration attempts and failed security-question retrievals — which are security-relevant events (e.g., repeated failed sign-ups, potential enumeration probing, or backend errors that may carry internal detail) — are only visible in the end user's own browser console. There is no evidence of these events being sent to any server-side monitoring, alerting, or audit trail, and any structured error detail beyond the string constant used in tests would be exposed client-side rather than captured for incident investigation.

title: Non-atomic two-step registration (user creation + security-answer save) with no demonstrated rollback on partial failure
description: The successful-registration test shows RegisterComponent performing two independent, sequential backend writes: first userService.save(user) to create the account (mocked at line 147 to return an object containing the new id), then securityAnswerService.save(securityAnswerObject) using that UserId (mocked at line 148, expected object built at line 156). component.save() (line 157) drives both calls asynchronously (awaited at line 158), and the test separately asserts each call's arguments (lines 159 and 160) without any code path shown that ties the second write's success to the first, or that compensates/rolls back the created user if the second write fails. The only failure-path test exercised elsewhere in the file (lines 186-191) covers failure of the first call (userService.save) alone; there is no test or visible handling for the case where user creation succeeds but the subsequent security-answer save fails. In that scenario the design would leave a fully created user account with no security-question answer on record, undermining any downstream flow (e.g., password-reset via security question) that assumes every registered account has an associated answer — a workflow/state-consistency gap the design never closes.

title: Client-supplied UserId propagated to Recycle create request (potential mass assignment / IDOR)
description: The RecycleComponent builds the payload sent to RecycleService.save() (and ultimately POST /api/Recycles, whose handler lives outside this file) by embedding a UserId field that is populated purely from a prior client-side call to UserService.whoAmI(). The spec tests explicitly assert that the object handed to recycleService.save() contains a 'UserId' property (e.g. `{ UserId: undefined, AddressId: '1', quantity: 100 }` and `{ UserId: 42, ... }`), confirming that the client — not the server — determines and transmits the UserId value as part of the create request body. If the backend /api/Recycles handler persists this client-supplied UserId field directly (a common Juice-Shop-style mass-assignment pattern) rather than re-deriving the owning user from the authenticated session, an attacker can tamper with the outgoing request to set an arbitrary UserId, creating recycle records attributed to another user (an IDOR / broken object property level authorization). This file cannot confirm server-side enforcement since the route handler is in server.ts, but it demonstrates the client design trusts and forwards a sensitive ownership field.

title: Recycle submission workflow proceeds without verifying authenticated user
description: The save() workflow tested here does not appear to block submission when the current user cannot be identified. In the test 'should display pickup message and reset recycle form on saving', userService.whoAmI() is mocked to return an empty object (no id), yet component.save() still successfully calls recycleService.save() with a payload where UserId is undefined. This indicates the client-side design never gates the recycle creation action on successful identification/authentication of the user — the workflow trusts that the recycle request is legitimate regardless of whether an id was resolved. If the corresponding server-side endpoint (POST /api/Recycles, outside this file) does not independently enforce authentication before persisting the exposed request, an unauthenticated or session-less actor could submit recycle records, and — combined with the mass-assignment concern above — potentially assign them to an arbitrary UserId.

title: Security-relevant API/authentication failures only logged to browser console, no monitoring pathway
description: Tests 'should hold nothing on error from backend API' and 'should log the error on retrieving the user' confirm that when RecycleService.find() or UserService.whoAmI() (an identity-resolution call) fail, the component's ngOnInit() error handler does nothing more than call console.log(err) with the raw error value. There is no evidence in this file of the error being sent to any centralized logging/monitoring/alerting service, nor of any distinguishing context (user id, timestamp, correlation id) being attached. A failure of the whoAmI() identity check is a security-relevant event (it may indicate an authentication/session problem or an attack against the identity endpoint) and swallowing it into a client-only console.log means such failures are invisible to any server-side security monitoring, preventing detection or investigation of repeated failures (e.g., a brute-force or session-tampering pattern).

title: Weak client-defined password policy permits low-entropy passwords
description: The password FormControl only enforces a minimum length of 5 characters (Validators.minLength(5)) with no complexity requirements (no uppercase/lowercase/number/symbol mix enforced). This weak-policy value is picked up unchanged when save() is invoked, copied into the outgoing registration payload, and submitted to the backend via userService.save(user). A minimum length of 5 with no complexity checks makes accounts trivially vulnerable to offline/online brute-force and dictionary attacks once any credential list or password spraying is attempted against the login endpoint. Because this is the only visible password-strength gate in the registration flow, and it is far weaker than industry guidance (NIST recommends >=8, ideally longer, with breach-list checking), it establishes a real authentication weakness at account-creation time.

title: Account recovery relies on a single, user-chosen, plaintext-submitted security question/answer
description: During registration this component collects a security question selection and a free-text answer, using only a required-field validator on each, and submits them to securityAnswerService.save() to be tied to the new account as its account-recovery credential. There is no complexity/entropy requirement on the answer, the question set is a small predefined list typically containing commonly-guessable prompts, and only a single factor is required — no secondary verification step is ever constructed in this flow. The value passes from the two form controls, through save()'s payload assembly, into the initial registration call, and then — once the account is created and its id returned — into a second call that persists the answer keyed to that new UserId. Because this is registered as the primary recovery mechanism, an attacker who can guess or brute-force the low-entropy answer can leverage the recovery flow elsewhere in the app to take over the account. This is a design weakness in how the identity/recovery credential is established, and it changes who the application later believes is authorized to reset the password, making it also an authentication-outcome issue.

title: Server error responses logged to console without redaction

If the backend error payload includes stack traces, internal messages, or other diagnostic detail (common in Express/Node backends during misconfiguration or unhandled exceptions), that detail is dumped unredacted to the browser console at two separate points in this file. While this is client-side (visible to the user of that browser rather than a third party), it still represents logging of potentially sensitive/internal diagnostic data without any filtering, and can aid an attacker inspecting their own browser session to fingerprint backend internals during a registration-abuse attempt.

title: No client-side throttling/debounce on registration submission
description: save() performs no check to prevent it from being invoked repeatedly in rapid succession (e.g., no in-flight guard flag, no button-disable state tracked in this component, no debounce). Each invocation rebuilds the request payload and unconditionally fires a call to userService.save(user); on success, the callback chains a second unconditional network call to securityAnswerService.save(). Combined with the absence of any visible CAPTCHA or rate-limit awareness in this file, a scripted caller (or a user rapidly re-triggering the handler) could fire many paired registration/recovery-credential requests in quick succession, contributing to automated account-creation abuse if the backend does not independently enforce a limit. This is a resource-consumption gap at the client entrypoint that funnels straight into two chained backend write calls with no local mitigation.

title: Saved payment methods component renders child list with no visible ownership/authorization gating
description: This component is a thin wrapper that unconditionally renders PaymentMethodComponent (imported at line 7, used at line 14) with no input bindings, guards, or authorization checks of its own. The component class itself (lines 17-18) is empty — it does not verify that the currently authenticated user is the owner of the payment methods being displayed, does not receive or validate a user/account identifier, and delegates entirely to the child component and/or an out-of-file data service for what data gets shown. The @Component decorator (starting line 10) wires together a templateUrl (line 12) that presumably contains the markup invoking the child component, and an imports array (line 14) that registers PaymentMethodComponent as a standalone dependency — at no point in this configuration is any ownership, session, or account-scoping check introduced before the child is allowed to render. If the child component or its backing service trusts a client-supplied or route-supplied identifier to fetch payment methods (a common IDOR pattern in this codebase's sibling components), this component provides no compensating control to prevent one user's saved payment methods (e.g., truncated card numbers, cardholder names) from being rendered when another user's session or a manipulated identifier reaches it. Because the actual data-fetching and authorization logic live outside this file (likely in PaymentMethodComponent or a payment method service/API), this is reported as a design gap visible at the point where this file composes the view without asserting or enforcing any ownership check.

Because payment-method handling is a security-sensitive workflow (PCI-relevant data), the absence of any behavioral or negative test coverage means regressions that leak full card numbers into the DOM, into snackbar notifications (which are mocked here and never asserted against for content), or into console/log output would not be caught by this suite. This is a design/process gap: the test harness establishes no compensating control (assertion) to guarantee sensitive data never appears in rendered output or notification/log sinks, so an implementation change that violates that expectation would ship silently.

title: Client-controlled ownership fields (AddressId/UserId) sent unvalidated in recycle request
description: The recycle request object is built almost entirely from client-side state and then submitted verbatim to the backend. The AddressId comes from getMessage(id), a setter invoked by a child component (AddressComponent, outside this file) with no verification that the selected address actually belongs to the current user. The UserId is populated from a whoAmI() response (after the recycle object is reset to {}) but remains a plain, freely-editable field inside the 'recycle' object. When save() runs, it never checks the validity of the underlying form controls, blends in the previously-stored addressId, quantity, and optional pickup fields, and hands the whole object to recycleService.save() to be POSTed. Because this file performs no server-side re-derivation or ownership check at any point along this path, and simply trusts whatever identifier reaches getMessage() or whoAmI(), an attacker able to manipulate the outgoing request (e.g., via browser devtools or an intercepting proxy) can submit a recycling request tied to another user's address or identity. Whether the backend re-validates ownership of AddressId/UserId cannot be confirmed from this file, but the client establishes no defense-in-depth against it -- the classic 'client controls something the server should validate' pattern.

If the backend does not independently re-enforce these bounds (not visible from this file), an attacker could submit recycling requests with quantities outside the intended range, potentially abusing any reward/points logic tied to recycling volume.

title: Challenge description rendered as raw HTML (innerHTML) without visible sanitization/escaping
description: The spec asserts that when a challenge's `description` field is set to the literal string 'boom', the rendered DOM element with class `.description-row` has an `innerHTML` that *contains* the raw markup 'boom' (line 242). If Angular's default text interpolation (`{{ description }}`) were used, the resulting `innerHTML` of the host element would contain the HTML-entity-encoded form ('<b>boom</b>'), not literal tags. The fact that the test expects literal `` tags in the rendered innerHTML strongly implies the component template binds the challenge description via an `[innerHTML]` property binding (or similar raw-HTML insertion) rather than safe text interpolation. The `challenge` input, including its `description` field, is set directly from external/API data in production (challenges are created/fetched via `/api/Challenges` per the architecture map, and this endpoint has historically been reachable without strict admin authorization in vulnerable Juice Shop configurations). If the description field is rendered via `[innerHTML]` without a defense-in-depth sanitizer/allow-list beyond Angular's default DomSanitizer, or if `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` is used in the component (not visible in this spec file, but consistent with the observed rendering behavior), attacker/admin-controlled challenge descriptions containing HTML/script-bearing markup could execute in the browsers of all users viewing the scoreboard — a stored XSS via improper output handling. The actual template/component source (challenge-card.component.html / .ts) is outside this file, but this spec file is the concrete evidence establishing that raw HTML insertion is the intended, tested behavior of the component rather than an accidental defect.

Assertion confirms `compiled.querySelector('.description-row')?.innerHTML` contains the literal, unescaped markup 'boom', evidencing that the template renders the description as raw HTML (an innerHTML-style sink) rather than through Angular's default auto-escaping text interpolation.

title: Runtime value of 'difficulty' input is never validated, relying solely on a compile-time TypeScript union type
description: The component declares `difficulty = input.required<1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6>()` (line 10). This union type constraint (1|2|3|4|5|6) exists only at compile time in TypeScript; Angular's `input.required()` API performs no runtime validation or clamping of the value that is actually bound to this input at render time. If the value flowing into this component originates from data that is not fully trusted or sanitized before reaching the template binding (e.g. a challenge/product difficulty value coming from an API response or other externally influenced source consumed elsewhere in the application), the component will accept and attempt to render whatever numeric (or other) value is passed, since the type restriction is not enforced by any guard, default, or fallback in this file. This is a trust-assumption gap: the design assumes the caller/backend will always supply a value in the 1-6 range and never re-derives or validates it here, so any out-of-range or malformed value passed by a compromised or buggy upstream caller will propagate directly into whatever template logic renders the stars, with no defensive check in this component.

title: Unvalidated difficulty value causes lookup-table crash (client-side DoS) in score aggregation
description: The static method calculateDifficultySummaries builds a fixed lookup table (INITIAL_SUMMARIES) that only defines entries for difficulty keys 1 through 6, while the DifficultySummary interface's `difficulty` field type explicitly permits the value 0 (`0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6`). The function then indexes directly into this lookup using the caller-supplied `challenge.difficulty` value from each element of the `allChallenges` input without any bounds/range validation: `summariesLookup[challenge.difficulty].availableChallenges += ...`. If any challenge object flowing into this component has a `difficulty` of 0, or any other value not present in INITIAL_SUMMARIES (e.g. due to a malformed/attacker-influenced challenge record created via an administrative or otherwise reachable challenge-creation flow, such as the application's `/api/Challenges` endpoint noted in the route table), `summariesLookup[challenge.difficulty]` evaluates to `undefined`, and the subsequent property access throws a TypeError. Because `difficultySummaries` is a computed signal used to render the score board, this uncaught exception breaks rendering of the entire score-board page for every user viewing it, not just for the entity that supplied the bad data. This is a trust-assumption violation: the component design assumes upstream data always conforms to the 1–6 range without ever re-validating or defensively defaulting for out-of-range/unexpected difficulty values, even though the type system it defines for itself explicitly allows 0.

difficultySummaries computed signal calls calculateDifficultySummaries with the raw, unvalidated allChallenges() array on every change.

title: Unsanitized challenge dependency data exposed to (out-of-file) template without validation
description: The component exposes getter methods (isDependencyMissing, getDependencyDocumentation, getDependency) that read free-form fields (dep.name, dep.documentation) directly from the `challenge` input, which is populated from backend challenge data (ultimately sourced from the /api/Challenges endpoint and related challenge-configuration ingestion). These string values are returned to the associated Angular template (challenge-card.component.html, not present in this file) with no sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing applied in this component. If the accompanying template binds getDependencyDocumentation(...) or similar challenge-derived strings via an unsafe binding (e.g. [innerHTML] or bypassSecurityTrust*) rather than relying on Angular's default text interpolation, any attacker-influenced content in a dependency's documentation/name field (or in challenge().description/hint text carried on the same challenge object) would execute as markup/script in the browser of every user viewing the scoreboard. This file is the point where the untrusted data is received and forwarded unsanitized; the actual render sink is outside this file so the presence of unsafe binding cannot be fully confirmed here, but no defensive encoding step exists in this component to prevent it if such a binding exists.

title: Unguarded mutation of shared default filter-settings reference corrupts global default state
description: resetCategoryFilter() assigns this.categories directly to the module-level constant array DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING.categories (line 56), which is imported at line 3 from a shared module, instead of cloning it. Because arrays are passed by reference, this.categories now points to the same array object backing the application-wide default filter configuration, and that same reference is immediately broadcast to any listener via categoriesChange.emit(this.categories) at line 57. When the user subsequently interacts with the filter, toggleCategorySelected(category) is invoked externally (line 38) with the shared array still bound to this.categories. It checks isCategorySelected(category) (line 39), which delegates to the includes() check at line 47-48 against the same shared array. When the category is not already present, the else branch at line 42 executes this.categories.push(category), mutating the shared DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING.categories array object in place. The mutated, now-permanently-altered array is then emitted again at line 44. Because this constant is imported from a shared module, all future component instances and subsequent resets inherit the corrupted default. This is a design flaw: the component's reset invariant ('go back to default state') is violated by relying on a mutable shared reference rather than deriving a fresh copy, e.g. via [...DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING.categories]. Impact is limited to score-board challenge filtering UI state, but it demonstrates a state-integrity design gap where a value assumed to be a stable default is in fact caller-mutable global state that persists corruption across the whole running application instance.

The if condition calls isCategorySelected(category) to decide whether to remove or add the category, routing execution to the push branch.

The corrupted, permanently-mutated categories array is emitted via categoriesChange and becomes the new 'default' for all subsequent resets and component instances sharing the module.

title: Score board trusts client-held 'solved' flags with no server re-validation in this rendering path
description: HackingChallengeProgressScoreCardComponent computes the count of solved hacking challenges purely by filtering the `allChallenges` input array on the client-held `challenge.solved` boolean (lines 15-17). The component performs no re-verification of this flag against any trusted source at render time — it simply trusts whatever object array is passed in via the Angular `input()` signal. Because this file is the terminal consumer of the data (it only renders a count), the security guarantee that 'solved' accurately reflects a validated, server-confirmed state depends entirely on upstream code outside this file. If any upstream path (e.g., a caching layer, a locally-modified store, or a compromised/parallel API response) supplies a manipulated `EnrichedChallenge[]` with `solved: true` entries, this component will display an inflated/incorrect progress score without any independent check. This is a design gap rather than an implementation bug: the component never establishes or enforces that the count it displays is authoritative — it is architected purely as a pass-through aggregator of caller-supplied state, and the resulting readonly `solvedChallenges` signal (finalized at line 17) is exposed directly for template consumption with no intervening trust check. Impact is limited to displayed/cosmetic integrity of the score board UI (assuming actual challenge completion is authoritatively tracked and enforced server-side elsewhere, which is outside this file and cannot be confirmed from here).

computed() derives solvedChallenges by filtering on challenge.solved without any check that the flag originates from a trusted/authoritative source.

The computed() call closes here, finalizing readonly solvedChallenges as a public class member; this is the terminal point in this file where the unverified, filter-derived count becomes the authoritative value exposed to the template/parent for display.

title: Local backup/restore of score-board state wired without confirmation guard or audit logging in dialog component
description: This component is the 'additional settings' dialog for the Score Board and injects LocalBackupService directly (line 14), making it available to the associated template (score-board-additional-settings-dialog.component.html, referenced via templateUrl at line 9), which is not part of this file and presumably binds buttons to LocalBackupService methods (e.g. export/import or restore of local application/progress state). The TypeScript class itself contains zero logic: no method wraps calls to localBackupService with a confirmation step, input validation of an imported backup, or any logging/telemetry call marking that a state-overwriting action was invoked. The DI mechanism (inject, imported at line 1) and the service type itself (imported at line 2) are pulled straight into the component and exposed as a bare public field with no intervening abstraction. The component's imports array (line 12) wires up only Material dialog/button/icon UI modules and translation support -- no interceptor, confirmation service, or logging service is included that could gate or observe calls made against localBackupService from the template. Because all safety and audit controls for a potentially destructive, irreversible action (overwriting local application state from an externally supplied backup file) would have to live entirely in the invisible template/service layer, the component as designed provides no defense-in-depth at this layer: if the template simply calls a restore/import method on click, a user (or a tampered backup file) can silently overwrite local state with no confirmation dialog logic present here and no record of the action being taken. This is reported at low-to-moderate confidence because the template and LocalBackupService implementation, where the actual guard or logging might exist, are outside this file and were not observed.

No wrapper method, confirmation guard, validation, or logging call exists in this component around use of localBackupService; any destructive action triggered from the template bypasses this layer entirely with no controls added here.

title: Tutorial-mode restriction appears to be enforced only as a client-side UI warning
description: The spec file exercises TutorialModeWarningComponent's tutorialModeActive() computed signal, which derives its state purely from client-supplied inputs: an 'applicationConfig' object (with challenges.restrictToTutorialsFirst) and an 'allChallenges' array (with tutorialOrder/solved flags) that are set directly via fixture.componentRef.setInput(...) in the test (lines 34-37, 47-49, 54-68). The tests confirm that this component's only observable behavior is to toggle a boolean that presumably drives a warning banner in the UI, based entirely on data handed to it as inputs. Nothing in this file (nor implied by its tests) shows any server-side re-validation preventing a user from solving challenges out of tutorial order — the component only decides whether to *display a warning*, not whether to *block* the action. If the broader application relies on this same restrictToTutorialsFirst/tutorialOrder logic (or a client-only equivalent) as the actual enforcement mechanism for the 'solve tutorial challenges first' workflow, rather than a UI hint layered on top of a server-side check, an attacker could bypass the intended step-ordering simply by not rendering/using this component (e.g., calling challenge-solving APIs directly), since the true business rule (workflow order) is only encoded/tested here as a client-visible warning condition and not as an authoritative, server-enforced gate. This file cannot show whether server-side enforcement exists elsewhere, so this is flagged as a design-trust concern rather than a confirmed bypass.

Test sets 'applicationConfig' input (challenges.restrictToTutorialsFirst) directly, another client-observable/configurable value driving the workflow decision.

defaultChallenges is constructed as plain test data with tutorialOrder and solved fields cast 'as any' (line 24), the same shape later fed straight into the component's input without any intermediate validation or server round-trip visible in this file.

fixture.detectChanges() triggers Angular change detection, causing the component's tutorialModeActive() computed signal to evaluate purely from the two inputs just set, with no external/server check interposed.

A second test re-sets applicationConfig.challenges.restrictToTutorialsFirst to false at will and re-derives tutorialModeActive() without any recomputation trigger beyond the input change, confirming the warning state is entirely a function of caller-supplied config with no independent enforcement path visible.

component.tutorialModeActive() is asserted to reflect only these client-supplied inputs; the test suite gives no evidence of any corresponding server-side enforcement of tutorial-first ordering, suggesting the control may be UI-only.

title: Insecure default filter setting exposes disabled challenges by default
description: The DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING constant sets showDisabledChallenges to true, meaning that by default the score board UI will display challenges that have been explicitly marked as disabled. Disabled challenges are typically hidden because they are incomplete, broken, contain sensitive hints/solutions under development, or are otherwise not meant to be visible to regular users. A permissive-by-default value here means every user who loads the score board (before any explicit user opt-in) is shown this normally-hidden content, rather than the safer default of hiding it until a user explicitly opts in. If any consumer of this filter setting relies on it as the sole gate for what disabled-challenge metadata gets rendered client-side (rather than the server independently withholding disabled-challenge data), this design choice becomes a direct information disclosure vector: the client trusts a default value of 'show everything' instead of failing closed. Even if there is a server-side check elsewhere, choosing an insecure default here is a design flaw — the file that defines the canonical default filter state opts to reveal rather than conceal by default, which is backwards from a security-by-default posture (deny/hide by default, allow/reveal by explicit action).

trace.description: DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING is the canonical default state consumed by the score-board component (outside this file) whenever no user-specific filter preference has been set or on first load.
The FilterSetting interface declares showDisabledChallenges as a boolean flag that controls whether disabled challenges are rendered in the challenge list.

showDisabledChallenges is defaulted to true, meaning disabled/hidden challenges are shown to the user by default rather than requiring an explicit opt-in, an insecure 'fail open' default for content visibility.

title: Tutorial-mode restriction relies entirely on client-supplied state (trust boundary violation)
description: The tutorialModeActive computed property determines whether the 'restrict to tutorials first' policy is currently being violated by reading applicationConfig() and allChallenges() - both Angular input() signals fed to this component from its parent (ultimately from client-side application state / REST responses already fetched into the browser). The component never re-verifies against a server-issued, tamper-proof indicator; it simply recomputes a boolean from data that lives entirely in client memory and can be freely altered (e.g., via Angular DevTools, a modified component input, or a crafted API response) before this getter runs. The computed() block (line 18) reads both signals; if the restrictToTutorialsFirst flag (line 19) is falsy, the guard short-circuits to false at line 20, meaning that simply flipping this single client-held boolean off disables the restriction entirely regardless of actual challenge-solve state. Otherwise, execution falls through to the return expression starting at line 22, which pulls the full allChallenges() array, filters it down to tutorial-order challenges at line 23, and finally evaluates every(challenge => challenge.solved) at line 24 - a predicate driven entirely by the client-supplied `solved` field on each challenge object. If this flag (or the underlying challenge.solved / tutorialOrder fields) is the mechanism by which the UI decides to gate access to non-tutorial challenges elsewhere in the score-board feature, an attacker can simply ensure the client-side data used here reports all tutorial challenges as solved (or the restriction flag as false), causing tutorialModeActive to evaluate to false and the restriction warning/gate to disappear - while the actual solve-state on the server is unaffected. This is a trust assumption violation: a restriction that the design should have the server authoritatively enforce is instead derived purely from data the client already possesses and controls at every step of this computation chain.
