applicationConfig is likewise an externally-supplied input signal carrying the restrictToTutorialsFirst policy flag, sourced from client-held configuration state.
The restriction check reads applicationConfig()?.challenges?.restrictToTutorialsFirst directly from the client-controlled signal with no server round-trip or signed/immutable indicator.
The computed() wrapper reads both client-controlled signals together to derive the security-relevant tutorialModeActive decision, with no server round-trip performed inside this evaluation.

If the client-held restrictToTutorialsFirst flag is falsy, the function returns false immediately — an attacker who can influence this single client-side boolean disables the whole restriction path with no server confirmation.
The array is filtered down to challenges with a non-null tutorialOrder, still entirely client-supplied challenge metadata.

The final security decision is made by .every(challenge => challenge.solved), negated to produce tutorialModeActive — a predicate computed purely from client-supplied challenge.solved flags with no server-side re-validation, so the restriction can be defeated by manipulating client-held challenge state.

tutorialModeActive is derived purely by filtering/every-checking client-supplied challenge.solved and challenge.tutorialOrder fields, producing the boolean that (if used elsewhere to gate UI access) can be trivially manipulated client-side to defeat the tutorial-first restriction.

title: Client-controlled visibility flag for disabled/hidden challenges (showDisabledChallenges)
description: The `fromQueryParams` function reads the `showDisabledChallenges` value straight from the URL query string and uses it, unvalidated and unauthenticated, to toggle whether disabled/hidden challenges are shown in the score board (`filterSetting.showDisabledChallenges = queryParams.showDisabledChallenges === 'true'`). There is no server-side or role check anywhere in this file that gates who may set this flag — any user can simply append `?showDisabledChallenges=true` to the score-board URL to flip the visibility of challenges that the application intends to keep hidden (e.g. challenges disabled via feature flags, unreleased content, or admin-only test challenges). Because the decision of what is 'visible' is made entirely on data the client supplies via a URL parameter rather than being derived/authorized by the server, this is a trust-assumption violation: the client determines an access-level-like property instead of the server. The concrete attack scenario is: an unauthenticated or low-privilege visitor edits the query string to include `showDisabledChallenges=true`, and the resulting FilterSetting causes normally-hidden challenge metadata to be rendered in the UI, potentially leaking information about challenges/features not yet meant to be exposed.

The presence of showDisabledChallenges in the URL is checked with no whitelist/role validation.

filterSetting is initialized as a clone of DEFAULT_FILTER_SETTING; this safe default is about to be overwritten by unvalidated client input for showDisabledChallenges with no intervening authorization check.

title: Unvalidated status and category/tag values accepted from query string into filter domain
description: fromQueryParams assigns `status`, `categories`, and `tags` directly from raw query-string values without validating them against the set of legal/expected values (e.g. an enum of known statuses such as 'solved'/'unsolved'). The design never establishes or enforces a bound on what these fields may contain before they become part of the application's FilterSetting state, which is subsequently likely used to filter/query challenge data (in a caller outside this file). Because the server (or downstream consumer) is expected to trust this client-derived filter state as if it were validated, arbitrary or malformed values can propagate into filtering logic used elsewhere in the SPA. While the direct blast radius from this file alone is limited to UI filtering, the pattern is a textbook 'trust assumption violation' — the client fully controls a value that should be constrained/validated by the code that consumes it, and no whitelist or type check exists in this file to bound it.

title: Client-side model exposes full hint text alongside unlock counters, suggesting entitlement is enforced client-side rather than server-side
description: The EnrichedChallenge interface, which models data received by the score board frontend from outside this file (presumably a REST response from the server), pairs a plain `hintText: string` field directly with `nextHint`, `hintsUnlocked`, and `hintsAvailable` numeric counters. This shape strongly suggests the design delivers the actual hint content to the browser as part of the challenge object and then relies on the client-side counters (`hintsUnlocked` vs. `hintsAvailable`) to decide whether to display it in the UI, rather than having the server withhold hint text until it has been legitimately unlocked (e.g., via hint-point purchase). If that is the case, the trust boundary is violated: the sensitive/spoiler data (hint text, and potentially `originalDescription`, which could reveal solution details) is already present in the client's Redux/Angular state and any network response, and can be read directly from browser memory or dev tools regardless of the `hintsUnlocked` counter's value. This is a design flaw because the mandatory 'unlock' workflow step (spending hint points) can be bypassed entirely without touching the counters at all — the data was never actually withheld. The concrete population/fetch logic that fills these fields lives outside this file, so this finding traces the shape of the trust boundary as expressed by the type; it cannot be fully confirmed without seeing the code that assigns these properties on the client or the corresponding server endpoint.

hintText is declared as a plain string field on the client model, implying the actual hint content is delivered to the browser regardless of unlock state.

originalDescription is carried on the same object as the hint fields, meaning the full challenge description (which may also embed solution hints) is delivered to the client alongside the hint payload, widening the same trust-boundary gap.

nextHint tracks which hint index is next to reveal, another client-held counter that, like hintsUnlocked, is only useful as a gate if the corresponding hintText is not already present in full — confirming the counters are meant to control display of data already delivered rather than to request it fresh from the server.

hintsUnlocked is a separate counter field used (presumably by UI components elsewhere) to gate display of hintText — a client-side enforcement point for what should be a server-enforced entitlement, since the data itself (line 5) is already present.

title: Visibility of environment-disabled challenges enforced only client-side
description: The scoreboard's disabled-challenge filter (filterSetting.showDisabledChallenges) is a pure client-side UI toggle over a challenges array that already contains the full EnrichedChallenge objects for challenges disabled in the current deployment environment (challenge.disabledEnv !== null). The design assumes the client can be trusted to hide these entries; nothing in this file (or apparently upstream, since the data must already be present in the array for the filter to operate on it) prevents an attacker from bypassing the UI filter, e.g. via browser devtools or directly inspecting/mutating the underlying component state, to view hint text, descriptions, tags and other metadata for challenges meant to stay hidden because required backend functionality is unavailable in this environment. Because the disclosure boundary ('this challenge should not be visible in this environment') is enforced purely as a rendering filter rather than at the point the data is fetched/served, the control can be trivially defeated by any client capable of running JavaScript in the page - a trust-assumption violation where the server should decide what disabled-environment challenge data reaches the client rather than relying on the client to filter it for display.

Visibility of the disabled challenge is gated solely by the client-supplied boolean filterSetting.showDisabledChallenges, a display-only control that can be bypassed by manipulating client-side state directly, exposing the already-loaded disabled challenge's metadata.

title: Tutorial-first workflow restriction is enforced only as a display filter with no server-side gate
description: The 'restrictToTutorialChallengesFirst' logic computes, purely in the client, whether a non-tutorial challenge should be shown in the scoreboard list based on the solved/difficulty state of tutorial challenges. This treats an ordering/workflow rule ('finish tutorial challenges before attempting others') as a pure UI/display concern with no corresponding server-side workflow enforcement visible from this file. Because the entire computation (which tutorial challenges exist, whether they are solved, and the current difficulty threshold) is derived from client-held data and used only to filter what's rendered, a user can trivially attempt any challenge outside of this intended progression by not relying on the scoreboard UI at all, or by altering the client-side filterSetting/challenges state feeding this computation. This is a workflow-bypass style design gap: the ordering constraint exists only as convenience/UX in this file and is not a real access control.

If restrictToTutorialChallengesFirst is falsy the check is skipped entirely; this client-supplied flag is the sole gate for whether the rule applies at all.

The decision to reveal a later-stage challenge in the list is based purely on this client-side computed threshold, with no corresponding requirement enforced elsewhere that tutorial challenges must actually be completed before other functionality can be exercised.

title: Component error handling only writes raw error to console.log with no monitoring/alerting
description: The spec at lines 139-144 asserts that when the HintService.put() call fails, the ScoreBoardComponent's unlockHint() error handler calls console.log(error) with the raw error value returned by the observable (in this test, the literal string 'Error'). This test reveals the actual error-handling design of the component: failures on a security-relevant operation (hint unlocking, which is gated by score/challenge state) are only written to the browser console and are not sent to any application-level logging/monitoring service, not surfaced to the user as a security event, and not rate-limited or alerted on. In a real deployment this means repeated failed hint-unlock attempts (e.g., an attacker probing the hint API) leave no server-side or centralized trace — only a client-side console.log that the operator never sees. Additionally, whatever error object/response the backend returns (which could include stack traces or internal details in a misconfigured backend) would be dumped straight to the browser console, which is a client-side sink visible to anyone with dev tools open, rather than being sanitized before display.

HintService mock is wired into the component via TestBed providers, which is the mechanism by which the mocked put() (and its thrown error) actually becomes the service instance the component's unlockHint() code calls into.

title: Challenge solved/coding-status state is mutated purely from unauthenticated-looking websocket payload fields with no ownership or integrity check
description: onChallengeSolvedWebsocket and onCodeChallengeSolvedWebsocket accept an externally supplied payload object and use only a 'key' field to look up and mutate a challenge's 'solved' / 'codingChallengeStatus' state in the client-side model (lines 146-181). The tests show the handlers gracefully ignore an undefined payload (lines 184-194) but there is no evidence in this file (or reachable from it) that the payload's other fields (name, challenge, flag, hidden, isRestore, codingChallengeStatus) are validated, that the key is checked against a known/expected set of challenges, or that the source of the socket event is otherwise authenticated/authorized for this specific state change. Because the client trusts whatever 'key' arrives on the socket channel to flip solved/coding-challenge state used for the score-board UI (progress indicators, notifications), any component or actor able to emit or replay a message on this socket channel (e.g., via a compromised dependency, a misconfigured socket namespace, or business logic elsewhere that forwards attacker-influenced data onto this channel) can flip arbitrary challenges to 'solved' in the UI without any server-side re-validation visible at this layer. The pattern is repeated identically across three separate handler paths in this file (plain challenge-solved, find-it code-challenge-solved, fix-it code-challenge-solved), showing this is the systemic design of the component rather than an isolated oversight. This is a trust-boundary/design gap: the client never re-derives or confirms solved-state server-side before rendering it as truth.

title: Stored XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml on challenge description
description: Challenge data is fetched from the backend (challengeService.find, line 67) and each challenge's description field is passed directly into Angular's DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() (line 82) without any HTML sanitization or allow-listing. bypassSecurityTrustHtml explicitly disables Angular's built-in auto-escaping/sanitization for that value, and the resulting SafeHtml is bound (presumably via [innerHTML]) in the companion template so any HTML/script content in challenge.description will be rendered and executed verbatim in the victim's browser. Since challenge descriptions are ultimately server-controlled content, and the architecture summary shows a POST /api/Challenges endpoint that can create/modify challenge records, any actor able to influence a challenge's description field (an admin panel, a data-import route, or a compromised challenge record) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes for every user who opens the score board. There is no sanitizer, allow-list, or context check anywhere along the path from the API response array, through the combineLatest merge, the subscribe callback, and the per-challenge map/spread transformation, down to the bypass call - the bypass is unconditional for every challenge in the list.

this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(challenge.description as string) explicitly bypasses Angular's HTML sanitizer, marking the raw server-supplied string as safe HTML for direct DOM insertion via [innerHTML] in the template.

title: Client trusts itself to mark hints as unlocked without visible cost/authorization enforcement
description: unlockHint() (lines 181-189) is invoked purely from client-side interaction (e.g. a 'use hint' button) and immediately calls hintService.put(hintId, { unlocked: true }) to flip the hint's unlocked flag, then re-runs ngOnInit() to refresh state on success. In Juice Shop's design, hints are supposed to cost points/coins or be gated behind some prerequisite, but nothing in this file re-derives or validates that cost/eligibility before issuing the unlock request - the component simply forwards the caller-supplied hintId and challengeKey straight into a PUT request with a hardcoded unlocked:true payload. If the backend handler for this PUT endpoint does not independently re-verify that the unlock is legitimate (e.g., enough points spent, hint not already unlocked, valid challenge state), an attacker could call the underlying REST endpoint directly (bypassing this component) with an arbitrary hintId to unlock any hint for free. This file demonstrates the client-side trust assumption - the value that gates a security-relevant state transition (hint unlocked) is sent as a flat boolean from the client with no accompanying proof of payment/state between the point the hintId/challengeKey parameters are received and the point the PUT request is dispatched. The actual enforcement (or its absence) lives in the hint service/backend, outside this file.

hintService.put(hintId, { unlocked: true }) sends a flat 'unlocked: true' state change to the backend for the given hintId, with the client never proving prerequisite conditions (e.g., payment) were met within this file's logic.

title: Raw error objects logged to browser console on hint-unlock failure
description: In the error callback of the hintService.put() subscription (line 187), the raw error object `err` is passed directly to console.log() with no filtering or redaction. Depending on what the HttpClient error object contains (HTTP response body, headers, URL, or backend stack trace/message forwarded in the response), this can leak internal implementation details, request URLs, or other sensitive diagnostic information into the browser's developer console. The subscribe() call at line 183 registers an observer object literal (opening at line 183 and closing at line 188) whose error branch is defined at line 187 with no intermediate transformation, redaction, or structured-logging wrapper between the network call and the console.log invocation - the raw error reaches the console verbatim. This is client-local logging (not a network-exposed log store), but it is still an example of unredacted error data being written to a persistent, inspectable log surface without any structured/security-aware logging strategy, and it provides no security-relevant event correlation (no context about which user/hint/attempt failed beyond the raw error).

title: DOM-based Reflected XSS via search query parameter bypassing Angular sanitization
description: The filterTable() method reads the 'q' query parameter directly from the URL (this.route.snapshot.queryParams.q), trims it, and then passes it to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), explicitly disabling Angular's automatic HTML sanitization. The result is stored in searchValue, typed as SafeHtml, which strongly implies it is bound in the component template (search-result.component.html, not shown) via an [innerHTML] binding. Because the value originates directly from an attacker-controlled URL query string and is never sanitized (no HTML-entity encoding, no allow-list, no library such as DOMPurify is used), a URL like /search-results?q= will execute arbitrary script in the victim's browser when they visit a link containing this parameter. This is a classic DOM-based / reflected XSS.

Truthiness check on queryParam gates entry into the block that processes and later trusts the raw value; empty/undefined values skip to the else branch (line 151), so any non-empty attacker string proceeds.

title: Stored XSS via product descriptions trusted as raw HTML
description: After fetching the product list from the backend (productService.search('')), trustProductDescription() iterates every product and calls DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() on the raw description field, unconditionally marking it as safe HTML with no validation, allow-listing, or sanitization library applied. Product descriptions are data that, in this application, can originate from privileged-but-still-attacker-reachable flows (e.g., product creation/edit in Juice Shop is a known stored-XSS vector). Because the sanitizer bypass is applied indiscriminately to every product's description before rendering (likely via [innerHTML] in the child ProductComponent, outside this file), any HTML/script content persisted in a product description will execute in the browser of every user who searches or browses products. The rendering sink itself lives in product.component's template, outside this file, but the trust decision is made here.

title: Client-side authentication state trusts mere presence of a localStorage token without validation
description: isLoggedIn() determines the user's authentication state purely by checking whether the key 'token' exists in localStorage, with no verification of the token's signature, structure, expiration, or authenticity. Because localStorage is fully writable by any script running in the page's origin (including via any XSS elsewhere in the app, such as the reflected/stored XSS findings above) or manually via browser devtools, an attacker can trivially set localStorage.setItem('token','anything') to flip this method to return true, causing any UI logic in this component (or others) gated on isLoggedIn() to behave as though the user is authenticated. This is a purely cosmetic/client-side check; if any authorization-sensitive UI decision in this component relies on it without server-side re-verification, it can be bypassed trivially.

title: Client-controlled continueCode cookie is trusted to auto-restore challenge progress without server-side authentication
description: The tests in this file demonstrate that the ServerStartedNotificationComponent reads a client-side cookie named 'continueCode' and, upon receiving a 'server started' socket event, uses that value directly to call ChallengeService.restoreProgress() and restore a player's hacking progress — with no further identity check shown anywhere in the test suite. Because the cookie is entirely under the browser/client's control (the test literally sets it with cookieService.put('continueCode', 'CODE') at line 93, exactly as an attacker-controlled browser would), any party who can guess or obtain another user's continueCode value can have their progress silently restored/hijacked, since the server-side trust boundary the design relies on is a client-supplied token stored in a plain cookie rather than a server-verified session artifact. The restoreProgress mock (line 42) is configured to unconditionally succeed with of({}) regardless of what continueCode value is supplied, mirroring that the flow exercised by these tests never demonstrates the value being independently verified before the socket callback (captured at line 95, invoked at line 96) proceeds to restore state and confirm the 'server started' event fired (line 97). The test suite also confirms the cookie value is left completely unchanged/unvalidated after use (line 98: expect(cookieService.get('continueCode')).toBe('CODE')), i.e., the code path never re-derives or invalidates the value server-side within the flow exercised by these tests. This is a classic trust-assumption violation: the client supplies a value the server (via the socket handler) should independently authenticate before granting a state-restoring action.

The mocked socket 'on' handler captured at index [0][1] represents the restore-progress callback that will use the cookie value when the server-started event fires.

title: Failed automatic progress-restore attempts (potential continueCode guessing) are only surfaced via unmonitored browser console.log with no rate-limiting or audit trail
description: The test 'should log errors during automatic progress restore directly to browser console' (lines 123-133) confirms that when the underlying ChallengeService.restoreProgress call fails (e.g., because an invalid/guessed continueCode was supplied), the component's only response is to call console.log(err) in the client's own browser. The flow begins by configuring the restoreProgress mock to throw (line 125) and setting the same client-controlled continueCode cookie used in the companion finding (line 126), demonstrating this failure path is reached through the identical untrusted-cookie channel. console.log is stubbed with a spy (line 127) before ngOnInit is invoked (line 128); the socket handler is captured (line 129) and then invoked (line 130), driving the component through its error-handling branch, after which the test confirms the 'server started' handler ran (line 131) and that the sole handling of the failure was a console.log call with the raw error (line 132). There is no evidence in this component/spec of any security-relevant event being sent to a server-side logging or monitoring system, no correlation ID, and no throttling/lockout logic for repeated failed restore attempts. Since continueCode is a client-controlled value used to restore progress (see companion finding), an attacker enumerating/guessing continueCode values to hijack other players' progress would generate only client-local console output that the attacker himself controls and can simply ignore — the server/operations team receives no signal of the failed attempts, and there is no compensating control (rate limiting, alerting) for this inherently abusable, unauthenticated restore operation.

title: Reflected DOM XSS: search query bypasses Angular sanitization before being trusted as HTML
description: The spec confirms that SearchResultComponent.filterTable() takes the raw 'q' query parameter from ActivatedRoute.snapshot.queryParams — an attacker-controlled URL parameter — and passes it directly, unmodified, to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(). Angular's bypassSecurityTrustHtml explicitly disables the framework's built-in output encoding for the wrapped value, and the test at line 221 proves the component calls it with the raw payload '<script>scripttag</script>' with no sanitization, escaping, or allow-listing applied first. A second test (lines 204-210) shows an even more dangerous payload ('<iframe src="javascript:alert(`xss`)">...') is accepted and even causes a socket.emit('verifyLocalXssChallenge', ...) call carrying the raw payload — confirming this is a known/tracked DOM XSS surface baked into the component's design rather than an oversight caught anywhere in this code path. Any value subsequently bound in the template via [innerHTML] (or similar) using this trusted value would execute attacker-supplied script in the victim's browser purely by visiting a crafted URL such as /search-results?q=<script>...</script>.

Test explicitly asserts sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml was called with the raw '<script>scripttag</script>' query value, proving the component disables Angular's auto-sanitization for user-controlled search input before it is bound into the DOM.

title: Stored XSS: product description bypasses Angular sanitization before being trusted as HTML
description: The spec proves that when ProductService.search() returns product records, the component takes the 'description' field — persisted product data that can originate from product-management/admin input or other user-controlled workflows — and passes it verbatim to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() without any HTML sanitization or allow-listing. The mock is first defined with a benign default return value, then the test overrides it with a malicious description; component.ngAfterViewInit() is invoked to pull that data through the component's normal initialization/subscription path, fixture.detectChanges() drives Angular's rendering/processing pipeline, and the final assertion shows the exact unmodified payload reaching bypassSecurityTrustHtml(). Because bypassSecurityTrustHtml explicitly marks content as safe for HTML binding, any script/markup stored in a product description will execute in the browser of every user who views the search results.

title: Client-side login state derived from mere presence of a localStorage token, not its validity
description: isLoggedIn() is shown by the spec to return true purely based on whether a 'token' key exists in localStorage, with no verification of the token's signature, expiration, or authenticity. The path runs from a baseline where the token key is explicitly removed (client-writable localStorage confirmed as the external state source), through an assertion that isLoggedIn() correctly reports false in that state, to a second step where the test writes an arbitrary non-JWT string ('abc') into the same key with no validation performed anywhere in between, after which isLoggedIn() reports true. This is a client-side identity decision that can be trivially spoofed by any script running in the page (e.g., via the XSS findings above, or simply through DevTools) to flip UI gating that depends on isLoggedIn(), since the decision never inspects the token's structure or authenticity.

title: API failures logged only via raw console.log with no structured/security monitoring
description: The spec confirms that when ProductService.search() fails, the component's only response is to call console.log(error) directly with the raw error value, with no structured logging, telemetry, or reporting to any monitoring service. The path runs from the mocked API failure, through the equivalent error setup in the dedicated console-logging test, through the console.log spy installation, through the component's initialization call that subscribes to the failing observable and triggers its error handler, through the change-detection pass, to the final assertion that console.log was invoked directly with the raw error value 'Error'. Any failure of these calls — which could include authorization failures, malformed responses, or backend errors carrying diagnostic details — is only visible in the end user's own browser console and is not captured for security monitoring or incident investigation.

title: Read-only editor state enforced only client-side, not backed by server-side validation
description: readOnlyExtensions() configures a CodeMirror editor to be non-editable purely through client-side state flags (EditorView.editable.of(false) and EditorState.readOnly.of(true)). These are UI-layer conveniences implemented entirely in JavaScript running in the user's browser. They can be trivially bypassed by an attacker using browser devtools to call the CodeMirror API directly (e.g. dispatching a transaction bypassing the readOnly guard), by monkey-patching the EditorView/EditorState objects before this module initializes them, or simply by crafting and sending the underlying HTTP request that would normally carry the editor's content directly, without ever touching the UI. If any caller of this file (e.g. a code-snippet viewer, a challenge display, or any feature where content displayed via this editor is later submitted/trusted as unmodified) relies on this 'read-only' configuration as a security boundary rather than re-validating the submitted content server-side, that is a trust-assumption violation: the client is trusted to enforce a restriction that only the server can meaningfully enforce. The actual caller and how the editor's content is subsequently used (submitted, compared, persisted) is outside this file, so the impact depends on that usage, but the control itself, as implemented here, provides no security guarantee.

title: Component error handling only logs raw errors to browser console with no structured/security logging
description: This spec file locks in (via `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')`) the production behavior of TokenSaleComponent.ngOnInit(): when the ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() call fails, the component's error handler passes the raw error value directly to console.log. This test formally certifies that error handling for a failed backend call consists solely of a client-side console.log statement with no structured logging, no correlation ID, no reporting to a monitoring/alerting backend, and no sanitization of the error content before it is printed. Because console.log output is visible to anyone with access to the browser's developer console (including the end user or anyone inspecting the page), any sensitive detail present in the underlying HTTP error object (e.g., backend stack traces, internal error messages) would be exposed client-side rather than being captured by a security monitoring pipeline. This test, by asserting exact equality with the raw error argument, encodes and validates the insecure/incomplete logging behavior rather than a structured logger call, meaning a security event (a failed configuration retrieval, which could indicate backend issues or probing) goes essentially unlogged for detection/alerting purposes and is only surfaced to whichever client happens to trigger it.

title: Configuration fetch errors silently swallowed via console.log with no structured/security logging

This is a client-side console statement, not a security-relevant log sent to any monitoring/alerting backend, so operators have no visibility into repeated configuration-fetch failures (which could indicate backend tampering, misconfiguration, or probing). Additionally, because the raw error object is logged rather than a sanitized message, any sensitive details the backend includes in error responses (stack traces, internal URLs, etc.) would be exposed to anyone with access to the browser console on that machine. This is a weak/incomplete logging practice: no correlation ID, no distinction between expected and security-relevant failures, and no forwarding to any monitoring system.

title: Test confirms DOM XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml on unsanitized orderId
description: The spec file exercises and asserts a code path in TrackResultComponent where the order tracking number (orderId), which ultimately originates from external/user-controlled data (an order created via the order-creation flow or a route/query parameter used to look up an order), is wrapped in a `...` string and passed directly to Angular's DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml without any HTML encoding or sanitization step. The test at lines 63-69 explicitly sets component.orderId to a string containing an HTML tag (`Link`), feeds it back through the mocked TrackOrderService.find() response, calls ngOnInit(), and then asserts that sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml was called with the raw, unescaped HTML embedded inside a wrapper. This proves that the underlying component (track-result.component.ts, not directly visible here) explicitly disables Angular's built-in output encoding for this field and trusts it as safe HTML, which is then presumably bound via [innerHTML] in the template. The wiring that makes this observable is itself part of the defect's demonstrated path: the test double for DomSanitizer is constructed with bypassSecurityTrustHtml as a bare jest/vitest spy (line 30-32), then explicitly configured as a pure passthrough that returns its argument completely unchanged (line 34) — i.e., the mock performs literally zero sanitization, and the separate sanitizer.sanitize function (which might otherwise strip dangerous content) is mocked independently to always return an empty object (line 35), meaning it is never relied upon for this field. This mocked sanitizer is then injected into the component in place of the real Angular DomSanitizer via the TestBed providers array (line 45), so any call the component makes to bypassSecurityTrustHtml during ngOnInit resolves to the harmless-argument passthrough, letting the raw HTML travel untouched all the way to the assertion. If an attacker can control the orderId value (e.g., by crafting an order with a malicious order number, or if orderId is taken from a URL parameter), the payload would execute as HTML/script in the browser of any user who views the tracking page, since bypassSecurityTrustHtml removes Angular's sanitization protection and no other sanitizer is used for this value in the asserted path.

The mocked TrackOrderService.find() is configured to return this same orderId value as part of the order data, simulating the API response the real component consumes.
component.ngOnInit() is invoked, triggering the component's internal logic (defined in track-result.component.ts, outside this file) that processes the orderId and wraps it in a <code> tag.

The DomSanitizer test double is constructed, defining bypassSecurityTrustHtml as a bare spy function with no sanitization logic of its own — the control that should neutralize the payload is only a stub at this point.

bypassSecurityTrustHtml is explicitly implemented as an identity passthrough ((args) => args), so whatever HTML the component hands it is returned completely unmodified — no encoding, stripping, or validation occurs at this control point.

This passthrough sanitizer mock is registered as the DomSanitizer provider for the component under test, so the component's internal call to the injected sanitizer resolves to the harmless-passthrough implementation rather than real sanitization.

The test asserts sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml was called with the raw, unescaped HTML string ('Link'), confirming the component explicitly bypasses Angular's HTML sanitization for this value before it is rendered (likely via an [innerHTML] binding in the template), enabling DOM-based XSS if orderId is attacker-controlled.

title: Privileged UI/role decision based on client-decoded, unverified JWT payload
description: isAccounting() determines whether the user is shown accounting-only functionality by calling loginGuard.tokenDecode() and reading payload?.data?.role directly from the decoded JWT, with no signature verification performed in this file (or visibly by the injected LoginGuard call). Client-side JWT decoding (e.g. jwt-decode) only base64-decodes the payload; it does not cryptographically validate the token. Any code path that can place an attacker-controlled token string into local storage (a stored-XSS gadget elsewhere in the app, or direct devtools/localStorage tampering during testing) can inject a payload with role: 'accounting' and the sidenav will treat the user as an accounting user. Because this is the only authorization check exercised in this file to gate a privileged menu item, and it is deciding function-level access based on client-trusted, signature-unverified data, it represents both a broken function-level authorization pattern and a cryptographic/authentication trust failure (decision made on unverified token data). Real enforcement must additionally exist server-side, but this file's own authorization gate is defective on its own terms.

trace.description: isAccounting() is invoked (presumably from the template) to decide whether to render accounting-only navigation items.
loginGuard.tokenDecode() decodes the JWT stored client-side without this file performing or requiring any signature verification.
roles module is imported to supply the roles.accounting constant that the decoded, unverified claim will be compared against.
LoginGuard is injected as the component's source of decoded-token identity, establishing the dependency this decision relies on.
The role claim from the unverified decoded payload is compared directly to roles.accounting and used as the sole authorization decision for showing privileged functionality.

title: Authentication state derived solely from presence of an unvalidated localStorage token
description: isLoggedIn() and the ngOnInit login-state branch treat the mere existence of a 'token' key in localStorage as proof of authentication, without validating its signature, structure, or expiration. Because localStorage is fully readable and writable by any JavaScript running in the page's origin (including injected/XSS scripts, or via direct browser devtools manipulation), a caller can trivially satisfy this check by writing any non-empty string to localStorage['token']. The consequence of this unvalidated check is that getUserDetails() is triggered to fetch and display data as if the session were valid. Combined with isAccounting() reading role claims from the same unverified token, this establishes an authentication decision point in the file that never confirms the token is genuine, only that a value is present. This is a design and cryptographic-authentication weakness: the token is used as a bearer-only truth of identity without integrity verification at the point this file consumes it.

isLoggedIn() repeats the same pattern: truthiness of localStorage.getItem('token') is treated as the authentication signal, exposed for use elsewhere (e.g. templates) to gate UI.
Because the raw presence check succeeded, getUserDetails() is called to populate authenticated user data without any prior validation of the token's authenticity.
The raw token value from localStorage is returned/used as the logged-in indicator with no validation of signature or expiry performed in this file.

title: Session/auth token persisted in localStorage, exposing it to XSS-based theft
description: The application stores its authentication token in localStorage ('token' key) rather than in a secure, httpOnly cookie, as evidenced by logout() explicitly removing it from both localStorage and cookieService. Tokens in localStorage are accessible to any script executing in the page context, meaning any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the SPA (a realistic risk in a large Angular app with many components) can be leveraged to exfiltrate the authentication token and fully impersonate the user, including any accounting-role claims read from it by isAccounting(). This is a standard session-management/cryptographic-authentication weakness: sensitive bearer credentials are placed in a storage mechanism with no XSS isolation.

isLoggedIn() again reads localStorage.getItem('token') directly, confirming localStorage remains the sole in-page store consulted for the live session token throughout the component's lifetime.

title: Security-relevant events (login-state transitions, config/version fetch failures) are only console.log'd, never reported or monitored
description: Every subscribe() error handler in this file (application version fetch, last-login-IP save on logout, score-board status fetch, user details fetch, application configuration fetch) simply does console.log(err) with no structured logging, telemetry, or alerting. Additionally, the logout flow (logout()) and login-state transition handling in ngOnInit perform no security-event logging of authentication state changes at all — there is no record retained anywhere (beyond the browser console, invisible to any backend monitoring) of login/logout occurring, or of failures fetching authenticated user data (which could indicate token tampering or backend authorization failures). Because this is purely client-side console output, none of it reaches any monitoring or alerting system, meaning repeated failures (e.g., many failed whoAmI calls indicating invalid/tampered tokens) are never observable operationally.

getUserDetails() failures (which could indicate an invalid or expired token being used) are only logged via console.log with no structured/security logging.
The application-version fetch in ngOnInit likewise only console.log(err)'s failures, establishing the pattern repeated across the component's initialization path.
saveLastLoginIp()'s error handler also only console.log(err)'s any failure, so even the one security-adjacent call made on logout has no durable failure record.
getScoreBoardStatus()'s error handler continues the same console-only pattern for a challenge-state-relevant fetch.
getApplicationDetails()'s configuration-fetch error handler again only console.log(err)'s, confirming no path in this file ever escalates a failure beyond the browser console.

title: Challenge 'continue code' treated as bearer credential, stored in JS-readable cookie and auto-applied via URL parameter
description: The component reads 'continueCode', 'continueCodeFindIt' and 'continueCodeFixIt' values directly from cookies via ngy-cookie's CookieService (which exposes document.cookie to JavaScript) and immediately forwards them, only URI-encoded, to ChallengeService.restoreProgress()/restoreProgressFindIt()/restoreProgressFixIt(). These continue codes function as bearer secrets that let the backend restore a specific user's challenge-solve state — effectively an authentication/authorization decision (whose progress gets applied to the current session). Three design/crypto weaknesses stem from this: (1) because the cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript (not HttpOnly), any XSS elsewhere in the app can exfiltrate the continue code and later replay it to hijack/merge another user's hacking progress; (2) each code is passed to its respective challenge-service method as an encodeURIComponent-escaped value only after a bare truthiness check (no further validation), strongly implying it is embedded in a GET request URL/path, which means it will be captured in browser history, in any Referer headers sent to third-party resources, and in server access logs — a classic 'credential in URL' exposure; (3) the client-received cookie value is trusted at face value and automatically triggers a state-restoring action on the 'server started' socket event with no user confirmation and no re-verification visible here of server-side ownership/binding of the code to the authenticated session, meaning any actor able to plant this cookie in the victim's browser (e.g. cookie tossing from a sibling subdomain) can silently force progress-state changes for all three challenge tracks (regular, FindIt, FixIt).

continueCode read from a client-side, JavaScript-accessible cookie via CookieService.get — a bearer-style secret exposed to any XSS on the page.
Same pattern repeated for continueCodeFindIt, URI-encoded and forwarded to restoreProgressFindIt.
Same pattern repeated for continueCodeFixIt, URI-encoded and forwarded to restoreProgressFixIt.

Bare truthiness check gates continueCodeFindIt before it is forwarded, mirroring the same unvalidated-trust pattern.
Bare truthiness check gates continueCodeFixIt before it is forwarded, mirroring the same unvalidated-trust pattern.

Cookie-derived secret is URL-encoded and handed to ChallengeService.restoreProgress(), which (outside this file) issues the network call that applies the progress — exposing the credential in the URL/logs and trusting client-supplied state to drive an identity-linked action.

title: Authentication token persisted in dual, JavaScript-accessible client storage (cookie + localStorage)
description: clearProgress() removes a 'token' value from both CookieService (line 98) and localStorage (line 101), which shows the authentication token is being maintained redundantly in two client-accessible stores. Both the cookie (accessed here through the JS-level CookieService API, implying it is not HttpOnly) and localStorage are readable by any JavaScript executing in the page context. Storing the same session/auth token in multiple JS-accessible locations widens the attack surface for token theft via any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the SPA — an attacker who achieves script execution can read the token from localStorage even if the cookie were hardened, and vice versa. The surrounding statements in the same function show this token-clearing sits alongside clearing of challenge continue-codes and session/local UI-preference state, confirming this is one deliberate, sequential cleanup routine rather than an isolated line, and that the 'token' credential is treated identically to non-sensitive UI state in both of its JS-exposed stores. This is a weak session-token handling pattern (OWASP A07) rather than a defect fixable in this file alone, but this file is where the dual-storage design is directly observable.

Same auth token additionally removed from localStorage, confirming redundant storage of the session credential in a location fully exposed to any XSS-executed script.

title: Raw error objects logged to console and interpolated into user-facing translation strings
description: When restoreProgress fails, the full error object is written to the browser console via console.log(error) and is also passed as an interpolation parameter into a translated notification string ('AUTO_RESTORE_PROGRESS_FAILED', { error }), which is then displayed to the user by being assigned into the component's bound hackingProgress.autoRestoreMessage property. HTTP error objects from Angular's HttpClient can contain response bodies, headers, and stack/debug information; logging them unfiltered to the console and surfacing them in the UI risks leaking backend implementation details, internal error messages, or (depending on backend behavior) sensitive fragments of the response — with no redaction and no structured/security-relevant event logging distinguishing this from a normal debug trace. The same unredacted console.log(error) pattern repeats for both FindIt (line 72) and FixIt (line 81) restoration failures.

title: DOM XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml() on reflected order-tracking ID
description: The component reads the `id` query parameter directly from the URL (`this.route.snapshot.queryParams.id`) and passes it, unsanitized and unvalidated, to `trackOrderService.find()`. The value returned in `results.data[0].orderId` is then wrapped in a literal `...` HTML string and explicitly marked as trusted via Angular's `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml()`. This call deliberately disables Angular's built-in auto-escaping for whatever ends up in `results.orderNo`, which is subsequently bound into the DOM (via `[innerHTML]` in the companion template, outside this file) as trusted HTML. In OWASP Juice Shop's tracking flow, when no matching order exists the backend response echoes back the caller-supplied order ID field, so an attacker can put an XSS payload (e.g. ``) directly in the `id` query string of the track-result URL. Because the sanitizer bypass is applied unconditionally to attacker-influenced content with no HTML/context sanitization performed first, this is a classic reflected/DOM XSS sink: the source is a URL parameter, the taint travels through an HTTP round trip, and the sink is an explicit security-bypass API rather than the framework's safe default binding.

Unvalidated orderId is sent to TrackOrderService.find(); the backend endpoint (outside this file) returns results.data[0], whose orderId field can echo back caller-supplied content (e.g. when no matching order exists).

results.data[0].orderId is interpolated into a raw HTML template string and passed to sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), explicitly disabling Angular's output sanitization for this value with no prior encoding/validation.

results.orderNo (now a trusted SafeHtml object) is later bound in the companion template (track-result.component.html, outside this file) typically via [innerHTML], causing any embedded markup/script in the tainted orderId to execute in the victim's browser.

title: Authentication token persisted in JS-accessible cookie and localStorage (XSS-exploitable token theft)
description: The test suite demonstrates that upon successful 2FA verification, the component under test (TwoFactorAuthEnterComponent) stores the raw authentication token both in a cookie (readable via cookieService.get('token'), which — unlike a server-set httpOnly cookie — is written by client-side JavaScript and therefore cannot carry the httpOnly flag) and duplicated into localStorage. Any token stored in localStorage or in a JS-writable/readable cookie is directly retrievable by any script running in the page context. This is a classic authentication/session-management weakness: if an attacker achieves any XSS on the origin, they can read `localStorage.getItem('token')` or `document.cookie` and exfiltrate the session token, fully impersonating the victim without needing to defeat the actual login or 2FA check. The full path runs through two separate test blocks that both drive component.verify() with a mocked token-bearing response and then assert the token landed in a JS-readable store: first the cookie store, then again for localStorage — confirming the component performs this dual, unencrypted persistence as its normal, designed behavior rather than as a test artifact.

component.verify() is invoked, causing the component to process the mocked token response and persist it into client-accessible storage.
Assertion confirms the token is written into a cookie readable via cookieService.get('token') — a JS-writable cookie, not a secure server-issued httpOnly cookie.
Mock configures TwoFactorAuthService.verify() to return a response object carrying { token: 'TOKEN' }, simulating the external server payload entering the component.
A second test block re-exercises the same verify() flow, this time to check localStorage persistence of the same token value.

component.verify() is invoked again, this time the internal logic additionally persists the token into localStorage.
Assertion confirms the same bearer token is duplicated into localStorage.getItem('token'), directly readable by any script (e.g. via XSS) running on the page.

title: No brute-force / rate-limiting protection evidenced on 2FA verification endpoint
description: The full test suite for the 2FA entry component contains only a single failure-path test (lines 125-129), which merely asserts that component.errored becomes true after a failed verify() call. There is no test exercising repeated failed attempts, lockout, throttling, or backoff behavior, and the component's observable behavior on failure is limited to flipping an 'errored' flag with no indication of attempt counting or rate limiting being enforced client- or server-side. The path from the failed-verification entrypoint to the sole observable effect passes through a single, unconditional call to component.verify() with no intervening attempt-counter, delay, or lockout check. Since MFA codes are typically short (4-6 digit) values, the absence of any rate-limiting control on the verification step is a design gap: an attacker who has already obtained a valid session (post-password, pre-2FA) can attempt to brute-force the second factor without being throttled, defeating the purpose of the MFA control.

component.verify() is invoked unconditionally, with nothing observed in this path (no attempt counter, no cookie/localStorage lockout flag, no delay) gating or throttling repeated calls.

Only observable effect of a failed verification attempt is component.errored being set to true — no lockout counter, delay, or attempt-limiting behavior is asserted anywhere in this test file, suggesting no such control exists in the component under test.

title: No logging/monitoring of failed two-factor authentication attempts observable in component behavior
description: The test for a failed 2FA verification (lines 125-129) shows the component's entire failure response is setting an internal `errored` boolean; there is no evidence of any security event being emitted, logged, or reported (e.g., to an analytics/audit service) when a 2FA verification fails. The call path goes directly from the mocked failure response through a single, side-effect-free verify() invocation to a purely UI-facing flag, with no logging call interposed anywhere along that path. Failed MFA attempts are a canonical security-relevant event that should be logged/monitored to detect credential-stuffing or brute-force attacks against the second factor. Based on the behavior exercised by this test suite, no such logging occurs.

component.verify() processes the failure; nothing in the observable path forwards this event to any audit/log service before updating UI state.
Only assertion made is on the local 'errored' UI flag; no audit/log call is exercised or verified, indicating the failed-authentication event is not recorded anywhere observable.

title: Authentication token stored in client-accessible storage (localStorage and cookies) with no evidence of protective flags
description: The spec file confirms, through the behavior it asserts on SidenavComponent.logout(), that the application's session/authentication token is persisted in two client-JavaScript-accessible locations: browser localStorage (key 'token') and a cookie managed via CookieService (also key 'token'). Storing a bearer/session token in localStorage (and in a cookie without any visible HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite configuration in this file) means any JavaScript running in the page context — e.g. injected via an XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the SPA — can read document storage and cookies (unless CookieService enforces HttpOnly, which client-side JS cannot do) and exfiltrate the token, enabling full session hijacking. This is a classic weak session-management pattern: the mere fact that logout() must explicitly call localStorage.removeItem('token') and cookieService.remove('token') shows the token is written to both readable stores during login, with no compensating control (token binding, short TTL enforcement, rotation) visible from this file.

A second test 'should remove authentication token from cookies' confirms the same token value is also mirrored into a cookie via cookieService.remove('token'), with no JS-visible configuration in this file indicating HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite protections.

component.logout() is invoked; internally this triggers the removal of the 'token' entry from localStorage, meaning the token was resident there in JS-readable form up to this call.

component.logout() is invoked again; this same call path also triggers cookieService.remove for the token, confirming logout() must clear two separate stores to fully invalidate the session client-side.

expect(cookieService.remove).toHaveBeenCalledWith('token') confirms the cookie-based copy exists as a second, parallel storage location for the same sensitive value, with no HttpOnly/Secure attributes observable from this file.

expect(removeItemSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('token') establishes that the token lives in a JS-readable store for the lifetime of the session, making it a direct target for token theft if any XSS sink exists elsewhere in the SPA.

title: Privileged UI (accounting/admin menu) gated solely on client-decoded, unverified JWT role claim
description: SidenavComponent.isAccounting() (exercised at lines 126-130, 132-136, 330-339, 390-404) determines whether to display the 'Go to accounting page' menu entry purely by calling loginGuard.tokenDecode() and inspecting a role field in the decoded payload. The tests show this decision is driven entirely by whatever tokenDecode() returns — a decode operation, not a documented signature-verification step — and by the mere presence of a 'token' key in localStorage (line 391, 399, 407, 423, 440). No test in this file exercises or requires a server round-trip to re-validate the role before rendering privileged navigation. If tokenDecode() only base64-decodes the JWT payload (as its name implies) without verifying the signature, an attacker who can place an arbitrary/self-signed or algorithm-confused token into localStorage (e.g. via a prior XSS, or via directly editing localStorage in devtools) can set role: 'accounting' and cause the client to reveal/enable admin-only functionality that a purely client-trust design assumes is safe to gate this way. This couples a client-side authorization decision (access-control) to an unauthenticated trust of decoded token contents (crypto-auth) — even though the underlying backend endpoints would still need their own authorization, the SPA's own gating logic is not itself validating the token's authenticity.

Test sets loginGuard.tokenDecode.mockReturnValue({ data: { role: roles.accounting } }) and asserts component.isAccounting() === true, confirming the component trusts the decoded payload's role field directly with no additional verification step visible.

A negative-case test sets tokenDecode to return role 'customer' and confirms isAccounting() is false, proving the same unauthenticated decode value is compared directly against a role string on every invocation of isAccounting().
In the template-rendering test, localStorage.setItem('token', 'token') establishes only presence-based login state (not validity) as the first gating condition for showing logged-in-only navigation.

Template test confirms the privileged 'Go to accounting page' link is rendered in the DOM whenever tokenDecode returns the accounting role and a 'token' key merely exists in localStorage, i.e. the sensitive navigation entry is exposed based on unauthenticated client-side decoding rather than a verified, server-confirmed role.

title: Security-relevant failures (user detail lookup, login-IP persistence, version/config retrieval) are only surfaced via console.log with no structured or monitored logging
description: Across multiple tests, the component's error-handling paths for security-relevant operations — retrieving the current user's identity (getUserDetails/whoAmI), retrieving scoreboard/challenge state, retrieving application configuration, persisting the last login IP (saveLastLoginIp), and retrieving application version — are all shown to funnel failures into a bare console.log(err) call and nothing else. Tracing the full set of these tests shows this is not an isolated case but a systemic pattern repeated at every error branch in the component: the caught error object is passed unmodified to console.log with no structured logger, no correlation ID, no severity classification, and no forwarding to any server-side or monitored sink. Because this is the only observable handling behavior, an attacker who can trigger repeated failures (e.g. of whoAmI or the security-relevant saveLastLoginIp audit call) leaves no server-side or monitorable trace beyond the individual user's own browser console, defeating detection or investigation of anomalous or malicious activity.

The same pattern recurs for getApplicationDetails(): configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration is made to throw and console.log is again the sole observed handling path, confirming this is systemic across the component rather than a single overlooked branch.

Similarly, 'should log error when retrieving application version fails' shows ngOnInit's failure handling for administrationService.getApplicationVersion also terminates at console.log('VersionError'), confirming a systemic pattern across the component of using an unmonitored client console as the sole error-reporting sink for security-adjacent operations.

title: Client-supplied user ID used to fetch arbitrary user details without authorization check
description: The component reads an `id` value directly from `MAT_DIALOG_DATA` (injected dialog data, ultimately originating from whatever UI component opened this dialog) and passes it unchecked into `userService.get()` to retrieve full user details, which are then bound to `this.user` and rendered in the template. There is no verification in this file that the currently authenticated user is authorized to view the profile of the user identified by `dialogData.id`. If the dialog-opening code (outside this file, e.g. an admin/user listing) allows the id to be influenced by the caller, or if this component is reachable with an arbitrary id (for example via URL/route state manipulation or by tampering with the value passed into the dialog), an attacker could view another user's details (email, address, payment info, etc. depending on what UserService.get returns) simply by supplying a different numeric id. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client trusts that dialogData.id is safe to use for a data fetch, and the file performs no access-control decision of its own, relying entirely on an unverified upstream/server check that cannot be confirmed from this file.

The returned user object (potentially another user's PII) is assigned to this.user with no ownership/authorization verification performed in this component, and is then rendered in the associated template.

title: Security-relevant fetch failures only logged to browser console with no structured handling or reporting
description: When fetching a user's details fails (which could indicate an authorization failure, e.g. a 403/401 from the backend when a user attempts to view another user's data, or any other error), the entire error object is passed to `console.log(err)`. This is the only handling of the failure: there is no differentiation between an authorization-denied event and a generic network error, no user-facing indication, and no forwarding to any monitoring/alerting mechanism. From a security-monitoring standpoint this means access-control-denial events surfacing through this UI path leave no durable, correlatable trace beyond an ephemeral browser console entry, which is not visible to backend operators and cannot be used to detect or alert on repeated unauthorized access attempts. Additionally, dumping the raw error object to the console risks incidentally exposing internal response details (e.g., stack traces, request URLs with the target id, HTTP body) into an unmonitored client-side log sink.

trace.description: userService.get(this.dialogData.id) call whose failure path is a security-relevant event (possible authorization denial or data-access failure).
userService, the object whose call can produce the security-relevant failure, is injected here.

The subscribe object's `next` branch closes without any related security-relevant success logging (e.g. no confirmation of which user record was accessed), so the same subscribe block also has no success-path audit trail before the error branch is reached.
Error handler only performs console.log(err) — no structured security event logging, no distinction of auth-failure vs. generic error, no reporting to any monitoring system.

title: No client-side rate limiting or lockout on 2FA token verification enables brute-force of 6-digit code
description: The verify() method submits the user-entered 6-digit token to twoFactorAuthService.verify() on every call, and the only handling of a failed attempt is to flash an 'errored' flag for 5 seconds (line 64-67) before resetting it — there is no attempt counter, exponential backoff, or lockout enforced in this component. A 6-digit numeric TOTP-style code has only 1,000,000 possible values. If the backend endpoint this file calls does not itself throttle or lock the account (which cannot be confirmed from this file, but nothing in this client enforces it either), an attacker who has already obtained a valid session cookie/localStorage precursor (e.g., via a leaked email/password) can script repeated calls to this verify flow to brute-force the second factor, defeating the purpose of MFA. This is both a missing-rate-limiting design flaw and a bypassable-MFA authentication weakness.

fields.token is sent to twoFactorAuthService.verify() with no client-side throttling of repeated submissions.
The raw form value is read into fields, extracting the attacker-controllable token with no attempt-count tracking attached to it.
On failure, only a transient UI flag is set (line 64-67); no attempt counter, backoff, or account lockout is enforced, allowing unlimited retry attempts against the second factor.

title: Authentication token persisted in localStorage, exposing it to XSS-based theft
description: Upon successful 2FA verification, the session/auth token returned by the server is written directly into localStorage (line 53) in addition to a cookie (line 56). localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript executing in the page's origin, so any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the application (or a malicious third-party script/dependency) can read this token via `localStorage.getItem('token')` and exfiltrate it, allowing full session hijacking without needing to steal the cookie. This is a session-management weakness: sensitive authentication material should only live in an httpOnly cookie, never in script-accessible storage.

title: Session cookie set without Secure/SameSite hardening flags
description: The authentication token is also placed in a cookie via cookieService.put('token', authentication.token, { expires }) (line 56). Only an 'expires' option (8 hours) is configured; no 'secure', 'sameSite', or 'httpOnly'-equivalent options are passed. Without the Secure flag, the cookie can be transmitted over plain HTTP if the app is ever reached that way (mixed content, downgrade, or misconfigured environment), and without SameSite it is more exposed to being sent along with cross-site requests, weakening CSRF defenses for whatever consumes this cookie. This is a misconfiguration of the session token's storage attributes and compounds the crypto-auth weakness of exposing the token to script access via localStorage as well.

title: Failed second-factor authentication attempts are not logged
description: The error handler for a failed 2FA verification (lines 63-69) only toggles a local UI 'errored' boolean for 5 seconds and returns the error object — it performs no logging, telemetry, or reporting of the failed authentication attempt (e.g., no call to an audit/logging service, no increment of a failure counter sent to the backend). Since this is the client-side surface for a sensitive authentication decision (second factor verification), the absence of any client-side security event emission means that, unless the backend independently logs failed verify attempts (unknown from this file), there is no way to detect a brute-force or credential-stuffing campaign targeting the 2FA endpoint from the information available in this component.

title: User-detail retrieval failures are only console-logged, never security-monitored
description: The spec explicitly asserts (and therefore documents/locks in) that when UserDetailsComponent.ngOnInit() fails to retrieve a user (userService.get() errors), the component's only reaction is `console.log(err)`. This is confirmed by the test 'should log the error on retrieving user', which mocks a failed HTTP call with throwError('Error') and expects console.log to have been invoked with the raw error. The UserDetailsComponent (referenced but not shown in this file) is exercised here by the admin/user-detail dialog, which is typically used to inspect a specific user's data (a security-relevant, potentially privileged operation, e.g. reachable from an admin panel or user list). A failure here — such as a 401/403 from an authorization check, or a 404 from an enumeration attempt against /api/Users/:id — is swallowed into the browser console with no server-side audit trail, no alerting, and no user-facing error surfaced. This means an attacker probing user IDs for enumeration, or triggering repeated failed lookups, leaves no trace that operators can use to detect or investigate the activity; the only record exists transiently in the requesting browser's own devtools console, which is neither centralized nor monitored. This is both a logging/monitoring gap (no server-side or centralized capture of a failed sensitive data-retrieval event) and a design gap: the component's error-handling design has no differentiated, monitored response to access-denial vs. not-found vs. server error conditions for what appears to be a privileged 'view another user's details' workflow.

title: Component trusts client-mocked user object without shape/authorization validation
description: The test 'should set the retrieved user' shows that ngOnInit() takes whatever value userService.get() resolves to (here, arbitrarily the string 'User') and assigns it directly to component.user with no validation of shape, ownership, or authorization scope. While this is a unit test using a stub, it reveals the underlying component design: the retrieved value is trusted and rendered/used as-is. The userService.get mock itself (defined generically at line 24, with only a permissive default of({}) set at line 26) is never constrained to any expected user-record shape, and the test freely substitutes an arbitrary primitive ('User') as a stand-in for a full user object at line 62 — illustrating that nothing in the component's consumption path enforces a schema or an identity check on the response before binding it. If the real backend endpoint underlying this flow (e.g., GET /api/Users/:id per the route list) does not perform proper authorization checks server-side, the client component has no compensating control — it will happily bind and display whatever record is returned, including another user's data, since there is no verification here that the returned record's identity matches the identity that was requested/authorized. This is a design gap: the file establishes no expectation that the component should validate the returned principal identity against the requested one before trusting/rendering it.

title: Disabling 2FA requires only password, no second-factor re-verification (MFA step-up bypass)
description: The spec confirms that the component's disable() flow only collects a password value from twoFactorDisableForm and invokes twoFactorAuthService.disable with a single 'password' argument — no TOTP token is required or passed. Disabling two-factor authentication is a sensitive, security-downgrading operation that should require proof of possession of the second factor (the current TOTP code) in addition to the password, exactly as the setup flow requires both password and initialTokenControl (see lines 118-119, 124). Because the disable operation only re-checks the first factor, an attacker who has obtained a user's password alone (e.g. via credential stuffing, phishing, or a leaked password reused elsewhere) can fully disable 2FA protection on the account without ever needing the physical/soft token, defeating the purpose of 2FA. This is both a weak MFA implementation (crypto-auth) and a workflow design flaw that omits a mandatory step-up check for an inherently risky operation (insecure-design).

title: Raw TOTP secret exposed as a plaintext DOM data attribute
description: The component renders the TOTP secret not only into the otpauth:// URL used to generate the QR code (line 100) but also directly into a 'data-test-totp-secret' attribute on the visible '#initialToken' input element, as confirmed by the test asserting input.getAttribute('data-test-totp-secret') equals the raw secret value. Placing the raw shared secret into a queryable DOM attribute (rather than confining it to the QR code image alone) unnecessarily widens the exposure surface: any script with DOM access (e.g. via an XSS vector elsewhere on the page, a malicious browser extension, session-replay/analytics tooling that snapshots the DOM, or simple browser devtools inspection) can trivially read the plaintext TOTP seed. This weakens the confidentiality guarantee of the shared secret that underlies the 2FA scheme.

title: Failed 2FA-status fetch only logged to browser console, no security event logging
description: When fetching the account's 2FA status fails (e.g., due to a session problem, token tampering, or an authorization failure while checking a security-relevant state), the only observable handling is a generic client-side console.log('Failed to fetch 2fa status') call. This is confirmed by the test which stubs console.log and asserts it was called with that static string when the status observable throws. There is no evidence of this security-relevant failure being reported to any server-side logging/monitoring/alerting system, no request/correlation identifier, and no distinction between transient network errors versus potential attack indicators (e.g., repeated failures that might indicate session hijacking attempts). Because browser console output is only visible to the local client and is not captured by any centralized monitoring, security teams have no way to detect or investigate patterns of failures in 2FA status checks.

title: Unencoded user email interpolated into otpauth:// URI enables QR/URI parameter injection
description: When building the TOTP provisioning URI for the QR code, the application code encodes the application name with encodeURIComponent but embeds the user's `email` value (returned from the 2FA status service call) directly into the URI template without any encoding: `otpauth://totp/${encodedAppName}:${email}?secret=${secret}&issuer=${encodedAppName}`. If the email value contains URI-structural characters such as `&`, `#`, `%`, or additional `key=value` pairs, it can alter the structure of the otpauth URI — for example appending or overriding the `secret` or `issuer` query parameters that an authenticator app will parse when the QR code is scanned. The inconsistent treatment (appName is encoded, email is not) shows encoding was considered for one field but omitted for another value that flows into the same executable/structured context (a URI consumed by an authenticator app parser). Because email addresses are frequently accepted with loose validation at registration, this is a realistic injection vector into a security-critical artifact (the 2FA secret provisioning URI).

title: TOTP secret and setup token disclosed to any authenticated session without password re-verification
description: The 2FA setup flow reveals the plaintext TOTP secret and a one-time setupToken as soon as updateStatus() is called — which happens automatically in ngOnInit() for any authenticated user whose 2FA is not yet enabled. No password or additional re-authentication is required to view this sensitive secret; the only gating factor is holding a valid session, and the status()/config() calls and the conditional that follows check only whether 2FA is already configured, never who is asking or whether they have recently proven their password. The password field (twoFactorSetupForm passwordControl) is only required later, at the point of confirming setup with a 6-digit token (setup() method), not to view/generate the secret itself. This means an attacker who obtains a victim's session (e.g., via session fixation, an XSS elsewhere in the app, or a shared/unlocked browser) can silently harvest the TOTP secret and setup token displayed/stored by this component without ever knowing the account password, undermining the intended two-factor protection the secret is meant to establish. A sound design would require re-authentication (password) before disclosing new 2FA secret material.

title: Failed 2FA setup/disable attempts are not logged anywhere
description: The error handlers for both the 2FA setup confirmation (setup()) and 2FA disable (disable()) flows silently swallow failures: they only reset form control pristine state and set a local `errored` flag for UI display. Unlike updateStatus()'s error handler, which at least writes to console.log (line 83), these security-relevant failure paths — a wrong password or wrong TOTP token during setup, or a wrong password during 2FA disable — produce no log output or telemetry at all, at any point along either handler's execution. Repeated failed attempts here are exactly the kind of event (potential brute-forcing of the 6-digit TOTP code, or attempts to disable 2FA with guessed passwords) that should be observable for security monitoring. While actual audit logging is normally a server-side responsibility, this client file is the only place these specific failure events are currently handled, and it discards them at every step without any record, making it harder to detect or investigate abuse from the client side.
