title: Wallet top-up amount is validated only on the client side (trust-boundary violation)
description: The test suite (lines 85-94) confirms that WalletComponent enforces the deposit amount range [10, 1000] exclusively through an Angular Reactive Forms validator on `balanceControl`. This is a client-side-only control: nothing in this spec (or the mocked WalletService) shows the same bound being re-derived or re-checked server-side before the PUT request is issued (walletService.put is mocked to always resolve with `of({})` regardless of the value passed, see lines 33/36). Because Angular form validators run only in the browser, an attacker can bypass them entirely by calling the underlying REST endpoint directly (e.g. via curl/Postman) with an out-of-range or negative amount, since the client component is not the actual enforcement point — it merely disables the submit button in the UI. This is a design gap: the value that governs an economic operation (wallet balance top-up) is asserted only by a client-side rule that the server must independently reproduce, and this spec gives no evidence that such server-side re-validation exists in the flow this component drives.

title: Backend errors are dumped directly to the browser console with no structured security logging
description: The spec at lines 103-108 explicitly documents and asserts the component's design: when the balance-fetch API call fails, the raw error value is passed straight to `console.log`. This confirms a logging design where failure of a security/financial-relevant operation (wallet balance retrieval) produces only an unstructured client-side console entry, visible to anyone with browser DevTools, and with no server-side or centralized security monitoring, no correlation ID, and no distinction between benign and suspicious failures (e.g., repeated failures that might indicate probing or tampering with the wallet endpoint). Because this is asserted as the expected/desired behavior in a test, it reflects the actual production design of the component: raw backend error content (which could include internal error details) ends up in client logs instead of being funnelled through an application-level security event/monitoring pipeline, making it impossible to detect or alert on repeated failed wallet API calls from the server side.

title: Client-controlled wallet top-up amount trusted for downstream payment flow
description: The wallet top-up amount entered by the user is only validated client-side via Angular reactive-form Validators (required, min(10), max(1000)) on the balanceControl (line 30). When the user proceeds, the raw form value is read directly from the control inside continue() (line 43) and written unmodified into sessionStorage under the key 'walletTotal' (line 44). The component then immediately navigates to the /payment/wallet route (line 45), which presumably reads this sessionStorage value to determine how much to charge or credit. Because Angular Validators are enforced purely in the browser and sessionStorage is fully attacker-writable, a user can trivially bypass the min/max constraints (e.g., via browser devtools: sessionStorage.setItem('walletTotal', '999999') or a negative/fractional value) either before calling continue() or between the setItem call and the navigation, and there is no re-derivation or server-side revalidation of this monetary value visible anywhere in this file's flow before it is handed off to the payment step. This is a trust-boundary violation: the client determines a value the server should be authoritative over (the top-up/payment amount), and the design never re-validates it downstream in a way traceable from this component.

This is a permissive default: instead of an allow-list of known custom elements, the entire module loses a built-in safety net that would otherwise flag unexpected/unknown bindings at build time. In a wallet/web3 context where templates may render externally influenced data (addresses, balances, transaction metadata) via bindings, removing this check increases the chance that an unsafe or unexpected binding pattern in the component template goes unnoticed during development/review.

title: Server-supplied configuration value trusted and concatenated directly into DOM classList without validation
description: The constructor subscribes to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() and, on receipt, takes conf.application.theme — a value originating from a backend configuration endpoint outside this file's control — and directly concatenates it into a CSS class string that is added to the overlay container's DOM classList. Tracing the full path: the OverlayContainer service is injected as a class field, then captured into a local constructor variable, then its element-fetching method is invoked, and finally the tainted, unvalidated theme string is concatenated and passed straight into classList.add(). There is no allow-list check, type check, or sanitization of the theme value anywhere along this path before it is used to mutate the DOM. The design assumes the configuration source is always trustworthy and well-formed; if that trust assumption is ever violated (compromised/misconfigured backend, MITM on the config endpoint, or a supply-chain issue in the config service), the value flows straight into a DOM API. classList.add() will throw on strings containing whitespace, but arbitrary single-token class names (e.g., matching real CSS selectors elsewhere in the app) can still be injected to enable CSS-based UI manipulation such as clickjacking-style overlay tricks or hiding/revealing elements, without any server-side or client-side validation layer catching it.

title: No error handling or logging on configuration subscription — failures silently swallowed
description: The subscription to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() only provides a 'next' handler; there is no error callback and no logging of failures anywhere in the callback body or at the point the subscription is closed. Walking through the callback: the DOM-mutating statement executes across the container-fetch and classList mutation lines, and the subscribe() call is closed immediately afterward with no second (error) or third (complete) argument supplied. If the configuration fetch fails, returns malformed data, or is tampered with in transit, the failure is silently dropped with no record left for monitoring or incident investigation. For a module that governs UI theming tied to server configuration, this is a minor but real logging/monitoring gap: an operator cannot distinguish 'configuration service is being attacked/tampered with' from 'nothing happened' by inspecting logs, because no log entry is ever produced on the error path.

The subscribe call closes without an error handler; any error emitted by the observable is unhandled and unlogged, leaving no trace for security monitoring.

title: Raw provider/contract error messages surfaced directly to the user without sanitization
description: In depositETH, withdrawETH, and getUserEthBalance, any exception thrown by the ethers.js provider/contract call (which can include internal RPC error payloads, contract revert reasons, or library-internal details) is assigned verbatim to this.errorMessage (error.message) which is presumably rendered in the UI. There is no filtering or generic error mapping before display. While this is a client-side/blockchain-library error rather than a server-side leak, it can still surface unexpected internal details (e.g., RPC endpoint specifics, contract state) to the end user, which is a weak error-handling control comparable to debug-information exposure.

title: Backend-configurable banner content rendered as raw HTML without sanitization control
description: The spec explicitly documents and asserts that the welcome banner's `message` property, which originates from the backend-provided application configuration (`ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration`), is 'interpreted as HTML' when rendered. One test (lines 83-89) shows that `ngOnInit()` takes the mocked configuration object and assigns its `welcomeBanner.title`/`welcomeBanner.message` fields directly onto `component.title`/`component.message` with no transformation or sanitization visible. A second test (lines 158-165) then demonstrates the consequence of that same property being bound in the template: setting `component.message = 'welcome!'` and calling `fixture.detectChanges()` causes an actual `` DOM element to be created in the rendered output, i.e. the component binds this value with an HTML-interpreting sink (consistent with `[innerHTML]`) rather than treating it as plain text. Chaining these two tests shows the full path: unsanitized backend-controlled config data flows straight through `ngOnInit` into `component.message` and then straight into an HTML-rendering sink with no allow-listing or DomSanitizer step exercised anywhere in the suite. Any origin able to influence the configuration payload (a compromised/misconfigured backend, an admin-editable banner setting, or a MITM on the config endpoint if not otherwise protected) can inject arbitrary markup/script into every visiting user's page.

After fixture.detectChanges(), the test asserts a real <em> element exists in the rendered DOM, confirming the template renders `message` as raw HTML rather than escaped text — with no sanitization step exercised or verified in the test suite.

title: Configuration-fetch failures are only logged to browser console with no structured/monitored logging
description: When the configuration service call fails, the component's error handling (exercised by this spec) results only in a `console.log` call with the raw error value ('Error'), per the assertion `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')` at line 110. There is no evidence in this test suite of the failure being reported to any monitoring/alerting system, sent to a logging service, or surfaced with a correlation ID. A backend configuration outage or tampering (e.g., an attacker disrupting the config endpoint, or repeated failures indicating probing/DoS) would go undetected by operators, since the only observable signal is a client-side console.log statement visible solely to the individual browser session. Additionally, logging the raw error object to console risks exposing internal backend error details (stack traces, endpoint URLs, or other diagnostic information) to anyone with access to browser devtools.

The test confirms the only observable handling of this security/operationally-relevant failure event is a call to console.log with the raw error — no structured logging, monitoring hook, or alerting path is exercised.

title: Sandbox feature route registered without any access-control guard
description: The Web3SandboxModule registers a top-level route (path: '') that renders Web3SandboxComponent with no canActivate/canLoad guard attached anywhere in this file. Given the naming ('web3-sandbox'), this is very likely an experimental/testing surface intended for restricted or internal use, yet the routing configuration here treats it identically to a public feature — no role check, no authentication gate, and no environment gate (dev-only) is expressed at the module or route level. The route object itself (lines 16-19) carries only 'path' and 'component' fields; no 'canActivate', 'canLoad', or 'data.roles' property is present. That bare route is then registered into the router via forChild (line 25), the @NgModule decorator that hosts it (line 22) applies no route-level providers/guards either, and Web3SandboxComponent is declared as a direct standalone import of the module (line 33) with the module class itself (line 37) adding no constructor-level authorization check before allowing the component to render (the constructor at lines 41-50 only wires theme/config, never checks user identity or role). Any user who can reach the router path this module is mounted under gets full access to whatever the sandbox component exposes.

title: CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA disables Angular template validation for this module
description: The module declares schemas: [CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA], which tells the Angular compiler to accept any unknown element and attribute name in this module's templates without complaint. This relaxation is scoped to the entire @NgModule (starting at line 22), applies across the full imports list (lines 23-32) and specifically covers Web3SandboxComponent, which is pulled in directly as a standalone import at line 33 — that import list closes at line 34 — meaning the schema relaxation the module declares at line 35 governs exactly the sandbox component's template. This is a broad relaxation of the compiler's built-in safety net (unknown-element/unknown-property errors) that would otherwise catch mistakes such as accidentally binding to a native DOM property/attribute that has security implications, or loading of unexpected custom elements, precisely on the module most likely to contain experimental, less-reviewed markup.

title: Server-supplied configuration value applied to DOM classList without validation and without error handling
description: The constructor subscribes to configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() and directly concatenates the returned conf.application.theme value into a CSS class name added via classList.add(). The services used in this callback are captured just beforehand: configurationService is injected at line 38 and re-bound to a local const at line 42, and overlayContainer is injected at line 39 and re-bound to a local const at line 43, both purely to be closed over by the subscribe callback at line 45. Inside that callback, conf.application.theme is concatenated with the literal string '-theme' with no validation of its shape (line 48), the DOM container element is retrieved via .getContainerElement() (line 47), and the unvalidated composed string is handed to classList.add() (line 46). Critically, subscribe() at line 45 supplies only a success handler — no error callback and no catchError — so if the configuration request fails, returns malformed data, or if classList.add() throws a DOMException because the theme string contains invalid characters (e.g. whitespace), the failure is silently swallowed with no logging, leaving no audit trail of a configuration or DOM-mutation anomaly.

title: Unverified remote Solidity compiler binary fetched and executed without integrity check
description: The compileAndFetchContracts() method builds a compilerInput object whose 'version' field is a URL pointing at https://binaries.soliditylang.org/bin/<file> (constructed from the compilerReleases lookup table) and hands it, together with the user-edited Solidity source (this.code from the CodeMirror editor), to the third-party 'solidity-browser-compiler' package. That package is expected to fetch the referenced soljson-*.js binary over the network and load/execute it in the browser (this is how emscripten-compiled solc distributions are consumed) in order to compile the supplied source. There is no subresource-integrity hash, checksum, or signature verification of the fetched compiler binary anywhere in this code path. If the CDN (binaries.soliditylang.org) is compromised, subject to DNS/traffic manipulation, or if a future version string ever became attacker-influenced, the application would load and execute arbitrary third-party JavaScript in the same origin as the rest of the Juice Shop application, giving that script access to the DOM, localStorage, cookies, and any in-page secrets — a classic software/supply-chain integrity failure (OWASP A08). Because the version keys are currently limited to a hardcoded map, exploitability today depends on compromise of the external distribution point, but the missing integrity check is a genuine and traceable defect in this file.

The template literal concatenates selectedVersion into the fixed external URL https://binaries.soliditylang.org/bin/<selectedVersion>, with no integrity/checksum metadata attached to the resulting reference.

title: Client-side 'session' authorization flag not reset on connection/chain-verification failure
description: The boolean this.session is used as the sole gate before allowing sensitive wallet-signed operations (contract deployment with a transaction value, and arbitrary function invocation with a transaction value) in deploySelectedContract() and invokeFunction(). handleAuth() only sets this.session = true after successfully confirming the connected chain id equals the Sepolia target (line 324-330), and only sets it to false when the chain check explicitly fails (line 325). However, if any step earlier in the try block throws (e.g. the wallet_addEthereumChain request at line 305 is rejected by the user, or connect()/disconnect() fails), execution jumps straight to the catch block at line 333, which only logs the error and never resets this.session. Because handleChainChanged() re-invokes handleAuth() on every wallet chainChanged event, a user who previously had session=true and then switches networks or rejects a subsequent connection prompt will keep a stale session=true value even though the wallet is no longer verified to be on the expected chain/account. The gating logic therefore does not correctly represent the current authorization/verification state at the moment deploySelectedContract()/invokeFunction() are called, since the check depends on a flag that is not reliably re-derived on every relevant network state change.

title: Raw error object logged to browser console without redaction
description: When the application configuration fetch fails, the raw error object returned by the HTTP client is passed directly to console.log with no filtering, redaction, or environment gating. If the ConfigurationService's underlying HTTP call surfaces backend error bodies, stack traces, request URLs, or other diagnostic details in the error object, all of that is written unfiltered to the browser's developer console. This is a debug-style diagnostic output left active in what appears to be production code (no environment.production guard), and it is the kind of place where sensitive response data (e.g., internal error messages, tokens, or trace details echoed by a misconfigured backend) could end up exposed to anyone who opens the browser console. It also represents a missed opportunity for structured, centralized error/security logging (no correlation ID, no severity classification, no reporting to a monitoring service) — a failed configuration fetch is silently dumped to console with no further handling.

title: Component swallows configuration-fetch errors into raw console.log with no structured/security logging or monitoring
description: The spec explicitly asserts (and thereby documents/locks in) that when ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration() errors out, the WelcomeComponent's ngOnInit handler responds by calling console.log(err) with the raw error value and does nothing else (no user-facing error state, no telemetry/monitoring hook, no structured logger). This is a client-side logging/monitoring failure: (1) errors are dumped straight to the browser console rather than through any structured logging/monitoring pipeline, so there is no way to detect or alert on repeated configuration-fetch failures (which could indicate backend tampering, an outage, or an attacker probing the API); (2) whatever the underlying HTTP error object contains (status text, response body, headers) is logged verbatim to a channel any user or extension with devtools access can read, risking disclosure of backend implementation details; (3) from a design perspective, the only 'error handling' the component performs for a failed trust-relevant configuration fetch (which drives security-relevant UI behavior like the welcome banner) is a console print — there is no retry, no fallback-safe default enforcement, and no reporting path, meaning failures here are silently invisible to any monitoring system even though this configuration establishes application-level settings.

title: Unbounded canvas creation with no debouncing or prior-instance cleanup
description: shootConfetti() unconditionally creates a new full-viewport canvas element and appends it to document.body every time it is invoked (lines 9-18), without checking for or removing any confetti canvas created by a previous invocation whose 6-second removal timeout (lines 39-41) has not yet fired. If this exported function is reachable from a code path that can be triggered repeatedly in quick succession (e.g., a UI event handler wired to a server-controlled trigger, or invoked programmatically many times before the cleanup timeout elapses), a caller could cause unbounded accumulation of full-screen, fixed-position canvas elements (z-index 2000), each with its own canvas-confetti renderer instance (with a resize listener attached) and two concurrent particle-animation loops, degrading rendering performance and consuming client memory/CPU (a client-side resource-exhaustion condition). The design never establishes a cap, a singleton guard, or a debounce on invocation frequency, so even a correctly-written caller cannot prevent pile-up if invocation frequency is not controlled elsewhere; the only cleanup mechanism is a fixed 6-second timer per call rather than a bound on concurrently-live instances. Because the entrypoint/caller of shootConfetti() is outside this file, reachability and actual trigger frequency cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: Exported shootConfetti() function; caller is outside this file and could invoke it repeatedly without any rate limit.
A brand-new canvas element is created on every call with no check for an existing/prior confetti canvas still pending removal.
New canvas is appended to document.body unconditionally, so multiple full-viewport canvases can stack up if invoked repeatedly.

The new canvas is styled as a fixed, full-viewport overlay (position/left/right/width/height set at lines 10-14), so each additional un-cleaned instance is a full-screen element, not a cheap off-screen node.

confetti.create(canvas, {resize:true}) instantiates a new renderer bound to this canvas with a window resize listener; each un-cleaned prior invocation leaves its own renderer/listener alive concurrently.
First shoot() call starts a particle animation loop (225 particles) on this instance's canvas, adding to whatever animation loops earlier un-cleaned invocations are still running.

Second shoot() call starts a further concurrent particle animation loop (225 particles) on the same canvas, doubling the per-invocation animation cost that piles up if shootConfetti is called again before cleanup.

Cleanup only occurs 6 seconds later via timeout(6000).then(() => canvas.remove()); until then each invocation's canvas/animation remains live, and there is no upper bound on concurrently live canvases.

title: Stored XSS via unsanitized welcome-banner message sourced from remote configuration
description: The component fetches application configuration from a remote/external configuration service and, without any sanitization or encoding, assigns the attacker/admin-influenced welcomeBanner.message field directly to this.message (a property whose default value at line 28 is raw HTML markup, including <a>, <strong>, <h1> tags). This strongly indicates the template (welcome-banner.component.html, not visible in this file) binds message via [innerHTML] rather than as plain text, since the default value is pre-formatted rich HTML. Because the configuration is loaded dynamically from a backend/YAML-driven config (per the architecture, there is a /file-upload route that accepts YAML configuration uploads which can alter application.welcomeBanner settings), any actor who can influence this configuration source can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into message, which is then rendered unsanitized to every visitor who is shown the welcome banner. The same unguarded pattern is used for the sibling title field, showing the assignment block treats the entire welcomeBanner config object as trusted without any validation gate beyond a simple truthiness check.

A bare truthiness check (config?.application?.welcomeBanner) is the only gate before the override is applied — it validates presence, not content, so any HTML/script payload in the field passes through unfiltered.
this.title is likewise overwritten from the same unvalidated config object, showing the whole welcomeBanner payload is trusted wholesale.

this.message is a rich-HTML string by design (default value shown here contains raw

title: Reverse tabnabbing via target="_blank" links without rel="noopener noreferrer" in banner HTML
description: The default welcome-banner message embeds anchor tags with target='_blank' pointing to https://owasp.org and https://owasp-juice.shop but omits rel='noopener noreferrer'. When this HTML is rendered (presumably via innerHTML binding in the associated template), the opened tab retains a window.opener reference back to the Juice Shop page, allowing the destination page (or, if the message is later attacker-controlled per the injection finding above, an attacker-supplied link) to run window.opener.location = 'https://phishing-site' and redirect the original tab to a phishing page while the user believes they are still on the legitimate site. There is no intermediate processing step between the literal definition of this markup and its use as the rendered value — the same string literal is both where the unsafe attribute is declared and what is eventually rendered.

title: Client-side-only enforcement of mandatory tutorial completion (restrictToTutorialsFirst)
description: When the server-provided configuration indicates hackingInstructor.isEnabled and challenges.restrictToTutorialsFirst are both true, the component's only enforcement mechanism is to set dialogRef.disableClose = true and showDismissBtn = false, which merely hides the UI's dismiss button and disables the Material dialog's built-in close affordance. This is a purely presentational/client-side control: it does not prevent a user from bypassing the workflow by interacting with the application through other means (direct API calls, browser devtools manipulation of the Angular component state, keyboard shortcuts, or simply not opening the dialog at all) to reach challenges/scoreboard without completing the intended tutorial-first workflow. Because the actual business rule ('users must complete tutorials before accessing other functionality') is never enforced server-side and is trivially bypassable client-side, this is a design flaw rather than an implementation bug.

title: Configuration-fetch failures are only logged to browser console with no structured monitoring

There is no structured client-side error reporting, telemetry, or security-relevant event capture for this failure. While this is a client-side component (so 'logs' are local to the user's browser rather than a centrally monitored log store), a failure here silently degrades security-relevant behavior (e.g., the restrictToTutorialsFirst enforcement at lines 43-46 never activates if the config call fails), and there is no mechanism to detect or alert on repeated/anomalous configuration-fetch failures that could indicate tampering with the configuration endpoint or a denial-of-service against it.

title: Production environment relies on implicit relative host with no explicit secure transport enforcement
description: The production Angular environment configuration sets `hostServer: '.'`, meaning all API requests made by the frontend will be resolved relative to whatever origin/protocol served the SPA, rather than pinning to an explicit, trusted, HTTPS-only backend origin. This file is the single source of truth for how the built frontend decides where to send authentication tokens, session cookies, and sensitive API calls in production. Because the value is a bare relative path with no scheme or host validation, if the application is ever served over plain HTTP (e.g. behind a misconfigured reverse proxy, CDN, or an attacker performing a downgrade/host-header attack), the SPA will silently issue all API traffic — including credentials — to that same insecure origin without any code-level control preventing it. There is no accompanying enforcement (e.g., a hardcoded HTTPS scheme, HSTS-related config, or origin allow-list) in this file to prevent the app from operating over an insecure channel. Tracing the value's path: it is declared on line 8, the object literal containing it is closed and finalized for export on line 9, that same object is bound to the exported `environment` constant on line 6, the `production: true` flag on line 7 sits alongside it with no transport-security override, and the resulting relative host string is what downstream consumers (outside this file) use as the API base for every request.

The file itself contains no safeguard, assertion, or runtime check that verifies the replacement actually happened — the security-relevant decision (whether to run Angular in development mode with verbose error output, disabled AOT/production optimizations, and easier introspection of application internals) is entirely delegated to angular.json build configuration that is not visible from this file. This is a design flaw in the sense that the file establishes no self-enforced invariant — it never re-derives or validates its own security posture, it simply trusts an external, unverified process to overwrite it correctly.

title: Tutorial content documents an unmitigated DOM-based XSS in the product search feature
description: This file is not application logic itself but a 'hacking-instructor' walkthrough that drives the user through the Juice Shop's own DOM-based XSS in the product search box. The hint sequence has the learner type a payload into the '#searchQuery input' field and then asserts (via waitForElementsInnerHtmlToBe) that the resulting markup is written verbatim as the innerHTML of the '#searchValue' element. The assertions at lines 82 and 99 confirm that raw, unescaped HTML/JS supplied by the user (including an <iframe src="javascript:alert(...)"> payload) ends up as the literal innerHTML of a DOM node, and the accompanying hint text at line 96 explicitly instructs the learner to confirm the resulting alert() box — i.e. the payload executes. This proves that somewhere in the application's search-result rendering code (outside this file, e.g. the Angular component that binds the search term to innerHTML or uses a DomSanitizer bypass), user input from the search box is inserted into the DOM without HTML-encoding or sanitization, allowing arbitrary script execution in the victim's browser (classic DOM XSS). While this specific file only contains the instructional metadata/test-hooks, it directly documents and helps trigger a real unmitigated injection sink elsewhere in the frontend. Because the actual sink (the innerHTML assignment in the search-result component) is not visible in this file, this finding is reported at reduced confidence, tracing from the point where this file receives/validates the tainted DOM state.

title: Admin section route accessible without server-enforced authorization (confirmed by embedded hacking-instructor tutorial)
description: This file is the in-app 'hacking instructor' tutorial for the 'Admin Section' challenge. Its hint sequence explicitly walks the user through discovering and successfully navigating to the /administration Angular route, and its resolver `waitForAngularRouteToBeVisited('administration')` (line 83) marks the challenge as solved the moment the route is visited — not after any credential or role check. Before that, the /admin route probe at line 72 resolves via `waitForAngularRouteToBeVisited('admin')` (line 76) on navigation alone. The preceding 'must be logged in as admin' hint (line 18) is explicitly marked `unskippable: false` (line 20) and its resolution (`waitForAdminLogIn()`, line 21) is only ever used to gate that one optional hint—not the actual route-visiting hints later in the array—so a player can skip past the login guidance entirely and proceed straight to the /admin and /administration navigation hints. The congratulatory hint (line 86, '🎉 Congratulations! You successfully accessed the admin section!') fires purely on route navigation, and the explanatory hint at line 91 confirms the intended discovery path is simply inspecting Angular JS bundles for route paths, requiring no authentication step whatsoever. Most tellingly, the final hint (line 101) explicitly invites the player to 'try to access the admin section without admin credentials. What do you think would happen?' — directly confirming that the admin UI section is reachable without any working authorization gate. This is the classic Broken Function Level Authorization pattern: a privileged UI surface (admin section) reachable via direct client-side navigation, gated (if at all) only by an Angular route guard that this same tutorial demonstrates can simply be bypassed by typing the URL. The design defect is that 'is this user an admin' is never re-derived/enforced server-side for the purpose of gating access to the admin section route itself; it is left entirely to optional, skippable client guidance and client-side routing, which the tutorial explicitly shows can be bypassed.

title: Client-controlled userId trusted as feedback author (Broken Access Control / IDOR by design)
description: This tutorial file documents and walks the user through exploiting a genuine design flaw in the Juice Shop feedback feature: the application's feedback form contains a hidden `userId` field whose value is read directly from client-side DOM state and, per the hint text and the resolved-callback logic, is submitted to the server as the authenticated author of the feedback. The hint text at lines 24-25 explicitly frames this as 'broken access controls' where the user must 'impersonate another user while providing feedback,' and line 31 states that without the exploit the feedback would 'be posted by yourself while logged in or anonymously while logged out' — meaning the server is not deriving the author identity from the authenticated session/token, but instead trusting a value the client can freely edit. Lines 37-55 walk the tester through discovering the hidden field via DevTools (opening dev tools at line 43, being told there is 'more than meets the eye' at line 49, and being instructed to manipulate the hidden field's value at line 55). The resolved() handler at lines 58-66 then operationalizes the attack: it captures the field's initial value (line 58), enters a polling loop (line 60) that repeatedly checks the live DOM value (line 61) and only breaks once it detects the tampered value differs from the original (line 62), sleeping between checks (line 64) until the user has substituted another user's id. Once the tamper is confirmed, the hint at line 70 instructs the user to submit the form, and the sink at line 73 waits for the actual submit-button click that ships the forged userId to the server. This is a textbook trust-assumption violation (OWASP A04): the server should independently derive the feedback author from the authenticated session rather than accepting a client-supplied identifier, but the design here allows any authenticated (or possibly unauthenticated) user to attribute feedback to an arbitrary other user by editing a hidden form field. While the server-side handler that ultimately persists this feedback lives outside this file, this file itself is the concrete evidence of, and walk-through for, the insecure design: an identity value that should be authoritative-server-derived is instead client-supplied and blindly trusted, enabling impersonation, reputational/defamation abuse, and data integrity violations against arbitrary victim accounts.

title: web3WalletABI interface exposes classic deposit/withdraw pattern consistent with a reentrancy-vulnerable contract
description: The web3WalletABI (lines 1113-1214) describes a wallet-style contract with ethdeposit(address _to) payable (credits an address supplied by the caller rather than msg.sender), a balances(address) mapping, a userWithdrawing(address) tracking value, and a withdraw(uint256 _amount) function with no 'from' parameter (implying it withdraws from the caller's tracked balance via an external call). This shape - a balance mapping combined with a withdraw function and a state variable named 'userWithdrawing' - is the textbook layout of contracts vulnerable to reentrancy (external call before state update), and the ABI itself declares a ContractExploited event, strongly indicating the underlying on-chain contract already anticipates being drained via a known exploit path. The presence of a bare receive() payable fallback alongside ethdeposit's balance bookkeeping means ETH can enter the contract without being credited to any tracked balance, creating a divergence between the contract's real ETH balance and its internal accounting that a reentrant withdraw call could exploit. Because this file is the sole interface the frontend uses to construct calls into this contract, the frontend has no encoded safeguard (e.g., confirmation, warning, or restriction) before allowing any wallet-connected user to invoke withdraw or ethdeposit on behalf of another address. The actual Solidity implementation is outside this file, so exploitability cannot be fully confirmed here, but the interface itself is a strong signal of an insecure-by-design contract exposed without any client-side compensating control.

title: BeeFaucetABI withdraw function exposes an unrestricted token faucet with no visible per-user rate limiting
description: BeeFaucetABI (lines 1059-1112) exposes balance/getBalance view functions and a withdraw(uint8 amount) function with no other input (no address cap, no cooldown parameter, no signature/allowlist argument). As presented to the frontend, any caller can invoke withdraw repeatedly to drain the faucet's token balance up to the uint8 range (0-255) per call, with nothing in the interface indicating a per-address or per-time-window limit is enforced. The token() accessor confirms the faucet dispenses a specific ERC20 token whose supply is finite and drainable. If the underlying contract does not itself impose such limits (which cannot be confirmed from this ABI alone), this is a faucet-drain design flaw: the process this file's interface encodes (dispensing tokens on request) has no conserved quantity check ever re-derived server/contract-side beyond what the ABI shows, allowing an attacker to call withdraw in a loop and exhaust the token supply intended for legitimate users.

the parameter is named 'amount' and is passed directly into the withdrawal call with no accompanying address allowlist, cooldown token, or signature parameter visible in the interface to bound repeated calls.
the amount type closes as uint8, capping a single call at 255 but leaving no interface-level mechanism limiting how many times withdraw can be called by the same caller.
withdraw is declared nonpayable/callable by any address per this interface, with no rate-limit or per-caller cap encoded, enabling repeated draining of the faucet balance.

title: Hardcoded admin credentials shipped in frontend JavaScript bundle
description: This file is compiled into the Angular frontend bundle and is served to every visitor of the application (it is part of the hacking-instructor tutorial module, exported as PasswordStrengthInstruction and imported by the instructor UI). It hardcodes the real administrator account's email address ('admin@juice-sh.op') and, across the sequence of hint objects, the actual admin password in full ('admin123') — first as the literal string used by waitForInputToHaveValue comparisons at each stage of the tutorial (lines 55, 61, 67, 73). Because these are plain string literals embedded directly in TypeScript source that ships to the client, any user can retrieve the working admin credentials simply by reading the compiled JS bundle or the repository source — without performing any of the guided 'exploitation' steps the challenge pretends to walk them through. This exposes a live, functioning credential pair in cleartext client-side code, and constitutes both a cryptographic/authentication failure (a real secret embedded in code, not derived at runtime, not one-way hashed for comparison) and a security misconfiguration (secret material shipped in a public-facing frontend artifact). While this is a deliberately vulnerable training application (OWASP Juice Shop) so the pedagogical goal is arguably the weak password itself, the concrete artifact — the admin's actual working password value hardcoded and shipped in cleartext in a publicly downloadable JS file — matches the sink pattern for hardcoded credentials regardless of the surrounding intent, and would be flagged as such in any generic secret-scanning or code review process.

The real administrator email address 'admin@juice-sh.op' is hardcoded as a literal argument to waitForInputToHaveValue.
Partial password fragment 'admin1' hardcoded as a comparison literal, part of the progressive disclosure of the full password.
First password-stage literal 'admin' hardcoded as a comparison value passed to waitForInputToHaveValue, the base of the real admin password being progressively revealed in source.
Third password-stage literal 'admin12' hardcoded as a comparison value passed to waitForInputToHaveValue, one digit short of the full working password.

The full, working administrator password 'admin123' is hardcoded in cleartext as the final comparison literal passed to waitForInputToHaveValue, exposing the complete working credential in client-shipped source code.

title: Tutorial confirms SQL-injection based authentication bypass allowing full account takeover without credentials
description: This file is the guided-hint definition for the 'Login Bender' challenge. It walks the user step-by-step through building and submitting the payload bender@juice-sh.op'-- as the email field value (with an arbitrary, unvalidated password), explicitly stating that this comments out the password-check clause of the backend's login SQL query and results in a successful, authenticated session as the Bender user (line 111: user is told they have been logged in as Bender). While the vulnerable query itself lives in the (external, not shown) login route handler, this file is direct, first-party evidence that the application's credential-verification logic concatenates unsanitized user input into a SQL statement, that no server-side check exists to prevent the password clause from being neutralized by injected SQL comment syntax, and that doing so results in the identity-resolution step (login) authenticating the caller as an arbitrary victim account without knowledge of that account's password. The full path runs: the tutorial first has the user supply the victim's real email unaltered (line 78) and any non-empty password (line 84), then submit an ordinary login attempt that fails because the password is wrong (line 90) -- demonstrating the normal, non-bypassed path is enforced. The tutorial then explicitly names the exploit technique, instructing the user that appending `'--` to the email will comment out the password-check clause of the DB query (line 98), has the user overwrite the email field with the injection payload bender@juice-sh.op'-- (line 101), and has the user resubmit the login form (line 107), which is where the crafted value reaches the external login handler and its SQL execution. The outcome (line 111) confirms the credential check was bypassed and the session was issued for the victim identity. Per the authentication-outcome anchor, a defect that lets an attacker skip a credential check and control whose identity is selected is both an authentication failure and, because it grants access to another user's account/resources without any ownership or authorization check, an access-control failure. It is also an insecure-design failure: the login workflow's core security invariant -- 'a session is only issued when a correct password is supplied' -- can be fully bypassed while every individual step (submit email, submit password, click login) succeeds and returns normally, which is the definition of a business-logic/design-level authentication bypass rather than a mere implementation bug in one field.

Hint's resolved condition requires the exact payload bender@juice-sh.op'-- in the email field, confirming the challenge is designed around a SQL-comment injection that truncates the query's password-check clause before it reaches the backend credential verification code.
Hint has the user fill the #password field with an arbitrary non-empty value, since the real password is assumed unknown; this value will be forwarded unchanged to the login submission.

User clicks #loginButton with the unmodified email/arbitrary password combination; the tutorial's next hint (line 93) confirms this legitimate-path attempt fails, establishing that only the credential-verification query itself stands between the caller and the victim's session.

Final hint confirms the outcome: the caller is now logged in as Bender, i.e. the identity-resolution/session-issuance decision was successfully manipulated by the SQL-comment injection, completing the authentication bypass and unauthorized account access.

Clicking #loginButton submits the crafted email (with arbitrary/unvalidated password from line 84) to the login handler; per the challenge design, the backend's credential-verification query executes with the injected comment, bypassing the password check and authenticating the request as the victim (Bender) identity, confirmed at line 111.

title: Instructional evidence of SQL Injection authentication bypass on /login (admin account takeover)
description: This file is the walkthrough/hint script for the 'Login Admin' challenge in OWASP Juice Shop. Its hint chain explicitly documents and verifies a real SQL Injection vulnerability in the application's login flow: the email field value is concatenated directly into a SQL query on the server (referenced but not shown in this file), so an attacker who submits `' OR true--` as the email (with any password) causes the WHERE clause to always evaluate true and the trailing `--` to comment out the rest of the query (including the password check), resulting in the attacker being authenticated as the first matched user — which the hints confirm is the administrator account. This file does not perform the query itself (the /login route handler lives outside this file), but the hint text at lines 34, 39, 72, 77-124 explicitly walks a user through constructing and confirming a working SQL injection authentication bypass against the real endpoint, and line 124 confirms success ('You have been logged in as the administrator'). Because this defect changes who the application believes the caller is (authentication bypass via injection on the credential-verification query), it is both an injection finding and a credential/authentication finding.

title: Verbose server error exposes raw SQL query and database engine details on failed /login requests
description: The hint chain describes the server's 500 error response to a malformed login request as containing the SQLITE_ERROR message and the entire raw SQL query text in the network response body (line 72). This confirms that the /login endpoint (outside this file) does not sanitize or generalize error output before returning it to the client: it leaks the underlying database engine (SQLite), the query structure, and presumably the concatenation points used to build the query. This kind of verbose error disclosure is a misconfiguration that materially assists an attacker in constructing the SQL injection payload documented in the companion finding, since it reveals exactly how user input is embedded in the query.

Resolver waitInMs(10000) advances the tutorial past the generic on-page error before the user is told where to look for the real diagnostic detail.
Hint explicitly directs the user to the browser's JavaScript console or network tab, i.e., the raw HTTP response, to find more information than the generic on-page error shows.
Resolver waitInMs(10000) advances the tutorial after directing the user to inspect the network response, immediately before the disclosure is confirmed.

Hint confirms the 500 response to POST /login contains the SQLITE_ERROR and the entire SQL query text, i.e., the server (outside this file) returns raw database error detail and query structure to an unauthenticated client instead of a generic error message.

title: Client-shipped walkthrough hardcodes a working SQL-injection authentication-bypass payload for a specific real user account
description: The exported LoginJimInstruction object is bundled into the frontend application and is reachable by any visitor of the shop (no server-side authorization gate is visible in this file, and the hint content is delivered as static instructional data consumed by the hacking-instructor module). It walks the reader step by step through discovering the email address of a named real account ('Jim'), then hardcodes the exact working exploit string `jim@juice-sh.op'--` as the value the email field must contain (line 90) and instructs clicking the login button (line 96) to complete authentication as that user without any password. This is not a hypothetical description of a flaw elsewhere — it is the literal payload needed to defeat the password-check clause of the login query, embedded and validated (via waitForInputToHaveValue) directly in production frontend source. Anyone who loads the client bundle (whether or not they are meant to be doing the 'Login Jim' training exercise) can read this file and obtain a ready-to-use credential-bypass string for a specific victim account. Because the mechanism being defeated is the login/password-verification decision itself, this also changes who the application believes the caller is — the anchor pattern for an authentication-bypass finding — and the design provides no compensating control (e.g., restricting the hint content to users who have already legitimately solved a prerequisite, or gating disclosure of the working payload behind server-side verification of intent) before revealing a payload that grants access to another user's account.

Clicking #loginButton with the injected email submits the bypass to the (external) login endpoint, resulting in successful authentication as Jim without any valid password — confirmed by the success message at line 100.

title: Attack walkthrough against a named victim account is exposed to any client with no authorization or audience restriction
description: The instructional content in this file (which product-review-based email harvesting to use for account takeover, per line 46) is embedded as ordinary exported data in the production frontend source rather than being restricted to an authorized training context. Nothing in this file establishes that only users who are permitted to perform this exercise (e.g., in an isolated test/training deployment) can access these step-by-step account-takeover instructions; as authored, the object is unconditionally exported and available to whatever consumer loads it, with no per-user or per-role check gating disclosure of the exploit technique against a specific victim identity ('Jim'). This is analogous to a diagnostic/training capability left enabled without restriction in a production-facing bundle, and it also reflects an access-control gap in that the mechanism grants procedural access to another user's account (Jim's) with no verification that the requester is authorized to assume that identity.

title: Basket ownership determined by client-controlled sessionStorage 'bid' value enables Horizontal Privilege Escalation (BOLA)
description: This file is the in-app instructor for the 'View Basket' challenge, and it explicitly documents (and validates as the intended solution) an access-control flaw in the target application: the identifier used to determine which shopping basket to display ('bid') is stored client-side in sessionStorage and is trusted by the application when the basket view is subsequently loaded. The instructions walk the user through reading the current 'bid' from sessionStorage (line 59), waiting/polling until that stored value is observed to change (lines 61-64, confirming the write actually took effect client-side and is what the app will read next), being told to overwrite it with an arbitrary value from the browser DevTools (line 55), then navigating away and back to the basket view (line 76) so the app re-reads the tampered identifier, polling until the displayed 'itemTotal' changes to prove different basket data was loaded as a direct consequence of the client-supplied 'bid' (lines 81, 83, 86) — without any server-side check that the authenticated user actually owns the basket referenced by that ID. The design flaw is that the server derives which basket to render from a value that originates from, and can be freely modified by, the client, rather than deriving/verifying the basket-to-user mapping server-side from the authenticated session. This is both a textbook Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) issue — a resource identifier supplied by the caller is used to fetch another user's data without an ownership check — and an insecure design issue, since the design never establishes a rule that the basket ID must belong to the current session's authenticated user; trusting a client-held identifier as sufficient authorization is the flaw itself, not just a missing input check. The hint content explicitly confirms successful exploitation: 'Congratulations! You are now viewing another user's shopping basket!' (line 92).

trace.description: Client-side code reads the basket identifier 'bid' from sessionStorage — a value that is attacker/browser-controllable and not cryptographically bound to the authenticated session.
Instruction explicitly guides overwriting the session-stored 'bid' key to 'a different value', demonstrating that this client-held identifier is mutable and used to select which basket is displayed.

After navigating away and back to the basket view, the code waits for 'itemTotal' in sessionStorage to change, confirming the app re-fetches basket contents keyed by the tampered 'bid' without an intervening ownership check (the actual fetch/authorization logic lives outside this file, in the basket route handler / service the app calls when the basket view loads).

The resolved() handler compares the live sessionStorage 'bid' value against the originally captured one, gating progression on the value having been changed — confirming the app treats whatever is currently stored in 'bid' as the active basket reference.

The handler polls via sleep(100) until the change is detected, actively waiting for the attacker's overwritten 'bid' to be in place before letting the tutorial (and by extension the app's basket-loading flow) proceed.
Instruction directs the user to navigate to any other screen and then back to 'Your Basket', forcing the application to re-fetch basket data using the now-tampered 'bid' value from sessionStorage.

The handler compares the current 'itemTotal' to the previously captured value, using a change in displayed total as proof that a different (non-owned) basket's contents were successfully loaded and rendered with no ownership check having blocked it.
The handler again polls via sleep(100) until the itemTotal changes, waiting for confirmation that the foreign basket's data has been served to the attacker's session.

The challenge is marked resolved once another user's basket contents are displayed to the attacker's own authenticated session, confirming the missing per-resource ownership check (BOLA) enabled by trusting the client-supplied basket ID (insecure design).

title: Score Board page protected only by 'security through obscurity' (unauthenticated, unlinked route)
description: This file is the in-app tutorial ('hacking-instructor') that walks a user through discovering the application's Score Board page. The hint text itself documents the actual security control (or lack thereof) protecting this sensitive internal page: it is not protected by authentication or authorization, and its only 'protection' is that no link to it exists in the navigation or sidebar (lines 22-23). The tutorial then walks the user through progressively more concrete discovery steps: first telling them to guess the URL or comb through client-side JavaScript (lines 28-29), then narrowing this to inspecting the DevTools Sources tab or continuing URL guessing (lines 34-35, gated on waitForDevTools() at line 37), then explicitly restating the same guidance a final time (line 40) as an unskippable step (line 43, unskippable: true) whose completion condition is simply that the Angular route 'score-board' was visited (line 44) — with no indication anywhere in this flow of an authorization check gating that navigation. This is a textbook insecure design: a page that exposes sensitive internal state (which security challenges/vulnerabilities have been solved on this instance — effectively a diagnostic/monitoring surface) is reachable by any unauthenticated user who guesses the URL or reads the client bundle, because the design relies on obscurity (absence of a nav link, requiring DevTools/URL discovery) rather than an actual access-control check. Since routing tables, JS bundles, and network requests are all attacker-visible, this 'protection' provides no real security boundary. The actual vulnerable route/component is not present in this file (it is defined elsewhere, e.g., the Angular routing module), so this file is used here as documentary evidence of the design decision and the entrypoint into the exposed page; the concrete authorization gap in the route handler itself cannot be directly confirmed from this file alone.

Hint explicitly states there is no link to the Score Board in the navigation or side bar — the only 'defense' is that the route is unlinked, not that it requires authorization.

Third hint instructs the user to start guessing the Score Board URL directly.
Same hint continues, alternatively instructing the user to comb through client-side JavaScript code for the route information — confirming the route/path is discoverable from the shipped JS bundle.
Third hint's completion condition (waitInMs) simply advances the tutorial after a delay, with no check that any authorization boundary was crossed during discovery.
Fourth hint tells the user the JavaScript code can be found in browser DevTools via F12, further operationalizing the client-side discovery path.
Hint text continues, directing the user into the DevTools interface to locate the route.
Fourth hint's completion condition is merely that DevTools was opened (waitForDevTools()) — again no authorization check, just confirmation the discovery tool was used.

Fifth hint restates the guidance to look through client-side JavaScript in the Sources tab or continue URL guessing, reinforcing that this is the sanctioned/expected discovery method rather than a flaw the app tries to prevent.

This step is marked unskippable: true, meaning the tutorial forces the user through this URL-guessing/JS-inspection discovery path as the canonical way to reach the Score Board, cementing that obscurity (not access control) is the intended barrier.

The final challenge-completion condition is simply that the Angular route 'score-board' was visited (waitForAngularRouteToBeVisited('score-board')), confirming that direct client-side navigation to the route succeeds with no authorization gate visible in this tutorial's model of the flow.

title: Bootstrap failures only logged to browser console, no security monitoring/reporting
description: The Angular application bootstrap process (bootstrapApplication) is the single entrypoint for the entire SPA. Its failure handler at line 130 does nothing but console.log(err) the error object. This is the only error-handling path visible for a catastrophic failure of the application's initialization (which could be caused by a malicious script injection, tampered dependency, CSP violation, or a compromised interceptor/guard failing to load). Because the error is only written to the local browser console, there is no telemetry, alerting, or centralized logging of this security-relevant event — an operator has no way to detect that clients are failing to bootstrap (e.g., due to an attack on the delivery pipeline or a supply-chain compromise of one of the many imported modules) unless a user manually reports it. There is also no correlation ID or user context attached to the log, making any post-hoc investigation impossible even if a user did share their console output.

trace.description: bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, providers) is invoked as the top-level entrypoint of the SPA; this call can reject if provider construction or module initialization fails.

The provider array (many Angular Material modules, guards, and application services) is passed to bootstrapApplication; any failure anywhere in this large dependency graph surfaces as a rejected promise.
The providers option object is opened; every entry inside it is a candidate point of failure that will ultimately surface only through the single catch at the end of the chain.

importProvidersFrom(...) pulls in dozens of Angular Material and third-party modules (Routing, TranslateModule, CookieModule, FileUploadModule, etc.); failure of any one propagates up through the same unmonitored path.
provideHttpClient(withInterceptorsFromDi()) configures the HTTP client stack used for all backend communication; misconfiguration or failure here also funnels into the same unlogged catch.
provideTranslateService({...}) begins configuring the translate loader with a remote-fetched asset prefix; a failure loading translation config is likewise only caught generically at the end.
The providers array is closed, completing the full set of dependency-injection configuration whose failure is funneled to a single generic handler.
.catch((err: Error) => console.log(err)) is the sole handling of a bootstrap failure — logged only to the local browser console with no remote logging, alerting, or monitoring integration.

title: Production hardening (enableProdMode) conditionally gated on externally-defined environment flag with no visible enforcement
description: Angular's production mode (which disables development-only checks, verbose error messages, and Angular DevTools hooks) is only enabled when environment.production is truthy (lines 77-79). The value of environment.production is defined in a separate file (./environments/environment) which is not visible here, and this file performs no independent validation that the correct environment file was used for the build. If a build pipeline misconfiguration or a wrong environment file substitution causes environment.production to be false in a production deployment, the application will run in development mode in production, exposing debugging information, enabling Angular DevTools introspection of internal component/service state (including potentially sensitive service data such as WalletService, AddressService, PaymentService), and increasing the client-side attack surface. This file offers no defense-in-depth (e.g., no build-time assertion, no runtime check reconciling the environment against the actual deployment) for this critical security-relevant configuration path.
