Only this i18n restoration branch logs anything, and only on failure (logger.warn); no branch logs a successful restoration, leaving no audit trail for a security-relevant remediation action.

title: One-time startup restoration is an insufficient compensating control for file-overwrite vulnerabilities
description: This function's entire purpose is to undo unauthorized modification of application files (legal.md, the promo video, i18n translation files) that other parts of the application allow to be overwritten (the naming 'restoreOverwrittenFilesWithOriginals' implies a known write-primitive elsewhere, e.g. path-traversal/zip-slip during upload). The design relies exclusively on restoring the known-good copies once, at process startup (called from restoreOverwrittenFilesWithOriginals()). There is no integrity check performed at request time, no periodic re-validation, and no detection of tampering while the process is running. Once the server has booted, an attacker who can re-trigger the underlying overwrite (a vulnerability presumably located in another file, e.g. the upload handlers referenced in the architecture summary) can overwrite these files again and they will remain compromised - served to every subsequent user - until the process is restarted. Treating a boot-time file copy as the security control for an ongoing overwrite primitive is a workflow/trust-boundary design gap: the server never re-derives or re-verifies the integrity of these files after the initial restore.

Function returns after the one-time restore; the application has no further mechanism (in this file) to detect or repair renewed tampering with these files while running.

title: Unguarded dictionary lookup on domain reachability failure can throw an unhandled exception and crash the process
description: checkIfDomainReachable(domain) assumes that whatever string is passed as `domain` is always a key present in the static `domainDependencies` map. Inside the catch block that handles a failed fetch(), the code does `domainDependencies[domain].dependentChallenges.forEach(...)` without first checking that `domainDependencies[domain]` is defined. Contrast this with the sibling function `checkIfEnvironmentVariableExists`, which does guard the equivalent lookup with `if (variableDependencies[varName])` before dereferencing it. If `checkIfDomainReachable` is ever invoked (now or by a future caller) with a domain string that is not one of the two static keys in `domainDependencies` (currently only 'https://www.alchemy.com/' and the value of application.chatBot.llmApiUrl at import time), the `.dependentChallenges` access throws a TypeError inside the catch block. Because there is no outer try/catch, this becomes an unhandled exception in an async function, which surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection at startup and can crash the whole process rather than fail gracefully like the rest of the precondition checks are designed to do. This is a trust assumption the design never enforces (the function signature accepts an arbitrary string but the implementation silently requires it to be a member of a fixed, narrow set of keys).

title: Outbound fetch to configuration-supplied LLM API URL and reusable domain-fetch helpers with no destination validation
description: checkIfDomainReachable and checkIfLlmModelAvailable are exported utility functions that take a raw URL/domain string and pass it directly into fetch() with no scheme allow-listing, no hostname allow-listing, and no check against internal/loopback/link-local address ranges (e.g. cloud metadata IPs). In this file they are invoked with the value returned by config.get('application.chatBot.llmApiUrl'), which is an externally overridable configuration value (Juice Shop's config layer supports environment-variable and config-file overrides). Nothing in this file validates that llmApiUrl points to an intended external LLM provider rather than an internal service (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/ or http://localhost:<admin-port>/). The value flows unchanged through a conditional gate and a second function call before reaching a second unvalidated fetch, so every hop preserves the lack of validation rather than introducing one. Because these are generic, exported, unvalidated 'fetch this URL' helpers, any other part of the application (or a future caller) that passes attacker- or admin-influenced input into them would create a full SSRF primitive; even within this file, the missing origin validation on a configuration-controlled endpoint is a security-relevant gap consistent with the guidance that config-driven URLs used for outbound calls still need destination validation.

title: Config validation admits an unrestricted, unvalidated notification poll URL and unbounded poll frequency
description: checkForIllogicalCombos() is the only gate that runs before a systemWideNotifications configuration is accepted as valid at startup. When configuration.ctf.systemWideNotifications.url is present, the function only checks that pollFrequencySeconds exists, is a number, and is greater than zero (lines 178-182). It never validates the URL value itself: no scheme check, no host allow-list, no rejection of loopback/link-local/private-network/metadata addresses (e.g. 169.254.169.254). It also never enforces any upper bound (minimum interval) on the poll frequency — a value like 0.001 passes the '> 0' check. Because this is the designated security/sanity gate for this configuration block, its failure to constrain the destination and the polling rate is a design and configuration defect in its own right: the resulting boolean is folded straight into the overall startup success flag and, once true, the whole configuration — including the unrestricted URL and unbounded cadence — is logged and treated as fully validated, letting the rest of the application (and any client that polls this URL) act on it unrestricted. If this configuration block can be influenced by anything other than a fully-trusted static ops file (the codebase exposes a YAML/config file-upload route elsewhere in server.ts per the architecture map), an attacker-influenced destination and polling rate would sail through this check unnoticed.

Closing of the validation block: when the (weak) checks pass, execution falls through with success still true — no rejection path exists for a bad URL or an unreasonably tight frequency.

title: Unsanitized configuration-derived strings written directly into security log lines (log forging)
description: Several validation routines interpolate free-form string fields taken directly from the products/memories configuration objects into logger.warn() calls, wrapped only in an ANSI-coloring helper (colors.italic / colors.red), with no escaping of control characters (newlines, carriage returns, ANSI escape sequences). checkUniqueSpecialOnProducts (lines 103-113) logs product.name verbatim; checkUniqueSpecialOnMemories (lines 151-161) logs memory.caption verbatim; checkSpecialMemoriesHaveNoUserAssociated (line 144) logs a memory.user value verbatim. These fields are ordinary display-name/caption strings sourced from the configuration store (config.get('products') / config.get('memories'), lines 27-28), which is exactly the kind of free-form text field that a log-forging attack abuses: an entry containing embedded newlines or ANSI sequences can fabricate fake log lines or corrupt terminal/log-viewer output, undermining the integrity of the security log stream used to detect configuration tampering. If the underlying configuration objects can be influenced by anything other than a fully-trusted static file (the wider application exposes a YAML config-upload route per the architecture map), this becomes directly attacker-reachable; even absent that, it is a control gap in how this file writes untrusted-shaped data to logs.

title: Startup validator trusts configuration store contents without verifying provenance, including fields tied to security-relevant behavior
description: This file's entire design is to gate startup on the assumption that config.get('products'), config.get('memories'), and config.util.toObject() represent a trusted, operator-authored configuration (lines 26-28, 54, 163). The validator checks internal consistency (uniqueness, required keys, illogical combinations) but never checks where the configuration values originated. The wider application (per the provided architecture) exposes a route that accepts uploaded YAML/config-like files (handleYamlUpload). If that upload path is capable of contributing to the same configuration namespace this file reads from, the trust boundary this validator relies on — 'this data comes from a static, ops-controlled file' — no longer holds, and every check in this file (including the URL/poll-frequency check discussed separately) is validating attacker-reachable data as if it were operator data, without any provenance or integrity check. This is reported as an insecure-design gap in this file rather than a proven exploit, because the merge/upload code path itself is outside this file and not directly observable here.

title: Intentional XXE: external entity substitution and filesystem access enabled in XML parser
description: parseXmlString() parses caller-supplied XML using libxml2-wasm with XML_PARSE_NOENT (substitute entities) and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD (load external DTDs) both enabled, and loadLibxml2() explicitly calls xmlRegisterFsInputProviders() to grant the WASM sandbox host filesystem access specifically so that external entities such as file:///etc/passwd resolve. The code comments confirm this is deliberate ('intentionally vulnerable to XXE'). Because the function accepts an arbitrary string and applies no schema restriction, entity allow-listing, or disabling of external/network entity resolution, any caller that forwards untrusted XML (e.g., an uploaded file, imported data, or API body) into parseXmlString allows an attacker to embed a DOCTYPE with a SYSTEM entity pointing at a local file or (depending on transport support) an internal URL, and have its contents substituted into the returned document text (line 39's toString() surfaces the resolved entity content back to the caller). This is a textbook XXE injection: attacker-controlled XML content is interpreted by the parser as directives that read host filesystem contents, and the vulnerable configuration is a security misconfiguration deliberately baked into the parser defaults with no safe fallback, making it also an insecure design choice (no compensating control such as sanitization, allow-listing of DOCTYPE, or restricting resolvable URI schemes exists anywhere in this exported function).

loadLibxml2() dynamically imports libxml2-wasm's Node.js filesystem input providers.

The IIFE returns the loaded libxml2 module (with filesystem entity resolution now globally enabled) to be cached and reused for every future parseXmlString call.
loadLibxml2 resolves libxml2Promise and hands the libxml2 module back to parseXmlString, which will use it to parse the untrusted `data`.
The tainted call awaits loadLibxml2(), pulling in the WASM parser and its filesystem-access setup before any parsing of `data` occurs.
The tainted `data` string and the XXE-enabling `option` bitmask are bundled together into the vm sandbox object that will be handed to the parser.
vm.createContext(sandbox) materialises the execution context carrying the untrusted `data` and unsafe `option` flags into scope for the parse call.

vm.runInContext executes XmlDocument.fromString(data, { option }), parsing the attacker-controlled XML with entity substitution and external DTD loading active; any SYSTEM/external entity in `data` is resolved against the filesystem and its content becomes part of the parsed document, later returned via xmlDoc.toString() at line 39.

title: Entity-expansion (billion-laughs) DoS mitigated only by wall-clock timeout, not by memory/expansion limits
description: The comment at lines 29-32 acknowledges the entity-expansion bomb risk from enabling XML_PARSE_NOENT and attempts to mitigate it purely via a vm.runInContext timeout (default 2000ms). A vm timeout only interrupts JavaScript execution at safepoints; it does not bound the memory or CPU already consumed by the underlying native/WASM libxml2 call before the call returns control to JS, and does not cap the depth or ratio of entity expansion during parsing. An attacker-controlled XML payload with a nested entity-expansion bomb (e.g., classic 'billion laughs') can therefore still cause severe memory exhaustion or a long, uninterruptible native computation inside the single vm.runInContext call before any timeout has a chance to act, since XmlDocument.fromString itself is the operation being timed and may not yield until it completes or the process is starved. There is no compensating control here such as a maximum entity expansion count, maximum node/document size limit, or streaming parse with resource caps — the design relies solely on a coarse timer around an operation whose resource consumption isn't otherwise bounded.

XML_PARSE_NOENT enables entity substitution, the mechanism entity-expansion bombs abuse to cause exponential memory growth.

title: No security logging around XXE-capable XML parsing

If an attacker attempts to exfiltrate local files through XXE, or repeatedly probes with entity-expansion payloads, there is no log entry produced by this file to detect or later investigate the attempt. This is a straightforward absence of security-relevant event logging for an operation that is explicitly documented (in the surrounding comments) as high-risk.

vm.createContext(sandbox) sets up the parse execution with no correlation ID or request-tracing hook that would let a later investigation tie this parse back to a specific request/user.

The XML is parsed with XXE-enabling options and no logging (success, failure, or entity-resolution events) is emitted anywhere in this function, leaving no audit trail of potentially malicious XXE payloads or expansion-bomb timeouts.

title: Unvalidated webhook destination passed directly to outbound fetch (SSRF / caller-controlled destination)
description: The exported `notify` function accepts a `webhook` parameter that defaults to `process.env.SOLUTIONS_WEBHOOK` but can be overridden by any caller. This value is passed directly into `fetch()` with no validation of scheme, host, or IP range (no allow-list, no check against private/internal address ranges or cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254). If any code path in the application (now or in the future) passes a caller/user-influenced value into this parameter, the server will make an outbound POST request — carrying internal telemetry (hostname, OS version, app name, NODE_ENV, application version) — to an attacker-chosen destination. Even restricted to the env-var default, the design establishes no compensating control (origin allow-listing) around what is effectively an outbound HTTP client with a variable target, which is the design gap this playbook flags: the function trusts the destination without ever validating or re-deriving it server-side.

webhook value is used unmodified as the fetch target URL, with no scheme/host/IP validation or allow-list check.
The only gate on webhook is `if (!webhook) return` — a presence check, not a validation of scheme, host, or origin; any non-empty string is allowed through unmodified.

title: Outbound webhook request has no timeout/abort control
description: The fetch() call to the webhook endpoint has no AbortController/timeout configured anywhere in its options object (method, headers, and body are set, but no `signal` or timeout mechanism). If the configured (or caller-supplied) webhook host is slow, unresponsive, or intentionally stalls the connection, the awaited fetch will hang indefinitely, tying up the request-handling context. Since notify() is invoked on challenge-solve events, a slow or malicious webhook target can be used to accumulate hanging outbound connections/resources over repeated challenge solves, degrading server responsiveness.

title: Unhandled fetch failures for security-relevant webhook notification are not logged
description: There is no try/catch around the fetch() call. If the webhook URL is malformed, the DNS lookup fails, the connection is refused, or the TLS handshake fails, the promise rejects and propagates as an unhandled exception rather than being logged. This is a security-relevant event (a solution/telemetry webhook delivery failure) that goes completely unrecorded, preventing operators from detecting delivery failures, misconfiguration, or an attacker interfering with webhook delivery (e.g., DNS poisoning/blocking). The only logging present (line 40) assumes the fetch resolved successfully to a Response object and is never reached on rejection.

title: Webhook URL (potentially containing embedded secret tokens) logged in plaintext
description: The full webhook URL is written to the application log at info level via `colors.bold(webhook)`. Many real-world webhook integrations (e.g., Slack/Discord/Teams incoming webhooks) embed a secret authorization token directly in the URL path or query string. Logging the entire URL string means that secret is persisted in plaintext application logs, exposing it to anyone with log access and increasing the blast radius if logs are later exposed or exfiltrated.

title: SSRF and unbounded resource consumption via unrestricted URL fetch in downloadToFile
description: downloadToFile(url, dest) accepts a URL from a caller and passes it directly to the `download` npm package with no destination allow-listing, no protocol restriction beyond what an upstream caller might apply, no response-size cap, and no timeout, then writes the entire response body to disk. Per the routing architecture, this function backs the unauthenticated route POST /profile/image/url (profileImageUrlUpload), which lets any unauthenticated caller supply an arbitrary URL to be fetched server-side. The only related validation helper in this file, isUrl(), merely checks that the string begins with the substring 'http' via startsWith(url,'http'), which itself is implemented as str.indexOf(prefix) === 0 — a pure prefix check with no host/origin comparison. This is satisfied equally by http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, http://localhost/admin, or any other internal/private-network target — it is not an SSRF allow-list. Because download() buffers the fetched response fully before it is written with fs.writeFileSync inside the function's try block, an attacker can also point the URL at a very large or slow endless response to exhaust server memory/disk, causing denial of service.

isUrl() only checks that the string starts with 'http' — a weak scheme-only check, not a host/origin allow-list, so internal or metadata-service URLs pass identically to legitimate ones.
await download(url) performs an outbound HTTP(S) request to the fully attacker-controlled URL with no destination restriction, no size limit, and no timeout.
isUrl(url) is the exported validation helper a caller would use to gate this URL before invoking downloadToFile; it forwards the value into startsWith rather than performing any host validation.
startsWith is implemented as str.indexOf(prefix) === 0, confirming the check only inspects the first characters of the URL string and cannot distinguish public from internal/metadata hosts.

fs.writeFileSync(dest, data) writes the entire fetched response — of unbounded size — to disk, completing both the SSRF request and the unbounded resource consumption.

title: Unsanitized filename extraction (extractFilename) enables path traversal when used to build a file-write destination
description: extractFilename(url) takes the substring of a caller-supplied URL after the last '/', URL-decodes it, and strips a trailing query string, returning the raw result with no sanitization against directory-traversal sequences ('../'), absolute-path prefixes, or null bytes. This function is exported and, given it operates on the same kind of URL accepted by profileImageUrlUpload/downloadToFile in this file, is a plausible source for the filename component of a destination path passed to downloadToFile's `dest` parameter. If a caller (outside this file) builds `dest` by joining an upload directory with this decoded filename, a URL such as .../..%2f..%2f..%2fserver%2fviews%2fevil.ejs would decode to a path-traversal filename, letting fs.writeFileSync (line 117) write the downloaded content outside the intended upload directory — an arbitrary file write.

title: CTF flag integrity relies on SHA-1 HMAC and a statically-loaded fallback key
description: ctfFlag(text) signs challenge-completion text with HMAC-SHA1 using a key resolved by getCtfKey(): it prefers process.env.CTF_KEY but, when that is unset, falls back to synchronously reading a fixed relative file path 'ctf.key' and caching it for the process lifetime. If CTF_KEY is not configured per-deployment (the common case for default installs), every instance uses the same shipped key file, meaning anyone who can read or already knows the default key material can forge a valid HMAC for arbitrary challenge text without ever exercising the corresponding vulnerability — subverting the flag mechanism's purpose of proving a challenge was actually solved. SHA-1 is also a deprecated digest algorithm; while HMAC-SHA1 is not broken by SHA-1 collision attacks, pairing a deprecated primitive with a potentially non-unique/default key compounds the weakness of this integrity check.

title: Unbounded in-memory accumulation in parseJsonCustom with no size or depth limits
description: parseJsonCustom(jsonString) feeds a caller-supplied string directly into a clarinet streaming JSON parser and accumulates one entry per key/value event into an in-memory array with no cap on string length, key count, or nesting depth. If this exported helper is reachable from an endpoint that accepts user-controlled JSON text, an attacker can submit an extremely large or highly repetitive payload (e.g., millions of keys) to drive unbounded memory and CPU consumption during parsing and array accumulation, causing degraded service or an outage.

title: BOLA: Address CRUD lacks per-user ownership scoping
description: The Address model exposes a UserId foreign key and a primary key id, and per the architecture context, the auto-generated CRUD surface (/api/Addresss, /api/Addresss/:id, with pagination) reads/updates/deletes Address records by their id. Nothing in this file enforces that lookups, updates, or deletes are scoped to the UserId of the currently authenticated caller. If the auto-generated route layer performs a plain findByPk/update/destroy on `id` (which is the typical behavior of such generic CRUD scaffolding), any authenticated user can access, modify, or delete another user's shipping address simply by supplying a different numeric id — a classic BOLA. The model itself provides no ownership-check hook (e.g., no scope, no beforeFind/beforeUpdate hook comparing UserId to the session user) to compensate for a route layer that might be missing this check.

title: Mass assignment of UserId enables address ownership takeover
description: The Address model exposes UserId as a directly-writable attribute alongside all other user-supplied fields (fullName, mobileNum, zipCode, streetAddress, city, state, country). There is no explicit allow-list or exclude-list configured in this file to prevent UserId from being set via a caller-controlled create/update payload. If the auto-generated CRUD route for /api/Addresss binds the request body directly to Address.create()/update() (the typical behavior for such generic scaffolding), an attacker can include a `UserId` field in the request body pointing at another user's id, either creating an address record falsely attributed to another user, or updating an existing address's UserId to reassign it — enabling account/data confusion, spoofed order records, or worse, taking over another user's address by rewriting the UserId on an address record they can otherwise reach.

title: Design never derives address ownership server-side
description: The business rule that an address belongs to exactly one user and can only be created/managed by that user is never enforced anywhere in this model. UserId is treated identically to any other attribute (fullName, city, etc.) rather than being a trust-boundary field that the server must derive from the authenticated session rather than accept from the client. This is a design gap, not just a missing check: even if a single validation were added elsewhere, the model provides no structural mechanism (hook, scope, immutable field) to guarantee that UserId always reflects the true owner, so any future code path that persists an Address using client-supplied data will silently reproduce the same flaw.

title: Free-text address fields persisted without sanitization (stored XSS risk)

These fields commonly get rendered later in address lists, order confirmations, invoices, or admin views. If any downstream template renders these values without context-appropriate escaping, an attacker can store a payload like `<script>` in fullName or streetAddress that executes when viewed by the address owner or, worse, by an administrator reviewing orders/complaints. The rendering sink is outside this file, but the persistence point that accepts unsanitized free-form text is here.

title: BasketItem model lacks ownership scoping, enabling BOLA via auto-generated CRUD routes
description: The BasketItem model defines only ProductId, BasketId, id and quantity (lines 19-22) with no user-ownership field and no hook or association constraint that ties a BasketItem to the currently authenticated user. The architecture notes this model is exposed through an auto-generated CRUD REST surface at /api/BasketItems and /api/BasketItems/:id. Because the model itself carries no owner reference and defines no per-instance authorization logic, any authenticated user who knows or guesses a BasketItem id can read, update, or delete a record belonging to a different user's basket via the :id route, since the generic CRUD layer performs lookups by primary key (id) without an application-level 'does this basket belong to me' check baked into the model. This is a textbook BOLA: authentication does not imply per-resource authorization, and the missing ownership check has to live somewhere — it clearly is not enforced here.

title: Mass-assignable BasketId allows injecting items into another user's basket
description: BasketId is defined as a plain INTEGER attribute (lines 31-33) with no restriction on which values a client may supply when creating or updating a BasketItem. If the auto-generated CRUD create/update route (POST/PUT /api/BasketItems, /api/BasketItems/:id) binds request body fields directly onto the model — the standard behavior for this kind of scaffolding — an attacker can set BasketId to a value belonging to a different user's basket, effectively adding products to (or modifying quantities within) someone else's shopping basket. The model provides no allow-list or read-only marking that would prevent BasketId from being caller-controlled; the server should instead derive BasketId from the authenticated user's own session-associated basket rather than trusting the client-submitted value.

If this value flows into checkout/price-calculation logic elsewhere in the application (quantity * unit price), a negative quantity submitted through the mass-assignable create/update CRUD endpoint could reduce or invert the computed basket total, and an unbounded large quantity could cause integer overflow or inventory-logic abuse. The design never establishes an enforced bound on this business-critical quantity value at the point where it enters the system, leaving that invariant entirely to code outside this file (or nowhere at all).

title: UserId is a freely-assignable model attribute enabling basket ownership hijacking (mass assignment)
description: The Basket model declares UserId as a plain CreationOptional<number> attribute (line 21) and configures it in Basket.init as an ordinary INTEGER column (lines 36-38) with no restriction, default-value derivation from session, or allow-list annotation anywhere in the model. Any caller elsewhere in the application that persists a basket by spreading request-body fields into Basket.create()/Basket.update() (a common Sequelize pattern) will happily accept an attacker-supplied UserId value, because the model itself provides no barrier. This allows an authenticated attacker to create or reassign a basket to point at another user's UserId, or to hijack an existing basket by updating its UserId, leading to basket/coupon takeover and potential viewing or manipulation of another user's shopping basket. Because the model does not mark UserId as a derived/server-only field (e.g., via a setter guard or omission from allowed init attributes), the ORM layer treats it identically to any other caller-controllable column. The class generic binds UserId into both InferAttributes and InferCreationAttributes, the Basket.init call wires the field into the schema's argument object, and the exported symbol is what makes this configuration reachable from any importer.

title: Basket model provides no ownership-scoping mechanism for per-user resource isolation
description: The Basket model's primary key (id, auto-incrementing integer, lines 30-34) is the only lookup key defined in this file. There is no default scope, class-level helper method, or association constraint in this model that ties a basket lookup to the currently authenticated user's UserId. Because basket ids are sequential and globally unique (not partitioned per-user), any code elsewhere that resolves a basket purely by primary key (e.g., Basket.findByPk(id) driven by a route parameter) will return a basket belonging to any user, not just the caller, unless an ownership check is added at the call site every single time. The model itself establishes no structural guarantee against this: the options object passed to Basket.init (lines 40-43) only sets tableName and the sequelize instance — it contains no defaultScope or scopes option that could have enforced a UserId filter at the model level — which is a design-level gap. The natural, most convenient way to query this model (by id alone) is also the unsafe way, and the model provides no safer alternative.

title: CAPTCHA answer persisted in plaintext with no expiry or one-time-use control
description: The Captcha model stores the challenge text (`captcha`) and its solution (`answer`) side-by-side as plain STRING columns (lines 19-20, 29-30), with no hashing/salting of the answer and no field tracking whether a given captcha has already been solved/consumed or when it expires. A CAPTCHA is a security control meant to prove a human solved a one-time visual challenge; persisting the answer in cleartext in the same row as the challenge, without any expiration or 'used' flag in the schema, means (a) any code path anywhere in the application that reads this table (an admin tool, a backup, a debug export, or a bug in another file that queries Captchas) discloses the plaintext solution, and (b) nothing in the schema itself prevents the same captchaId/answer pair from being validated repeatedly (replay), because there is no consumption state stored at all. This is a design gap visible directly in the model definition: the schema never establishes the invariant 'an answer, once verified, cannot be reused,' so no amount of correct handler logic elsewhere can enforce that invariant without extending this schema.

title: Card model exposed via auto-generated CRUD with no ownership scoping and writable UserId (BOLA + Mass Assignment)
description: The Card Sequelize model defines UserId as a plain, freely-writable INTEGER attribute (line 18, 29-31) alongside the payment fields (fullName, cardNum, expMonth, expYear). Per the architecture context, this model is exposed via an auto-generated CRUD surface at /api/Cards and /api/Cards/:id (both paginated), which is the classic finale-rest style scaffolding used elsewhere in this codebase. Because the model itself contains no ownership-scoping hook (no default scope, no beforeFind/beforeUpdate hook restricting rows to req.user.id, no attribute-level restriction on UserId), two exploitable conditions exist: (1) BOLA - any authenticated user can request GET /api/Cards/:id for an id belonging to a different user (the id primary key defined at line 19 is the identifier the generated per-record route keys off of) and receive that user's full card record, because nothing in this file (or presumably the generated controller) filters the lookup by the caller's own UserId; (2) Mass assignment - because UserId is a normal writable attribute with no allow-list/exclude configuration, a POST or PUT to the auto-generated endpoint can set UserId directly, letting an attacker associate a forged/stolen card to another user's account or hijack an existing card record's ownership. The controller/route wiring that would perform the ownership check is outside this file, but the model provides no compensating control of its own, and the field itself is designed to be caller-writable through the entire registration pipeline from Card.init() through to model export.

title: Unrestricted mass-assignment of pricing fields on Delivery model

title: Mass-assignable CAPTCHA answer and UserId fields enable verification bypass and BOLA
description: The ImageCaptcha Sequelize model declares 'answer' (the secret value a user must submit to pass the CAPTCHA) and 'UserId' (the association that ties a CAPTCHA challenge to the account it was issued for) as ordinary, unrestricted model attributes (lines 20-22, 34-36). Sequelize models exposed this way allow any caller that invokes Model.create()/update()/build() with a raw object (e.g., derived directly from req.body in a route handler outside this file) to set every declared attribute, including 'answer' and 'UserId', unless the call site explicitly passes a 'fields' allow-list. Because this model file defines no restriction, no virtual/read-only marking, and no hook (beforeCreate/beforeValidate) that strips or re-derives these fields server-side, a caller that persists a new ImageCaptcha record from untrusted input could set the 'answer' field to a value of their choosing (potentially self-supplying the answer they will later submit, defeating the purpose of the CAPTCHA) or set 'UserId' to an arbitrary user id (associating a captcha challenge/answer with a victim account rather than the caller's own session, an object-level authorization violation). The full path runs from the class's attribute declarations, through every field registered in ImageCaptcha.init (none of which are marked read-only or excluded from mass assignment), through the model options that bind the attributes to the 'ImageCaptchas' table, to the final export that hands the unrestricted model to any external caller. The actual route handler that calls into this model is outside this file, so the exploitability depends on how the caller constructs the create/update payload, but the model itself provides no defense-in-depth against this class of misuse at any point along that path.

While CAPTCHA answers are lower-value secrets than passwords, storing them in cleartext with no built-in expiry mechanism at the model layer is a design choice that removes a compensating control (short-lived, non-reusable secrets) that would otherwise limit the blast radius of a data exposure.

title: Database query logging disabled, eliminating SQL-level audit trail
description: The Sequelize connection is initialized with `logging: false` (line 42), which globally suppresses all query logging for every model operation performed through this connection (all CRUD operations across Users, Products, Complaints, SecurityAnswers, Wallets, Cards, etc. — i.e., every table in the application). In the event of a suspected SQL injection, account takeover, or data exfiltration incident, responders have no query-level trail to reconstruct what was actually executed against the database, only whatever the application layer chose to log elsewhere (if anything). This is a design decision baked into the shared DB client construction, not a per-call omission.

title: Mass assignment of UserId allows forging feedback under another user's identity
description: The Feedback model declares a `UserId` attribute (line 23) as a plain nullable INTEGER with no `set()` override, no allow-list restriction, and no derivation from the authenticated session — unlike the `comment` and `rating` fields, which both have custom `set()` interceptors. This model backs the auto-generated CRUD routes `POST /api/Feedbacks` and `PUT /api/Feedbacks/:id` (outside this file). If those routes bind the request body directly onto the model (the standard behavior for this codebase's auto-CRUD surface), a caller can include an arbitrary `UserId` value in the JSON body and have it persisted verbatim, letting User A submit feedback that is attributed to User B, or spoof feedback as an admin/other account.

title: Stored comment field defaults to weaker sanitization (sanitizeSecure) unless a specific challenge flag is enabled
description: The `comment` field's Sequelize `set()` interceptor (lines 41-49) chooses between two sanitization functions based on a runtime feature/challenge flag: `security.sanitizeHtml(comment)` is used only when `utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.persistedXssFeedbackChallenge)` is true; otherwise the normal/default code path uses `security.sanitizeSecure(comment)`. The security posture of a persisted, user-controlled free-text field (`comment`) is thus determined by an external, potentially attacker-influenced or environment-dependent flag rather than by a single robust sanitizer applied unconditionally. If `sanitizeSecure` is a weaker/legacy sanitizer (as historically in this codebase, e.g. simple tag-stripping regex rather than a full HTML sanitizer), attacker-supplied comment text can persist HTML/script payloads that later render as stored XSS wherever feedback comments are displayed (rendering sink is outside this file). Even setting aside the specific strength of `sanitizeSecure`, tying the sanitization strategy to a challenge-tracking flag rather than to a fixed, defense-in-depth-appropriate control is itself an insecure design choice for a field that is always attacker-controlled and always persisted.

title: Stored XSS: description sanitization bypassed when restfulXssChallenge is enabled
description: The `description` field's Sequelize setter conditionally skips output/input sanitization entirely. Even outside the specific challenge-toggle mechanism, the design pattern of gating a security control (sanitization) behind a runtime flag rather than enforcing it unconditionally is itself a design flaw — the safe path is opt-in, not the safe default.

title: No functional-level authorization boundary defined for inventory-altering fields, enabling stock/purchase-limit tampering
description: Inventory quantity and per-user purchase limits are business rules that should only ever be set by trusted server-side/admin logic (e.g., restocking, promotional limit changes). This model file defines no constraint, hook, or separation that prevents a regular authenticated (or, if the auto-CRUD route lacks auth, unauthenticated) user from directly setting an arbitrary quantity or nulling out limitPerUser (default is null, meaning 'no limit' — line 47) through the standard create/update path. An attacker could set a product's quantity artificially high to guarantee stock availability, or set limitPerUser to null/very high to defeat anti-hoarding / fair-purchase business logic elsewhere in the application that reads this field to cap checkout quantities. Because the model provides no economic invariant (e.g., quantity must be derived from stock movements, not set directly by API callers), the design itself permits inventory-value creation/manipulation if the wrapping route does not independently enforce admin-only access — which cannot be confirmed from this file and is a documented architecture concern (auto-generated CRUD routes for this model exist with no visible field restriction here).

title: quantity and limitPerUser lack minimum-value validation, permitting negative inventory/limit values
description: Both quantity (line 36-40) and limitPerUser (line 42-47) are validated only with Sequelize's isInt check. Neither enforces a lower bound (e.g., min: 0). If these fields are reachable by any write path (the auto-generated CRUD update endpoint for this model, or internal restock/order logic that trusts the persisted value), a negative quantity or negative limitPerUser can be persisted. Downstream business logic that treats quantity as a non-negative stock counter (e.g., decrementing on purchase, comparing against limitPerUser to gate checkout) may behave incorrectly when fed a negative value — for example, a negative quantity could make a decrement operation increase apparent stock, or a negative limitPerUser could be interpreted as 'no limit' by permissive comparison logic, defeating anti-hoarding checks. This is a design gap: the model is the single place where these invariants should be enforced (validate block) and it does not do so.

title: Mass assignment on UserId/AddressId enables creation of recycling requests under another user's identity
description: The Recycle model declares UserId and AddressId as plain, freely-settable attributes (lines 20-21, 30-35) with no allow-list, no default binding to the authenticated session, and no beforeCreate/beforeUpdate hook that forces UserId to equal the requesting user's own id. This model is the backing store for the auto-generated CRUD routes POST /api/Recycles and PUT /api/Recycles/:id (outside this file, in server.ts). Because the generic CRUD handler typically maps the entire request body onto the model's create/update call, a caller can supply an arbitrary UserId (impersonating another user) or an arbitrary AddressId (referencing another user's address) in the request body. The model provides no server-side control that would prevent this — the field is indistinguishable in the schema from any other caller-writable field. This is a textbook mass-assignment / object-property-level-authorization gap: nothing in this file stops the caller from setting a field (UserId) that should only ever be derived server-side from the authenticated session.

title: BOLA: Recycle records reachable by primary key with no ownership scoping (GET/PUT/DELETE /api/Recycles/:id)
description: The model exposes a numeric primary key id (lines 19, 36-40) and a UserId foreign key (line 20), but nothing in the model enforces that lookups be scoped to the owning user. The architecture indicates auto-generated CRUD routes GET /api/Recycles/:id, PUT /api/Recycles/:id, and DELETE /api/Recycles/:id exist (in server.ts, outside this file) that almost certainly resolve the record via a direct primary-key lookup (e.g., findByPk(id)). Since the model provides no scoped query helper, default scope, or hook that filters by the authenticated user's id, any authenticated user who can guess or enumerate another user's recycle id can read, modify (change quantity/pickup address/date), or delete that other user's recycling request — a classic BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) pattern. Two users (User A, User B): User A creates a recycle at id=5; User B can GET/PUT/DELETE /api/Recycles/5 by simply substituting the id, since the model has no per-record ownership check baked in and there is no visible external enforcement layer for this data.

title: Unscoped listing of all users' recycling requests via GET /api/Recycles
description: The Recycles table stores per-user records (UserId, AddressId, quantity, isPickup, date) but the model defines no defaultScope, no association-based restriction, and no field-level exclude/include list. Given the auto-generated CRUD route GET /api/Recycles (paginated) documented in the architecture, the natural behavior of a generic list handler backed by this model is to return all rows across all users, including their UserId and AddressId, to any authenticated (or possibly unauthenticated) caller. This leaks which users are recycling, their quantities, and which address records they use, without any per-user filtering enforced at the model layer — an access-control / insecure-design gap since the design never establishes a rule that recycle listings must be scoped to the requester.

title: Ownership foreign keys left updatable (mass-assignment reassignment) for sensitive models, unlike BasketItem
description: Nearly every belongsTo(UserModel) association in this file explicitly sets constraints: true and foreignKeyConstraint: true to enforce referential integrity at the database level (AddressModel 25-31, BasketModel 33-39, CardModel 49-55, ComplaintModel 57-63, MemoryModel 77-83, PrivacyRequestModel 85-91, RecycleModel 109-115, WalletModel 137-143). This is unlike FeedbackModel's identical omission at 65-69, which carries an explicit comment ('no FK constraint to allow anonymous feedback posts') showing that omission there is an intentional, reviewed exception — no such rationale exists for ImageCaptcha or SecurityAnswer. title: Security question lookup table fully mutable via unrestricted auto-generated CRUD
description: SecurityQuestion is a small, shared reference model (id, question) used to populate the list of security questions offered during registration and used later for the password-reset / forgot-password flow. The model is registered with Sequelize and exported for use by the application's generic REST CRUD layer (per the routing summary, /api/SecurityQuestions and /api/SecurityQuestions/:id are auto-generated CRUD endpoints backed by this model). Nothing in this file restricts which fields are writable or asserts that mutation of this table requires an elevated/admin role: the class declaration exposes 'id' and 'question' as plain attributes (lines 15, 19, 20), the init call (line 24) wires them into Sequelize with no lifecycle hook, the column definitions for both 'id' (lines 26-29) and 'question' (lines 31-33) carry no access-control metadata, and the model options block (lines 35, 37-39) only sets tableName and the sequelize connection — no scope, hook, or permission gate is attached anywhere in this construction. Because security questions are a security-relevant control (they gate account recovery), any actor able to reach the generic create/update/delete CRUD surface for this model (POST/PUT/DELETE /api/SecurityQuestions[/:id]) can insert new questions, rewrite existing ones, or delete questions relied upon by other users' account-recovery configuration, without the file establishing any ownership or role check. This is a function-level authorization gap: only listing/reading questions should plausibly be available broadly, while create/update/delete should be admin-only, but the model provides no such distinction, so protection depends entirely on the mount configuration outside this file.

title: Reflected XSS / injection via unsanitized URL embedded in Error message forwarded to error handler
description: The Angular client-serving middleware takes the raw request `url` (attacker-controlled path, including query string and any characters the client sends) and, for any path not starting with '/api' or '/rest', concatenates it directly into an Error object's message string: `new Error('Unexpected path: ' + url)`. This error is then passed to `next()`, which hands it off to Express's error-handling middleware (not present in this file). In OWASP Juice Shop and similarly structured Express apps, the downstream error handler commonly renders the error message into an HTML error page or JSON/HTML hybrid response without additional encoding. Because `url` is fully attacker-controlled (it can contain arbitrary characters including `<script>` tags, HTML entities, or quotes since Express does not restrict raw path/query content before this handler runs), an attacker can craft a request path such as `/<script>alert(1)</script>` or a query string designed to break out of the error page's markup, causing the error handler to reflect executable HTML/JS back to the victim's browser (reflected XSS) or, at minimum, leak the raw internal path structure verbatim in a diagnostic message (information disclosure). No sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing is applied to `url` before it is embedded into the Error message in this file. The control flow that lets the tainted value reach the sink is a simple two-way branch: if the url does not start with '/api' or '/rest' (line 13), the else branch (line 15) is entered unconditionally with no further checks, and the raw url is concatenated straight into the Error message (line 16) which is immediately forwarded via next() (line 16). The actual rendering/encoding behavior lives in the error-handling middleware, which is outside this file, so exploitability depends on how that handler emits the message — but this file introduces the tainted, unencoded string that reaches that sink.

Raw, unsanitized url is concatenated directly into a new Error's message string: 'Unexpected path: ' + url.
Because neither prefix matched, execution falls into the else branch with no intervening sanitization, transformation, or encoding of the tainted url value.

Tainted Error (carrying the raw url in its .message) is passed to next(), forwarding it to Express's error-handling middleware (outside this file) which likely renders the message into an HTML/diagnostic response without further encoding.

title: SecurityAnswers auto-generated CRUD exposes all users' security-question mappings without ownership scoping (BOLA)
description: The SecurityAnswer model exposes UserId, SecurityQuestionId and answer as plain, directly settable attributes with no allow-list or ownership guard defined in this file (lines 20-23, 29-47). If the auto-generated create/update handlers for /api/SecurityAnswers pass the request body straight into SecurityAnswer.create()/update() (the typical pattern for this app's auto-CRUD surface, confirmed by the architecture notes listing this model's CRUD routes), an attacker can supply an arbitrary UserId in the body rather than having it derived from the authenticated session. Because UserId only carries a uniqueness constraint (line 31) and not an ownership check, an attacker whose target has not yet registered a security answer can create one on the victim's behalf with an answer of the attacker's choosing, or - via PUT on a known/enumerated id - overwrite an existing answer belonging to another user. This directly compromises the security-question-based password recovery mechanism: the attacker later answers their own chosen question/answer during the victim's password reset flow to seize the account. This is a mass-assignment/API-property-authorization defect whose impact is specifically an authentication/account-recovery bypass.

title: Deterministic, unsalted HMAC of low-entropy security answers enables offline dictionary/rainbow-table attacks
description: The answer setter (lines 44-46) runs every security-question answer through security.hmac(answer) with no per-record salt or pepper visible at this call site, and no work-factor/iteration parameter (unlike a password-hashing KDF such as bcrypt/argon2/scrypt). Security-question answers are inherently low entropy (e.g., pet names, mother's maiden name) drawn from a small guessable space. Because the same plaintext answer always produces the same stored value for a given global HMAC key (no per-record randomness), an attacker who obtains the SecurityAnswers table (e.g., via the BOLA/list exposure described in the companion finding, or a database leak) can precompute HMAC values for common answer dictionaries once and match them across every user's row instantly, exactly as with unsalted password hashes. This differs from acceptable practice (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt with per-record salt and cost factor) and materially weakens the confidentiality of the recovery-answer store.

title: Wallet balance field is directly mass-assignable with no field-level protection
description: The Wallet Sequelize model declares balance (line 21, defined in init at lines 35-41) as a plain, fully writable integer attribute. There is no read-only marker, no exclusion from bulk attributes, and no application-level guard visible in this file that would prevent a caller-supplied value for balance from being written directly via Wallet.update(req.body, ...) or Wallet.create(req.body) in a controller outside this file. Juice Shop's wallet feature is intended to only change balance through recorded top-up/transaction operations, not by directly setting the stored balance value. Because the model itself provides no allow-list or protected-field mechanism, any code path elsewhere that spreads request body fields into a Wallet create/update call would let an attacker set their balance to an arbitrary value (including a very large positive number), which is a mass-assignment / broken object property level authorization risk as well as an insecure design issue (balance should be a derived/computed value from an immutable transaction ledger, not a directly settable column).

title: No lower-bound (non-negative) validation on wallet balance
description: The balance column is validated only with isInt: true (line 38); there is no min: 0 (or any other bound) constraint. The design intent of a wallet balance is that it should never go negative and should be conserved/only change through well-defined transaction operations. Because the model itself enforces no floor, any code path that decrements or sets balance (e.g., an order/payment deduction, or a direct update as described in the mass-assignment finding) can drive the balance below zero, or a caller who successfully reaches the balance field can set it to a negative number that still passes model validation. This is an insecure design gap: the invariant 'balance must never be negative' is a business rule this file is responsible for enforcing at the data layer, and it does not.

title: Admin application-configuration endpoint reachable without authentication (Broken Function Level Authorization)

title: Unauthenticated access to admin-labeled version disclosure endpoint
description: The route GET /rest/admin/application-version is registered with no authentication or authorization middleware (per the routing map) yet its path clearly signals an admin-only/internal operation. title: Broken Object Level Authorization on GET /rest/basket/:id — any user can read any other user's basket
description: The retrieveBasket handler takes the basket id directly from the URL path parameter and uses it as the sole lookup key against BasketModel with no check that the requesting user (or any authenticated identity at all) actually owns that basket. The route is registered with no authentication middleware ('auth: none'), and even if a session were present, the handler never compares the basket's owning UserId against the caller's identity before returning the full basket contents (including joined Product data) in the JSON response. This is the textbook BOLA pattern: an attacker can enumerate basket ids (they are typically small sequential integers) and retrieve the shopping basket contents — items, quantities, pricing exposure via nested Products — belonging to arbitrary other users, with zero authentication and zero ownership check. Because the route has no auth middleware at all, this is doubly severe: not only is there no per-object ownership check, there isn't even an authentication gate to identify who is asking. The path from the tainted id to the disclosed response runs unbroken through the lookup, the Products-existence check, and the per-product name translation loop — none of which introduce an ownership or authorization decision.

title: Excessively permissive TOTP time-window tolerance enables brute-force of 2FA codes
description: Both the 2FA login verification (verify) and the initial 2FA setup verification (setup) call otplib's verifySync with `epochTolerance: 30`. TOTP codes are normally valid for a single ~30s window plus at most one adjacent window (tolerance of 1). A tolerance of 30 time-steps extends the acceptance window to roughly ±15 minutes around the current time, meaning any of dozens of previously-valid or soon-to-be-valid 6-digit codes will be accepted as correct. This dramatically increases the number of guesses that will succeed within a given wall-clock period, and effectively multiplies the value of any brute-force attempt against the totpToken/initialToken parameter, since each guess is checked against ~60 valid codes instead of 1-3. Combined with the fact that the rate limiting applied to this route (visible only in the route registration, not in this file) is a simple 100-requests/5-minutes window rather than a hard lockout, an attacker with a valid tmpToken (obtained after supplying only the user's password) has a meaningfully higher chance of guessing a currently-accepted TOTP code than the algorithm's default security margin intends.

title: Disabling 2FA does not re-verify the second factor, allowing MFA to be defeated with password alone
description: The disable() handler treats disabling two-factor authentication — a highly sensitive operation that removes a security control the user opted into — as protected solely by a password re-entry check (`user.password !== security.hash(password)`). It never asks the caller to supply a current, valid TOTP code from the authenticator device, even though verify() (the login path) demonstrates the application knows how to check a TOTP token. Because the design never establishes 'possession of the second factor' as a requirement for turning that factor off, an attacker who has obtained the user's session (e.g., via a stolen/leaked authentication token) and the user's password (but never had access to the TOTP device — the entire point of 2FA) can permanently strip 2FA protection from the account in one call. This defeats the security guarantee 2FA is meant to provide: that account-security-relevant actions require both factors, not just the one factor that was already compromised.

title: Non-constant-time comparison of password hash during step-up authentication
description: In both setup() and disable(), the confirmation password supplied by the caller is compared against the stored password hash using JavaScript's strict inequality operator (`user.password !== security.hash(password)`). String comparison in JavaScript engines short-circuits at the first mismatching character, which can create a timing side-channel that leaks information about how many leading characters of the hash match. While remote timing attacks over a network are harder to exploit than local ones, this is nonetheless the wrong primitive for comparing security-sensitive secrets; a constant-time comparison function should be used instead. This is on the credential-verification decision path that gates two sensitive account operations (2FA setup and 2FA disable).

Because the implementation lives outside this file, this cannot be fully confirmed here, but the call site in this file is the point where that weak primitive — if it is indeed a fast unsalted hash — is used to gate two security-sensitive account operations (enabling/disabling 2FA). If the stored password hash were ever exfiltrated, a fast unsalted hash would allow rapid offline cracking, defeating the purpose of using a hash at all.

title: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via vm sandbox / notevil eval on user-controlled orderLinesData
description: The b2bOrder handler takes body.orderLinesData directly from the unauthenticated POST /b2b/v2/orders request and, when the rceChallenge/rceOccupyChallenge feature flag is enabled, passes it verbatim into a notevil 'safeEval' call executed inside a Node vm sandbox (vm.createContext + vm.runInContext). Both notevil and Node's built-in vm module are well-documented as escapable sandboxes (they do not provide true isolation against constructor-chain / prototype-pollution based escapes), so an attacker who controls the string passed to safeEval can typically break out of the sandbox and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node process, leading to full remote code execution on the server. Because the route carries no authentication or authorization middleware ('auth: none'), any anonymous network caller can reach this dangerous sink directly by POSTing a crafted orderLinesData payload — there is no login, role check, or ownership check of any kind gating an operation that evaluates caller-supplied code server-side. This is simultaneously an injection flaw (untrusted input reaches a code-evaluation sink), an access-control failure (a maximally dangerous operation is reachable without any authentication), and a design flaw (deliberately exposing a code-evaluation entrypoint to unauthenticated network callers is unsafe by construction regardless of the sandboxing technique used).

title: No rate limiting on expensive/dangerous code-evaluation endpoint enables repeated exploitation and DoS

Because the endpoint is unauthenticated, an attacker can send an unbounded number of requests, each spinning up a new VM context and evaluating attacker-supplied code for up to 2 seconds. This allows both (a) brute-force attempts at a sandbox-escape payload with unlimited tries, and (b) a straightforward denial-of-service by saturating the event loop / process with repeated 2-second synchronous evaluations, since Node's vm timeout mechanism does not reliably stop CPU-bound synchronous execution and each concurrent request still consumes a worker thread/event-loop slot.

title: Hardcoded wallet mnemonic seed phrase committed to source code
description: The submitKey handler compares the user-supplied req.body.privateKey against the real secret using JavaScript's strict equality operator (===) at line 15, and again for address/publicKey at lines 18 and 20. String equality in JavaScript engines short-circuits on the first mismatched character, producing a measurable timing difference between guesses that share a longer common prefix with the real secret and those that do not. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and returns different HTTP status/messages instantly, an attacker can perform a timing side-channel attack, submitting many candidate strings and measuring response latency to incrementally recover the private key character-by-character rather than needing a brute-force of the full keyspace. This is a genuine cryptographic-authentication weakness: the comparison of a secret credential must be constant-time to avoid disclosing information through timing.

title: Password change succeeds without verifying current password when 'current' parameter is omitted
description: The handler only validates the caller's current password when the `currentPassword` variable is truthy: `if (currentPassword && security.hash(currentPassword) !== loggedInUser.data.password)`. Because this is a short-circuit `&&`, an attacker who holds a valid session/bearer token (e.g. obtained via XSS, a leaked token, or a shared/public device) can simply omit the `current` query parameter entirely (or send an empty string) to skip the verification check completely, and proceed straight to `user.update({ password: newPasswordInString })`. This defeats the entire purpose of requiring a current-password re-confirmation before a sensitive account-security operation, enabling full account takeover by anyone who merely possesses a valid session token without ever needing to know the victim's actual password. This is a credential-verification decision (an authentication-outcome anchor) that is silently bypassed by omitting client input, so it is both a design/access-control defect and an authentication failure.

title: Operator-precedence bug corrupts last-login timestamp used for security monitoring
description: The expression `new Date(parsedToken?.iat ?? 0 * 1000).getTime()` is affected by JavaScript operator precedence: multiplication (0 * 1000) binds tighter than the nullish-coalescing operator, so the expression evaluates as `parsedToken?.iat ?? 0`, not `(parsedToken?.iat ?? 0) * 1000` as apparently intended. Since JWT `iat` is expressed in seconds while JS Date expects milliseconds, this produces a wildly incorrect lastLoginTime (effectively near the Unix epoch) for every user with a token. Because this value is the application's only visible record of a user's last login exposed through this administrative listing, its corruption undermines the reliability of an audit/monitoring data point that an operator would use to detect suspicious login activity or investigate an incident.

if (userToken) allows control flow to reach the timestamp computation for this user.
The corrupted lastLoginTime value is included in the per-user response object and returned to the caller as the audit-facing 'last login' data point.

Operator precedence bug (`?? 0 * 1000` instead of `(?? 0) * 1000`) causes iat (seconds) to be used directly as a millisecond timestamp, producing an incorrect lastLoginTime that is returned as part of the security-relevant audit data.

title: Hardcoded, non-cryptographic Hashids salts allow forgery/decoding of 'continue codes' representing challenge-solved state
description: All three handlers (continueCode, continueCodeFindIt, continueCodeFixIt) construct a Hashids instance with a hardcoded literal salt string ('this is my salt', 'this is the salt for findIt challenges', 'yet another salt for the fixIt challenges') and a fixed, fully alphanumeric alphabet. Hashids is a reversible obfuscation/encoding scheme, not a cryptographic MAC or signature - it provides no integrity or authenticity guarantee. Because the salt and algorithm are hardcoded directly in source (and this is an open-source codebase, so the salt is public knowledge to any attacker who reads the repository), anyone can independently instantiate the same Hashids configuration client-side and (a) decode any continueCode returned by these endpoints to enumerate exactly which challenge IDs are solved, and (b) encode an arbitrary, attacker-chosen set of challenge IDs into a syntactically valid continueCode. If any other part of the application accepts a continueCode as input to restore/mark challenges as solved (the conventional purpose of a 'continue code' feature), an attacker can forge a code for challenges they never actually solved, effectively achieving progress/privilege escalation over the scoring or challenge-completion system without performing the underlying work. The endpoints themselves are also registered with no authentication middleware, so this forgeable, security-relevant token is generated and exposed without any access control at all. The core defect is using a non-cryptographic reversible encoding library, configured with a secret embedded in source code, as if it were a secure integrity-protected token for representing security-relevant application state.

trace.description: continueCode() returns an Express handler registered at GET /rest/continue-code with no authentication middleware; req/res are received directly from the outside caller.

Hashids instance constructed with a hardcoded, publicly-visible salt string 'this is my salt' and a full alphanumeric alphabet - no cryptographic key management, no rotation, no secret derived from server-side configuration.

IDs of solved challenges are encoded via the weak, reversible Hashids scheme rather than a signed/HMAC-protected token, so the resulting value carries no integrity guarantee against tampering or forgery.
An empty ids array is initialized to accumulate the identifiers that will become the security-relevant payload of the continue code.

The handler iterates every challenge in the in-memory challenges cache, inspecting each challenge's solved flag - this is the point where global, security-relevant state is pulled into the value that will be encoded.

Each solved challenge's id is pushed into the ids array with no filtering, deduplication, or server-side authorization check beyond the solved flag - this array becomes the raw input to the weak encoding step.

The forgeable continueCode is returned to the caller in the JSON response; because the same hardcoded salt/algorithm can be reproduced by any attacker, this value (and any equivalent value an attacker crafts) is subsequently trusted elsewhere in the application as evidence of legitimately solved challenges.

title: Same forgeable-encoding defect repeated for coding-challenge 'findIt' and 'fixIt' continue codes
description: continueCodeFindIt and continueCodeFixIt repeat the identical pattern: a Hashids instance is built from a hardcoded salt literal and used to encode the IDs of ChallengeModel rows whose codingChallengeStatus meets a threshold (>=1 for findIt, >=2 for fixIt), then returned unauthenticated to the caller. As with continueCode(), the salts ('this is the salt for findIt challenges', 'yet another salt for the fixIt challenges') are hardcoded in source and Hashids provides no cryptographic integrity, so an attacker who knows (or reads) the salt can craft a continueCode claiming any coding-challenge IDs as find-it/fix-it complete. Combined with the complete absence of authentication on these routes, any client can both read out which coding challenges are completed and forge a code asserting arbitrary completion - enabling the same progress-forgery risk described for the base continueCode endpoint, doubled across the two coding-challenge tiers (continueCodeFixIt at lines 37-48 follows the exact same sequence of steps against a third hardcoded salt).
