Hashids instance built with hardcoded salt 'this is the salt for findIt challenges' - same weak, non-cryptographic construction as the base continue code, reproducible by any attacker who reads the source.
IDs of challenges with codingChallengeStatus >= 1 are fetched and (line 32) encoded with the forgeable Hashids scheme, with no signature or server-side verification token accompanying the value.
An empty ids array is initialized to accumulate the coding-challenge identifiers that will be encoded into the continue code.
The handler iterates the returned challenge rows, beginning the loop that transfers each qualifying challenge's identity into the payload to be encoded.
Each challenge's id is pushed into the ids array with no additional integrity binding, becoming the raw input to the weak encoding step.
The ids array is passed to hashids.encode(), the concrete weak-cryptography operation that turns the completion state into a value secured only by the hardcoded salt rather than a signature or HMAC.

The forgeable code is returned in the JSON response to an unauthenticated caller; equivalent defect exists in continueCodeFixIt at lines 37-46 with a third hardcoded salt ('yet another salt for the fixIt challenges').

title: Unauthenticated exposure of internal CTF configuration data
description: The GET /rest/country-mapping route is registered with no authentication or authorization middleware (per routing metadata: auth: none). The handler reads an internal configuration value (ctf.countryMapping) directly from the application config store and returns it verbatim to any caller via res.send(countryMapping) (line 17), with no check that the requester is an authenticated user, let alone an administrator or CTF organizer. This configuration object is intended to support the FBCTF integration (mapping flag/country identifiers used by the CTF scoring bridge) and is internal operational data rather than public application content. Because there is no authentication gate on this route at all, any anonymous client can enumerate or scrape this internal mapping data at will. While the handler itself performs no per-resource ownership check (there is no resource id here, so classic BOLA does not apply), the broader problem is a function-level authorization gap: a configuration-disclosure endpoint that should plausibly be restricted to CTF administrators/organizers is reachable by anyone, and the file provides no server-side check to change that. There is also no rate limiting on this handler, so it can be scraped/polled repeatedly, though the impact of that alone is low since the response is small and static.

trace.description: Exported handler is registered at GET /rest/country-mapping with no auth middleware (per provided routing metadata: auth: none); caller/router lives outside this file.
Handler reads internal configuration value ctf.countryMapping directly from the application config module without any authorization check on the requester.
Handler enters try block unconditionally for every request, with no gate based on caller identity or role.
Truthiness check on the fetched config value decides which branch executes; it checks only whether the value exists, not who is asking.
Else branch is taken when the config value is present, proceeding to return it to the caller with no further access check.

When config is absent, an Error is thrown, driving the alternate response path that differs observably (500) from the success path (200), letting an unauthenticated poller fingerprint server configuration state.
Catch block handles the thrown error on every failing request with no rate limiting or lockout after repeated failures.
Warning is logged on every failed request but no throttling/alerting threshold is applied to repeated failures from the same source.
500 response returned to caller on the failure path, and 200 with data on the success path (line 17) — both reachable an unlimited number of times per caller.
Internal configuration data is sent verbatim to the unauthenticated caller via res.send(countryMapping).

title: No rate limiting on config-exposing endpoint enables unrestricted scraping
description: The countryMapping handler has no per-IP or per-session rate limiting applied within this file, and per the routing metadata is also unauthenticated. Because the operation is cheap (a config lookup and a send), the primary consequence is low-impact enumeration/scraping capability rather than a DoS vector, but the combination of no authentication and no throttling means the endpoint can be polled at will by automated clients to continuously harvest the country mapping configuration, or to probe for configuration presence/absence (the 500 vs 200 status difference at lines 17/21 reveals whether ctf.countryMapping is configured on the server, which is a minor information-disclosure/fingerprinting primitive).

trace.description: Handler registered at GET /rest/country-mapping with no auth and (from this file) no rate-limiting logic applied before processing the request.
Every invocation performs a config lookup with no throttling or caching control visible in this file.
Response is returned unconditionally on every call, allowing unrestricted repeated polling.

title: Missing authentication enforcement allows anonymous review creation
description: The route PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews is registered with no authentication middleware, and the handler itself does nothing to compensate: it calls security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) to resolve the caller's identity but never checks whether the result is defined, never verifies a valid session/token was presented, and the code flows straight from that resolution into the try block and the insert call with no conditional gate in between. An attacker with no session at all can PUT a review for any product id and receive a 201 success. This is a Broken Function Level Authorization / missing authentication defect: a write operation that should require a logged-in identity is reachable by anyone.

trace.description: Handler for PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews, registered in server.ts with auth: none, receives req/res from an unauthenticated caller.
user is resolved from the request via security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) but the result is never checked for null/undefined, and 'user' is never referenced again in the function.
Execution enters the try block with no conditional guard on 'user' or any auth-status check separating identity resolution from the write operation that follows.
reviewsCollection.insert() executes unconditionally, creating a review regardless of whether a valid authenticated identity was present, and returns 201 success.

title: Mass assignment of review 'author' field enables identity spoofing
description: The inserted review document sets author directly from req.body.author (client-controlled) instead of deriving it from the resolved authenticated user's identity (e.g., user.data.email as is standard practice elsewhere in this codebase). The 'user' object obtained on line 16 is fetched but discarded, and instead the client-supplied author string on line 22 is used verbatim inside the document literal passed to insert(). Because the application never enforces that the review's stated author matches the caller, any client can submit a review whose author field names an arbitrary other user (or arbitrary string), impersonating them in a persisted, publicly visible record. This is a classic Mass Assignment / Broken Object Property Level Authorization defect: a sensitive identity-bearing field is bound straight from caller input with no allow-list or server-side derivation.

trace.description: req.body.author is read directly from the client-supplied request body.
The resolved authenticated user object is fetched but discarded - never used to set or validate the review's author, despite being available.
Handler for PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews receives req containing both the caller's session/token material and an arbitrary req.body.
reviewsCollection.insert() persists the review with the caller-supplied author value verbatim, allowing impersonation of any name/email in a stored review.

title: Unbounded, unauthenticated review creation with no size or rate limits
description: The handler accepts arbitrary-length req.body.message and req.body.author values and inserts them into MongoDB with no length validation, no request body size cap visible in this file, and no rate limiting anywhere on the code path from receiving the request to executing the insert. Combined with the missing authentication check (see related finding), any anonymous caller can repeatedly invoke this endpoint with large payloads and an arbitrary product id, growing the reviews collection unbounded and consuming storage/CPU/memory, or flooding a product with spam reviews.

trace.description: Handler for PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews accepts req.params.id and req.body without any request-level authentication or size constraints applied in this file.
req.body.message is used without any length or content validation before persistence.
Execution proceeds straight into the try block with no validation step limiting payload size, field length, or call frequency before the write is attempted.
req.body.author is likewise used without any length or content validation before persistence, compounding the unbounded-input surface.
reviewsCollection.insert() is called with no throttling or cap, allowing repeated/large insertions to be triggered by a single caller with no restriction.

title: BOLA: Duplicate BasketId parameters allow writing items into another user's basket
description: addBasketItem() re-parses the raw request body with a custom parser (utils.parseJsonCustom) that preserves every key/value occurrence, including duplicates, into arrays. The ownership check at line 37 only inspects the FIRST occurrence of BasketId (basketIds[0]) against the caller's own basket id (user.bid). However, the object that is actually persisted uses the LAST occurrence of each key (basketIds[basketIds.length - 1], productIds[productIds.length - 1], quantities[quantities.length - 1]). An attacker can therefore submit a request body containing two 'BasketId' entries: the first equal to their own basket id (which satisfies the ownership check) and a second equal to a victim's basket id (which is what actually gets used to build and save the BasketItemModel). This lets an authenticated user add arbitrary products/quantities into another user's basket, a classic BOLA / object-level authorization bypass.

All 'BasketId' occurrences from the body are pushed into the basketIds array, not just one.

Matched quantity values are pushed into quantities, preserving duplicates.
End of per-entry key matching; loop continues to next entry.

The authenticated user's own basket id (user.bid) is resolved for comparison.

ProductId assigned from productIds[productIds.length - 1] (last occurrence), independent of what was validated.

The basket item object actually persisted uses basketIds[basketIds.length - 1] (the LAST supplied BasketId), which was never checked against the caller's identity, and is saved at line 48.

title: Fail-open basket ownership check when user identity is absent
description: The ownership check at line 37 is gated behind `user &&`. If security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) returns a falsy value (e.g. the request has no valid token and the appendUserId middleware, defined outside this file, does not reject unauthenticated calls but merely attempts to decorate req), the entire ownership condition short-circuits to false and the code falls through to the else branch, creating a basket item for whatever BasketId was supplied with no validation whatsoever. This is a fail-open authorization design: absence of an established identity should deny the write, not skip the check.

user is derived from security.authenticatedUsers.from(req); if no valid session is present this evaluates to a falsy value.

The condition `user && ...` short-circuits when user is falsy, skipping ownership validation entirely and allowing the else branch (lines 40-49) to build and save a basket item for any BasketId supplied by the caller.

title: Check-then-use mismatch: quantity/stock validation reads a different value than what is persisted
description: The route chain for POST /api/BasketItems runs quantityCheckBeforeBasketItemAddition() before addBasketItem(). That pre-check validates req.body.ProductId and req.body.quantity, which come from the standard (single-value) JSON body parse. However, addBasketItem() independently re-parses the raw body with a duplicate-key-preserving custom parser and uses the LAST occurrence of ProductId/quantity to actually build and persist the BasketItemModel. By submitting duplicate ProductId/quantity fields (a low value that passes validation, followed by a different value used for persistence), an attacker can have the stock/per-user-limit check performed by quantityCheck evaluate a harmless value while an entirely different, unchecked value (e.g. an oversized quantity or a different product) is what actually gets saved.

addBasketItem(), invoked next in the chain, independently re-parses the raw body preserving all duplicate key occurrences.
The basket item to persist uses quantities[quantities.length - 1] — the LAST occurrence — which may differ from the value validated by quantityCheck.

Every 'quantity' occurrence is pushed into the quantities array, preserving duplicates not visible to the earlier check.

title: PUT /api/BasketItems/:id performs no ownership check before allowing an update to proceed
description: quantityCheckBeforeBasketItemUpdate() is the sole handler registered for PUT /api/BasketItems/:id. It looks up the basket item purely by its primary key (req.params.id) with no WHERE clause tying it to the requesting user's own basket (item.BasketId vs. the authenticated user's bid). The user object is fetched at line 68 but is never used to verify ownership of the item found at line 67 — it is effectively dead code with respect to authorization. If req.body.quantity is absent, next() is called unconditionally (line 75), and if present, only a stock/limit check is performed (line 73) before calling next(), which passes control to a generic update handler (outside this file). Any authenticated user can therefore target another user's basket item id and have this file's gate pass the request through with no ownership enforcement.

An error is thrown only if the item does not exist at all — not if it belongs to a different user.

title: No validation that quantity is a positive integer allows stock/limit checks to be trivially bypassed with negative values
description: quantityCheck() compares the caller-supplied quantity directly against product.limitPerUser and product.quantity using >= comparisons, with no prior validation that quantity is a positive integer. A caller can supply a negative quantity (e.g. -5); since limitPerUser and stock are positive numbers, both `product.limitPerUser >= quantity` and `product.quantity >= quantity` evaluate to true regardless of actual stock or per-user caps, so next() is called and the negative-quantity basket item is persisted by addBasketItem(). This is a design gap: the server never establishes that quantity must be a positive integer before it is used in business logic and eventually in price/total calculations downstream.

product.limitPerUser >= quantity is trivially satisfied for any negative quantity, bypassing the per-user purchase cap.

The corresponding product/limit record is fetched for comparison against the unvalidated quantity.

product.quantity >= quantity is likewise trivially satisfied for a negative quantity, so next() is invoked and the negative-quantity item proceeds to be persisted via addBasketItem() (line 46-48), enabling downstream price/total manipulation.

title: Unbounded processing of duplicate-key raw request body without size limits
description: addBasketItem() iterates over the entire array returned by parsing the raw request body, with no cap on the number of key/value entries. An attacker can submit a body containing an extremely large number of ProductId/BasketId/quantity entries; the loop still processes every entry into memory (three growing arrays) on every request. There is no visible size or count limit applied in this file before the loop runs.

Each entry is tested against 'quantity'.
Matches are appended to quantities without any cap.
End of per-entry processing; loop proceeds to next entry regardless of how many have already been processed.
Three arrays (productIds, basketIds, quantities) grow unbounded per request before a single basket item is ultimately built and saved.

title: Unauthorized basket-write attempts are not logged
description: When the ownership check fails (line 37-38), the handler simply responds with a 401 error and no security-relevant event is recorded (no log of the user id, attempted basket id, or IP). Repeated probing for other users' basket ids (as exploited by the duplicate-key BOLA above) would leave no audit trail to detect or investigate the attack.

The authenticated user's own basket id is resolved for the comparison that will determine whether a denial is logged-worthy.
Ownership mismatch condition evaluates true, leading to the denial branch.
On ownership mismatch, a 401 response is returned with no logging of the security-relevant denial (attempted basket id, acting user, etc.).

title: Arbitrary field selection via `fields` query parameter exposes sensitive user model properties (e.g. password hash, TOTP secret)
description: The handler builds a whitelist-free field selector: it splits the caller-supplied `fields` query parameter and, for every requested field name, indexes directly into the full `user.data` object (`user?.data[field as keyof typeof user.data]`) and copies whatever value is found into the response, as long as it is not `undefined`. The only case that returns a fixed, safe subset of fields (`id`, `email`, `lastLoginIp`, `profileImage`) is the else-branch that runs when no `fields` parameter is supplied at all. As soon as an attacker supplies `?fields=password` or `?fields=totpSecret,role,deluxeToken` (or any other property that exists on the in-memory user record, such as password hash, security answer, TOTP secret, deluxe/role flags, etc.), the code happily returns it because there is no explicit allow-list of exposable fields — only an implicit exclude via the untouched else branch. This is classic Broken Object Property Level Authorization: the client, not the server, decides which internal model properties are disclosed. Because this endpoint requires no authorization middleware beyond the caller holding a valid session cookie (their own), the caller can dump other normally-hidden attributes of their own account record, including the password hash, enabling offline cracking regardless of the account owner's actual password strength, and disclosing internal flags (isAdmin/role-like data) that should never be attacker-visible.

The raw string is split on commas into an array of arbitrary property names with no allow-list filtering.
Each attacker-supplied field name is iterated without validation against a safe-field whitelist.
The field name is used to index directly into the full internal user.data object, retrieving any property that exists there (password, totpSecret, role, deluxeToken, etc.).
The dynamically-built baseUser object, potentially containing sensitive internal fields, is assigned into the response payload.
The full internal user object (user.data) is loaded from authenticatedUsers via the session cookie token; this becomes the object the attacker-controlled field names will index into.
baseUser is initialised as an empty object that will be filled purely from attacker-chosen keys rather than a fixed safe shape.
The conditional branches into the unrestricted, caller-driven field-selection path whenever any fields were requested, bypassing the safe fixed-field branch entirely.
The attacker-named property's value (e.g. password hash, totpSecret, role, deluxeToken) is copied verbatim from user.data into baseUser under the caller-chosen key.
res.json(response) returns the caller-selected fields directly to the client.

title: JSONP callback support on authenticated whoami endpoint enables cross-site exfiltration of session data
description: When the caller supplies a `callback` query parameter, the handler switches from `res.json` to `res.jsonp`, wrapping the JSON response in a JavaScript function call named by the caller. Because this endpoint is reached via a simple cross-origin GET (browsers automatically attach the session cookie to such requests, and there is no CORS restriction visible in this handler nor any CSRF/Origin check performed before branching to jsonp), a third-party website can embed a script tag pointing at this endpoint with an arbitrary callback name to have the victim's browser execute the response as script in the attacker page's origin, handing the victim's own currentUser data (id, email, lastLoginIp, profileImage, and — combined with the fields mass-selection defect above — password hash, TOTP secret, role, etc.) directly to attacker-controlled JavaScript. This defeats the Same-Origin Policy protection that res.json responses normally enjoy (plain JSON is not directly executable/readable cross-origin as a script include), and is a textbook JSONP-based cross-site data leak / session riding vector. This is a misconfiguration: enabling a JSONP escape hatch on a cookie-authenticated endpoint that returns user-identifying data, without any origin validation or restriction on which endpoints may use it.

The response still contains the authenticated user's session-derived data (identified via the browser-supplied cookie), which will be embedded in the jsonp wrapper.
The user record is loaded from authenticatedUsers using the cookie token; this session-bound data becomes the payload that will later be serialized into the jsonp callback wrapper.
The user data (baseUser) is assembled into the response object that the callback branch at line 52 will hand to res.jsonp unchanged.
res.jsonp(response) emits the sensitive user payload as an executable script fragment invoking the attacker-chosen callback, which a cross-origin script include can capture.

title: Unauthenticated Broken Object-Level Authorization on Basket Coupon Application
description: The applyCoupon handler accepts an arbitrary basket id from the URL path and performs BasketModel.findByPk(id) followed by an update of the basket's coupon field, with no check anywhere in the handler that the requester is authenticated, nor that the basket identified by `id` belongs to the caller. The route is registered with auth: none, so any unauthenticated party can PUT to /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon for any numeric basket id and mutate another user's basket state (setting or clearing its coupon/discount), and can also enumerate which basket ids exist via the differing 200/404 responses. This is a textbook BOLA: the identifier that selects the resource is fully caller-controlled and no ownership/session check is interposed between lookup and mutation. The only conditional gating execution (line 19) tests mere existence of the basket, never ownership, so the flow proceeds straight from an unvalidated identifier to a cross-account write.

trace.description: applyCoupon handler receives params.id and params.coupon from the PUT /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon route (registered with auth: none); no authentication/session context is consulted anywhere in this function.
The caller-supplied basket id is taken directly from params.id with no validation that it belongs to the current user.
BasketModel.findByPk(id) loads the basket purely by primary key, with no WHERE clause or subsequent check tying the basket to the authenticated user.

The only gating condition checks whether the basket exists at all (`if (!basket)`); it does not verify the basket's owner matches the caller, so any existing basket id passes this check and execution continues.
basket.update({ coupon: ... }) mutates the target basket's coupon/discount state for whatever basket id was supplied, completing the unauthorized cross-account write.

title: No Rate Limiting Enables Coupon Brute-Forcing on a State-Changing Endpoint
description: The coupon parameter is decoded and validated purely in-process via security.discountFromCoupon with no throttling, lockout, or attempt tracking. Because the endpoint requires no authentication and accepts a coupon string on every request, an attacker can script repeated PUT requests against /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon, iterating over the coupon code space (or a candidate list) until a valid coupon is found, then apply it to any basket id. The full per-request path — decoding, validating, resolving the basket, and persisting — executes with no delay or counter at any stage, so each guess is answered immediately and cheaply, making automated brute-force discovery of valid discount codes unbounded.

trace.description: Handler for PUT /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon accepts an arbitrary coupon string on every invocation, with no auth or throttling middleware visible in this file.
security.discountFromCoupon(coupon) is invoked synchronously on the raw caller-supplied string for validation, with no attempt counter, delay, or lockout around this call.
The raw coupon string is decoded via decodeURIComponent on every request with no per-request cost limiting or attempt counting.
coupon is finalized to either the guessed value or null purely based on the immediate validation result, with no record kept of the attempt.
The target basket is loaded with no throttling applied before this potentially repeated lookup.
Existence check passes through for any valid basket id, allowing the guess-and-apply cycle to continue unimpeded.
The basket is updated with the guessed coupon value with no rate-limit-triggered rejection at this persistence step.
Basket id is extracted, establishing the target basket that will receive the (potentially already-used) coupon.

On a successful guess the discount is applied and returned immediately; failed guesses simply return 404, allowing the caller to iterate rapidly without any penalty, enabling automated brute-forcing of valid coupon codes across arbitrary basket ids.

title: Stateless Coupon Validation Allows Unlimited Reuse of a Single Discount Code
description: Coupon validity is determined purely by decoding the coupon string (security.discountFromCoupon) with no persisted record of which coupons have already been redeemed, by whom, or how many times. Nothing in this handler marks a coupon as consumed or checks a usage table before applying the discount to basket.coupon. As a result, the same coupon code — once known or brute-forced — can be applied repeatedly to any number of different baskets (including baskets belonging to other, unauthenticated targets per the access-control finding), defeating the intended single-use/promotional-limit business rule and creating unbounded discount/financial exposure.

trace.description: Handler receives basket id and coupon code from the request path.

The coupon is written onto the basket and the discount honored (line 25-26) with no server-side tracking that would prevent the identical coupon from being applied again to this or any other basket.

This handler performs no encoding or validation on `id` before embedding it in the message, and the code path leading there — lookup followed by the not-found branch — does not filter or sanitize the value in between.

title: BOLA: attacker-controlled UserId in memories lookup bypasses ownership check
description: The data export handler authenticates the caller via the Bearer token (line 18-19) and derives the trusted user's email/id from the session store, but when querying the MemoryModel it uses req.body.UserId directly instead of the authenticated user's own id (loggedInUser.data.id). Any authenticated user can therefore supply another user's UserId in the POST body and receive that user's memory records (image URLs and captions) in the exported data at line 107. This is a textbook Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) flaw: the server trusts a caller-supplied identifier to select the resource instead of deriving it from the verified identity, exposing private uploaded images/captions belonging to other accounts. Note orders and reviews queries in the same handler correctly use the server-derived email (lines 33, 40), highlighting that the memories query is the inconsistent, unprotected path.

title: Arbitrary local file read via 'layout' parameter protected only by a weak denylist
description: The POST / handler accepts a client-supplied 'layout' field in the request body and resolves it to an absolute filesystem path with path.resolve(req.body.layout) without any allow-listing or containment to a safe base directory. The only protection is a hard-coded denylist of three literal substrings ('ftp', 'ctf.key', 'encryptionkeys'). Any other path — including absolute paths like /etc/passwd, application source files, or other secrets not matching those three strings — passes the check unmodified. The (still user-controlled) layout value is then spread into the view-render call together with the rest of req.body, and the resulting rendered response is truncated and returned to the caller. This pattern is the classic denylist-vs-allowlist failure: the control was built to block three specific known-sensitive files rather than to restrict the resolved path to an intended directory, so it does not actually prevent path traversal or arbitrary file access — it is trivially bypassed by requesting any file whose absolute, lower-cased path does not contain those three substrings.

Any anonymous caller can invoke this endpoint repeatedly and receive the entire delivery-method table in a single response. While the current dataset may be small, the code establishes no control to prevent the result set or the request rate from growing unbounded — if the underlying table grows (e.g., via admin-managed delivery methods) or the endpoint is hit in a tight loop, this becomes a straightforward amplification/DoS vector against the database and the response payload size, with no application-level defense in this handler.

Because these routes carry no authentication middleware (auth: none), the only identity signal available to isDeluxe is whatever the client chooses to send, and this file has no visibility into, nor does it enforce, how that identity claim is cryptographically verified before being trusted to select which price field is returned. If the verification performed by security.isDeluxe (outside this file) is weak or bypassable, an attacker could spoof deluxe status to view (and potentially propagate downstream to order/pricing flows) discounted pricing data without ever authenticating. This is flagged as a trust-boundary concern in this file because the pricing/authorization decision is made per-request based on an identity claim on a route explicitly configured with no auth layer, and the same unverified pattern is repeated identically in the second handler.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of asset explicitly stored under a 'private' directory
description: The route registered for this handler (GET /the/devs/are/so/funny/they/hid/an/easter/egg/within/the/easter/egg) has no authentication or authorization middleware applied. The handler unconditionally serves a static file located at 'frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/threejs-demo.html'. The directory name 'private' signals that this asset was intended to be gated behind some access control (e.g., only reachable after completing a prior challenge or being authenticated), yet the exported handler performs no session check, no role check, and no verification of any prerequisite state before calling res.sendFile. The file even imports the application's own challenge-gating helper module (challengeUtils) and challenge state cache (challenges) at the top of the file, but the handler body never calls into either of them to make an authorization decision — those imports sit unused as far as this handler's control flow is concerned. Any unauthenticated caller who discovers or guesses the route path receives the private asset with a 200 response. This is a Broken Function-Level Authorization pattern: a resource whose own storage location indicates it should be restricted is served to anyone who can reach the URL, with the URL string itself acting as the only (and non-cryptographic) barrier.

title: Security-through-obscurity used as the sole access control for a 'private' resource

The handler itself contains no logic to verify that the requester has satisfied any prerequisite (e.g., completed an earlier stage, is authenticated, or holds a specific role) before returning the file content. Notably, the file imports both the challenge state cache (challenges) and the challenge-gating helper (challengeUtils) — the exact tools this codebase uses elsewhere to condition behaviour on game/authorization state — yet the handler never invokes either import to make that decision here; the design never establishes a re-derivable trust decision, it only trusts 'nobody will guess/find this path.' Any leak of the URL (browser history, referrer headers, shared links, crawling, source maps, or documentation) permanently and irrevocably exposes the asset to anyone, with no way to detect or revoke access after the fact. A correctly implemented version of this same code (obscure path + unconditional file serve) is still exploitable by design once the path is known.

title: Insufficient-funds check silently bypassed when the user has no wallet record

title: Poison Null Byte Bypasses File Extension Allow-list, Enabling Arbitrary File Disclosure from ftp/ Directory
description: The file-serving handler validates the caller-supplied filename against an extension allow-list (.md, .pdf, or the literal 'incident-support.kdbx') BEFORE the value is normalized/stripped of a poison null byte. An attacker can request a filename crafted like 'target-file%00.md' (or equivalent null-byte-containing sequence). endsWithAllowlistedFileType() sees the '.md' suffix and passes the check, but security.cutOffPoisonNullByte(file) then truncates the string at the null byte, producing a completely different filename ('target-file') that never itself satisfied the extension check. This resulting filename is then handed directly to path.resolve('ftp/', file) and served via res.sendFile with no further validation of extension, ownership, or intended public-accessibility. This is the classic 'poison null byte' bypass: validation is performed on a value that is subsequently mutated before use, so the check provides no real guarantee about what is actually served. The impact is disclosure of arbitrary files present in the ftp/ directory regardless of their extension or confidentiality (e.g., internal notes, backup files, credential-bearing files), since the only real gate (the extension/allow-list check) is trivially defeated. This is also a design flaw: the code performs an authorization/validation decision on a value and then discards that value in favor of a derived one without re-validating, meaning the control can never be relied upon to restrict which files are servable.

However, this function's body is completely empty — no logging, alerting, metrics increment, or security-event record of any kind occurs. This is a clear point in the code where a security-relevant event (a validation-bypass file disclosure) is recognized structurally but not recorded, meaning operators have no way to detect, investigate, or respond to exploitation of this endpoint from logs alone.

title: Potential Directory Traversal via Encoded Path Separators Surviving the Naive Slash Check
description: The only defense against directory traversal is a literal check for the '/' character in the raw file parameter (line 18), performed before any decoding normalization. If the externally-imported security.cutOffPoisonNullByte() function performs additional decoding of the string (common in null-byte-stripping utilities that also handle URL-encoded sequences), a caller could submit a double-encoded or otherwise obfuscated path-traversal sequence (e.g., an encoding of '../') that contains no literal '/' at the time of the line-18 check but resolves to actual path-separator characters afterward. Because path.resolve('ftp/', file) is called on the post-processing value without re-checking for traversal sequences, this could allow escaping the intended 'ftp/' directory. This cannot be fully confirmed without the implementation of cutOffPoisonNullByte, which resides outside this file.

Traversal defense consists only of rejecting a literal '/' in the raw, undecoded value.

path.resolve('ftp/', file) combined with res.sendFile serves whatever path the mutated value resolves to, with no re-validation for traversal.

title: Unauthenticated /rest/languages endpoint performs unbounded, uncached, expensive file I/O and CPU work on every request
description: The GET /rest/languages route is registered with no authentication middleware and calls getLanguageList(), which on every single request: (1) reads and JSON.parses the full English reference translation file, (2) attempts to read/parse a backend translation file, (3) calls readdir on the frontend i18n asset directory, and then (4) for every file returned by readdir, asynchronously reads and JSON.parses both the frontend and (optionally) backend translation file and runs calcPercentage, which iterates over every key of the file content and compares it against every key of the English reference content (an O(n) full-object diff per file, per request, executed twice — once for the frontend comparison and once for the backend comparison). None of this work is cached, memoized, or throttled, and the endpoint requires no authentication and no session/API key. Because response time and resource cost scale with the number and size of language files and none of the computed results are cached between requests, an attacker can repeatedly invoke this public endpoint to force the server to repeatedly perform many synchronous-style file reads and full-object key comparisons, consuming CPU and file-descriptor/I/O resources. Combined with the total absence of any visible rate limiting or per-IP throttling in this file, this creates an amplification vector for denial of service: a small number of requests forces disproportionately large repeated I/O + parsing + diffing work with no caching layer to short-circuit repeat requests.

Every request enumerates all files in the frontend i18n asset directory via readdir with no caching of the file list or its contents between requests.
For every file found, the handler spawns an async read+parse+diff operation (languagePromises.map), scaling total work with the number of language files present, on every single request.
For each file, a second file read against the corresponding backend translation file is also performed per request, doubling I/O load, again uncached.

Reads the backend English reference translation file from disk on every request (inside a try block), adding further uncached I/O to each call.
Reads each individual locale file from disk per request, per file, uncached.
JSON.parses each locale file's full content per request, per file.
Invokes calcPercentage against the full parsed locale content to compute the frontend translation percentage — first of two diff computations per file.
JSON.parses the backend locale file content per request, per file.
Invokes calcPercentage a second time per file to compute the backend translation percentage, doubling the CPU-bound diff work triggered per request.

Promise.all awaits every per-file read/parse/diff task concurrently for every incoming request, with no memoization or caching of results reused across requests, so the full cost is paid again on each call.

calcPercentage performs a full key-by-key comparison of the entire parsed JSON object against the English reference object for every file, on every request, with no memoization — the CPU-bound sink that an attacker can trigger repeatedly and cheaply since the endpoint is unauthenticated and un-rate-limited.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of cryptographic key material via serveKeyFiles handler
description: The exported serveKeyFiles() middleware reads an arbitrary filename from the route parameter `params.file` and, after only a superficial check, streams the corresponding file from the `encryptionkeys/` directory back to the caller with res.sendFile. There is no authentication or authorization check anywhere in this handler — any caller who can reach the mounted route (the mount point is defined outside this file, e.g. in server.ts) can request any filename inside that directory. Given the directory is literally named 'encryptionkeys', it is expected to contain private/public keys used for cryptographic operations such as JWT signing. If the private signing key (or any other secret key material) is stored there under a guessable or discoverable filename, an unauthenticated attacker can retrieve it directly. Possession of a private signing key lets an attacker forge arbitrary, validly-signed authentication tokens (e.g. JWTs) for any user, which is a direct authentication-bypass outcome, not just a confidentiality loss. Notably neither branch of the conditional (success at line 14 or the 403 rejection at lines 16-17) ever performs an identity or permission check — the only gate on the whole function is the cosmetic slash test.

The raw, attacker-controlled filename is assigned to `file` with no authentication check performed anywhere in this handler.
Only a weak blacklist check (absence of '/') gates the request; there is no verification of caller identity or of which specific key the caller is entitled to retrieve.
Even the rejection branch (triggered only by presence of '/') confirms the check is purely about filename shape, not about caller identity or entitlement to the key.
res.sendFile serves the requested file straight out of the encryptionkeys/ directory to the unauthenticated caller, disclosing key material such as a private signing key.

title: Weak blacklist-based path validation permits directory traversal / path bypass
description: The handler attempts to prevent path traversal by rejecting only filenames that contain a literal forward slash (`file.includes('/')`). This is a blacklist of a single character rather than a canonicalization check (verifying the resolved absolute path is still inside the intended base directory) or a strict allow-list (e.g. matching only `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$`). This control is fragile: on any deployment where the OS path separator differs from '/', such as Windows, a value like '..\\..\\..\\windows\\win.ini' contains no forward slash and passes the check at line 13, yet path.resolve at line 14 will honor backslashes as path separators and can escape the encryptionkeys/ directory entirely. More generally, the design relies on excluding a single 'bad' character instead of positively constraining the input, which is the textbook fragile-blacklist pattern that breaks under encoding or platform differences — a canonicalization/startsWith check on the resolved path (or an allow-list of exact known filenames) was never implemented.

Untrusted filename value is captured without any normalization.

Validation is a single-character blacklist (`!file.includes('/')`) instead of resolved-path containment verification or a strict filename allow-list; this does not account for OS-specific separators such as backslash on Windows.

title: No security logging of access or denied access to key files
description: Access to files under the encryptionkeys/ directory is a security-sensitive event (potential exposure of cryptographic key material), yet the handler contains no logging of successful file serves (line 14) nor of rejected/suspicious requests that trip the traversal check (lines 16-17, where the response is a 403 and an Error is passed to next() with no log entry written first). Without a log record of which filenames were requested, by whom, and whether the request was allowed or denied, there is no way to detect reconnaissance or exfiltration attempts against key material, nor to reconstruct an incident timeline afterward.

title: CAPTCHA verification fails open when no matching CAPTCHA record exists
description: The verifyImageCaptcha() middleware, which gates POST /rest/user/data-export, queries for a recent CAPTCHA belonging to the requesting user and only rejects the request if a CAPTCHA record IS found AND the answer is wrong. If no CAPTCHA record is found at all (captchas[0] is falsy) — e.g. because the caller never requested a CAPTCHA via GET /rest/image-captcha, or because more than 5 minutes elapsed, or because the UserId lookup does not match any row — the code treats this as success and calls next() unconditionally. This means the entire anti-automation control can be trivially bypassed by simply calling the data-export endpoint without ever having solved a CAPTCHA, since 'no CAPTCHA on record' is treated identically to 'CAPTCHA correctly solved.' This is a workflow/business-logic design flaw: the mandatory verification step can be skipped by omission rather than defeated, and it also removes the intended throttle against automated bulk data-export requests.

title: Unauthenticated caller reaches CAPTCHA verification with unfiltered UserId, potentially matching another user's CAPTCHA
description: verifyImageCaptcha() derives UserId from security.authenticatedUsers.from(req); if the caller is not authenticated (or the token/session lookup fails), UserId resolves to undefined rather than the handler rejecting the request outright. This undefined value is placed directly into the Sequelize where clause (where: { UserId, createdAt: {...} }). Depending on Sequelize's handling of undefined where-values, this can cause the UserId filter to be silently dropped, so the query returns the most recently created CAPTCHA belonging to ANY user rather than being scoped to the caller. Combined with the fail-open behavior on the following line, this weakens the intended per-user isolation of the CAPTCHA check and lets an unauthenticated or improperly-authenticated caller reach the protected next() step without the verification being properly scoped to their own identity.

title: No rate limiting on CAPTCHA generation endpoint allows unbounded database writes
description: GET /rest/image-captcha (imageCaptchas()) generates a new CAPTCHA and unconditionally persists it as a new row via ImageCaptchaModel.build(...).save() on every request from any authenticated user, with no rate limit, cap, or cleanup visible in this file. A user (or automated script using valid credentials) can call this endpoint repeatedly to grow the ImageCaptchaModel table without bound, consuming database storage and degrading performance over time. There is no visible pagination, size cap, or throttling control on this write path.

Because this endpoint gates the sensitive user data-export functionality, repeated failed verification attempts (e.g., from automated guessing or abuse attempts) are indistinguishable from normal traffic in application logs, preventing detection of brute-force or automation attempts against this control.

title: TOCTOU race condition on review 'like' check allows duplicate likes and likesCount inflation
description: The handler checks whether the current user has already liked a review (line 31) and only then increments the shared likesCount counter (lines 35-38) and later appends the user's email to the persisted likedBy array (lines 43-52). Between the initial check and the final persistence of likedBy, the code deliberately calls `await sleep(150)` (line 41, explicitly commented as an 'Artificial wait for timing attack challenge'), which widens the window during which the server-side likedBy array has NOT yet been updated. An attacker can fire many concurrent POST /rest/products/reviews requests for the same review id before any of them finishes its full read-modify-write cycle. Each concurrent request will pass the 'already liked' check at line 31 (since none of the prior requests have finished writing likedBy yet) and will unconditionally execute the `$inc: { likesCount: 1 }` update at lines 35-38. This lets a single user inflate a review's likesCount an arbitrary number of times, and the final $set of likedBy (lines 49-52) is subject to a last-write-wins race that can leave likedBy and likesCount permanently inconsistent. This is a business-logic/economic-imbalance design flaw (a resource meant to be limited to 'one like per user' can be multiplied) and, because it is achievable purely via request concurrency against an endpoint with no throttling, it also constitutes unrestricted resource consumption at the business-logic layer.

title: Unvalidated request body 'id' used directly as MongoDB query filter (NoSQL injection)
description: `req.body.id` is taken from the request body with no type checking (not required to be a string/ObjectId) and is used directly as the `_id` filter value in multiple MongoDB operations: `db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id })` (line 25), `db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, ...)` (line 36), the re-fetch (line 43), and the final update (line 50). Because Express parses JSON bodies, an attacker can submit `id` as an object containing MongoDB query operators (e.g. `{"$ne": null}`, `{"$gt": ""}`, or a regex operator) instead of a scalar id. Depending on the underlying MongoDB/mock driver's handling of such filters, this can cause the query to match an unintended document (a review the attacker does not know the id of), bypass the intended per-id targeting of the endpoint, or otherwise manipulate query logic. No allow-listing, type coercion, or ObjectId validation is performed on `id` before it reaches any of the four filter objects it flows into.

title: Raw internal error object returned to client on failure
description: In the inner try/catch block, any error thrown while re-fetching the review or updating likedBy is returned directly to the caller via `res.status(500).json(err)` (line 55), rather than a sanitized message. Depending on the error type (e.g., a MongoDB driver error, or a TypeError from accessing `.likedBy` on a null updatedReview at line 44), this can leak internal implementation details such as stack traces, driver/library version strings, or internal query structure to an authenticated attacker who can trigger this path (e.g. by racing requests or supplying a malformed id). Neither catch block (inner at lines 54-56, outer at lines 57-59) logs the error server-side, so there is no record of the failure for detection or investigation.

title: Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read via Weak Blocklist Filter on Log File Name
description: The serveLogFiles handler takes an attacker-supplied route parameter (params.file) and passes it into path.resolve('logs/', file) before serving it with res.sendFile. The only validation performed is a check that the string does not contain a forward slash (line 13). This is a blocklist approach that fails to account for several traversal techniques: (1) a single '..' segment contains no slash and is accepted, causing path.resolve to walk up one directory level from the 'logs/' base (e.g., to the application root); (2) on Windows deployments, backslash is a valid path separator recognized by Node's path module but is not filtered, so a value like '..\..\..\windows\win.ini' or an absolute drive-letter path such as 'C:\secrets.txt' contains no forward slash yet fully escapes or overrides the intended 'logs/' base directory (path.resolve treats an absolute second argument as replacing the first entirely); (3) the JS-level check operates purely on the literal '/' character rather than on the resolved, canonicalized path, so any OS-level separator or absolute-path syntax that is not '/' bypasses it. The correct control - resolving the path and verifying the result is still contained within the 'logs/' directory (e.g., via path.relative or startsWith on a normalized/absolute base) - is never performed. As a result, a caller who can reach this route can potentially read arbitrary files on the server filesystem outside the intended logs directory, depending on OS and deployment specifics.

Successful file reads via this endpoint (line 14) are also not logged. This prevents detection of reconnaissance or exploitation attempts against the file-serving mechanism, and prevents reconstructing an attack timeline if traversal succeeds through one of the bypass techniques described in the companion finding.

title: Unsafe/unbounded YAML deserialization via vm sandbox (potential DoS / weak sandbox boundary)
description: handleYamlUpload takes the raw bytes of an uploaded .yml/.yaml file and executes `yaml.load(data)` inside a Node vm context. Node's `vm` module is explicitly documented as NOT a security boundary and can be escaped by crafted input; it also does not limit memory allocation, only CPU time (via the 2000ms timeout). An attacker-controlled YAML payload (e.g. deeply nested aliases / 'billion laughs' style structures, or very large strings) can cause large memory allocations before the timeout fires, and the code only reacts to the resulting 'Invalid string length' / 'Script execution timed out' errors after the fact rather than preventing the resource spike. This is both an unsafe-deserialization pattern (parsing fully untrusted content with a generic YAML loader inside a non-hardened sandbox) and a resource-consumption risk on an unauthenticated endpoint.

title: Zip Slip: weak path-containment check allows arbitrary file write within the application directory
description: extractZipBuffer iterates entries from an attacker-supplied zip file and writes each entry to disk. The path-traversal guard `absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))` only checks that the resolved path is a substring of the process working directory path. Because path.resolve('.') is the app's cwd, ANY path that normalizes to somewhere inside the cwd will satisfy `.includes(...)` — the check does not restrict writes to the intended 'uploads/complaints/' subdirectory. An attacker can craft a zip entry name such as '../../some/other/file.js' that still resolves under the cwd but outside uploads/complaints, allowing arbitrary file creation/overwrite anywhere within the application's directory tree (source files, config, static assets, etc.). This is the classic Zip Slip vulnerability and is reachable from the unauthenticated POST /file-upload endpoint whenever the fileWriteChallenge flag is enabled.

No maximum file size is ever enforced in this file. Combined with the fact that the file is buffered in memory (uploadToMemory) before being handed to the zip/xml/yaml handlers, an attacker can submit an arbitrarily large file (or a file that decompresses/parses into a huge structure) and consume server memory/CPU, since there is no application-level cap prior to processing.

title: checkFileType middleware computes but never enforces file type

This is a trust-boundary/design flaw: the server treats a client-supplied filename string as authoritative for deciding how to process file content.

title: XML parse result (potential XXE output) reflected back to the client in error responses
description: handleXmlUpload parses fully untrusted XML file content with parseXmlString (implementation in ../lib/xml, not visible in this file). The inline comment 'XXE attacks in Docker/Heroku containers regularly cause "segfault" crashes' indicates the parser is known to be susceptible to XML External Entity processing. Whatever parseXmlString returns is truncated to 400 characters and embedded directly into an Error message that is passed to next() and ultimately returned to the requesting client. If the underlying parser resolves external entities (local file inclusion or an outbound network/SSRF request to an entity URI), the resolved content would flow back into this same response, giving an unauthenticated caller an oracle to exfiltrate local files or probe internal network endpoints via the file-upload endpoint.

title: SQL Injection in login query enables full authentication bypass
description: The login handler builds a raw SQL query by directly interpolating req.body.email and the hashed req.body.password into a template literal, then executes it with sequelize.query(). Because the email value is concatenated into the SQL string without parameterization or escaping, an attacker can supply a value such as `' OR 1=1-- ` (or `admin@juice-sh.op'--`) as the email field to short-circuit the WHERE clause and authenticate as an arbitrary user, or even always match the first row returned, without knowing any valid password. Because this query is the credential-verification statement that decides whether login succeeds and which user identity is subsequently trusted (a session token is issued from its result at lines 22-25), this defect both is a SQL injection and directly yields authentication bypass.

An attacker can send unlimited login attempts (including automated password-spraying or brute-force attacks against the SQL injection vector above) with no server-side friction, since every failed attempt simply returns a 401 and the handler returns immediately for the next request.

title: Unauthenticated /metrics endpoint exposes internal business and system telemetry
description: The GET /metrics route is wired (per the routing table) to metrics.serveMetrics() with auth: none — no authentication or authorization middleware is applied. serveMetrics() (lines 84-89) unconditionally serves the full Prometheus registry to any caller by writing register.contentType as the response Content-Type and returning await register.metrics() as the body. That registry, populated by observeMetrics() (lines 91-224) and refreshed on a 5-second setInterval loop (lines 158-218), includes sensitive/internal business data with no access restriction: total wallet balance across all users (walletMetrics, defined lines 147-150, set line 211), total and per-type registered user counts (userMetrics/userTotalMetrics, defined lines 136-145, set lines 208-210), total orders placed (orderMetrics, defined lines 131-134, set line 206), a cheat-detection score (cheatScoreMetrics, defined lines 120-123, set line 202), coding-challenge solve/accuracy progress (defined lines 102-129, set lines 198-204), and Node.js process/runtime internals from Prometheus.collectDefaultMetrics({}) (line 93). All of these Gauge/Counter objects register themselves into the same shared `register` (line 25) that serveMetrics() reads from, so every value the periodic update loop computes from live database queries (Promise.all at lines 183-196) becomes visible to an unauthenticated caller the next time it hits /metrics. Any unauthenticated actor can repeatedly scrape this endpoint to harvest business intelligence (revenue proxy via wallet balance, growth via user counts, security posture via cheat score/challenge completion) and perform reconnaissance on the server's runtime characteristics. Because there is also no rate limiting or caching in front of register.metrics(), an attacker can hit this endpoint at will, causing repeated metric aggregation work on every request — a classic unauthenticated, unrestricted diagnostic endpoint.

title: Mass assignment of UserId allows memory creation under arbitrary user identity
description: The addMemory handler builds the record to persist directly from the raw request body, taking UserId from req.body.UserId with no validation that it matches the authenticated caller. Although the route is documented as passing through a security.appendUserId() middleware, the handler code itself never re-derives the owner from the authenticated session - it simply trusts whatever UserId value is present on req.body at the time MemoryModel.create(record) is called. The record object literal is assembled across lines 12-16, with the UserId field taken verbatim from client input at line 15 and the object fully formed by line 16 before being handed to the persistence call. This is the classic mass-assignment / trust-assumption-violation pattern: the resource owner is a security-sensitive property that should be computed server-side from the session, not accepted from client input. If the upstream middleware fails to overwrite the field (e.g., different key casing, conditional logic, or ordering issue) or the value can be re-added elsewhere in the pipeline, an authenticated attacker can create memory records that are attributed to a different UserId than their own, corrupting another user's memory history / attributing content to a victim.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint returns every user's memory records with joined user data
description: GET /rest/memories is registered with no authentication/authorization middleware ('auth: none') and the handler performs MemoryModel.findAll({ include: [UserModel] }) with no filter on the requesting user, and no attribute allow-list on the included UserModel. This is a textbook BOLA / broken function-level authorization: there is no ownership check at all (not even an authentication check), so any anonymous party can enumerate all users' uploaded images/captions and, depending on the UserModel's default attribute scope (not restricted here via an attributes clause), potentially sensitive user fields as well.

title: Premium content paywall bypass — no authentication or payment verification
description: The route /this/page/is/hidden/behind/an/incredibly/high/paywall/that/could/only/be/unlocked/by/sending/1btc/to/us is registered with no authentication or authorization middleware (per the routing table: auth: none), and the servePremiumContent handler itself performs zero checks before serving the protected asset. The URL and comments imply a business rule: access to this wallpaper is supposed to require payment (1 BTC) — i.e., a premium/paid entitlement. However, the handler unconditionally calls res.sendFile() on the private asset for any request, authenticated or not, paid or not. This is a Broken Function Level Authorization / Broken Access Control defect (any anonymous caller who discovers or guesses the URL gets the protected resource) and simultaneously an Insecure Design defect: the design never establishes or checks a purchase/entitlement fact server-side before granting access to a resource explicitly gated on payment. title: BOLA: Order history scoped by lossy, collision-prone email obfuscation instead of user identity
description: The GET /rest/order-history handler resolves the authenticated user from the bearer token, then instead of scoping the order lookup by the user's stable identifier (loggedInUser.data.id, which is already available), it replaces every vowel in the user's own email address with '*' and uses that lossy string as the sole filter for the orders query. Because the transformation collapses many distinct email addresses onto the same obfuscated value (e.g. 'bob@test.com' and 'bab@test.com' both become 'b*b@t*st.com'), any two accounts whose emails share the same consonant skeleton and vowel positions will retrieve each other's order history. An attacker can register (or already control) an account whose email collides with a victim's email under this transformation and then call this endpoint with their own valid session to receive the victim's order data (items purchased, delivery status, pricing) — a functional Broken Object Level Authorization even though the attacker is fully 'authenticated'. This is also a design flaw: the endpoint never derives ownership from the trusted, unique user id already present on loggedInUser.data, choosing instead a weak derived string for matching.

title: Unbounded order dataset returned with no pagination in allOrders handler

title: NFT wallet ownership claimed via unauthenticated, unverified self-reported address
description: walletNFTVerify() reads req.body.walletAddress directly from the request and treats presence of that address in the addressesMinted set (populated by an on-chain 'NFTMinted' event listener) as proof that the requesting caller owns/controls that wallet and therefore solved the challenge. There is no cryptographic proof of wallet ownership (e.g., a signed nonce/message verified against the address) and no authentication binding the HTTP caller's identity to the wallet address. Since NFT mint events and minter addresses are public on-chain data (visible via any blockchain explorer or by simply listening to the same contract events), any unauthenticated caller can submit an address that someone else used to mint the NFT and be credited with 'Challenge successfully solved', without ever controlling that wallet. This is a trust-assumption violation: the server accepts a client-supplied identity claim (wallet address) as fact instead of independently verifying control of the private key, which is also an authentication-outcome defect because the endpoint is effectively an identity-resolution/verification decision ("is this caller the owner of this wallet") that is never actually checked.

title: Unauthenticated event-listener endpoint vulnerable to race-driven resource duplication and unbounded memory growth
description: GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen has no authentication and no rate limiting. It checks the module-level flag isEventListenerCreated, and only after several asynchronous steps (dynamic import, WebSocketProvider construction, Contract construction, error-handler wiring, event subscription) sets the flag to true at line 29. Because the check at line 16 and the flag update at line 29 are separated by multiple awaited/sequential async operations, concurrent requests arriving before the flag is set will all pass the guard and each spin up a new WebSocketProvider and Contract event subscription. An attacker who repeatedly hits this public, unauthenticated endpoint concurrently (especially exploiting the reset of isEventListenerCreated to false on any websocket error at line 21) can cause repeated/duplicate outbound WebSocket connections to the upstream Alchemy endpoint, consuming server sockets/memory and potentially exhausting the configured Alchemy API key's connection/rate quota. Additionally, addressesMinted (line 10) is an in-memory Set with no size cap or eviction, growing unboundedly as mint events arrive, with no pagination/cleanup logic in this file.

title: Unauthenticated access to file explicitly stored in a 'private' asset directory
description: The route handler servePrivacyPolicyProof() serves the file 'frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/thank-you.jpg' to any caller with no authentication or authorization check whatsoever. The route is registered with auth: none, and the handler itself performs zero identity or entitlement checks before calling res.sendFile(). Notably, the file imports 'challenges' (line 8) and 'challengeUtils' (line 9) — modules used elsewhere in this codebase to gate or verify state before granting access to a resource — yet neither import is ever referenced in the handler body, confirming that no verification, state check, or challenge-solved gate was wired between the request entering the handler (line 11) and the file being served (line 13). The file path itself contains the segment 'private', indicating the resource was intended to be gated behind some access control, yet the only 'protection' is that the route path is an obscure, hard-to-guess URL. Security through URL obscurity is not an access control — once the path is discovered (via source review, directory brute-forcing, referrer leakage, browser history, proxy logs, or simple guessing) any unauthenticated party can retrieve the private resource. This is a textbook broken access control pattern: authentication is entirely absent, and there is no per-user or per-role entitlement check gating a resource whose own file path declares it private.

title: Sensitive/internal-looking resource exposed via static endpoint without an access-control layer
description: The handler statically resolves and returns a file from an 'assets/private/' directory without any middleware-level access restriction (no auth, no role check, no referer/session check). This is a misconfiguration of the route: a resource path that the application's own directory naming convention marks as private is wired into a publicly reachable, unauthenticated route. The 'challenges' data-cache import at line 8 is available in this file but unused, meaning no lookup against stored state occurs to decide whether the private resource should be released for this particular request; the path.resolve() call at line 13 builds the absolute path directly from a hardcoded string with no runtime restriction layered on top. There is no security header, no cache-control restriction, and no gating logic differentiating this endpoint from any other fully public static asset, even though the directory naming and route registration pattern suggest it should require some form of restricted access.

trace.description: Route exported for registration; per the routing table this path has auth: none applied by the framework configuration outside this file.
Handler body contains no configuration or check narrowing exposure of the 'private' resource.
The 'challenges' datacache is imported but never queried, so no runtime configuration or state check restricts release of the private file.
Static file under the 'private' asset directory is served directly to the unauthenticated caller.

title: No logging of access to the private proof resource
description: Retrieval of a resource stored under a 'private' asset path is a security-relevant event (it indicates discovery of a hidden/undocumented endpoint and retrieval of a gated file), yet the handler performs no logging of the access — no requester IP, no timestamp, no correlation ID is recorded before or after sendFile() is called. Even the imported challengeUtils module (line 9), which elsewhere in this codebase is associated with recording/solving challenge state, is never invoked here to record that this private endpoint was reached. Without any log entry, there is no way to detect repeated probing/enumeration of this hidden route, nor to reconstruct who accessed the private resource and when, undermining incident detection and response for what is otherwise treated as a sensitive resource.

trace.description: Handler is invoked for every request to the hidden, unauthenticated route.
No logging statement exists anywhere in the handler body prior to fulfilling the request.
challengeUtils import remains unused, so no state-recording or audit hook fires on this access path.
The private file is served with no record created of the access event.

title: Unauthenticated checkout allows BOLA on arbitrary basket IDs
description: The POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout route is registered with no authentication middleware (per routing metadata: auth: none). The handler takes `id` directly from `req.params.id` and looks up the basket with `BasketModel.findOne({ where: { id }, ... })`. The only gate before all downstream processing is a plain existence check (`if (basket != null)`) — the caller's identity, if any, is only used to derive an email string for display, never to compare against the basket's owner. Because the route requires no login at all, any anonymous caller can invoke checkout for any basket ID, causing product quantities to be decremented, basket items destroyed, a PDF order confirmation generated, and (if `req.body.UserId` is supplied) wallet balances of arbitrary accounts to be debited or credited. This is a textbook BOLA: the resource identifier is taken from the request and used for a state-changing lookup with zero ownership or authentication verification.

trace.description: req.params.id (basket identifier) taken from an unauthenticated route (POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout, auth: none per routing metadata)
Basket looked up by id alone via BasketModel.findOne, with no check that the requester (if authenticated at all) owns this basket
if (basket != null) is the only gating condition before all subsequent processing — a pure existence check, not an ownership check
security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) optionally resolves a caller identity, but the result is never compared to the basket's owner
email is derived (or defaulted to '') from the optional customer object; control flow proceeds identically whether or not a real authenticated user exists
fileWriter 'finish' handler schedules the destructive/state-changing completion of the order for this basket id
Loop iterates over basket.Products (with BasketItem) to process each line item
quantityRow fetched per product with no lock, readable identically by a concurrent request for the same basket
newQuantity computed by subtracting the current basket item quantity from the just-read stock — if invoked twice concurrently, both computations subtract from the same stale base value
QuantityModel.update persists the decremented quantity before the basket is marked processed, so a concurrent duplicate call can repeat this mutation
Basket items destroyed and order finalized (line 162 insert, line 175 doc.end) for whatever basket id was supplied, without ownership verification

title: Client-supplied UserId drives wallet debit/credit — arbitrary account financial manipulation
description: The handler uses `req.body.UserId`, a value fully controlled by the caller, to decide which user's WalletModel record to debit and credit, instead of deriving the acting user's identity from the authenticated session. The wallet-payment sub-block (guarded by `paymentId === 'wallet'`) performs a balance check and conditional decrement against that client-supplied UserId; but the bonus-crediting block that follows is reached unconditionally whenever `req.body.UserId` is present and the wallet debit sub-block did not early-return on insufficient balance — meaning even a non-wallet payment (paymentId !== 'wallet') still results in an arbitrary account being credited with `totalPoints`. Since the checkout route itself requires no authentication, an attacker can invoke checkout supplying any victim's UserId to inflate their wallet balance, or attempt to drain a victim's wallet balance via the wallet-payment debit path. This is both a broken object-property-level-authorization issue (UserId is a mass-assignable field controlling a sensitive model operation) and a broken access-control issue (identity for a financial action is taken from client input, not the session).

WalletModel.decrement executed against req.body.UserId's wallet
Branch checks req.body.orderDetails.paymentId === 'wallet'; when false, the debit sub-block is skipped entirely but the outer UserId-gated block continues
Balance sufficiency check (wallet != null && balance >= totalPrice) decides between decrement and an early-return failure

WalletModel.increment unconditionally credits bonus points to req.body.UserId's wallet with no ownership/session check

title: Forged coupon discount — discount validity computed entirely from client-supplied, decodable data
description: When a basket has no server-tracked coupon (`security.discountFromCoupon` returns falsy), `calculateApplicableDiscount` falls back to `req.body.couponData`, a base64 string fully controlled by the client. It is decoded and split into a coupon code and date, then checked against the hardcoded `campaigns` table (lines 205-214) present in this very source file. Because the valid codes and exact millisecond timestamps are static and visible in source, an attacker can construct a matching couponData value offline and obtain discounts up to 75% on any order without ever having been issued a real coupon by the business logic. The design trusts client-supplied data for a value (discount) that should only ever be derived from server-side, single-use, tracked coupon records.

couponDate parsed as a Number from couponData[1], again fully attacker-supplied

Decoded values are matched against the hardcoded campaigns table and, on match, the discount percentage is applied to totalPrice at line 113/116

title: Unauthenticated, unrate-limited checkout triggers expensive PDF generation and disk writes
description: placeOrder is reachable with no authentication and performs multiple expensive operations per invocation: dynamic import of pdfkit, PDF document construction (multiple text/draw operations), and a synchronous-style file write to `ftp/order_<id>.pdf` via fs.createWriteStream, plus several DB round-trips (quantity lookups/updates, wallet lookups, order insert). There is no rate limiting, no body size cap, and no restriction that would prevent a caller from repeatedly invoking this endpoint (even against a basket with few or no items) to exhaust disk space (many small PDF files under ftp/), CPU, or DB connections. Because the endpoint requires no authentication, the attack surface is the entire internet.

PDFDocument dynamically constructed and rendered per request with no throttling
id taken directly from request params with no rate limiting or authentication gate before expensive work begins
BasketModel.findOne executed per request (DB round trip joining Products) with no throttle
if (basket != null) is the only gate before the expensive PDF-generation path is entered
pdfFile filename constructed fresh per request
new PDFDocument() instantiated per request — non-trivial object/rendering construction with no throttle
