title: Race window between stock/wallet mutation and basket item destruction enables duplicate processing
description: Quantity decrements (lines 77-80) and wallet increments (line 155) occur synchronously during PDF text generation, but the corresponding BasketItemModel.destroy that would prevent re-processing of the same basket only executes inside the asynchronous `fileWriter.on('finish', ...)` callback (lines 47-57), after the PDF has been fully written to disk. Between the start of the loop and that finish event there is a window during which a second concurrent request for the same basket id would find the same, not-yet-destroyed BasketItem rows and again decrement product quantity and again credit wallet bonus points, effectively allowing duplicate order settlement (double stock deduction, double bonus credit) for a single purchase. There is no locking, idempotency key, or basket-status check guarding against concurrent invocation.

trace.description: Checkout invoked with basket id; no state/status check prevents concurrent invocation for the same basket
Quantity decrement performed per basket item during PDF generation, before the basket is marked processed

BasketItemModel.destroy (the only guard against reprocessing) runs asynchronously in the fileWriter finish callback, well after the quantity/wallet mutations, creating a race window for duplicate processing

title: No security-relevant logging on financial checkout events
description: The checkout flow performs sensitive financial mutations (wallet debit/credit keyed by client-supplied UserId, coupon/discount application, order creation) but the only observability on failure or success paths is a generic `next(error)`/`next(new Error(...))` call or a silent successful mutation, with no structured audit log capturing which UserId was targeted, which basket, the discount source, or the outcome. Combined with the earlier findings (arbitrary UserId, forged coupon), the absence of an audit trail means abuse of these flows (wallet draining/inflation, discount forgery) would leave no distinguishable record for detection or incident response.

trace.description: Wallet-affecting checkout branch driven by client-supplied UserId
Insufficient wallet balance failure only forwarded to generic error handler, no audit log of the attempted UserId/amount
Wallet-payment branch decision made with no record of which payment path was selected
Balance sufficiency check determines success/failure of a financial mutation with no logging either way
Credit block entered (try) with no pre-mutation logging of the target UserId or the amount about to be credited
WalletModel.increment executed silently — no log record of the credited UserId/amount is produced
Order inserted into ordersCollection with no accompanying audit/security log entry recording the acting identity or discount source used

title: Object-level authorization for all card operations depends entirely on an externally-set req.body.UserId field
description: All three handlers (getPaymentMethods, getPaymentMethodById, delPaymentMethodById) scope their CardModel queries using req.body.UserId taken directly from the request body, rather than reading the identity from a verified session/request object independently inside this file. The route table shows the only protection applied is security.appendUserId() middleware (defined outside this file), which is presumably responsible for overwriting req.body.UserId with the authenticated user's id before these handlers run. This file performs no independent verification that req.body.UserId actually corresponds to the authenticated caller - it simply trusts whatever value is present on req.body when the handler executes. This is a fragile authorization boundary: if the middleware merges rather than strictly overwrites the field (e.g. req.body.UserId = req.body.UserId || user.id), is ever skipped due to a routing change, or the field name later changes, an attacker can supply an arbitrary UserId in the JSON body of a GET/DELETE request and read or delete another user's stored payment card. The same unverified-trust pattern is repeated identically across all three exported handlers: each one re-declares an async function that immediately consumes req.body.UserId (and, for the id-scoped handlers, req.params.id) into a Sequelize where-clause, and in every case the code proceeds directly from the query result to building a response or performing the destructive action, with no re-derivation of caller identity and no secondary ownership comparison anywhere in the file. This also constitutes an insecure design choice: using a body-supplied field as the sole authorization anchor for GET/DELETE endpoints (where request bodies are non-standard and easy to overlook or misconfigure) rather than deriving the identity from the trusted session object at the point of use, culminating in an unguarded destructive delete operation.

Once the query returns, the code proceeds to populate the response object purely based on whether card is non-null, with no additional comparison of the returned card's UserId against a value derived independently of req.body.

The success/failure branch is gated solely on whether the query matched (card != null), i.e. on the same untrusted req.body.UserId used to build the query, not on any separately-verified ownership fact.

title: Detected unauthorized card access/deletion attempts are never logged
description: When a lookup or delete operation fails to match a card for the given id/UserId combination, both getPaymentMethodById and delPaymentMethodById explicitly label the response as 'Malicious activity detected' - i.e., the application's own logic recognizes this as a potential security event (an attempt to access or delete a card that does not belong to, or does not exist for, the supplied UserId). The path from receiving the request to emitting that label passes through the scoped lookup and the null-check branch that decides whether the event is 'legitimate' or 'malicious', yet at no point along that path is any logging, auditing, or alerting call made. The event is only communicated back to the calling client via a 400 response and is otherwise discarded. This means security teams have no record of repeated BOLA probing attempts (e.g., an attacker iterating card IDs to enumerate/access other users' cards), preventing detection, investigation, or alerting on this attack pattern. The identical gap exists in delPaymentMethodById (lines 71-74), which reaches the same unlogged 'Malicious activity detected.' response via CardModel.destroy returning a falsy result.

When card is null (no matching record for that id+UserId pair, i.e. not owned by the caller or non-existent), the code explicitly treats this as a security-relevant condition.

title: Unbounded result set returned by GET /api/Cards
description: getPaymentMethods loads all CardModel rows matching the UserId filter via CardModel.findAll with no limit, offset, or pagination applied, and builds the full result array in memory before returning it in a single response. The accumulator array is declared up front and then populated by iterating every row returned by the unbounded query, with no cap on iteration count or on the number of items pushed into the response payload. If a user account accumulates a very large number of card records, this endpoint will attempt to load, transform, and serialize all of them in one request, with no defensive upper bound anywhere in the handler.

title: Full SSRF via unrestricted profile-image URL fetch, with fetched content exposed on a public path
description: The handler takes req.body.imageUrl directly from the client and passes it unmodified to fetch() with no scheme, host, or IP-range validation (no check against loopback/private ranges, no allow-list of remote hosts). This lets an authenticated caller force the server to make an arbitrary outbound HTTP(S) request to any destination reachable from the server's network position, including internal services, admin interfaces, or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254). Critically, the response body of that request is then streamed to disk under frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/uploads/<userId>.<ext>, a path that is served statically by the application. Because the extension defaults to 'jpg' for any URL whose trailing segment isn't a known image extension, essentially any response body (metadata JSON, internal API responses, admin page HTML, etc.) gets persisted and becomes retrievable by simply visiting the resulting public asset URL. This converts what looks like a 'blind' SSRF primitive into a fully exploitable one: an attacker can read the contents of internal-only resources through the public static file. The route itself has no authentication middleware applied at the routing layer (auth: none); protection depends entirely on the in-handler cookie/token lookup, so any caller who can present or forge a valid session cookie can trigger this.

The truthy loggedInUser check gates execution into the fetch branch but performs no validation of url itself.

Response body is streamed verbatim to a file under the publicly served frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/uploads/ directory, exposing fetched content (potentially from internal/metadata endpoints) at a predictable public URL.

title: Stored XSS via arbitrary remote SVG content persisted as a user's profile image
description: The extension used to save the fetched remote content is derived purely from the tail of the attacker-supplied URL and is allowed to be 'svg' (line 28). The raw response body is written to disk unmodified (no sanitization of the SVG markup, no stripping of <script> tags or event handlers) and then registered as the user's profileImage via UserModel.update. SVG files containing embedded <script> elements or JS event handlers can execute script when the image is later opened directly or embedded in a context that permits SVG scripting, giving stored XSS in the attacker-chosen victim account's (their own, but reachable by other users viewing the profile/avatar) rendering context. The rendering/consumption sink lives outside this file (frontend templates/avatar rendering), but the unsanitized persistence point is here.

title: Fallback path stores raw attacker-supplied URL as profileImage without validation
description: When the fetch/write attempt throws (e.g., non-OK response), the catch handler falls back to storing the raw, attacker-controlled url string directly as the user's profileImage field (line 36) with no validation of scheme or content. Because profileImage is very likely rendered as an or similar attribute elsewhere in the frontend, a value such as a javascript: or data: URI, or a URL containing markup-breaking characters, could result in script execution or other injection when the profile page is rendered for the affected user. This is a second, independent persistence point for unsanitized data distinct from the SSRF-fetch path.

title: Unbounded outbound fetch and disk write with no size limit, timeout, or rate limiting
description: The handler fetches an attacker-chosen URL and streams the entire response body to disk (lines 24-30) with no timeout on the fetch call, no maximum content-length check, and no cap on how many times a given user can invoke this expensive operation. An attacker can point imageUrl at an endpoint serving an extremely large or slow/never-ending response, tying up server memory, disk space, and file-descriptor/connection resources per request, and can repeat this with no rate limiting to amplify the effect into a denial-of-service condition. The route also lacks any authentication middleware at the routing layer (auth: none in the route table), further widening exposure to whoever can present a session cookie recognized by security.authenticatedUsers.

title: Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read via Incomplete Blacklist on Quarantine File Server
description: The exported serveQuarantineFiles() middleware takes the caller-supplied route parameter `file` and uses it to build a filesystem path that is then streamed back to the client with res.sendFile(). The only defense against directory traversal is a single check that rejects the value if it contains the forward-slash character ('/'). This is a blacklist of one character rather than a proper containment check (e.g. resolving the path and verifying it is still inside the intended base directory, or using res.sendFile's built-in `root` option which enforces exactly that). As a result: (1) any traversal technique that does not rely on a literal forward slash in the value that reaches this code is not blocked — most notably backslash-based traversal ('..\\..\\..\\windows\\win.ini' or absolute drive paths such as 'C:\\secret.txt') on any deployment where Node's path module resolves using Windows semantics, since path.resolve() here uses the platform-default path implementation and backslash is never checked; (2) the check operates purely on string content and gives no assurance about the resolved path's final location — it is a fragile, incomplete substitute for verifying containment inside 'ftp/quarantine/'. Because there is no authentication or per-user check on this handler either, any caller who can reach this route can attempt to read arbitrary files reachable via traversal, turning what should be a scoped 'download a quarantined upload' feature into a potential arbitrary file disclosure primitive. The correct control — comparing the resolved absolute path against the resolved base directory, or passing `{ root: path.resolve('ftp/quarantine/') }` to res.sendFile — is absent.

Tainted value is assigned to local variable `file` with no type/format normalization.
Validation is a single blacklist check for the literal '/' character only; backslash, absolute Windows paths without slashes, and other traversal encodings are not rejected.

res.sendFile(path.resolve('ftp/quarantine/', file)) resolves and serves the file without verifying the resolved path is still contained inside the 'ftp/quarantine/' directory, and without using res.sendFile's `root` containment option.

title: Quarantine File Endpoint Serves Files With No Visible Authentication or Ownership Check
description: The serveQuarantineFiles() handler performs no authentication check, session validation, or per-user ownership verification before resolving and streaming the requested file back to the caller. Any party able to reach this route (its mounting/auth-middleware, if any, is outside this file) can request any filename in the quarantine directory by guessing or enumerating names, with no check that the requester is the user who uploaded/owns that quarantined file. If this route is mounted without an authentication middleware upstream, this is a straightforward BOLA-style exposure of quarantined uploads belonging to other users.

The only gate before serving the file is the slash-content check — not an authorization check.
File is served to the caller with no verification that the caller is entitled to access this particular quarantined file.

title: Rejected Path-Traversal / Malformed Filename Attempts Are Not Logged
description: When a request contains a '/' in the file parameter (a strong signal of a directory-traversal probing attempt), the handler simply sets a 403 status and passes a generic Error to next() — there is no security-relevant log entry (source IP, attempted filename, timestamp) recorded for this rejected attempt. This prevents detecting or investigating repeated path-traversal probing against this endpoint.

Value is assigned to `file` and carried into the validation check without being recorded anywhere.

The conditional evaluates whether `file` contains '/'; when it does, execution takes the else branch (line 16) that rejects the request — this is the security-relevant decision point that goes unrecorded.
On detecting a suspicious value (contains '/'), the code only sets HTTP status 403 and forwards a generic error to next() with no logging of the offending value or requester.

title: Unauthenticated CPU/memory-intensive file processing before authentication check enables DoS
description: The route POST /profile/image/file is registered with no authentication middleware (auth: none) and relies entirely on an in-handler cookie/token lookup at line 35. However, the expensive work — accepting the full uploaded buffer (already fully buffered in memory by the upstream multer middleware) and running file-type magic-byte detection via fileType.fromBuffer(buffer) — happens at lines 17-34, before the authentication check at lines 35-39. This means any anonymous caller, without a valid session cookie, can force the server to perform this buffering and CPU-bound file-type detection work repeatedly with no rate limit, no session requirement, and no size cap visible in this handler. Because the auth check is the last gate rather than the first, the design does not prevent unauthenticated resource consumption; it only prevents unauthenticated file persistence. Repeated anonymous large uploads can degrade or exhaust server memory/CPU (denial of service) before ever being rejected.

title: No file size limit or rate limiting before writing arbitrary-size buffer to disk
description: After the (late) authentication check, the handler writes the entire uploaded buffer directly to disk with fs.writeFile at line 43, with no size validation performed anywhere in this file and no rate limiting on the endpoint. An authenticated user (or, combined with the prior finding, effectively any repeated caller once past the fileType check) can repeatedly submit large image-typed payloads to this endpoint, each of which is fully written to disk, with no visible cap on request frequency or payload size in this handler. This enables disk-space exhaustion and repeated disk I/O load through an ordinary, no-quota upload workflow.

Buffer is taken directly from the request with no size check applied in this handler.

title: Weak content validation (magic-byte sniff only) allows crafted polyglot files into publicly-served static directory
description: The only validation performed on the uploaded content is a magic-byte MIME sniff via fileType.fromBuffer (lines 24-34), which inspects the file's leading bytes to classify its type but does not otherwise validate the structural integrity or sanitize the remainder of the file's content. An attacker can construct a polyglot file that satisfies the magic-byte check for an image type (e.g., a valid JPEG/PNG/GIF header) while carrying additional embedded, non-image payload data appended after the valid header. Because the resulting file is written verbatim to a directory that is served as public static content (frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/uploads/), the crafted file becomes reachable via a predictable URL. Depending on how the static file server and any client-side consumers interpret such content, this can be leveraged for stored content-integrity abuse (e.g., serving attacker payload from a trusted origin path).

Unlike the file-write error path, there is no direct, explicit security-audit log entry recorded in this file for what is effectively a flagged 'illegal activity' / authentication-failure event, making it harder to guarantee this security-relevant event is captured and correlated for incident detection.

title: Unauthenticated notification-replay endpoint with no function-level authorization
description: The route GET /rest/repeat-notification is registered with no authentication or authorization middleware (per the routing table) and the handler itself performs no identity or role check whatsoever before executing its logic. It accepts an arbitrary `challenge` query parameter, looks up the corresponding challenge object, and — if that challenge is marked solved — re-invokes challengeUtils.sendNotification to resend/replay the 'challenge solved' notification. This functionality looks like a developer/testing utility (re-triggering a notification that would normally only fire once, at the moment a challenge is actually solved), which is exactly the kind of operation that should be gated behind an admin or internal-only check. Because no such check exists, any unauthenticated caller can invoke it for any challenge name they can guess or enumerate, effectively giving anonymous users the ability to force server-side notification logic to run on demand — a broken function-level authorization / debug-endpoint exposure.

title: Unbounded, unauthenticated notification replay enables resource-consumption DoS
description: Because the endpoint requires no authentication and there is no rate limiting, size cap, or per-user throttle visible in this handler, an attacker can invoke GET /rest/repeat-notification in a tight automated loop for any known solved-challenge name. Each call reaches challengeUtils.sendNotification (line 15) unconditionally whenever challenge.solved is true, with no check for whether a notification was already recently sent. If sendNotification performs work such as a database write and/or a broadcast to all connected clients (typical for a 'notification' subsystem), an attacker can force this expensive/broadcast operation to run at whatever rate their network allows, exhausting server resources (DB writes, memory, socket broadcast bandwidth) or spamming every connected client's UI — a denial-of-service vector reachable by anyone, with zero cost of entry (no login required) and no visible throttle.

title: Unvalidated decodeURIComponent on caller-controlled query parameter can throw an unhandled exception
description: query.challenge is passed straight into decodeURIComponent without validation or a try/catch. A malformed percent-encoded value (e.g. a lone '%' or an invalid escape sequence) causes decodeURIComponent to throw a URIError synchronously inside the request handler. Since this file contains no error handling around the call, the exception propagates to Express's generic error handler; depending on deployment configuration this can produce an unexpected 500 response and, if verbose error output is enabled, leak internal stack trace / file path information to an unauthenticated caller. This is reachable by anyone since the route requires no authentication.

title: Unauthenticated BOLA on GET /api/Recycles/:id exposes other users' recycle records
description: getRecycleItem parses the raw path parameter with JSON.parse and places the result directly as the value of the 'id' key in a Sequelize where clause, with no type check that the parsed value is a scalar (number/string). Because JSON.parse accepts arbitrary JSON structures, an attacker can supply a path segment that decodes to an object, e.g. a URL-encoded '{"$ne":null}' or '{"$gt":0}', which becomes 'where: { id: { $ne: null } }' (or an equivalent operator object). If the Sequelize configuration honors legacy/string operators (or any operator aliasing is enabled elsewhere in the app), this turns a single-record lookup into an operator-driven query that can match every row in the table, defeating the intended 'fetch one record by id' semantics. Because the query has no pagination/limit and the endpoint is unauthenticated, a successful operator injection lets an anonymous caller dump the entire Recycles table in one request — effectively obtaining the same 'list all recycle records' capability that the sibling endpoint (blockRecycleItems, line 23-26) was explicitly designed to block for GET /api/Recycles.

If the Sequelize configuration honors legacy/string operators (or any operator aliasing is enabled elsewhere in the app), this turns a single-record lookup into an operator-driven query that can match every row in the table, defeating the intended 'fetch one record by id' semantics. There is no logging of the failed id, the source IP, or the exception, for either parse failures or database errors. This is a security-relevant blind spot: repeated malformed-id probing (which is exactly the reconnaissance behavior an attacker performing the injection described in the sibling finding would exhibit) leaves no trace, preventing detection or investigation of an attack in progress.

title: Open Redirect via weak prefix/substring-based allowlist validation
description: The /redirect endpoint takes an arbitrary, fully-attacker-controlled URL from the 'to' query parameter and passes it straight to res.redirect() as long as security.isRedirectAllowed(toUrl) returns true. That function lives outside this file, but this file itself contains a locally-defined mirror of the intended validation logic, isUnintendedRedirect(), which determines whether a URL is allowed by checking utils.startsWith(toUrl, allowedUrl) against each entry in security.redirectAllowlist. A prefix/substring match on a full URL is not equivalent to validating the URL's origin: an attacker can construct a URL such as 'http://<allowedUrl-prefix>.attacker.com/...' or embed the allowed prefix as a path/query component of an otherwise attacker-controlled URL, and the startsWith check will treat it as allowed even though the browser will actually navigate to the attacker's domain. Because this is the same kind of check the actual gatekeeping function (security.isRedirectAllowed) is designed to perform, and no stronger URL-parsing/origin-comparison logic is visible anywhere in this file, the redirect target validation is a weak, bypassable control. The endpoint requires no authentication, so any external party can craft a link (e.g. in a phishing email) that appears to originate from the trusted application domain (juice-shop.example.com/redirect?to=...) but silently forwards victims to an attacker-controlled site — a classic open-redirect-enabled phishing/credential-theft primitive, and could also be chained with other flows (OAuth-style redirect_uri abuse, stealing referrer-embedded tokens, etc.).

Either way, the disconnect between the visible (unused) check and the actually-executed external check is a design/maintainability weakness that increases the chance a weak validation slips into or remains in production undetected.

title: Unencoded reflection of user-controlled URL into error message on rejected redirect
description: When a redirect target is rejected, the handler builds an Error whose message directly concatenates the raw, attacker-supplied toUrl value ('Unrecognized target URL for redirect: ' + toUrl) and forwards it to next(). This error is then handled by Express's error-handling middleware (outside this file). If that downstream handler renders error messages into an HTML response (which is the Express default behavior for many configurations, including stack-trace/error pages), an attacker can supply a 'to' parameter containing HTML/script content (since it is never rejected — it is exactly the value that fails isRedirectAllowed and is guaranteed to reach this error path) and have it reflected unescaped into the response, resulting in reflected XSS. Because this file does not encode, sanitize, or otherwise neutralize toUrl before embedding it into the Error message, and no validation restricts the character set of the 'to' parameter, the flaw exists here even though the actual HTML-rendering sink is in different (out-of-file) error-handling code.

title: Forgeable continue codes via hardcoded, publicly-known Hashids salts
description: All three handlers use the Hashids library purely as a reversible, non-cryptographic obfuscation encoding of internal challenge IDs, keyed with a salt string that is hardcoded directly in the source ('this is my salt', 'this is the salt for findIt challenges', 'yet another salt for the fixIt challenges'). Because this file (and the whole application) is open source, the salt, alphabet, and encoding scheme are fully known to any attacker. Hashids explicitly documents that it provides obfuscation, not security -- it is not a MAC or signature. As a result, an attacker can independently construct a Hashids encoder with the identical salt/alphabet, encode any arbitrary set of challenge IDs (including challenges never actually solved), and submit the resulting string as continueCode. The handler decodes it and unconditionally calls challengeUtils.solve()/solveFindIt()/solveFixIt() with true for every matching challenge, with no verification that the caller ever legitimately completed those challenges. This turns a token that is supposed to prove prior progress into a fully forgeable credential, letting anyone claim completion credit for arbitrary challenges. This is both a broken authentication-style token issue (hardcoded key enabling forgery of a completion assertion) and a business-logic design flaw (the server trusts a client-suppliable value instead of deriving completion state from server-side history).

Yet the handlers perform a state-changing operation -- marking challenges as solved in the shared, application-wide `challenges` datacache -- based solely on a client-supplied path parameter. There is no check tying the continueCode to any authenticated session/user, and no verification that the caller previously had legitimate access to whatever account originally produced that progress. Because challenge-solved state in this codebase is global (not scoped per authenticated user within this handler), any unauthenticated caller who can produce or guess/brute-force a valid-looking code can flip challenge state for the whole application instance, corrupting the scoreboard/progress tracking that the challenge-completion mechanism is meant to protect. This is a broken function-level authorization issue: a sensitive, state-mutating function is reachable with no identity check at all.

title: Unbounded, unauthenticated continueCode input enables repeated expensive decode calls (no rate limiting)
description: The three handlers accept an attacker-supplied continueCode path parameter that is only validated by a charset regular expression (/^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$/) with no length cap, then passed to hashids.decode(). Because the routes require no authentication (auth: none) and there is no visible rate limiting or request-size restriction in this file, an attacker can send a very high volume of requests, and/or very long candidate strings, causing repeated Hashids decode operations. While a single decode is cheap, the combination of (a) no authentication, (b) no rate limiting, and (c) no upper bound on continueCode length creates an unrestricted-resource-consumption vector: an attacker can flood these endpoints to consume CPU/connection resources, and can also use them for online brute-forcing of valid continue codes with no throttling to slow the attempt rate.

Combined with the lack of authentication on these routes, this removes any ability to detect or investigate abuse (e.g., mass forging of continue codes, or brute-force probing) after the fact, since there is no audit trail of who invoked these endpoints or what changed.

title: Unthrottled security-question guessing enables account takeover via password reset
description: The /rest/user/reset-password endpoint (registered with auth: none) allows resetting any account's password by supplying the account's email plus the answer to a single, typically low-entropy 'security question'. There is no rate limiting, attempt counter, CAPTCHA, or account lockout anywhere in the handler: an attacker can call this endpoint repeatedly with the same email and different guessed answers until security.hmac(answer) matches the stored hash, at which point the password is changed to an attacker-chosen value and the account is fully taken over. Because security question answers (pet name, birth city, etc.) have far lower entropy than a random token, and because the recovery flow relies on knowledge-based verification as the sole factor with no throttling, this is both a missing-control (resource-consumption) issue and a fundamentally insecure account-recovery design (insecure-design) whose exploitation directly defeats the authentication/ownership guarantee of the reset flow (crypto-auth, per the authentication-outcome anchor: a defect that lets an attacker resolve to another user's identity/credential control).

String equality in most JS engines short-circuits on the first differing byte, which can create a timing side channel that leaks information about how many leading characters of the hash match, theoretically aiding an attacker attempting to guess or forge the correct hash value. This is a weaker control than a timing-safe compare and sits directly on the authentication-decision path for the password-reset flow.

title: SQL Injection in product search via unparameterized query interpolation
description: The searchProducts handler takes the 'q' query parameter directly from the request, performs only a length cap (200 chars), and then interpolates it verbatim into a raw SQL string executed via sequelize.query. There is no parameterization (no use of Sequelize's `replacements`/`bind` options) and no escaping of SQL metacharacters such as single quotes. An attacker can close the LIKE string literal and inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. a payload like `')) UNION SELECT id, email, password, ... FROM Users-- ` would let the query return columns from the Users table (including email and password hash) disguised as product rows. Those rows are then iterated, passed through the i18n translation helper, and serialized straight back to the caller via res.json(). Because the endpoint requires no authentication, this is a fully unauthenticated SQL injection that can be used to read arbitrary data from any table in the database (Users, orders, security answers, etc.), not just Products — an authorization bypass achieved through injection, and a direct path to harvesting password hashes for offline cracking.

title: Unauthenticated, unbounded product search enables resource exhaustion and full data scraping
description: The /rest/products/search endpoint requires no authentication and applies no rate limiting, no pagination, and no LIMIT clause on the query. Every matching row from the Products table (or, via the SQL injection above, any table reachable through UNION) is loaded into memory, iterated to apply per-row translation processing, and then serialized in full into the JSON response. Because the query uses a leading-wildcard LIKE ('%...%') across two columns with no index-friendly prefix, each request forces a full table scan whose cost and result size scale with table size, not with any caller-supplied bound. An attacker can repeatedly issue empty or broad queries (e.g. q= or a single common character) to force expensive full scans, large in-memory arrays, and full result-set serialization on every request, with no throttling to stop high-frequency abuse — a straightforward denial-of-service vector against the database and application server, and a means of scraping the entire catalog in one request.

title: Database error internals passed through to error handler without sanitization
description: When the raw SQL query fails (e.g. due to a malformed injection attempt or a syntax error triggered by an attacker probing the query), the handler forwards error.parent — the underlying database driver error — directly to next(). If the downstream global error handler (outside this file) renders error details to the client, this can leak internal database schema/query information useful for refining injection attacks. Regardless of downstream behavior, this file makes no attempt to log the anomalous query attempt for security monitoring (e.g., logging the offending 'q' value and requesting IP when a query fails), so repeated SQL injection probing against this unauthenticated endpoint would go unnoticed.

title: Stored XSS via unsanitized true-client-ip header persisted to user record
description: The handler reads the attacker-controlled HTTP header 'true-client-ip' directly from the incoming request (line 18). If the header arrives as an array (line 19), only the first element is kept (line 20) — neither step performs any content validation. The value then reaches a branch gated purely on a feature/challenge flag (line 22): when utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.httpHeaderXssChallenge) is true, the if-body is empty (line 23) so the raw, attacker-controlled string flows through completely untouched; only in the opposite case is security.sanitizeSecure applied (line 24), meaning the sanitizer is not unconditionally enforced but is switchable by external/config state. The value then passes an emptiness check (line 26) — since the header was supplied, it is non-empty and the safe fallback branch (line 27, deriving from the raw socket address) is skipped, so the tainted value is preserved. It is finally persisted verbatim to the user's lastLoginIp column via user.update() (line 31). Because 'true-client-ip' is read straight off the request object with no upstream reverse-proxy validation, any caller can set this header themselves and inject markup/script (e.g. '<script>...</script>'), which is stored as-is and will render unescaped wherever lastLoginIp is later displayed (e.g. an admin user view outside this file) — a stored XSS. The conditional bypass of sanitization based on a flag rather than a fixed security policy is itself an insecure design choice.

title: Full user model instance returned in response, risking exposure of sensitive fields
description: The caller's identity, resolved from the session (line 16) and confirmed authenticated (line 17), is used to fetch the complete user record by primary key (line 30). No field projection or DTO is applied at the lookup. The subsequent update call returns the full updated Sequelize model instance rather than a restricted subset of fields (line 31), and this entire object is then serialized straight to the client via res.json() with no allow-list or exclusion of sensitive columns (line 32). Sequelize model instances typically include all persisted columns unless explicitly excluded, which for a User model commonly includes sensitive properties such as password hash, TOTP/2FA secret, or security-answer hash. Any authenticated caller therefore receives far more of their own record than the endpoint's stated purpose (saving a login IP) requires, and any future addition of a sensitive column to the model is automatically exposed here with no code change needed in this file.

title: State-changing database write performed via GET request with no CSRF/rate-limit control
description: The exported handler is registered (per the routing table) as GET /rest/saveLoginIp (line 15), a read-semantic verb used to perform a mutating action. Control flow proceeds through an in-handler session check (line 16) and the branch that treats the caller as authorized to mutate (line 17) — there is no additional CSRF token, origin check, or verb-appropriate guard here, only presence-of-session. The mutation is then wrapped in a bare try block (line 29) with no throttling or idempotency control, before the actual database write is executed on every matching request (line 30 fetch, line 31 update). Using GET for a mutating operation is a design flaw: GET requests are commonly triggered passively (image tags, link prefetching, caching proxies) and are typically not covered by CSRF protections applied to state-changing verbs, and there is no visible rate limiting anywhere in this path, so an authenticated caller (or anything able to cause their browser to issue this GET, e.g. via passive triggers) can invoke the write repeatedly and rapidly.

title: User account enumeration via unauthenticated security-question lookup
description: The handler exported from this file is registered as GET /rest/user/security-question with no authentication middleware (per routing context: 'auth: none'). It accepts an arbitrary `email` value from the query string and uses it to look up a SecurityAnswerModel joined to UserModel by that email. The response shape differs observably depending on whether a matching account exists: if a SecurityAnswer/User record is found, the associated security question object is returned (HTTP 200 with `{ question: {...} }`); if no account matches, an empty object `{}` is returned. Because this endpoint requires no authentication and no rate limiting is present in this file, an attacker can iterate over a list of candidate email addresses and use the differing response to determine which addresses correspond to registered accounts. This is a classic account-recovery/enumeration weakness: the account-recovery decision point (does this email have a security question configured, i.e., does the account exist) is disclosed to an unauthenticated caller with no throttling. This both weakens the authentication/recovery mechanism (crypto-auth: account-recovery decision leaking account existence, per crypto-auth playbook item 7 and the authentication-outcome anchor for password-reset/security-question decisions) and reflects an insecure design choice (insecure-design: the recovery workflow trusts the client-supplied email fully and never limits or obscures the account-existence signal) and is compounded by the total absence of rate limiting on a sensitive, unauthenticated lookup endpoint that also queries the database on every attempt (resource-consumption: missing rate limit permits automated brute-force enumeration and unbounded query volume).

title: No security logging for account-recovery probing on security-question endpoint
description: The security-question lookup endpoint, which is part of the account-recovery flow and is reachable without authentication, performs no logging of any kind — neither successful lookups (account exists) nor failed lookups (account does not exist). A high volume of requests to this endpoint from a single source, which would indicate an automated account-enumeration or password-reset probing attack, would go completely undetected because there is no log entry, counter, or alerting hook anywhere in the handler. This absence of logging for a security-relevant event (account-recovery/security-question probing) prevents detection, investigation, or after-the-fact reconstruction of an enumeration attack against user accounts.

title: NoSQL Injection via unparameterized $where clause built from request parameter
description: The order id path parameter is interpolated directly into a MongoDB $where clause, which is evaluated as raw server-side JavaScript by the database engine: `db.ordersCollection.find({ $where: `this.orderId === '${id}'` })`. When the reflectedXssChallenge flag is disabled, the id is passed through a regex that strips non-word/dash characters (line 15, first branch), which incidentally also blocks most $where breakout characters. However, when the flag is enabled, the code uses `utils.trunc(req.params.id, 60)` instead — truncation only limits length, it does not remove quotes, backslashes, or JavaScript syntax. An attacker can then supply a payload such as `' || '1'=='1` or `'; return true; var x='` to break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary JavaScript that MongoDB will execute for every document in the collection, enabling boolean-based data exfiltration, DoS via expensive/looping expressions, or (per the code's own comment 'Truncate id to avoid unintentional RCE') more severe execution effects. This is a textbook $where NoSQL injection: user input is embedded into an executable query structure with no parameterization.

title: Reflected XSS via order id echoed back in JSON response

If no matching order is found, the raw (still-tainted) id is placed back into the JSON response as `orderId` (line 20) and returned to the client (line 22). If any frontend view renders this order-tracking response without output encoding (a known Juice Shop challenge pattern for this exact endpoint), an attacker-controlled payload such as `<script>...</script>` supplied in the URL path is reflected back to the victim's browser, resulting in reflected XSS. The comment on line 14 ('Truncate id to avoid unintentional RCE') confirms the developers were aware this value is dangerous but only mitigated the RCE vector, not the XSS vector, when the challenge flag is on.

title: Unauthenticated order lookup allows enumeration of any user's order details (BOLA)
description: The /rest/track-order/:id route has no authentication or authorization middleware ('auth: none') and the handler performs no check that the requesting caller owns, or is otherwise entitled to view, the order identified by `id`. Any unauthenticated party can supply an arbitrary order id and receive that order's full record via res.json(result) at line 22. Since order ids are not scoped to a session/user in this handler, an attacker can enumerate or guess order ids (which may be sequential or otherwise low-entropy) to read other customers' order information — a classic Broken Object Level Authorization pattern. There is also no rate limiting, so an attacker can iterate over the id space quickly to harvest data for many orders in a short time.

title: Security control (input sanitization) toggled off by a feature flag instead of always-on
description: The strength of the sanitization applied to attacker-controlled input is conditioned on `utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.reflectedXssChallenge)` (line 15). This means the same production code path exposes two very different security postures depending on a runtime/config flag: strict character filtering in one branch, and mere length truncation (no character filtering) in the other. A security-critical sanitization routine should not be conditionally weakened by an external flag reachable through configuration; if that flag can be toggled (directly or indirectly) in any deployed environment, the $where-injection and reflected-XSS defenses documented above are silently disabled. This is a design flaw: the code's own safety property is not guaranteed by the design, only by the current value of an external switch.

title: NoSQL Injection via string-concatenated $where clause in product reviews lookup
description: The handler builds a MongoDB $where clause by string concatenation of a value derived from req.params.id: '{ $where: this.product == + id }'. When the internal feature flag noSqlCommandChallenge is enabled, the code deliberately bypasses numeric coercion (Number(req.params.id)) and instead only truncates the raw parameter to 40 characters via utils.trunc. Truncation is a length cap, not a content sanitizer or allow-list, so an attacker can still supply a short JavaScript payload (well under 40 characters) that breaks out of the numeric comparison and is evaluated as arbitrary JavaScript by the $where operator for every document in the reviews collection. The developer comment 'Truncate id to avoid unintentional RCE' shows the mitigation was consciously chosen, but a length cap does not prevent code injection, which is itself a design flaw. Because $where causes the supplied JavaScript to execute inside the same JS global scope as the request handler, the injected code can additionally reach globals defined by this file, such as the synchronous, blocking global.sleep function (capped at 2000ms) declared at the top of the file. Calling that function from inside the injected $where predicate, which runs once per document in the collection, synchronously blocks the Node.js event loop, and because the predicate is evaluated per-document, a single request against a collection with many reviews can multiply the blocking delay, amplifying a single HTTP request into a severe denial-of-service condition for the whole application.

title: Dead/inert NoSQL DoS timing instrumentation, measured latency never logged or acted upon
description: The handler explicitly measures query latency to detect NoSQL denial-of-service attacks, per the comment 'Measure how long the query takes, to check if there was a nosql dos attack'. It records t0 before the query and t1 after it resolves, but t1 is never compared to t0, never logged, never used to trigger an alert, rate limit, or any other response. The response is then sent unconditionally regardless of how long the query took, confirming that the timing measurement has zero effect on the code's behavior. This makes the stated detection control completely inert: even if an attacker triggers an abnormally slow $where-based NoSQL DoS query, there is no logging or monitoring output that would let operators detect, investigate, or respond to the attack from this code path.

title: Unauthenticated, unbounded, per-document $where query with no rate limiting or pagination
description: The GET /rest/products/:id/reviews route requires no authentication (per routing configuration) and executes a MongoDB $where query, which forces a full JavaScript evaluation per document rather than an indexed match, with no result pagination or size cap on the returned review set, and no per-IP/per-user rate limiting visible in this file. Even setting aside the injection risk in the sibling finding, an attacker can repeatedly invoke this endpoint (optionally against a product with a very large number of reviews) at high volume with no throttling, forcing repeated expensive per-document JS evaluation, a full in-memory iteration over every returned review, and unbounded result serialization, degrading service availability.

title: Broken Object-Level Authorization: any authenticated user can edit any other user's product review
description: The handler resolves the calling user via security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) at line 15 but never uses that identity to scope or validate the update. The MongoDB update statement (lines 16-19) is built solely from caller-supplied data: the filter uses only req.body.id (line 17), the $set payload uses only req.body.message (line 18), and the options object sets multi:true (line 19), so the update dispatches (line 16) against whatever document(s) match the caller-chosen id with no clause tying the matched review's author to the authenticated user. Authentication is checked (a user object is fetched) but authorization (ownership of the specific review resource) is never verified — the classic BOLA/API1 pattern, and also a case where the client fully controls which resource is targeted with no server-side re-derivation of scope.

title: NoSQL query-operator injection via unvalidated req.body.id enables mass update of unrelated reviews
description: req.body.message is written directly into the review document's message field via $set (line 18) with no validation, sanitization, or allow-listing of HTML/script content. The same call also sets multi:true (line 19), meaning the unsanitized payload can be written into more than one review document depending on the filter, widening the number of stored copies of the malicious content before it is persisted (line 16). Product reviews are conventionally rendered back to other users (e.g., on the product details page) in the Juice Shop frontend. A free-form text field persisted without encoding is the classic stored-XSS injection point; the rendering sink lives outside this file, but the unsanitized persistence here is what introduces the payload into data that will later be rendered as markup/script to other users, including admins.

title: Unbounded multi-document update with no rate limiting on a sensitive mutation endpoint
description: The update operation uses { multi: true } (line 19) with a filter that is entirely attacker-supplied (line 17) and no per-request size/count cap. There is no visible rate limiting or throttling on this PATCH endpoint. An attacker can repeatedly invoke this endpoint (potentially amplified by the NoSQL-operator-injection issue described separately) to trigger large-scale writes across the reviews collection, consuming database resources and degrading service for other users.

title: No audit logging of review-mutation events on an authorization-sensitive endpoint
description: This handler performs a data-mutating operation (updating review content, potentially for a review not owned by the caller) but never logs the acting user, the target review id, or the outcome of the operation. The update is invoked (line 16) and its result handled in the success branch of the promise (lines 20-21) with no logging statement anywhere in the chain before the response is returned to the client (line 22). Given the absence of an ownership check (see related access-control finding), the lack of any audit trail means an abuse of this endpoint to alter other users' review content cannot be detected, investigated, or attributed after the fact.

title: Stored XSS via unvalidated/unsanitized username field
description: The handler takes req.body.username directly from the client and persists it to the user record via user.update({ username: req.body.username }) with no validation, length limit, character allow-listing, or sanitization. Usernames are a conventional 'carrier' field that gets displayed elsewhere in the application (profile pages, admin user lists, order/feedback attribution, etc.). Because the value is stored verbatim, any HTML/script payload placed in the username field will be persisted and can execute wherever it is later rendered without escaping. Reaching the persistence call requires passing the authentication guard and the user-existence guard, but neither guard performs any content validation on the username value itself. The rendering sink is outside this file (likely the frontend templates or admin panel), but the injection point — free-form user text accepted and persisted with zero sanitization — is here.

title: Authentication cookie set without Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags
description: The updated Sequelize model instance is converted to a plain object via utils.queryResultToJson(savedUser) with no field allow-listing, then handed wholesale to security.authorize() to mint a new token, which is stored server-side and returned to the client as a cookie. If queryResultToJson does not strip sensitive columns (password hash, role/isAdmin, security answer, etc.), those values become part of the token payload that is base64-encoded (not encrypted) inside a JWT-style token and is therefore recoverable by the client or anyone who intercepts the cookie. This both leaks sensitive credential material client-side (crypto-auth) and represents an object-property exposure (api-property-auth) since no explicit allow-list of 'safe' fields is applied before the object enters the token/cookie flow.

If queryResultToJson does not strip sensitive columns (password hash, role/isAdmin, security answer, etc.), those values become part of the token payload that is base64-encoded (not encrypted) inside a JWT-style token and is therefore recoverable by the client or anyone who intercepts the cookie. title: Unbounded, unthrottled session-token issuance with no invalidation of prior tokens
description: Every successful call to this endpoint mints a brand-new token via security.authorize() and inserts it into the authenticatedUsers in-memory store via .put(), without ever removing or invalidating the caller's previous token. There is no rate limiting on this POST endpoint (it is reachable with auth:none at the routing layer, relying solely on an internal cookie check), so a single authenticated actor — or anyone who can replay a valid cookie — can repeatedly invoke it to grow the authenticatedUsers map without bound, consuming server memory, and can also keep an arbitrary number of old, still-valid tokens alive simultaneously for the same account (no session rotation/invalidation), undermining containment of a compromised session.

title: No audit logging of profile modification or authentication decisions
description: The handler performs a security-relevant state change (updating the account's username and reissuing an auth token) but never writes any audit/security log entry recording who made the change, from where, or when. The only log-adjacent action in the file is passing an Error to next() when a request is unauthenticated (line 20); every subsequent step — identity resolution, record fetch, mutation, serialization, token issuance, cookie assignment, and the final redirect — completes with no security event logged, removing the ability to reconstruct or detect abuse of the profile-update / token-refresh flow after the fact.

title: Username field accepted with no format, length, or uniqueness validation
description: The design never establishes any rule constraining the username value beyond 'copy it into the database.' There is no length cap, character restriction, or uniqueness check before persisting req.body.username, and neither of the two guards the request passes through (authentication check, user-existence check) performs any content validation on the value itself. This lets a user set their display name to an empty string, an extremely long string, or a value identical to another user's name/email prefix, enabling impersonation-style confusion or downstream processing issues (e.g., truncation, display collisions) — a business rule the server never derives or enforces itself, purely trusting client input.

title: Remote Code Execution via eval() on user-controlled username field
description: The handler retrieves the authenticated user's record and reads user.username (line 52). If the username matches the pattern #{(.*)} it extracts the inner content and passes it directly to JavaScript's eval() (line 61). Since 'username' is a free-form profile field that a user can set (elsewhere, outside this file, e.g. during registration/profile update), an attacker can set their own username to a value like '#{process.mainModule.require("child_process").execSync("...")}' and, upon visiting their own /profile page, trigger execution of arbitrary JavaScript with the privileges of the Node.js server process. This is a critical server-side code injection reachable purely by controlling a stored profile field and viewing one's own profile — no other privilege is required. The code path is also a design flaw: the application's design permits any value satisfying a regex from a user-writable field to be executed as code, rather than ever treating username as pure data.

title: Content-Security-Policy explicitly weakened with 'unsafe-eval'
description: The Content-Security-Policy header set for the profile page hardcodes 'unsafe-eval' in script-src (line 88). This directly undermines the browser-side defense-in-depth that CSP is meant to provide, and is especially dangerous on this exact page, which also contains a server-side eval() sink reachable via the username field (line 61) and renders user-controlled data into a Pug template (line 95). Even setting aside the eval() finding, permitting 'unsafe-eval' on an authenticated, data-rendering page removes one of the strongest mitigations against script injection succeeding in the browser.

CSP string is constructed with script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval', a permissive/dangerous directive.

title: CSP header/directive injection via unsanitized profileImage value
description: The Content-Security-Policy header is built by directly interpolating user.profileImage into a template string: `img-src 'self' ${user?.profileImage}; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'` (line 88). profileImage is a stored, user-controllable field (set via other routes such as profile image URL upload, outside this file) and is inserted without any validation, escaping, or origin allow-listing. If profileImage contains characters such as `;` or additional directive keywords, an attacker can inject or override CSP directives (e.g. append their own script-src/connect-src rules), weakening or rewriting the policy that is supposed to protect the page. This is a case of assembling a security-critical, browser-interpreted header via string concatenation of untrusted input rather than through a validating/escaping API.

title: Detected illegal/attack activity is not security-logged
description: Three separate points in this handler detect anomalous or clearly malicious conditions — no authenticated session (line 36), missing user record for an authenticated session (line 48), and a failed exploitation attempt of the eval()-based SSTI sink (line 97, catch block guarding the code at lines 85-95) — yet none of them write to any security/audit log. Each is only wrapped in a generic Error passed to next(), which becomes a normal error-handling/response path rather than a recorded security event. The successful case (eval() succeeding, line 55 sets `abused_ssti_bug = true`) is also never logged, and even when eval() itself throws (lines 62-64) the exception is silently swallowed with no logging at all, just a cosmetic fallback. This prevents detection, alerting, or forensic reconstruction of exploitation attempts against this endpoint.

title: Unbounded, expensive per-request template compilation with no rate limiting
description: On every single request to GET /profile, the handler reads a template file from disk (line 28) unconditionally — even before the authentication check at line 34 — performs a database lookup (line 41), applies a series of global regex replace operations across the whole template (lines 73-83), and then dynamically imports the Pug module and re-compiles the template from scratch (lines 86-87) instead of caching a compiled template. Combined with the fact that this route has no visible authentication/rate-limiting middleware at the routing layer (route table shows auth: none) and no throttling is present in this file, an attacker can repeatedly request /profile to force repeated disk I/O, DB queries, and template compilation, consuming CPU, DB, and file-descriptor resources on every hit. This is compounded by the eval() call on line 61 being executed on every request as well when a malicious username is stored, adding further per-request cost.

title: Possible use of weak hash for user email without visible verification
description: The handler calls security.hash(user?.email) (line 75) to derive a value embedded into the rendered template. The hashing implementation itself is defined in a module outside this file, so its algorithm cannot be confirmed here. Historically in this codebase family this helper uses a fast, unsalted hash (e.g., MD5) purely for a gravatar-style display value; if the same hash function or a related one is reused anywhere for security-sensitive purposes (e.g., token derivation), a weak/unsalted hash would enable precomputation attacks. This is flagged at low confidence because the algorithm cannot be verified from this file alone.

title: forgedFeedbackChallenge performs no verification or logging of impersonated feedback submissions
description: forgedFeedbackChallenge is registered as middleware on POST /api/Feedbacks (auth: none, per the routing table). Its name implies it should detect/verify whether a feedback submission has been 'forged' — i.e., submitted with a UserId/author identity that does not belong to the caller (a classic mass-assignment / impersonation vector on a public, unauthenticated endpoint). The implementation, however, does nothing but call next() unconditionally. No inspection of req.body (e.g., a UserId field that could be set to another user's id) occurs, and no security event is logged. Any attempt to forge feedback ownership passes through this file completely undetected and unrecorded, and the endpoint's actual identity-property protection (if any) is entirely delegated to code outside this file with zero defense-in-depth or audit trail here.

title: registerAdminChallenge / passwordRepeatChallenge / emptyUserRegistration are no-op stubs on the public registration route
description: POST /api/Users is an unauthenticated route (auth: none) that runs registerAdminChallenge(), passwordRepeatChallenge(), and emptyUserRegistration() as its dedicated verification middleware, each mounted as a separate handler on the same route per the routing table. Their names indicate they are the designated checkpoints for (a) detecting/preventing self-assignment of an admin role via the request body (a mass-assignment / privilege-escalation vector on registration), (b) validating that password and password-confirmation fields match, and (c) rejecting empty registrations. All three implementations simply call next() with no inspection of req.body whatsoever. This means the file that is supposed to be the security 'verify' layer for registration provides zero server-side verification of the role field, the password-confirmation field, or empty-submission cases across all three checkpoints, and produces no log/alert for any of these attempted abuses before the request reaches the real user-creation handler outside this file.

title: Unbounded in-memory array growth in captchaBypassChallenge enables memory-exhaustion DoS
description: captchaBypassChallenge runs on every POST /api/Feedbacks request (auth: none, per routing). It writes to req.app.locals.captchaBypassReqTimes at index (captchaReqId - 1) and then increments captchaReqId on every single call, with no upper bound, no cap on array size, and no eviction/rotation of old entries. Because this state lives in req.app.locals (shared, long-lived application state) and the endpoint is public and unauthenticated, an attacker can send an unbounded number of requests to continuously grow this array, consuming server memory proportional to the number of requests ever made. Nothing in this file caps request volume or array size, so this middleware — intended to support a CAPTCHA-bypass timing check — itself becomes a resource-exhaustion vector.

req.app.locals.captchaReqId++ unconditionally advances the counter on every request with no upper bound, guaranteeing the array indexed at line 21 grows without limit as long as the attacker keeps sending unauthenticated requests, exhausting server memory over time.

title: accessControlChallenges computes a UI-bypass signal but never enforces or logs it
description: accessControlChallenges derives `uiBypassed`, a signal indicating the request likely reached this route via direct API access rather than through the application UI (no `referer` header, or `sec-fetch-dest: document`). This is exactly the kind of signal used to detect function-level authorization bypass (a caller reaching a restricted operation by skipping the intended UI/workflow gate). It also destructures `url` from the request, presumably to correlate the signal with the specific restricted route being accessed. Both computed values are discarded — the function calls next() unconditionally without using either value to deny, redirect, or log the request. If any route relies on this middleware for an access-control decision, that decision never actually happens; at minimum, this represents a completely silent, unenforced/unlogged access-control checkpoint.

title: JWT / server-side / database security-event detectors are unconditional no-ops
description: jwtChallenges, serverSideChallenges, and databaseRelatedChallenges are exported as middleware factories whose names indicate they are the designated verification/detection points for JWT tampering or algorithm abuse, server-side request/template issues, and SQL/NoSQL injection indicators respectively. Each implementation only calls next() with no inspection of the request, token, or response at all. Whatever routes attach these (not visible in this file's provided routing sample) receive no verification and no security-event logging for these categories of attack from this file. In particular, jwtChallenges is the natural checkpoint for verifying JWT signature/algorithm integrity per its name, yet performs none — meaning any JWT-related authentication anomaly reaching this checkpoint is neither validated nor recorded.

title: Unbounded-length input to diceCoefficient/checkSystemPromptSimilarity with no size cap
description: checkSystemPromptSimilarity accepts a caller-supplied `submission` string (from a route outside this file, likely an LLM prompt/chat endpoint) and passes it, with no length validation, into diceCoefficient. diceCoefficient's only short-circuits are an exact-equality check and a minimum-length check (rejecting strings shorter than 2 characters) — neither bounds the maximum length. It then builds a full bigram Map over the first string and iterates every bigram of the second string, work and memory proportional to input length, with no cap enforced anywhere in this file. If the calling endpoint allows large free-form text submissions and is invoked repeatedly (e.g., once per chat message) without a length limit applied before reaching this function, an attacker could submit very large strings repeatedly to increase CPU/memory cost per request, degrading service.

title: Path traversal / arbitrary file read via unsanitized subtitles configuration value
description: videoPath() (line 85-91) passes the configured video filename through utils.extractFilename() before concatenating it onto the videos directory, stripping any directory components to prevent path traversal. getSubsFromFile() (line 79-83) does the exact same pattern for the 'application.promotion.subtitles' config value but omits the extractFilename() sanitization step entirely — the raw config string is concatenated directly into the filesystem path passed to fs.readFileSync. If this configuration value can be influenced by an outside party (the application architecture exposes a YAML config upload endpoint, POST /file-upload -> handleYamlUpload, which is a known mechanism for poisoning the 'config' module's runtime configuration in this codebase), an attacker can set application.promotion.subtitles to a path-traversal string (e.g. '../../../../etc/passwd' or a path to another sensitive file on disk) and have its contents read and returned to any unauthenticated client hitting GET /promotion. This is a clear asymmetry: the sibling function on the same file sanitizes an analogous config-derived filename, but this one does not, which is a concrete, demonstrable coding defect independent of whether the upload endpoint is confirmed reachable from here.

Unlike the application name at line 60, which is passed through entities.encode() before substitution, the subtitle content receives no encoding at all. If the subtitle file's content can be influenced by an attacker (e.g. via the path-traversal/config-poisoning primitive described in the companion finding, or if the subtitle asset is itself user-writable elsewhere in the application), a payload containing a closing '</script>' tag followed by arbitrary markup/script would break out of the intended context and execute in the browser of every visitor to /promotion, resulting in stored/reflected XSS against an unauthenticated, publicly reachable page.

title: Unvalidated HTTP Range header values flow into fs.createReadStream without bounds checking
description: getVideo() parses the client-supplied Range request header (req.headers.range, fully attacker-controlled) with a naive regex/split and feeds the results straight into parseInt without validating that the resulting start/end are non-negative integers, that start <= end, or that end < fileSize. A malformed Range header (e.g. 'bytes=-', 'bytes=abc-', 'bytes=99999999999-1') produces NaN or out-of-bounds values that are passed directly to fs.createReadStream({start, end}), which can throw synchronously (e.g. RangeError for invalid start/end combinations) or otherwise misbehave. There is no explicit validation layer rejecting malformed ranges before they reach the stream-construction sink, so any client can repeatedly send crafted Range headers to trigger error conditions on every request to this endpoint.

title: Missing error handling on video file stream can crash request handling
description: In the Range-request branch of getVideo(), the readable stream created by fs.createReadStream(path, { start, end }) is piped directly to the response with no '.on("error", ...)' listener attached. If the stream emits an asynchronous error (e.g. due to a filesystem-level issue triggered by an edge-case Range value, disk I/O failure, or a race where the underlying video file changes/disappears between the stat and the read), an unhandled 'error' event on a Node.js stream, by default, throws inside the event emitter and can crash the whole process if there is no listener to handle it. Because this endpoint is unauthenticated and directly driven by attacker-controlled Range headers, this is a low-effort denial-of-service surface.

title: Unhandled exception on template file read failure with no logging
description: promotionVideo() reads 'views/promotionVideo.pug' asynchronously and, on error, executes 'throw err' inside the fs.readFile async callback. This callback executes outside of Express's synchronous request-handling stack, so a thrown error here is not caught by Express's built-in error handling for synchronous route bodies; because the callback is declared 'async', the throw becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no .catch attached anywhere in the call chain. Depending on the Node.js runtime configuration, an unhandled rejection can terminate the process, and in all cases there is no log statement recording the failure, so an operator has no record that this occurred. This combines a resource-availability risk with a security-visibility gap: a failure condition that should be observable and handled gracefully instead is silently able to take down the service.

title: Blocking synchronous filesystem calls in unauthenticated, unthrottled request path
description: getVideo() calls fs.statSync() synchronously on every single request before any streaming begins, and getSubsFromFile() calls fs.readFileSync() synchronously on every request to /promotion. Both routes are unauthenticated and, as far as this file shows, have no request-size or request-rate controls applied. Synchronous filesystem operations block Node's single event loop for the duration of the call; under concurrent load (which an attacker can trivially generate against a public, unauthenticated endpoint), this degrades or stalls processing for all other requests being served by the same process, amplifying the impact of what would otherwise be a moderate load.

title: Template source built via raw string substitution before pug compilation
description: promotionVideo() builds the pug template source by performing raw string replacements (theme colors, application name, favicon path) directly on the file's text content, and only afterwards calls pug.compile() on the resulting string and executes it. This differs from the safe pattern of compiling a static template once and passing substitution values as locals/data at render time — here, arbitrary text is spliced into the *source* that the template engine parses and compiles. Although the currently substituted values originate from the application config module (theme palette, application.name, application.favicon) rather than directly from the request, if any of these configuration values become attacker-influenced (the architecture exposes a config-modifying upload route elsewhere in the application) and contain pug template syntax, this would result in server-side template injection with code execution during pug.compile()/fn(). Even absent a confirmed attacker-controlled config value, mixing string interpolation with template compilation is an insecure design choice that removes the safety pug's own locals mechanism would otherwise provide.

title: Path Traversal / Arbitrary Local File Read via unsanitized 'key' in checkCorrectFix
description: The POST /snippets/fixes handler (checkCorrectFix) takes 'key' directly from the JSON request body and concatenates it, without any sanitization, canonicalization, or allow-listing against known challenge keys, into a filesystem path: './data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml'. Because 'key' is typed only at compile time (ChallengeKey) and is never validated at runtime, an attacker can supply a value containing '../' sequences to escape the intended codefixes directory and reach arbitrary files elsewhere on disk whose name happens to end in '.info.yml'. Both fs.existsSync and fs.readFileSync use this tainted path, so the endpoint can be used to probe for and disclose the contents of files outside the codefixes directory. This is reachable with no authentication at all (route has no auth middleware), so any anonymous caller can attempt traversal. To reach the vulnerable concatenation, the request must first pass through readFixes(key) and the fixData.fixes.length gate, which only require that at least one legitimate codefix file exists for the (unrelated) key prefix match — an easy condition for an attacker to satisfy by reusing any valid challenge key while still supplying a malicious key value for the info.yml lookup.

title: Unsafe YAML Deserialization of File Content Reached via Path Traversal
description: The content of the file located via the attacker-influenced path (see path traversal finding) is passed straight into yaml.load with no schema restriction and no validation of the resulting object shape. If an attacker can place or reach a YAML file with dangerous tags at any path reachable through the traversal (for example a file dropped by another upload feature in the same application such as the YAML upload endpoint noted in the application's routing table), yaml.load may instantiate unexpected object types or, on vulnerable js-yaml configurations, execute embedded logic during parse. Even absent code execution, this is an untrusted-data deserialization sink: the parser output directly drives subsequent control flow (codingChallengeInfos?.fixes.find(...)) without validating that the parsed object actually has the expected shape, and the resulting explanation text can be surfaced back to the caller via res.__() without the file's provenance ever being checked.

title: Missing error handling around file I/O and YAML parsing can crash/hang the request
description: checkCorrectFix is an async Express handler with no try/catch around the fs.existsSync/fs.readFileSync/yaml.load sequence or around the optional-chained property access. If the file at the (attacker-influenced) path is malformed YAML, yaml.load will throw. Separately, codingChallengeInfos?.fixes.find(...) only guards codingChallengeInfos being null/undefined; if the parsed object exists but lacks a 'fixes' array (very plausible for any file an attacker manages to have parsed via the path-traversal issue, or even for a subtly malformed legitimate .info.yml), .find is called on undefined and throws a TypeError. Because the handler has no try/catch and no call to next(err), this becomes an unhandled exception inside an async function, surfacing as an unhandled promise rejection with no security logging of the event, and is reachable from a completely unauthenticated endpoint. Repeated triggering degrades or destabilizes the service.
