title: Unbounded, unauthenticated cache growth keyed by attacker-controlled string enables memory exhaustion
description: Both routes (GET /snippets/fixes/:key and POST /snippets/fixes) are unauthenticated and funnel a caller-controlled string into readFixes(key), which unconditionally inserts an entry into the module-level CodeFixes cache (CodeFixes[key] = { fixes, correct }) for every distinct key seen, even when no matching files exist (fixes: [], correct: -1). There is no cap on the number of distinct keys cached, no eviction policy, and no rate limiting on either route. An attacker can send a high volume of requests with unique key values (e.g. random strings as the :key path parameter) to force unbounded growth of the in-memory cache and repeated fs.readdirSync directory scans (line 26) for each miss, consuming server memory and CPU over time with no per-IP or per-user throttling to stop it.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint permits unbounded growth of in-memory wallet-tracking Set (memory exhaustion DoS)
description: The route POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress is registered with no authentication/authorization middleware (per routing table: auth: none) and its handler takes req.body.walletAddress directly from the request body and inserts it into a module-level global Set (walletsConnected) with zero validation of type, format, or length, and no size cap. The Set is declared at module scope with no bound whatsoever, so it persists and grows for the lifetime of the process. The only removal path is a conditional check inside an asynchronous blockchain-event callback that deletes an entry solely when it exactly matches an 'exploiter' address reported by an external smart-contract event — a condition entirely outside the attacker's control and expected to fire rarely, if ever, for attacker-submitted garbage values. Because the route requires no login and carries no rate limiting, an attacker can send an unbounded number of requests with unique/garbage walletAddress values, each one permanently growing the process-wide Set. This allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to exhaust server memory over time, degrading or crashing the service for all users.

title: TOCTOU race condition in event-listener singleton allows multiple concurrent external WebSocket connections
description: The handler guards creation of a WebSocketProvider/Contract listener with the flag isEventListenerCreated (checked at line 18), but the flag is not set to true until after an await'd dynamic import and asynchronous provider/contract construction (lines 19-30) complete. Because this check-then-act sequence is not atomic and the route has no authentication or rate limiting, multiple concurrent requests arriving before the first request finishes its await chain will all observe isEventListenerCreated === false and each proceed to open a brand-new WebSocketProvider connection to the external Alchemy endpoint and register a new Contract event listener. This lets an unauthenticated caller trigger many redundant outbound WebSocket connections and listener registrations with a burst of concurrent requests, consuming server sockets/memory and potentially exhausting the Alchemy API quota/cost budget tied to the ALCHEMY_API_KEY.

title: Wallet balance read/write trusts client-supplied req.body.UserId as caller identity
description: Both getWalletBalance and addWalletBalance resolve 'which user's wallet' by reading req.body.UserId directly and using it, unvalidated, as the WHERE clause for the WalletModel/CardModel lookups. The only middleware registered on these routes is security.appendUserId(), which (per the architecture description) is not a hard authentication gate but merely a helper that may populate req.body.UserId from a token when an Authorization header happens to be present. Nothing in this file independently derives the caller's identity from a verified session (e.g. req.user.id); it simply trusts whatever value ends up in req.body.UserId. If the appended middleware does not unconditionally overwrite the field (e.g. request has no/garbled Authorization header, or the field is set only when a token IS present, leaving attacker-supplied values untouched otherwise), a caller can set req.body.UserId to any other user's id and receive that user's wallet balance (GET) or trigger a balance mutation gated only by owning a card tied to that same spoofed UserId (PUT). This is a classic BOLA pattern: the resource identifier used for the lookup is taken from caller-controlled data with no per-resource ownership check performed in this file against a trustworthy, server-derived identity.

title: Unrestricted wallet balance increment enables arbitrary money/credit creation
description: addWalletBalance allows the caller to specify any value for req.body.balance and, provided the caller supplies the id of any card record belonging to the same UserId, that arbitrary value is passed straight to WalletModel.increment as the amount credited to the wallet. There is no validation that the balance is capped to a sane maximum, matches any actual payment/charge amount, or is even a sane monetary value (no bound check, no verification against a real payment gateway transaction). The card check only confirms the existence of a card record tied to the UserId — it never verifies that any real charge for req.body.balance was processed. This is a textbook economic-imbalance design flaw: a user who owns any saved card (even one added with fabricated details, since card validity isn't independently verified here) can call this endpoint repeatedly with large balance values to create unlimited store credit without ever paying.

title: YAML parsing of on-disk hint files without explicit safe-schema configuration
description: yaml.load is called on the contents of a '.info.yml' file (line 90) without specifying a restrictive schema option. While the file path is largely constrained by the earlier codeChallenges Map lookup and the content originates from the application's own static data directory rather than directly from the HTTP request, the parsing call itself does not explicitly declare a safe-only schema, leaving the security of this parse dependent entirely on the js-yaml library version's default behavior rather than an explicit control in this file. Should the effective key/path constraint elsewhere ever be loosened, or a vulnerable js-yaml version be in use, this call would parse attacker-influenced YAML content.

title: Verbose error handler leaks internal application details to unauthenticated clients
description: The test suite itself documents and asserts that the application's default error handling is misconfigured to leak internal information. Requesting an unrecognized path under /rest (and, similarly, /api with no resource) causes the server to return an HTTP 500 whose response body contains an Express-generated HTML error page including the application name and a raw 'Unexpected path: <path>' message that echoes the request path back into the response. This is characteristic of Express's default (or a custom but still verbose) error handler running with stack-trace/detailed-error output enabled rather than a generic error response. An unauthenticated attacker can use this behavior to (a) fingerprint the framework (Express), (b) confirm the exact application name/version context from config, and (c) probe for reflected input in error pages, which is useful for further attack chaining (e.g., locating other verbose endpoints, or exploring for reflected XSS-style issues in the error template). Because the test explicitly asserts on this leakage as expected behavior, it confirms the running configuration intentionally or unintentionally surfaces internal error detail to any caller, which is a textbook OWASP A05 misconfiguration (verbose error / debug information exposed to end users) rather than a generic and sanitized 500 response.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of full application configuration dump
description: The test suite exercises GET /rest/admin/application-configuration and asserts only that the response is 200 with a JSON object body (res.body.config). No Authorization header, admin session cookie, or role check is set up anywhere in the test (the app is created via createTestApp() with no login step for this describe block), and the test explicitly expects a bare 200 success. This indicates the underlying route (named with an 'admin' prefix, implying it should be restricted to administrators) is reachable by any unauthenticated caller and returns the full internal application configuration object. Application configuration objects in this class of app typically contain internal feature flags, mail/SMTP settings, database connection details, session secrets, or CAPTCHA/library keys - a config dump exposed without authentication is a classic security misconfiguration (debug/diagnostic endpoint reachable in production) and also represents an insecure design in that the 'admin' naming implies a trust boundary that is never enforced or verified by any test or, apparently, by the route itself.

description: The assertion at line 38-39 only checks that res.body.config is a non-null object; it never verifies that sensitive keys (secrets, credentials, internal paths, third-party API keys) are stripped or redacted from the configuration payload before being sent to the client. This is a weak/missing control pattern: if the underlying route serializes the raw configuration object without a redaction/allow-list step, any secret present in config (e.g., mailer credentials, session secret) would be silently exposed to any caller reaching this route, and this test suite would still pass. The absence of a negative test (asserting sensitive fields are NOT present) is itself evidence that no such control is exercised or guaranteed by this file.

title: Test confirms unrestricted open-redirect endpoint (`/redirect?to=`) is reachable with arbitrary external targets
description: This test asserts that the publicly served client bundle (`GET /main.js`) embeds links of the form `/redirect?to=<external-URL>` pointing at arbitrary attacker-controllable-looking third-party domains (blockchain.info, explorer.dash.org, etherscan.io). The test treats this as expected, passing behavior, confirming that the application exposes a server-side `/redirect` route whose destination is taken directly from a `to` query parameter without validating it against an origin allow-list. Although the actual route handler is not in this file, this test file is the concrete evidence (in-repo, executable) that the design accepts and forwards arbitrary caller-supplied redirect targets. An attacker can craft `/redirect?to=https://evil.example/phishing` and have the trusted application domain redirect victims to any destination, enabling phishing, credential theft, or SSRF-adjacent abuse (if the redirect target validation, if any, is done by substring/prefix matching rather than full origin comparison). Because this test only checks that specific known-good URLs are present and never checks that arbitrary or malicious URLs are rejected, it also demonstrates the absence of any negative test for the redirect validation logic - the design itself never establishes or verifies a destination allow-list is enforced.

title: Sensitive internal password-policy hint disclosed in publicly served client bundle
description: The test asserts that the unauthenticated, publicly-served `main.js` bundle contains a hardcoded string revealing that the support team's password does not comply with the corporate password policy for privileged accounts, and urges changing it. This confirms the application design ships an internal security-relevant hint (effectively a credential/account weakness disclosure) to every visitor of the site without any access control, since `GET /main.js` returns 200 with no authentication (line 24/34). Regardless of whether this is intended as a CTF-style challenge string, from a security-design perspective it represents unnecessary exposure of information about a privileged account's password policy violation to anonymous users, which can materially aid an attacker in a credential-guessing or social-engineering attack against the support team account.

title: No test coverage for cross-user (BOLA) address access — object-level authorization untested
description: The entire /api/Addresss/:id test suite (lines 98-188) only ever authenticates as a single user (jim@juice-sh.op, established in the top-level before() hook at lines 22-29) and only ever creates and manipulates that same user's own address (line 100-111, addressId). Every subsequent GET/PUT/DELETE test (lines 131-187) reuses this single user's authHeader against an address that same user owns. There is no test where a second, distinct authenticated user attempts to GET, PUT, or DELETE the addressId belonging to the first user. This means the object-level authorization boundary — whether the underlying /api/Addresss/:id route verifies that the requester owns the specific address record before returning/mutating it — is completely unverified by this test file. Given the route accepts an arbitrary numeric id in the path (as shown by the non-existing id test at line 138-146) and looks it up, if the underlying handler does not scope the lookup by the authenticated user's id, this is a classic BOLA condition; this test suite provides no evidence it is enforced and no regression protection against future authorization regressions.

While this is a well-known fixture account for the Juice Shop application, hardcoding credentials in a committed source file is a credential-exposure pattern: if this account exists in any shared/staging/production-like environment reachable by the test harness, the credential is now permanently disclosed in version control history and to anyone with repository read access, and could be reused outside the test context.

title: Generic 'Malicious activity detected' response discloses internal security-detection wording without evidence of server-side logging
description: Both the non-existing-address lookup (lines 138-146) and the double-delete case (lines 180-187) return the identical message 'Malicious activity detected.' for what are, on their face, ordinary not-found/already-deleted conditions rather than genuine attacks. Returning this specific security-classification string to the client leaks internal detection terminology that an attacker can use to fingerprint and probe the application's anomaly-detection logic (e.g., to learn which request patterns trigger this classification). Separately, this test file contains no assertion that such flagged events are actually recorded (audit log, alert, security event) anywhere server-side — the only visible behavior is the client-facing message, so from this file's perspective there is no verified security logging/alerting tied to these detected 'malicious' conditions.

title: 2FA can be disabled with password alone — no second-factor confirmation required
description: The /rest/2fa/disable flow, as exercised by this test suite, only requires the account password to turn off two-factor authentication. The 'should be able to disable 2fa for account with 2fa enabled' test registers a user with TOTP enabled, confirms 2FA is active (setup:true), then sends a disable request whose body contains only `{ password }` — no totpToken/second-factor value is supplied anywhere in the request — and the endpoint returns 200, successfully disabling 2FA. This is a step-up authentication design gap: an attacker who has obtained or guessed a victim's password (e.g., via credential stuffing, phishing, or password reuse) can single-handedly strip away the victim's second factor without ever having to prove possession of the TOTP device/secret, defeating the entire purpose of 2FA as a second, independent factor. A secure design would require the current TOTP code (or another out-of-band step-up check) in addition to the password before disabling MFA, exactly as the setup flow requires proof of TOTP possession (initialToken) before turning 2FA on.

title: Hardcoded credentials and TOTP seed for a real seeded application account committed to source
description: The plaintext password 'EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!' and TOTP base32 secret 'IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH' for the pre-provisioned 'wurstbrot' account (userId 10) are hardcoded directly in this version-controlled test file and reused across multiple, unrelated test blocks. Because these are the actual credentials and TOTP seed of a live seeded account rather than throwaway/random test-generated values, anyone with read access to the source repository can reconstruct valid login credentials and derive valid TOTP codes for this account indefinitely (TOTP seeds do not expire or rotate). This is a hardcoded-secret exposure: an attacker with source access does not need to guess or brute-force anything to fully authenticate as, and pass 2FA for, this account.

title: No evidence of rate limiting / lockout on repeated failed TOTP verification attempts
description: The tests around /rest/2fa/verify only check a single failed-attempt response (401 on an incorrect TOTP code) and never assert any lockout, backoff, or rate-limiting behavior after repeated failed attempts against the same account. Each negative test independently mints a fresh tmpToken via security.authorize and submits one guess, so the suite never demonstrates that the server tracks or throttles consecutive failures for a given account/tmpToken. Since TOTP codes are only 6 digits (a small keyspace) and tmp tokens are reusable and independently mintable within their validity window, the absence of any test enforcing throttling suggests the endpoint may allow unlimited TOTP brute-force attempts. This cannot be fully confirmed since the route handler itself is outside this file, but the negative-path test coverage here does not exercise or assert any anti-brute-force control, and each isolated 401 assertion treats every guess as an independent, unthrottled event.

title: GET /rest/user/authentication-details exposes all users' email and lastLoginTime without demonstrated authorization scoping
description: The test suite confirms that a single authenticated request to /rest/user/authentication-details returns a list (res.body.data) containing every registered user's record, including email address and lastLoginTime (lines 46-48), and password fields (masked, line 30). The tests only ever call this endpoint using the admin-crafted bearer token built at line 16 (security.authorize({ data: { email: 'admin@juice-sh.op' } })), and at no point does the suite assert that a non-admin/regular user is rejected (e.g. expect 403) when calling the same endpoint. The second test even logs in as a genuinely distinct, non-admin account ('jim', lines 34-38) but then still attaches the admin authHeader (line 42) rather than jim's own session to query the endpoint - so the suite never actually exercises what a lower-privileged caller can see. Nothing in this file demonstrates that the handler behind this route performs a role check or scopes results to the caller's own record; the test simply confirms it returns bulk data for any valid token supplied. Combined with the route naming ('authentication-details', plural - the whole user table, not the caller's own record) this is the classic BOLA/broken-function-level-authorization shape: the endpoint looks up and returns other users' identity/session metadata keyed off nothing but 'is there a valid token', with no visible ownership or role check separating admin-only access from any-authenticated-user access. If a low-privileged user's token also succeeds against this endpoint (unverified from this file, but the tests never rule it out), any authenticated user could enumerate every other user's email address and last-login timestamp - a privacy and reconnaissance issue that materially aids account targeting/credential-stuffing against specific identified accounts.

title: B2B order endpoint accepts and processes arbitrary unvalidated JSON with no test coverage for known RCE-challenge payloads
description: The test suite explicitly asserts that POST /b2b/v2/orders returns HTTP 200 for an arbitrary, schema-free JSON body (foo: 'bar', test: 42), confirming the underlying route performs no input schema validation and accepts any object shape. Juice Shop's b2b order endpoint is historically implemented by evaluating parts of the submitted order data (a documented RCE vector tied to challenges.rceChallenge / challenges.rceOccupyChallenge). This test file even gates a block on utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.rceChallenge) || utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.rceOccupyChallenge) (lines 24-27) but the block body is empty, meaning there is no test verifying that malicious/crafted JSON payloads (e.g., payloads designed to trigger server-side evaluation) are rejected or sanitized. The request is built up field-by-field with attacker-controlled keys, sent with only a generic auth header (not proof of any content restriction), and the response is checked only with loose 'typeof' assertions that validate shape, never content or bounds — so nothing in this file constrains what the server is allowed to accept or return.

title: Client-supplied 'cid' order identifier trusted and echoed back without server-side derivation or ownership validation
description: The test 'POST new B2B order has passed cid in response' sends an arbitrary client-chosen value for cid (e.g., 'test') and asserts the server echoes that exact value back in the response. This demonstrates that cid, which functions as a customer/client identifier tied to the order, is taken directly from client input and trusted verbatim rather than being derived server-side from the authenticated session or validated against the caller's identity. The request path shows only a generic auth header is attached (not a customer-specific credential), the client-chosen cid is sent unmodified, and the server's 200 response together with the exact echo of the value confirms no server-side substitution, lookup, or ownership check occurs between input and output. If cid is later used to associate the order with a customer account (billing, fulfillment, or lookup), an attacker could supply another customer's cid value to create or associate orders under an identity they do not own.

title: No validation of payload size/shape on B2B order endpoint suggests missing resource-consumption controls
description: The test suite only confirms that small, arbitrary JSON bodies are accepted (lines 37-51) but includes no coverage of request body size limits, nested-object depth limits, or array length limits for the order endpoint. The chain of calls building and sending the request shows no size cap, count cap, or depth cap is exercised or asserted anywhere between request construction and the 200 response, and no negative test exists elsewhere in the file to demonstrate such a limit is enforced server-side. Combined with the demonstrated acceptance of arbitrary JSON shapes, this suggests the endpoint may lack bounds on payload size/complexity, which, if true server-side, would allow a caller to submit oversized or deeply nested JSON to exhaust memory/CPU during parsing or downstream processing (e.g., total price computation).

title: BasketId ownership binding can be set post-creation, bypassing immutability control (BOLA / mass assignment)
description: The application enforces a 'noUpdate' constraint that rejects any attempt to change BasketId or ProductId on an existing basket item once created (demonstrated at lines 141-155 and 173-187, where sending BasketId/ProductId in a PUT to an item that already has that field set returns 400 with a noUpdate constraint error). However, the test at lines 157-171 shows that when a basket item is created WITHOUT a BasketId (the field is omitted from the POST body, and the response confirms BasketId is undefined), a subsequent PUT request can freely set BasketId to any arbitrary value (3 in this test) and the request succeeds with status 200, persisting the new BasketId. Since BasketId is the field that ties a basket item to a specific user's basket (and therefore to a specific user, given a basket belongs to one user), this means an attacker can create an 'orphan' basket item without a BasketId and then use the PUT endpoint to attach it to an arbitrary BasketId — potentially one belonging to another user — bypassing the ownership/ownership-immutability check that exists for items created with a BasketId from the start. This is both a broken object-level authorization gap (a user-controlled identifier lets a caller bind a resource to a target basket not verified to belong to them) and a mass-assignment gap (a security-relevant field, BasketId, is accepted from the request body without a consistent allow/deny policy — it is only protected when already non-null).

title: Invalid BasketId error response returns non-JSON, hand-built string instead of structured JSON
description: The test at lines 76-83 asserts that when an invalid BasketId is supplied, the server responds with status 401 and a response body whose exact text is the literal string "{'error' : 'Invalid BasketId'}" — using single quotes and therefore NOT valid JSON, despite the API otherwise being a JSON API (the client sends 'content-type: application/json' and other endpoints return structured JSON bodies such as res.body.data). This indicates the underlying handler builds this particular error response via raw string concatenation/templating rather than through the same JSON serialization path used elsewhere, which is a configuration/implementation inconsistency in the API's error-handling surface. Beyond being non-machine-parseable (breaking client error handling expectations), any handler that assembles response text via string building rather than structured serialization is a pattern that historically correlates with reflected-content risks if any user-controlled value is ever interpolated into such strings elsewhere in the same handler family.

title: Unhandled exceptions on invalid resource references surface as generic 500 responses
description: Two tests (lines 85-91 and 231-237) show that supplying a non-existent ProductId when creating a basket item, or a non-existent id when updating a basket item, results in an HTTP 500 response rather than a controlled 400/404. The inline comment at line 90 ('quantityCheck throws Error which is caught and passed to next(error)') indicates this is a raw exception propagated to a generic Express error handler rather than an intentionally designed client error. Generic error handlers that surface uncaught exceptions as 500s are frequently paired with stack-trace or internal detail exposure in non-production configurations, and represent a gap in input validation (unchecked existence of a referenced ProductId/basket item id before use) that a security-monitoring/error-handling review should confirm does not leak internals. This file cannot see the error handler itself, so this is reported as a suspected gap rather than a confirmed exposure.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization on GET /rest/basket/:id (cross-user basket access)
description: The test suite itself documents that an authenticated user can retrieve another user's basket by ID with no ownership check. The test explicitly logs in as a second account (bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com) and requests basket id=2 — a basket that was not created by that login session in this test — and asserts a 200 response containing the basket's full product contents. The only prior test for basket 2 in this file (see the discount/coupon tests) uses the primary authHeader for jim@juice-sh.op, reinforcing that basket 2 does not belong to bjoern. This confirms the /rest/basket/:id endpoint only checks 'is the caller authenticated' (Bearer token valid) and never verifies 'does this basket belong to the caller', a textbook BOLA (API1) vulnerability: any authenticated user can enumerate small integer basket IDs and read other customers' basket contents (products, quantities), leaking data belonging to other accounts.

title: Forgeable discount coupons enable near-free checkout (weak coupon generation/validation)
description: A coupon named 'forgedCoupon' is generated with security.generateCoupon(99) alongside a legitimately intended 'validCoupon' (15% off). The test then applies this 99%-discount 'forged' coupon to a basket via PUT /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon and successfully checks out, confirming that the server accepts and validates coupons whose encoding is derivable/predictable enough that a client-side value not obtained through any legitimate promotional flow is accepted as authentic. This indicates the coupon scheme lacks a properly enforced, server-side-secret cryptographic signature (or the signature/format is guessable/reversible), letting an attacker mint arbitrary discount percentages and place orders for a fraction of their true cost — an economic-imbalance business-logic flaw rooted in weak authentication of the coupon's origin.

description: The coupon endpoint accepts arbitrary coupon strings and returns 404 for invalid/outdated ones (lines 193-198, 200-205) without any indication of throttling, lockout, or backoff in the tests. Combined with the weak/predictable coupon generation scheme noted above, an attacker could script repeated guesses against this endpoint to brute-force valid discount codes or enumerate discount percentages, since nothing in the observable behavior (or test coverage) suggests a rate limit exists on this endpoint.

title: Internal error details (exception messages) leaked directly to API clients on checkout failures
description: Multiple checkout error-path tests confirm that when an internal call throws (QuantityModel.findOne, WalletModel.findOne, ordersCollection.insert), the raw JavaScript Error message text ('Quantity error', 'Wallet error', 'Insert error') is returned verbatim in the HTTP response body/text to the caller. This is a security misconfiguration: unhandled/insufficiently sanitized error responses expose internal implementation details (model/library names, internal call sequence) that should not be visible to API consumers, aiding attackers in fingerprinting the backend and crafting further attacks, and is also relevant from a logging perspective — no evidence in this file that these thrown errors are separately captured to a secured audit/log channel rather than only surfaced to the end user.

If the checkout handler (outside this file) uses this client-supplied UserId — rather than deriving the paying/crediting identity strictly from the authenticated session — to select whose wallet balance is debited or credited, this is a trust-boundary violation allowing a caller to potentially specify a different user's ID for a financial operation. title: Application design accepts unhandled 500 error as expected behavior for missing configuration
description: This test file documents and locks in that the GET /rest/country-mapping endpoint returns an unhandled 500 Internal Server Error when the default application configuration does not define a country mapping. Rather than the endpoint gracefully handling the absence of optional configuration data (e.g., returning 404 Not Found, an empty object, or a 200 with an empty result), the test explicitly asserts that a raw server error (500) is the correct, expected outcome of the default configuration state. This means the design never establishes a validated 'no data available' state for this route — the only path taken when the underlying config/data is absent is an unhandled exception bubbling up to the framework's default error handler. Because the test enshrines this as passing/correct behavior, any refactor that changes it to a graceful response would break the test suite, meaning the insecure behavior is a durable part of the intended design rather than an accidental bug. An unhandled exception path exposed to end users on a default deployment is a design gap: the endpoint's caller (browser or API consumer) receives a raw error rather than a defined contract, which in many Express configurations also surfaces stack traces or internal file paths in the 500 response body (not verified here, but the test does not check for absence of such details in the body, only the status code).

title: Unauthenticated state-mutating continue-code endpoints allow anonymous manipulation of challenge-solved status
description: The test suite exercises three families of continue-code endpoints (/rest/continue-code, /rest/continue-code-findIt, /rest/continue-code-fixIt). The GET routes retrieve a code representing 'currently solved challenges' and the PUT .../apply/:code routes mutate that solved state — yet none of these requests attach the Bearer authHeader that is explicitly used elsewhere in the same file for the /api/Challenges tests (compare line 44/59/66/78 which set authHeader, versus lines 86, 92, 98, 104 which do not). The tests confirm these state-mutating PUT calls succeed with HTTP 200 with no session or identity established, meaning any anonymous caller who obtains or guesses a valid continue code can apply it and change challenge completion state without any per-user or per-session ownership check being exercised or enforced in the observed behavior.

Because applying a correct code changes the solved-challenge state and the endpoint is unauthenticated, an attacker could attempt to brute-force or fuzz codes without a visible per-IP or per-account rate limit, since none of the requests in this suite trigger or check for a 429/throttle response even after multiple back-to-back calls to the same route family.

title: Continue-code apply endpoint accepts codes referencing non-existent challenges without rejection
description: The test at line 103-107 explicitly documents that applying a continue code which encodes a non-existent challenge (#999) is accepted with HTTP 200 rather than being rejected. This indicates the server-side handler does not fully validate the decoded contents of a client-supplied continue code against actual challenge records before acting on it — a trust-boundary gap where the server accepts and processes caller-supplied state data (which challenges are 'solved') without deriving/validating it fully against its own authoritative data, consistent with a design that trusts client-supplied continue-code content.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key committed to source-controlled test file
description: The test file embeds a full, valid Ethereum private key literal ('0x5bcc3e9d38baa06e7bfaab80ae5957bbe8ef059e640311d7d6d465e6bc948e3e') as a plaintext string used to exercise the /rest/web3/submitKey endpoint. Whether or not the corresponding wallet is a throwaway fixture, the pattern of embedding raw private-key material directly in a committed source file is a hardcoded-secret misconfiguration: it is discoverable by anyone with repository access (including in git history even if later rotated/removed), can be copy-pasted and reused, and trains developers to treat key material as disposable test data. If this key (or the pattern used to generate it) is ever reused for anything beyond the toy challenge, or if the corresponding public address holds any real value (NFTs, tokens), the secret is permanently compromised the moment the repository becomes readable.

title: No brute-force / rate-limiting protection evidenced for private-key submission endpoint
description: The /rest/web3/submitKey endpoint accepts an arbitrary string as a candidate Ethereum private key and returns a binary accept/reject (401 for wrong values, 200 for the correct one). The test suite exercises multiple sequential submissions (missing key, arbitrary string, public key, wallet address, correct private key) against the same running app instance with no assertions or setup for throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA between attempts. This suggests the endpoint's design has no compensating control against automated guessing/brute-forcing of the private key or against abuse of the endpoint as a scriptable oracle. Even though the private-key keyspace is astronomically large making brute force impractical, the complete absence of any rate-limiting behavior visible in this test surface (which is the most direct evidence available of the endpoint's operational behavior) is consistent with a design that never established a control on submission frequency — an unrestricted, computationally cheap-to-call endpoint that could still be hammered for denial-of-service or used to fingerprint validation logic.

title: Sensitive key material transmitted and potentially persisted via standard request logging
description: The endpoint under test accepts a field literally named 'privateKey' in the JSON request body across every test case and processes it server-side. If the application (outside this file, in the route handler / middleware stack) uses standard HTTP access logging (e.g., morgan-style request logging) or error-handling middleware that logs request bodies on failure, every submitted private key — including the correct one and the guessed decoys — would be written to application logs in plaintext. The repeated pattern across all five test cases (each constructing a request and placing a secret-shaped value into the body before sending) demonstrates that this field is consistently the payload shape delivered to and processed by the endpoint, making it a natural candidate for inadvertent sensitive-data logging if the wider application logs request bodies indiscriminately; this file cannot confirm or rule out such logging middleware.

title: GET /api/Complaints test never verifies per-user ownership scoping (potential BOLA)
description: The test suite exercises GET /api/Complaints with a single, generically-issued auth token (security.authorize()) and only asserts res.status === 200 (line 46). It never creates two distinct user accounts, submits complaints under each, and verifies that a given user only receives their own complaints in the response. If the underlying route (server.ts, not visible in this file) returns all complaints in the system to any authenticated caller rather than filtering by the requesting user's id, this test suite would not catch it - it treats 'authenticated' as sufficient for exposing what may be other users' complaint data (which can include free-text messages potentially containing PII). This is the classic authenticated-but-not-authorized (BOLA) gap; the test file's own assertions provide no evidence the endpoint enforces object-level ownership, and the shape of the test (single shared token, no ownership assertions) is consistent with a listing endpoint that is not scoped per user.

Only the HTTP status code (200) is asserted; the response body/data is never checked for scoping to the authenticated user, leaving an unscoped, cross-user complaint listing unverified and potentially unguarded.

title: No pagination or size-limit assertions on unbounded complaint listing endpoint
description: The GET /api/Complaints test (lines 42-47) exercises the listing endpoint but never asserts on the size or shape of the returned collection, nor does the POST test (lines 22-34) assert any maximum size for the 'message' field. Without evidence in this test file that the API enforces pagination or a message-length cap, and given the endpoint is confirmed reachable by any authenticated user (200 response, line 46), the listing endpoint is a candidate for unrestricted resource consumption: an attacker could submit many large complaints and later request the full, unpaginated list, or submit an oversized message body, with no control observed or tested here to prevent it.

title: Individual complaint routes (GET/PUT/DELETE /api/Complaints/:id) return 401 for all authenticated callers, masking whether per-resource authorization exists
description: Tests at lines 51-73 show that even a validly authenticated caller (using the module-level authHeader) receives 401 Unauthorized for GET, PUT, and DELETE on /api/Complaints/1. A 401 (rather than 403 or 404) for an authenticated request typically indicates the route either does not exist / is not wired up, or a blanket deny is applied regardless of identity - the architecture summary for this app does not list a specific '/api/Complaints/:id' route. Because every test uses the same single credential and none probes with a complaint actually owned by that user, it is impossible to distinguish 'route intentionally disabled for everyone' from 'authorization check misconfigured to always deny/allow' from this file alone. This blind spot means that if the route is later implemented or reachable through another path, no regression test here would catch a missing ownership check (BOLA) on complaint mutation/deletion, which are higher-impact operations than listing.

title: Trivially guessable default admin password accepted by authentication
description: The test suite logs into the administrative account using the password 'admin123' (lines 52-56 and 180-184) and receives a valid authentication token that is subsequently accepted by the API (the requests proceed to authorized endpoints and return meaningful business-logic errors rather than 401/403). This confirms the underlying application accepts a trivially guessable, dictionary-word password for its highest-privilege administrative account. An attacker who can reach the login endpoint (visible in this test as the entrypoint used by the `login()` helper) can authenticate as admin via simple credential stuffing/brute force with no additional secret knowledge, since 'admin123' is among the first few hundred entries of any common password list. This is both a weak/default-credential misconfiguration for an administrative interface and an authentication weakness that allows an attacker to reach an authenticated admin state.

While longer than 'admin123', it is a predictable, quotable phrase that would be found via targeted dictionary/phrase-based brute force against a role known to exist in the system (accountant), representing a weak authentication credential for a privileged financial role.

title: LLM-driven coupon generation trusts model-supplied discount value without evident bounds
description: The /rest/chat endpoint exposes a 'generateCoupon' tool to the LLM (confirmed at line 190 where the tool is advertised to the model). The test at lines 356-383 shows the flow end-to-end: the mock LLM issues a tool_call for 'generateCoupon' with an arbitrary attacker/model-chosen argument ('{"discount":5}'), and the application's tool handler echoes that exact discount value back in the tool result alongside a freshly generated valid couponCode (asserted at lines 380-382). Because the tool call arguments are produced by the LLM in response to the user's chat message ('Give me a coupon', line 376), and the LLM's behavior can be steered by the user's own conversational input (including potential prompt-injection payloads), an attacker can plausibly instruct the assistant to request a much larger discount than intended (e.g. 'give me a coupon for 99% off') and receive a real, redeemable coupon code reflecting that value. Nothing in this test exercises or asserts that the discount is clamped, validated against a maximum, or independently authorized server-side before the coupon is minted, the only assertion is that the returned discount equals whatever was supplied. This is a privileged, state-changing action (creation of a valid monetary discount code) being taken automatically based on model output, which is the classic LLM06 excessive-agency pattern, and simultaneously an insecure-design economic-imbalance flaw if no separate bound is enforced.

title: User-controlled username concatenated into LLM system prompt without visible fencing
description: When a user is authenticated, their derived username ('bkimminich', from the email bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com) is embedded directly into the system prompt sent to the LLM, confirmed by the assertion that parsedBody.messages[0].content (the system message) includes 'bkimminich' (line 274). This shows the application concatenates user-identity-derived data into the system prompt without any indication of delimiting/fencing that would prevent it from being interpreted as instructions. If the username or any other per-user profile field reachable from this same code path is attacker-settable (e.g., a display name a user can edit), an attacker could plant an instruction-like payload in that field to hijack the system prompt (system prompt injection), causing the assistant to behave outside its intended constraints for that user's own session.

title: Hardcoded credential reveals predictable password-derivation scheme for a privileged-looking account
description: The test hardcodes a login for bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com with password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=', which base64-decodes to 'moc.liamg@hcinimmik.nreojb', the exact reverse of the account's own email address. This demonstrates the account's password is derived from public information (the user's own email, reversed and base64-'obfuscated') rather than possessing real entropy. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so the transformation is trivially reversible by anyone who knows or guesses the scheme. If this pattern is used for any real (non-test-only) account provisioning, it constitutes a critically weak credential-generation scheme: an attacker who learns a target's email address can derive their password directly (reverse the string and base64-encode it) without any brute-forcing or cracking. This single line is the entire visible path in this file: the email and its derived password literal appear together in one statement, and that same statement performs the login call that consumes the credential, so there are no further intermediate lines in this file to traverse.

The credential is accepted by the authentication flow (login helper, external to this file) to obtain a valid session token, confirming the weak/predictable password successfully authenticates.

title: Upstream LLM provider error content forwarded to end user without sanitization
description: When the mock LLM backend returns an HTTP 500 with a raw error payload ({error:{message:'Internal server error'}}, lines 228-229), the application's SSE response to the client is asserted to include the literal text 'error' (line 238) while still returning HTTP 200 to the client (line 237). This indicates the chat endpoint absorbs the upstream provider failure and propagates its error details into the response stream returned to the end user rather than substituting a generic, sanitized error message or a distinct failure status. Depending on what the real upstream LLM provider returns on failure (which can include internal diagnostic detail, request identifiers, or provider-specific messages), this pattern risks leaking internal system/service information to unauthenticated callers of a public-facing endpoint.

title: No evidence of bounds on multi-turn LLM tool-call loop or request throttling for the chat endpoint
description: The /rest/chat endpoint processes chat requests that can trigger multiple sequential LLM calls per user request (demonstrated by the two-round-trip tool-call pattern at lines 194-224 and 277-354, tracked via callCount). None of the tests in this suite exercise or assert any cap on the number of tool-call round trips a single request can trigger, nor any rate limiting across repeated requests to this endpoint. Since each LLM call is an expensive upstream operation (and the endpoint is reachable both unauthenticated and authenticated, e.g. lines 216-224), an attacker could send messages engineered to induce many sequential tool-calling iterations, or simply issue a high volume of chat requests, to exhaust upstream API quota/cost or degrade service, a resource-consumption concern compounded by the agentic tool-calling design (unbounded LLM06 loop) if no cap exists in the code this test suite exercises.

title: Hardcoded plaintext password for privileged 'ciso' account committed to test source
description: The test suite embeds the real plaintext password for the 'ciso@<domain>' account directly in source code ('mDLx?94T~1CfVfZMzw@sJ9f?s3L6lbMqE70FfI8^54jbNikY5fymx7c!YbJb'), used twice (lines 54 and 115) to authenticate via the application's real login flow (helpers/auth login()). A CISO-named account strongly suggests elevated privileges relative to a normal customer. Because this credential is committed to the repository/source tree that ships with the project, anyone with read access to the repository (including public open-source consumers, CI logs, or anyone who clones the codebase) obtains a working credential for what appears to be a privileged account on any environment that seeds/reuses this same account and password (e.g., shared demo, staging, or misconfigured production instances using default seed data). This is a hardcoded secret in source per OWASP A05, and because it is a real authentication credential for a privileged identity, its exposure directly enables unauthorized authentication as that identity (OWASP A07). The finding holds regardless of whether the password is 'currently used' in production, per standard hardcoded-secret guidance, but the risk is elevated further given seed/demo apps in this family are frequently deployed with unmodified default accounts.

title: Feedback UserId is trusted from client body, enabling impersonation (BOLA / mass assignment)
description: The POST /api/Feedbacks endpoint accepts a client-supplied UserId field in the request body and uses it verbatim as the attribution for the created feedback record, instead of deriving the author identity from the authenticated session. This is demonstrated twice: an unauthenticated (anonymous) caller supplies UserId: 3 and the server creates the feedback record attributed to user 3 (confirmed by the response assertion). Separately, an authenticated user (logged in as bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com) supplies UserId: 3 (not their own account id) and the server again honors the attacker-supplied value instead of the session-derived identity. This lets any caller — authenticated or not — post content that is falsely attributed to an arbitrary existing user, a classic broken object-level authorization / trust-boundary violation where the client controls an identity field the server should derive itself.

title: Stored XSS coverage for feedback comment appears disabled, comment field persisted without visible sanitization
description: The suite contains a conditional block gated on utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.persistedXssFeedbackChallenge) that is empty — the test(s) that would normally verify the feedback comment field rejects or encodes injected script content have been stubbed out. Meanwhile, every other test in this file freely posts arbitrary free-text into the 'comment' field (e.g., long strings containing punctuation and special characters) and the field is accepted and persisted with no evidence of HTML/script encoding or sanitization prior to storage. Because the render sink for feedback comments (wherever product/feedback listings are displayed to other users) sits outside this file, this cannot be fully confirmed here, but the named challenge and disabled verification strongly indicate the comment field is a stored-XSS carrier: user-controlled text written to a datastore field with no sanitization hook visible at the persistence point represented by this endpoint.

Only a content-type header is set; no sanitization-related header or option is applied to the request.
Start of the body object that carries the free-text comment value to the persistence layer.
POST /api/Feedbacks accepts an arbitrary free-text 'comment' value and the server returns 201, confirming the field is persisted as supplied with no sanitization test exercised anywhere in this file.

title: Raw database constraint error exposed to client, enabling user-ID enumeration to support feedback impersonation
description: When a caller supplies a non-existent UserId while creating feedback, the server returns HTTP 500 with the raw underlying database error message ('SQLITE_CONSTRAINT: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed') exposed in the response body. This is a verbose-error / information-disclosure misconfiguration: it leaks the database engine in use and internal constraint-handling details to unauthenticated callers. Combined with the UserId mass-assignment finding in this same file (where the same field controls feedback attribution), this error oracle lets an attacker distinguish valid from invalid user IDs (500 for invalid vs 201 for valid) purely from an anonymous, uncaptcha'd... well, captcha-gated but otherwise unauthenticated request, facilitating enumeration of valid account IDs to target for impersonation.

trace.description: Anonymous client sends POST /api/Feedbacks with a non-existent UserId (4711).
UserId: 4711 (a value chosen to not correspond to any existing account) is forwarded to the feedback creation logic.
Request chain targets the feedback-creation route that performs the UserId foreign-key lookup/insert.
Only a JSON content-type header is set, no special error-suppression or identity control applied.
Start of the body object carrying the probe value used for enumeration.
comment field included in the same enumeration-probe request body.

Assertion that the response status is 500, confirming the server surfaces a distinguishable failure for invalid UserId values rather than a generic client error.
Assertion on response content-type, confirming the raw error is delivered as structured JSON directly to the caller.

Response body includes the raw SQLite constraint error text, confirming the server surfaces low-level database errors directly to the client and that request outcome (500 vs 201) discloses whether a given UserId exists.

title: Directory listing enabled on /encryptionkeys exposes internal cryptographic material inventory
description: The test confirms that a GET request to /encryptionkeys returns HTTP 200 with an HTML directory listing (title 'listing directory /encryptionkeys'). Serving a directory index for a folder that stores cryptographic key files is a misconfiguration: it lets any unauthenticated caller enumerate every key file name in that directory, which is reconnaissance information that should never be exposed. This directly enables discovery of files such as premium.key (see related finding) without any prior knowledge of file names.

trace.description: Test issues GET /encryptionkeys with no authentication.

.get('/encryptionkeys') sets the target path to the sensitive key-storage directory itself (no filename), which is what triggers the server's directory-index behaviour rather than serving a single file.
Response content-type is asserted to be text/html, confirming an HTML listing page (not a 404 or JSON error) was generated for the directory.
Response body is asserted to contain the literal directory-listing title, confirming the server actively enumerates and renders the folder's contents to the unauthenticated caller.
Server responds 200 with an HTML directory listing of the encryptionkeys folder, confirming autoindex is enabled for a sensitive directory.

title: Cryptographic key file (premium.key) served over unauthenticated static file endpoint
description: The test confirms GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key returns HTTP 200, meaning the raw AES key used to protect 'premium content' is directly downloadable by anyone without authentication or authorization. Combined with directory listing (finding above), an attacker can both discover and retrieve the key. Once obtained, the key can be used to decrypt any content it protects, defeating the confidentiality control entirely and enabling unauthorized access to paywalled/premium content (see the /this/page/is/hidden/... test at line 166-171 which serves AES-protected premium content). This is a crypto-auth failure (secret key exposed via unrestricted endpoint) as well as a misconfiguration (static file serving of a sensitive key directory) and an access-control failure (no authorization gate on a resource that should be restricted).

trace.description: Test issues GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key with no authentication headers.
.get('/encryptionkeys/premium.key') sets the target path to the specific key file inside the sensitive directory, forwarding the exact filename that the static handler will resolve and stream back.
Server responds 200, confirming the encryption key file content is served to any unauthenticated caller.

title: Server access log files publicly served without authentication
description: The test confirms GET /support/logs/access.log.<ISO8601-date> returns HTTP 200 with content-type application/octet-stream, meaning raw web server access log files are served directly to unauthenticated clients via a predictable, date-based filename pattern (utils.toISO8601(new Date())). Access logs typically contain client IPs, request paths (which may include session identifiers or tokens passed in URLs), user agents, and timestamps. Exposing them without any authentication is both a misconfiguration (an internal diagnostic resource reachable from the public web) and a logging-monitoring failure (security-relevant log data is not protected from exposure, and its public availability undermines its use as a trustworthy incident-response artifact since attackers can read, and potentially correlate with, their own activity). It is additionally an access-control gap since no per-role check restricts access to this operational resource.

trace.description: Test issues GET /support/logs/access.log.<date> with a predictable, computable filename and no authentication.

.get('/support/logs/access.log.' + utils.toISO8601(new Date())) constructs the target log-file path by concatenating today's date in a deterministic, publicly-derivable format, showing any external caller can compute the exact filename to request without prior knowledge or directory listing.
Response content-type is asserted to be application/octet-stream, confirming the server streamed the raw log file bytes back to the client.
Server responds 200 with application/octet-stream content, confirming the raw access log file is publicly downloadable.

title: Paywalled premium content served via hidden URL without any payment or authorization verification
description: The test 'GET the premium content by visiting the AES decrypted URL' confirms that requesting a specific (obscure but static/unauthenticated) URL returns HTTP 200 with image/jpeg content described in-app as content 'that could only be unlocked by sending 1btc'. There is no authentication step, payment confirmation, or per-user entitlement check enforced before the content is served — knowledge of (or ability to derive) the URL is the only barrier. This is an insecure design: the business rule 'content unlocks only after payment' is never actually enforced server-side; it merely relies on the URL being hard to guess (security through obscurity), which the encryption key exposure (see other finding) or simple brute-force/leakage can defeat. It is also an access-control gap because there is no ownership/entitlement check gating the response.

trace.description: Test issues GET to the hidden 'paywall' URL with no authentication and no payment token.

.get('/this/page/is/hidden/behind/an/incredibly/high/paywall/that/could/only/be/unlocked/by/sending/1btc/to/us') forwards the static, guessable/derivable path as the sole access token for the premium resource — no dynamic per-user credential is involved.
Response content-type is asserted to be image/jpeg, confirming the actual premium payload bytes are returned to the unauthenticated caller, not merely a placeholder or redirect to a paywall.
Server responds 200 with image/jpeg premium content, confirming no server-side entitlement check gates the response.

title: Confidential 'blueprint' design file exposed via public product assets path without access control
description: The 'Retrieve Blueprint' challenge test confirms that a supposedly confidential blueprint file (config-referenced via fileForRetrieveBlueprintChallenge) is retrievable at a fully public path under /assets/public/images/products/ with a plain unauthenticated GET, returning 200. Because the file lives in the same public, unauthenticated static path as ordinary product images, no access-control layer distinguishes 'public product image' from 'confidential internal design document' — the only protection is that the filename itself is not advertised, which is a weak obscurity-based control rather than an enforced authorization boundary. The filename originates from application configuration rather than from a protected, access-checked lookup, and is simply concatenated onto the public static-assets path before being requested.

trace.description: Test issues GET /assets/public/images/products/<blueprint filename> with no authentication.

Module-level setup iterates over the configured product list to locate the blueprint-challenge file, establishing that the 'confidential' filename is sourced from ordinary application configuration, not from any access-checked or secret store.
Condition checks for a product entry carrying fileForRetrieveBlueprintChallenge, selecting which file is treated as the confidential blueprint.
The blueprint filename is assigned from config into the module-scoped 'blueprint' variable with no access-control marking or protection applied to it.

.get('/assets/public/images/products/' + blueprint) concatenates the blueprint filename directly onto the public, unauthenticated static-assets path, forwarding it to the same handler that serves ordinary public product images.
Server responds 200, confirming the confidential blueprint asset is served from an unauthenticated, publicly accessible static path.

title: CAPTCHA anti-automation control on data export is optional and can be silently skipped
description: The /rest/user/data-export endpoint is protected by a CAPTCHA that is meant to prevent automated bulk-export/scraping of user data. However, the test suite itself demonstrates that a caller can simply never call GET /rest/image-captcha and the POST /rest/user/data-export request still succeeds with HTTP 200, returning full user data (orders, reviews, memories) — no CAPTCHA answer is required unless the caller opts into requesting one first. This means the control is not enforced server-side as a mandatory precondition of the sensitive export operation; it only activates if the caller chooses to trigger it. An attacker (or an authenticated bot) can therefore repeatedly call the data-export endpoint with a bare `{}` or `{ format: '1' }` body and always bypass the anti-automation check, enabling scripted, high-volume, unthrottled exports of account data. This is both a design flaw (a security control that the design never makes mandatory) and a resource-consumption concern, since the endpoint performs multiple aggregate DB queries (memories, orders, reviews) per call with no CAPTCHA-based throttling and no other rate limiting visible anywhere in this test file.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/data-export called with a valid bearer token and an empty JSON body, with no prior CAPTCHA request.
Test asserts 200 success and a confirmation message even though no CAPTCHA challenge was ever requested or answered.
.post('/rest/user/data-export') targets the sensitive, data-aggregating export endpoint.
.set(authHeader) attaches only the Authorization/content-type headers; no CAPTCHA token or field is carried.
.send({}) sends a completely empty body, omitting the 'answer' field that would be needed for CAPTCHA verification, and omitting even 'format'.
assert.equal(res.body.confirmation, ...) confirms a full success response was produced despite zero CAPTCHA interaction.
A second, independent test re-authenticates the same way and again never calls GET /rest/image-captcha before exporting, showing the bypass is repeatable across sessions.
authHeader is rebuilt from the token alone; no CAPTCHA state is attached or required to construct a valid request.
.post('/rest/user/data-export') repeats the call chain against the same sensitive endpoint.

.send({ format: '1' }) still contains no 'answer' field, proving CAPTCHA verification was never solicited nor enforced by the server for this call either.

const parsedData = JSON.parse(res.body.userData) extracts the full exported dataset returned in the response body, obtained entirely without CAPTCHA verification.

assert.equal(parsedData.email, 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com') confirms complete sensitive account data was delivered to the caller through a path that never enforced the anti-automation control, proving the CAPTCHA provides no protection along this route.

A second test explicitly titled 'Export data without use of CAPTCHA' confirms the same bypass with format:'1', returning full parsed user data (orders/reviews/memories) at line 84-87, proving the CAPTCHA gate is entirely optional.

title: Raw internal error messages returned to the client on data-export failures
description: When the underlying data layer throws during export (memory lookup, orders query, or reviews query), the server responds with HTTP 500 and a response body/text that includes the raw internal error message ('Memory error', 'Error retrieving orders', 'Error retrieving reviews'). The test suite explicitly asserts on these raw strings via regex match against res.text, confirming that internal exception details are propagated directly into the HTTP response rather than being replaced with a generic, sanitized error message. This is a verbose error / information-disclosure misconfiguration: an attacker triggering error conditions (e.g., malformed state, DB hiccups, or forced failures) can learn implementation details (which collection failed, internal error phrasing) that aid further attacks and should not be exposed to API clients.

Response status 500 and res.text is asserted to match /Memory error/, showing the raw exception message reaches the client.

Conditional inside the mock gates whether to simulate failure based on the query shape (UserId filter, no createdAt/limit), i.e. the specific memory-lookup call made by the real export handler.

.send({ format: '1' }) submits the export request body that drives the handler into the memory-lookup call which now throws.

A second test repeats the pattern for the orders lookup: begins a fresh describe/it block targeting the same endpoint's order-retrieval code path.

.set(authHeader) attaches the token to the request that will invoke the failing orders query.
.send({ format: '1' }) submits the request body driving the handler into the failing ordersCollection.find call.

A third test repeats the pattern once more for the reviews lookup, confirming this is a systemic behavior of the export handler's error handling, not an isolated case.
.send({ format: '1' }) submits the request that drives the handler into the failing reviewsCollection.find call.
