assert.match(res.text, /Error retrieving reviews/) confirms, for the third distinct failure path, that the literal internal error phrasing reaches the HTTP response body — establishing a consistent pattern across all three data sources aggregated by this endpoint of leaking internal error detail to API clients.

reviewsCollection.find mocked to throw; response text again asserted to contain the raw internal error phrase ('Error retrieving reviews') at line 368, confirming a consistent pattern of leaking internal error detail in API responses.

title: Weak / predictable seeded account credentials used for authentication
description: The test file authenticates against real application accounts using credentials that reveal a weak password scheme: the admin-equivalent test account 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' logs in successfully with password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=', which base64-decodes to the account's own email address reversed ('moc.liamg@hcinimmik.nreojb'). This is a trivially guessable/derivable password-generation pattern (reverse-and-encode the identity's own email) rather than a random secret, meaning anyone who knows the email can reconstruct the password. Separately, an 'admin@<domain>' account is authenticated using the extremely weak, commonly-guessed password 'admin123'. Both examples, if reflective of real seeded/default credentials in the target application (as opposed to purely synthetic test-only values), demonstrate a weak authentication/credential scheme: predictable derivation and trivial dictionary-guessable secrets for privileged or well-known accounts, enabling credential-guessing attacks that lead to full account (including admin) takeover.

trace.description: Login uses a password value that is the account's own email address, reversed and base64-encoded — a predictable derivation rather than a random secret.
A separate login as 'admin@<domain>' succeeds using the trivially weak, common default password 'admin123'.
authHeader = { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token, ... } turns the token obtained via the weakly-derived credential into a reusable bearer credential for subsequent requests.
A separate test constructs adminEmail = 'admin@' + config.get('application.domain'), targeting the well-known administrative account.
.set(authHeader) attaches the admin-derived token to an outgoing request, demonstrating the token from the weak credential is accepted for authenticating real API calls.

.send({ format: '1' }) completes a fully authenticated request to the sensitive /rest/user/data-export endpoint using only the trivially-guessable admin password, proving the weak credential grants full access to the account's protected functionality.
The resulting bearer token is used to authenticate and access the data-export endpoint, showing that possession of these guessable credentials yields a fully authenticated session.

title: Data erasure ('right to be forgotten') request does not actually delete the account
description: The test suite explicitly documents that a POST to /dataerasure/ returns HTTP 200 (success) for an authenticated user's erasure request, yet the same credentials continue to work for a subsequent login. This demonstrates that the erasure/deletion workflow is a no-op: the server accepts and confirms a data-erasure request without performing the underlying deletion the feature promises. This is a business-logic/design defect — a GDPR-style 'erase my data' request is a security- and privacy-sensitive irreversible operation, and the application's design provides no actual enforcement of the stated effect, misleading users into believing their account/data has been removed when it has not.

trace.description: Authenticated POST /dataerasure/ with the user's own email field submitted as an erasure request.
Server returns 200 with an HTML response, implying the erasure request was accepted/processed successfully.
.post('/dataerasure/') sets the erasure endpoint as the request target.
Cookie header carrying the session token is attached, establishing the authenticated identity whose data is nominally to be erased.
.field('email', 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com') supplies the target account's email as part of the erasure request payload.
assert.ok(res.headers['content-type']?.includes('text/html')) further confirms a normal successful HTML response, with no error or partial-failure indication returned to the caller.
.post('/rest/user/login') targets the standard login endpoint for the verification attempt.
Content-type header set to application/json for the login verification request.
.send({ email, password }) submits the same credentials used before the 'erasure' request, to test whether the account still exists/functions.

assert.equal(loginRes.status, 200) proves the login still succeeds after the 'successful' erasure request, confirming the erasure workflow never actually deleted the account or invalidated its credentials.
Test confirms via /rest/user/login that the same account credentials still work after the 'erasure', proving no account/data deletion actually occurred despite the successful response.

title: Path traversal / arbitrary local file read via user-controlled 'layout' parameter
description: The POST /dataerasure/ handler accepts a client-controlled 'layout' field and uses it directly to read/render a file on the server filesystem. Supplying a nonexistent relative path ('../this/file/does/not/exist') causes an unhandled filesystem error ('no such file or directory') to propagate back to the client, and supplying a valid traversal path ('../package.json') causes the server to read and embed the contents of a file outside the intended template/layout directory into the HTTP response. This is a classic Local File Inclusion / path traversal vulnerability: the server trusts a caller-supplied path with no allow-listing, canonicalization check, or directory confinement before performing a file-system read, and directly returns file contents to the requester.

trace.description: Authenticated POST /dataerasure/ sends a caller-controlled 'layout' field with a path-traversal value ('../this/file/does/not/exist').
Server responds with 500 and the raw filesystem error 'no such file or directory', confirming the 'layout' value is passed unvalidated into a file-read/render operation.
.post('/dataerasure/') targets the erasure endpoint, which internally renders a page using a layout template resolved from request data.
Cookie session token attached, satisfying the endpoint's authentication requirement (but not restricting the 'layout' value itself).
.send({ layout: '../this/file/does/not/exist' }) submits an attacker-controlled path-traversal value in the 'layout' field with no client- or server-side path restriction evident.
assert.ok(res.text.includes('no such file or directory')) confirms the raw OS-level error is surfaced, proving the 'layout' value reached an unsanitized file-system read/open call.
A second exploitation attempt begins: a new authenticated request is constructed against the same endpoint with a refined payload.
.post('/dataerasure/') again targets the vulnerable erasure/layout-rendering endpoint.
Cookie session token attached for the second request.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) shows the server successfully processed the traversal path this time, rather than rejecting it.
assert.ok(res.text.includes('juice-shop')) confirms content from package.json (a file outside the application's intended template scope) is present in the HTTP response body.
assert.ok(res.text.includes('......')) further confirms the arbitrary file's contents were read from disk and embedded/returned in the response, completing the arbitrary file read via path traversal.
Authenticated GET /dataerasure/ request begins for a user account lacking a security answer, using the token obtained at line 34.
.get('/dataerasure/') targets the erasure-form rendering endpoint, which requires the user's security answer to build the page.
Cookie session token attached, authenticating the request.
assert.equal(res.status, 500) shows the server fails internally while rendering the page rather than handling the missing-answer case gracefully.
assert.ok(res.text.includes('Error: No answer found!')) confirms the raw internal error string is returned directly in the response body to the client.

Sending layout='../package.json' yields HTTP 200 with the contents of package.json (a file outside the intended layout directory) embedded/returned in the response body, confirming arbitrary file read via path traversal.

title: Verbose internal error messages returned directly to the client
description: Multiple erasure-related error paths return raw internal error text to the HTTP client rather than a generic error message: 'Error: No answer found!' when a user lacks a security answer, and the raw OS-level 'no such file or directory' message when the layout path does not resolve. Returning internal exception detail/stack-derived strings in the response body is a diagnostic-information-exposure misconfiguration; it helps an attacker fingerprint internal logic (e.g., confirming that 'layout' reaches a filesystem call, or that account state depends on presence of a security answer row) which materially aided discovery of the path-traversal issue above.

trace.description: Authenticated GET /dataerasure/ for a user missing a security answer.
Server returns HTTP 500 with the internal error text 'Error: No answer found!' directly exposed in the response body.
Similarly, POST /dataerasure/ with an invalid 'layout' path exposes the raw filesystem error 'no such file or directory' in the response.

title: Predictable password derivation scheme observed in seeded credentials
description: The test's login credential for bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com is 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=', which base64-decodes to 'moc.liamg@hcinimmik.nreojb' — the user's own email address reversed. If this reflects an actual application-level pattern (e.g., a demo/seed account whose password is deterministically derived from its email), an attacker who knows or guesses the derivation function (reverse the email, base64-encode) could compute valid passwords for other accounts without any brute force, entirely bypassing normal authentication secrecy assumptions. This is only confirmable from this test file as applying to this one seeded account, so it is reported at lower confidence.

trace.description: Login call using password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=' for account bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com.

import { login } from './helpers/auth' — the credential pair is forwarded into this external helper (outside this file), which submits it to the application's authentication mechanism and returns a session token used throughout the remaining tests (e.g. line 37's Cookie header).

Base64-decoding this password yields the reversed email address itself, indicating a deterministic/predictable credential derived from a public identifier (the account's own email), rather than an independently chosen secret.

title: Test bootstrap unconditionally enables in-memory database with no environment guard
description: createTestApp() calls the production createApp() factory (imported directly from the main server module) with { inMemoryDb: true } and performs no check that this code path is actually running under a test environment (e.g. no NODE_ENV/CI assertion, no guard preventing this exported function from being invoked outside the test harness). Because this file directly reuses the production app factory rather than a fully isolated test-only bootstrap, and because the dangerous configuration flag (in-memory, non-persistent database) is passed unconditionally, any code path that manages to import and invoke createTestApp (or a similarly-shaped call to createApp with inMemoryDb: true) outside the intended test context would silently swap the persistent database for a throwaway in-memory one. This is a trust-assumption issue: the file assumes its own execution context (test runner) is enforced elsewhere, and the underlying design never re-validates that assumption at the point where the dangerous option is set. Concretely, if this module were ever reachable from a non-test entrypoint (e.g. accidentally bundled, imported by a diagnostic/admin route, or invoked via a test-only endpoint left enabled in a deployed environment), it would reset application state and bypass whatever persistence/audit guarantees the real database provides, with no log entry marking that a test/in-memory app instance was created.

trace.description: Exported async function createTestApp is a public entrypoint that any caller within the codebase (or, if misreachable, outside the intended test harness) can invoke.

The function unconditionally builds the { inMemoryDb: true } option object and passes it straight into the shared production createApp() factory, with no environment check (e.g. NODE_ENV === 'test') gating the call.

The module imports createApp directly from the production server module ('../../../server'), meaning this test helper wires itself to the exact same application factory used to boot the real application rather than a segregated test-only builder; the trust decision to reuse the production factory is made here.

createApp({ inMemoryDb: true }) is invoked, which per its signature controls whether the application backs itself with a persistent or throwaway in-memory database; this decision is made here without any verification that the caller is a legitimate test process, and no logging records that an in-memory (non-persistent) app instance was created.

title: Security regression tests for XXE and YAML-bomb DoS challenges are present but empty (no assertions executed)
description: The test file gates two blocks of test code behind `utils.isChallengeEnabled(...)` checks for `xxeFileDisclosureChallenge`, `xxeDosChallenge` (line 63) and `yamlBombChallenge` (line 70) — challenge flags that, in the underlying Juice Shop application, exist specifically because the `/file-upload` endpoint (and the `handleYamlUpload` handler referenced in the architecture summary) processes XML and YAML uploads that are historically vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) injection/file-disclosure and YAML-bomb style entity/alias-expansion denial-of-service. In this file, both conditional bodies (lines 64-67 for the XXE block, and the single-line body of the YAML-bomb block at line 71) are completely empty: the control flow enters the `if`, executes no statements (the intervening blank lines 64, 65, 66, 67 contain no `request(app)` calls, no payload construction, and no assertions), and falls straight through to the closing brace at line 68 without ever sending a crafted XXE or YAML-bomb payload to `/file-upload`. The second conditional at line 70 repeats the same pattern with its body closing immediately at line 71. This means that even though the application exposes challenge flags acknowledging these attack surfaces exist, the automated test suite performs zero verification of them at any point along this path. Any regression that reintroduces XXE parsing (allowing external entity resolution and file disclosure or SSRF via XXE) or unrestricted YAML alias/anchor expansion (allowing memory-exhaustion DoS from a small uploaded file) on `/file-upload` would go completely undetected by this test suite. The other tests in the file (lines 47-61) only confirm that plain `.xml` uploads now return HTTP 410, which does not exercise the YAML upload path or any XXE-specific payload variants, so it does not substitute for the missing coverage.

trace.description: Conditional test gate keyed off externally-configured challenge flags (xxeFileDisclosureChallenge, xxeDosChallenge) that exist because the /file-upload endpoint processes XML/YAML uploads susceptible to XXE and entity-expansion DoS.
The body of the XXE conditional block is empty — no request.post('/file-upload') with an XXE payload is issued and no assertion is made, so no verification of XXE protection occurs.
A second conditional gated on yamlBombChallenge, tied to the server's YAML upload handler (handleYamlUpload per routing table), is also present.
First line inside the conditional block: no test setup, request construction, or payload assembly occurs here; control simply falls through.
Second blank line inside the conditional block: still no request(app).post('/file-upload') call or XXE/YAML payload is issued.
Final blank line before the block closes; the challenge-gated test code that should exercise XXE file disclosure/DoS payloads never executes.
Closing brace of the XXE conditional block: control exits the block having performed zero verification of the endpoint's XXE handling.

The YAML-bomb conditional block body is empty, so no test ever submits a YAML entity-expansion payload to /file-upload to confirm the server bounds parsing/expansion, leaving a resource-consumption and injection (XXE) attack surface on this endpoint completely unverified by automated tests.

title: Disabled test for malformed Content-Length handling on file upload masks potential DoS/parsing weakness
description: The test at line 90 sends a file upload request with a deliberately tampered `Content-Length` header (set to '42', far smaller than the actual payload) to verify the server correctly detects the mismatch and fails gracefully (expected HTTP 500 with an 'Unexpected end of form' message). This test is explicitly skipped via `{ skip: 'Fails on CI/CD pipeline' }` on line 90, meaning the entire body of the test — resolving the fixture file path (line 91), constructing the supertest request against the running app (line 92), targeting the `/file-upload` route (line 93), setting the tampered `Content-Length` header (line 94), attaching the file payload (line 95), and both assertions verifying the failure status and error message (lines 96 and 97) — never executes in CI. The server's behavior when receiving a request whose declared body size does not match the actual transmitted size is therefore not continuously verified anywhere in the suite. Because Content-Length/body-size mismatches are a classic vector for request-smuggling and resource-exhaustion issues (e.g., a server that misparses a truncated multipart body could hang connections waiting for data that never arrives, or could be coerced into an inconsistent parsing state), disabling this regression check removes the only safeguard in this file that would catch a regression in how the upload handler bounds and validates incoming request size versus declared size.

title: Permissive CORS policy allowing any origin (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) is asserted as expected/intended behavior
description: The test suite explicitly asserts that every response from the application includes `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, meaning the CORS middleware is configured (by design, as confirmed by this passing test) to allow requests from any origin with no allow-list or origin validation. If any endpoint served by this application returns sensitive, user-specific, or session/cookie-bound data, a wildcard CORS policy combined with credentialed requests (or even non-credentialed but sensitive JSON) allows any third-party website to read the response via client-side JavaScript, defeating same-origin protections. Because this behavior is codified as a required/expected test assertion rather than flagged as a bug, it represents a hardcoded insecure default in the application's configuration that this test file locks in place. The actual CORS middleware configuration lives outside this file (likely in server.ts), but this file is the entrypoint that receives and validates the externally observable HTTP response, and it asserts the wildcard behavior as correct. Within this file the full path from request to assertion is: the request is issued against the app instance, the resulting status is checked as an intermediate gate, and only then is the wildcard-origin header value asserted as correct — there are no other intervening statements in this file that could have filtered, rejected, or overridden the response before the assertion locks it in.

Test asserts the response header 'access-control-allow-origin' equals '*', confirming and locking in a wildcard CORS policy applied by the server to all responses.

title: Generic error handler leaks internal request path / stack details in verbose 500 error page
description: The test confirms that requesting an unrecognized sub-path (e.g. '/rest/x') results in an HTTP 500 response whose HTML body contains a title reflecting the internal error message and the raw request path: '<title>Error: Unexpected path: /rest/x</title>'. This demonstrates the production error handler surfaces internal error text and unsanitized request data directly to unauthenticated clients instead of returning a generic, opaque error page. Exposing internal error text on every mismatched route helps attackers fingerprint the application's routing internals and error-handling framework, and reflecting the request path back in the response body without apparent escaping increases the risk that other reflected content in error paths could be leveraged for further attacks. This is a misconfiguration of the production error-handling behavior (verbose errors enabled) that this test explicitly validates as expected. Within this file, the path runs from the attacker-style request against the unknown sub-path, through the intermediate status-code gate that confirms the error handler (rather than a normal route) produced the response, to the final assertion that locks in the presence of the reflected, verbose error content in the response body.

title: Custom 'X-Recruiting' response header exposes internal/marketing information on every response
description: The test asserts that every response from the application includes a custom 'x-recruiting' header populated from a configuration value (application.securityTxt.hiring). While primarily a Juice-Shop-style easter egg, exposing a custom, non-standard header with internal configuration-derived content on every HTTP response increases the application's fingerprinting surface and reveals that internal configuration values are directly reflected into HTTP response headers on every request, which could be abused if the configuration value were ever attacker-influenceable or if it inadvertently carried more sensitive data in a different deployment. Within this file, the value flows from the request against the app, through the intermediate status-code check confirming a normal successful response, to the final assertion that ties the header's value directly to a live configuration lookup (config.get), demonstrating that the header content is sourced from application configuration and unconditionally attached to every response.

title: Login test helper exercises an unauthenticated, apparently rate-limit-free login endpoint
description: The exported login() function in this file drives the application's POST /rest/user/login endpoint, which per the routing metadata is reachable with no authentication or authorization middleware (auth: none) — expected for a login endpoint, but the helper itself performs no throttling, backoff, or attempt-count handling around repeated calls, and neither does anything visible in this file. Because this file is the canonical way tests (and, by extension, documentation of expected client behaviour) interact with the credential-verification endpoint, its unrestricted, single-shot request pattern with no signal of server-side rate limiting on the credential check is consistent with a brute-force-enabling gap: an attacker can submit unlimited email/password combinations against /rest/user/login. This is a credential-verification decision point (the authentication-outcome anchor), so a missing rate limit here is both a resource-consumption defect and an authentication (crypto-auth) defect, since it permits password brute-forcing. The actual enforcement (or lack thereof) lives in the server route handler outside this file, so this is reported with reduced confidence.

title: Public directory listing exposed on /ftp without authentication
description: The test at line 24 confirms that a GET to /ftp returns an unauthenticated HTML directory listing (title 'listing directory /ftp') with status 200. Directory listings on a publicly reachable endpoint let an unauthenticated attacker enumerate every file stored in the folder — including backup files, credential stores, and confidential documents that are exercised later in this same test suite (acquisitions.md, incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, quarantined malware). This is a design/configuration choice: the server actively serves a listing of internal file system contents to any caller, rather than restricting the endpoint or disabling directory browsing. An attacker simply requests /ftp to build a target list for further exploitation of the individual files below.

title: Confidential business document served without any access control
description: The test explicitly labeled 'GET the confidential file in /ftp' (line 74) confirms that /ftp/acquisitions.md — a document the application itself designates as confidential ('# Planned Acquisitions') — is retrievable by an unauthenticated request and returns 200 with its full contents. The design never establishes an authorization check for sensitive documents placed in the publicly served /ftp folder; any caller who knows or discovers the filename (trivially, via the directory listing at /ftp) can read confidential business information. This is a trust-assumption violation: the server treats presence of a file in a public folder as sufficient authorization to serve it, with no session, role, or ownership check.

description: The test at line 81-85 confirms that /ftp/incident-support.kdbx (a KeePass password database) is served with status 200 to an unauthenticated request. A .kdbx file is a credential store; exposing it publicly allows any attacker to download the vault and mount an offline brute-force/dictionary attack against its master password with no rate limiting or detection, since the download itself succeeds silently. Placing a credential store in a folder that is both listed (see /ftp finding) and served without authorization is an insecure design decision that treats a highly sensitive artifact the same as any static asset.

title: Extension allow-list on /ftp bypassable via null-byte-style encoded suffix, exposing backup files
description: Several tests show that files with disallowed extensions such as .bak are blocked with 403 when requested directly (lines 56-66), demonstrating an extension-based access control on /ftp. However, the test at line 127-133 shows that appending an encoded null-byte-like sequence and a permitted extension — '/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md' — bypasses this control and successfully returns the .bak file's contents (200, containing the epilogue-js dependency line) rather than being rejected. The extension filter is therefore not re-deriving/validating the true resource being served; it can be tricked by a crafted suffix into serving a file type it is explicitly designed to block. This is a design flaw in the access-control mechanism itself (the check is bypassable by construction, not merely missing one case), allowing disclosure of arbitrary backed-up source/config files (e.g., package.json.bak) that were deliberately blocked from direct access.

description: None of the tests in this suite assert or exercise any audit-log, alert, or monitoring behavior when sensitive resources are accessed — e.g., downloading the confidential acquisitions.md (line 74-79), the credential database incident-support.kdbx (line 81-85), or bypassing the extension filter to read package.json.bak (line 127-133). title: Unauthenticated public exposure of internal application log files
description: The test suite confirms that the route GET /support/logs/:file returns the contents of the application's access log file (e.g. access.log.<date>) with HTTP 200 and a Content-Type of application/octet-stream, and the request is made with no authentication token, cookie, or credential of any kind (see line 22-23). This indicates the underlying route handler (defined outside this file, in server.ts, but only observable here through its externally-visible behavior) serves internal operational log files to any unauthenticated caller. Access/error logs frequently contain sensitive operational data — request paths with query strings, IP addresses, user agents, session identifiers, internal error stack traces, and timing information — that is valuable to an attacker for reconnaissance, session hijacking, or building further attacks. Exposing these logs publicly also violates the principle that internal logs should be restricted to operators/admins.

title: Weak blacklist-only path traversal filter on log file name parameter
description: The /support/logs/:file route accepts an arbitrary, caller-controlled filename and reads a file from disk based on it (evidenced by the successful retrieval of access.log.<date> in the first test). The only protection demonstrated by this test suite is a check that rejects filenames containing a literal forward slash (tested here via the URL-encoded '%2f' sequence, asserting a 403 with the message 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!'). This is a single-character blacklist rather than a proper allow-list/canonicalization-based validation. It is not demonstrated (and nothing in this file or its assertions verifies) that other traversal vectors are blocked — e.g., backslashes ('..\\'), double-URL-encoded slashes ('%252f'), null bytes, or absolute paths without slashes on the resolved filesystem. Relying on a single blacklisted character for a file-read primitive is a design weakness typical of path-traversal-prone file-serving endpoints: an attacker who finds any encoding or path construction not covered by the forward-slash check could still read arbitrary files (e.g., /etc/passwd, configuration files, credentials) from the server's filesystem.

The path traversal payload uses only URL-encoded forward slashes to attempt to reach /etc/passwd, and the test only validates that this specific character (the forward slash) is rejected — no other traversal encodings, backslashes, or dot-dot sequences are exercised by this test suite.

The app instance handling this request was created in before() via createTestApp() with no additional filesystem sandboxing, chroot, or path-canonicalization middleware configured in this test setup, so the only defense exercised against traversal is whatever character-level check exists inside the route handler itself.

Assertion on the exact error text 'Error: File names cannot contain forward slashes!' confirms the server-side check is a narrow, single-character blacklist rejecting '/' specifically, rather than a canonical-path or allow-list validation — leaving other traversal techniques (backslashes, double-encoding, null bytes) for the same file-read sink untested and potentially unvalidated.

title: Test suite validates permanent public exposure of session/continue-code data via third-party paste site
description: The test at lines 68-73 fetches a public, unauthenticated Pastebin paste and asserts that it still contains a raw access-log line embedding what looks like a live session/continue-code parameter (`current=0Y8rMnww$*9VFYE%C2%A759-!Fg1L6t&6lB`). A companion test (lines 75-82) asserts that a public StackOverflow answer still contains the internal route `/rest/continue-code` and the exact query string used by the challenge board (`/api/Challenges/?name=Score%20Board`) plus a link back to the same paste. Together these tests encode, as expected/required application behavior, that sensitive access-log content (session-like tokens and internal API paths) remains permanently and publicly reachable on unauthenticated third-party infrastructure the application does not control. This is the textbook 'sensitive data present in logs, publicly exposed' pattern from the logging/monitoring playbook — except here the exposure is not accidental but is asserted as a durable requirement with no compensating control (no token rotation, no redaction, no expiry check) anywhere in the surrounding test logic.

title: Application design trusts mutable, unowned third-party content as ground truth for security-relevant challenge validation
description: Every test in this file fetches content from external domains the application does not control (pastebin.com, listverse.disqus.com, stackoverflow.com) and treats specific substrings within that live content as authoritative proof that a security challenge remains completable (lines 12-16, 20-25, 29-36, 39-48, 51-57, 61-65, 69-73, 76-81). There is no integrity check (e.g., content hash, pinned snapshot, checksum) — only a live network fetch followed by a substring match. Because the correctness of these checks (and, by extension, the challenge-verification logic elsewhere in the app that these tests exist to validate) is anchored to resources hosted and editable by unrelated third parties, an attacker or the third party itself can silently alter, remove, or replace the referenced content, and the design has no fallback or authenticity verification to detect tampering. This is a trust-boundary violation: security-relevant validation is delegated to infrastructure outside the application's control without any server-side re-derivation or integrity check.

title: Outbound fetch calls to third-party domains made without timeout, retry, or failure-handling controls
description: All fetch() calls in this file (lines 12, 20, 29, 39, 51, 61, 69, 76) make live network requests to external hosts with no timeout/AbortController configuration and no error handling around the fetch or the subsequent res.text() call. The pattern is repeated identically at every call site rather than routed through a shared, hardened client with bounded timeouts and retry/backoff — i.e., the missing control is systemic, not a one-off oversight. If any target host TCP-hangs or drips very slowly, none of these calls has a bound, which could hang test/CI infrastructure indefinitely, and mirrors an absent operational safeguard that would be dangerous if the same unbounded-fetch pattern were reused in non-test networking code.

title: Unauthenticated public exposure of internal /metrics endpoint (Prometheus metrics disclosure)
description: The test suite repeatedly calls `request(app).get('/metrics')` with no authentication token, session cookie, or authorization header of any kind, and asserts a 200 response containing detailed internal application telemetry: exact application version (major/minor/patch), per-difficulty and per-category challenge solve counts, a 'cheat score', coding-challenge phase progress (find-it/fix-it/unsolved), total registered user counts, live HTTP request counters by status code, and file-upload success/error counters by file type. None of these tests supply credentials or exercise any authorization check before hitting the endpoint, and every single one of the six separate unauthenticated calls across the file succeeds with 200 and yields the sensitive gauge/counter data asserted immediately after. This confirms the /metrics route is designed to be reachable by any unauthenticated caller, with no gate at any of the six call sites. Exposing this data publicly is a logging/monitoring and misconfiguration defect: internal operational metrics and diagnostic data (which in Prometheus-style exporters are conventionally restricted to internal/ops networks) are served to any anonymous client, letting an attacker fingerprint the exact software version for targeted exploit selection, monitor how many users are registered, and infer which security challenges/features have been solved or are misconfigured (the 'exposedMetricsChallenge' being tested here is itself the canonical OWASP Juice Shop vulnerability of an exposed metrics endpoint). Because there is no authentication gate at all (not merely a missing per-resource ownership check), this is also a broken function-level access-control gap: a diagnostic/administrative-grade endpoint that should require elevated privileges is reachable by anyone, repeatedly, without ever being challenged for credentials.

title: GET /rest/memories exposes all users' memory records without authentication
description: The test suite explicitly documents and asserts that GET /rest/memories returns HTTP 200 when called with no Authorization header at all (lines 23-27), and returns the same 200 status when called with a valid token belonging to a specific user (lines 29-38). There is no test anywhere in this file that verifies the response is scoped to the requesting user's own memories, nor any test that a second user's token yields a different (restricted) result set. Combined with the POST test at lines 89-103 showing that memories are persisted with an owner (`res.body.data.UserId`), this confirms memories are per-user resources, yet the GET endpoint the tests validate is reachable completely unauthenticated and returns 200. This is a textbook Broken Object Level Authorization / missing-authorization pattern: a resource collection tied to individual users is served to anonymous callers, allowing any unauthenticated attacker to enumerate memory records (which include captions and, per the upload flow, associated images) belonging to every user of the application. Because the entrypoint (the actual route handler in server.ts) is outside this file, the trace below documents the vulnerability as evidenced by this test file's own assertions of the endpoint's contract.

title: Unhandled server exception (HTTP 500) on invalid uploaded file type in POST /rest/memories
description: The test at lines 49-61 deliberately uploads a file with an invalid/unexpected type (a .docx disguised as an image field) to the authenticated POST /rest/memories endpoint and asserts the server responds with HTTP 500. A well-designed upload handler should validate the file type before processing and return a controlled 4xx response (as is correctly done for the 'file not passed' cases at lines 63-73 and 75-87, which return 400 with a clean error body). The fact that an invalid file type instead produces a 500 indicates the file-type/content validation is missing or incomplete and the server is throwing an unhandled exception during processing (e.g. during image parsing/resizing). This is significant for two reasons: (1) unhandled exceptions triggered by attacker-supplied file content can be a resource-consumption/DoS vector if the failing code path holds resources (memory, file handles, worker threads) before throwing, especially if repeated with many malformed uploads and no throttling; (2) default Express/Node error handlers frequently leak stack traces or internal file paths in the 500 response body when NODE_ENV is not 'production' or error handling middleware is not configured to sanitize output, which is a misconfiguration concern. This file cannot show the handler internals or response body, so this is reported as an inference from the documented status-code contract.

title: Weak, trivially guessable default administrator password accepted by login
description: The test 'POST login with admin credentials' asserts that the application successfully authenticates the built-in administrator account (admin@<domain>) using the password 'admin123' (line 76), returning HTTP 200 with a valid auth token. A hardcoded, low-entropy, dictionary-guessable password for a privileged administrative account is a critical authentication weakness: it can be found by any offline dictionary attack or even simple guessing, and once known (as demonstrated by its presence in this test file) grants full administrative access. This is both a weak-credential/authentication defect (crypto-auth) and a dangerous default-credential misconfiguration that should never survive into a real deployment.

title: Security-relevant login IP is trusted from a client-controlled header without validating a trusted proxy
description: The '/rest/saveLoginIp' behavior exercised by this test shows that the value of the client-supplied 'true-client-ip' request header is taken verbatim and persisted/returned as the authoritative 'lastLoginIp' for the account (line 178 sets the header to an arbitrary value '1.2.3.4', and line 182 confirms that exact attacker-controlled value is stored/returned as the recorded login IP). There is no indication in the observable behavior that this header is only honored when the request originates from a trusted reverse proxy. Any authenticated client can therefore forge the IP address recorded against their own account for any security-relevant logging, audit trail, or anomaly-detection purpose (e.g., masking the true origin of credential abuse, defeating IP-based fraud/brute-force detection, or falsifying evidence in an investigation). This is a security logging/monitoring integrity failure and a misconfiguration (trusting an unauthenticated forwarded-IP-style header without restricting it to known proxies).

title: Hardcoded weak credentials for privileged accounts committed to source-controlled test file
description: The test file hardcodes plaintext login credentials for multiple privileged accounts — the admin account ('admin123'), the accountant account ('i am an awesome accountant'), and a regular customer account ('ncc-1701') — and uses them repeatedly to authenticate against the running application via the login() helper. These are weak, low-entropy, easily-guessable passwords (e.g. 'admin123' is a textbook weak password) checked directly into the repository in plaintext rather than being sourced from a secrets manager, environment variable, or randomly generated per-test-run fixture. Because this is a version-controlled source file, anyone with read access to the repository (including public repositories, as is the pattern for OWASP Juice Shop-derived codebases) can read these exact strings. Every describe block in the file re-derives the same three credential sets from scratch and feeds them straight into login(), and the resulting bearer token is then used unmodified to authorize privileged API calls, so the weak/hardcoded value travels, unchanged, from literal string to live authorization header across every test in the suite. If the same seed/demo data or credential values are reused in any staging, demo, or production-adjacent deployment, this hardcoded credential set becomes a direct authentication bypass path: an attacker who reads the test suite obtains valid admin and accountant credentials without needing to guess or brute force anything.

title: Order-history test suite lacks cross-user ownership (BOLA) verification
description: The '/rest/order-history' GET test (lines 22-49) only verifies that an authenticated admin user can retrieve their own order history and asserts on the specific contents of the returned data. It never verifies that the returned records are scoped to the authenticated caller, and there is no companion test proving that a second, different user cannot retrieve or see order records belonging to the admin (or vice versa) through this same endpoint. Given that the sibling describe block in this same file ('/rest/order-history/orders') explicitly tests function-level authorization (which roles may call the 'all orders' endpoint), the absence of an equivalent object-level authorization test for the per-user order-history endpoint is a notable coverage gap: it leaves any BOLA defect in the underlying route handler (e.g., an order-history lookup that fails to filter strictly by the authenticated user's ID) undetected by this suite. Because the actual route handler lives outside this file, the presence of an actual BOLA defect cannot be confirmed from here, but the test file's design provides no regression protection against one, and any accidental broadening of the underlying query (e.g., a shared/incorrectly scoped filter) would not be caught by this file's assertions.

title: NFT-mint wallet ownership challenge verified by set-membership only, no proof of key ownership
description: The '/rest/web3/walletNFTVerify' endpoint (exercised by this test file) determines whether a user has 'solved' the NFT minting challenge purely by checking whether the client-supplied walletAddress string exists in a server-side Set (revealed by the test mocking Set.prototype.has/delete at lines 80-89 to force a match). There is no signature, nonce, or session binding shown anywhere in this test suite that would prove the caller actually controls the private key for the supplied wallet address. Since blockchain wallet addresses that have minted an NFT are public information (visible on-chain / via the listener), any user can submit someone else's already-minting wallet address in the JSON body and be credited with having solved the challenge, without ever owning or controlling that wallet. This is a trust-assumption violation: the server accepts a client-supplied identity credential (wallet address) as sufficient proof of an action performed by that identity, instead of requiring the caller to demonstrate control of the wallet (e.g., via a signed message).

title: Raw internal exception messages returned verbatim to the client in API error responses
description: Two test cases in this file demonstrate that when the underlying handlers throw an exception, the raw exception text is placed directly into the HTTP response body rather than being logged server-side and replaced with a generic client-facing message. In the nftMintListen error case, forcing an invalid ALCHEMY_API_KEY causes a 500 whose body is asserted to match /URL/i — meaning the internal error text (which is very likely to contain the constructed provider URL, and potentially the Alchemy API key embedded in it) is exposed to any caller who can trigger a 500. In the walletNFTVerify error case, a thrown Error with message 'Mocked error' is asserted to appear identically in res.body, confirming the pattern that internal exception messages are echoed straight back to API clients. This is a security misconfiguration (verbose error disclosure) and simultaneously a logging/monitoring failure: rather than capturing the exception server-side with correlation context and returning a sanitized message, the application surfaces internal state to the requester, aiding reconnaissance and potentially leaking secrets such as API keys embedded in constructed URLs.

title: Privacy request creation trusts client-supplied UserId without ownership enforcement (BOLA)
description: The POST /api/PrivacyRequests test authenticates as a single generic user (via the shared authHeader minted at line 14) and then submits a request body containing an explicit `UserId: 1` field. The test asserts that this succeeds with HTTP 201 and a valid created record, meaning the server-side handler accepts and honors an attacker/client-controlled UserId value in the request body rather than deriving the owning user strictly from the authenticated session. If the authenticated principal is not guaranteed to have id=1, this test demonstrates that any authenticated user can create (and, by extension, likely query/update) a privacy/deletion request record attributed to an arbitrary other user id simply by placing that id in the JSON body — a textbook BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) pattern. It is also a trust-assumption/insecure-design violation: the server should re-derive UserId from the authenticated session rather than accept it from the client for a data-subject-rights (GDPR-style) request, since these records determine whose personal data gets deleted or exported.

title: Password change credentials transmitted via GET query string
description: The '/rest/user/change-password' endpoint is exercised throughout this test file exclusively via HTTP GET requests with the current password, new password, and repeated password sent as URL query-string parameters (e.g. '?current=kunigunde&new=foo&repeat=foo'). Sensitive credentials placed in a URL are captured in server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and the Referer header of any subsequent third-party request made from the same page — none of which are protected the way a request body typically is. Every test case in this describe block (successful change, wrong current password, missing passwords, missing/invalid tokens, and a second distinct account) repeats the same GET-with-credentials-in-query pattern and each is asserted to reach the intended application logic (200 success or a specific validation error), confirming the endpoint fully processes this insecure transport shape rather than rejecting it.

title: Password reset relies on weak, guessable security-question answers with no evident rate limiting

The only negative-path test that resembles an authorization check is 'GET card by non-existing id returns 400' (line 130-136), which exercises a non-existent ID (999999), not another user's existing resource ID. Since payment card IDs appear to be small sequential integers (the test itself creates one and reads back res.body.data.id), and the only observed authorization gate is 'is the caller authenticated' (all 401 tests just check for a missing Authorization header, e.g. lines 104-117), this test file provides no evidence that the /api/Cards/:id handlers enforce per-resource ownership (e.g., WHERE userId = current_user AND id = :id) rather than a global lookup by id alone. This is a coverage gap for a PCI-sensitive resource (stored payment cards) and is consistent with a classic BOLA/IDOR pattern where authentication is checked but object-level authorization is never verified anywhere in the test suite that would catch a regression.

title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials used to obtain authentication token in test setup
description: The test bootstrap authenticates using a hardcoded plaintext email/password pair ('jim@juice-sh.op' / 'ncc-1701') and stores the resulting bearer token in a module-level variable that is reused as the identity for the entire file's authorization checks. While this is a well-known seeded demo account, hardcoding credentials directly in source (rather than via environment/config injection) is a weak pattern for authentication setup and, combined with the access-control finding above, means every 'authorized' assertion in this file rests on a single, statically-known identity rather than a properly parameterized/isolated test identity model. There is no intervening line between the credential submission and the token being captured into the shared header object -- the value passes directly from the login call to the authHeader assignment with no transformation or validation step in between.

title: NoSQL operator injection in review `id` field enables mass unauthorized modification of all reviews
description: The test 'PATCH multiple product review via injection' at lines 120-136 deliberately submits `id: { $ne: -1 }` as the review identifier to PATCH /rest/products/reviews with only a generic authenticated bearer token (authHeader). The test then asserts that the number of modified documents equals `totalReviews` — i.e. the total count of every review across every product in the catalog — proving the underlying handler passes the client-supplied `id` value directly into a MongoDB/NoSQL query filter without sanitizing operator objects and without any per-resource ownership check. Any authenticated user (not just the review's author) can use this to overwrite the message of every review belonging to every other user in a single request. This is simultaneously a Broken Object Level Authorization failure (no verification that the caller owns the review(s) being modified), an insecure design flaw (the server trusts a client-supplied identifier structure instead of deriving/validating it, and never bounds how many records a single mutation request can touch), and an unrestricted resource-consumption vector (a single authenticated request can trigger an unbounded bulk write across the entire reviews collection).

title: Weakly obfuscated (base64, non-cryptographic) hardcoded password used for authentication in test fixture
description: The login call at lines 92-96 and 106-110 uses a hardcoded password value `'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI='`, which is simply the reversed email string base64-encoded — not a hash or encrypted secret, but reversible obfuscation. If this pattern reflects how the application seeds/stores this credential (rather than only how the test authenticates), it indicates the credential is protected by an easily-reversible encoding rather than a proper password hash, and the plaintext-equivalent secret is embedded directly in source control. Even treated purely as a test fixture, a hardcoded, trivially-reversible credential for a real account name checked into the repository is an authentication weakness exposed to anyone with source access, and it is reused verbatim at a second call site, compounding the exposure.

title: Test-wide authorization header minted via `security.authorize()` without any credential verification
description: Line 18 builds a shared `authHeader` by calling `security.authorize()` (imported from ../../lib/insecurity) with no arguments and no prior login/credential check, then reuses this bearer token across multiple state-changing requests (e.g., lines 70, 125) as if it represents an authenticated, verified user. This file cannot show the implementation of `security.authorize()`, but its use here — producing a valid, accepted bearer token without any username/password/credential exchange visible in this file — is consistent with a token-issuance path that does not tie the token to a verified identity or that grants elevated/default privileges without an authentication step. Since this token is accepted by the review-edit endpoint for mutating resources, an authentication mechanism that can mint tokens without verifying identity would be a serious authentication bypass.

title: Unauthenticated PUT /api/Products/:id enables product tampering (Missing Function-Level Access Control) and persists unsanitized HTML (stored XSS)
description: The test at line 86 is explicitly named 'PUT update existing product is possible due to Missing Function-Level Access Control vulnerability' and asserts (rather than rejects) that an unauthenticated request succeeds. The request at lines 87-92 sends only a jsonHeader (content-type) with no Authorization/Bearer token — contrast this with the POST test (lines 45-55) and DELETE tests (lines 98-109) which correctly return 401 without/with authentication respectively. Here the PUT request without any authentication returns 200 (line 93) and successfully overwrites the product's description field with attacker-supplied content containing raw HTML markup (`More...`, line 91), which the API then returns verbatim (line 95), confirming no server-side sanitization or encoding is applied to a field that is displayed to users elsewhere in the application (rendering sink is outside this test file, in the product listing/detail UI). This is a real, demonstrated Broken Function-Level Access Control flaw: any unauthenticated caller can rewrite arbitrary product records. It simultaneously establishes a stored/persisted XSS vulnerability because the same unauthenticated write path accepts and persists raw HTML/script-capable markup for later rendering to any site visitor who views that product.

title: GET /api/Products returns unbounded product list with no pagination assertion
description: The test for GET /api/Products begins at line 30 with the request initiated, the .get('/api/Products') call at line 31 sends no pagination or limit query parameter at all. The response status is checked at line 32 and content-type at line 33, then at line 34 the response body is only asserted to be an array (Array.isArray), with no assertion of a maximum count, page size, or enforcement of any 'limit'/'offset' parameter. At line 35 the test then iterates a for-loop over the entirety of res.body.data, whatever size it may be, checking only field types (lines 36-41) without ever bounding how many records were returned. The loop closes at line 42 having iterated the complete, unbounded result set with no size cap verified anywhere in the test. If the underlying endpoint has no pagination/size cap (which this test does not exercise or validate), a public unauthenticated endpoint could be abused to force the server to serialize and return an unbounded result set on every request, consuming memory/CPU. Reachability of an actual unbounded-data condition in production cannot be fully confirmed from this test file alone.

title: Path-traversal protection implemented as a single-character blacklist rather than canonicalized allow-list check
description: The test suite confirms that the /ftp/quarantine/:file endpoint (defined outside this file, exercised here via supertest) rejects a traversal attempt only because the decoded filename contains a literal forward slash — the error text explicitly says 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!'. This reveals the server-side design relies on blacklisting a single character rather than resolving the requested path to its canonical absolute form and verifying it stays within the quarantine directory (an allow-list/prefix-check design). A blacklist of one character is a classic insecure-design pattern: any traversal technique that does not require a literal '/' in the raw parameter — e.g. platform-specific separators, double-encoding tricks that only become '/' after a later decode stage, or filesystem-specific alternate separators — is not exercised by this test and may not be caught by the underlying check. The test only proves the happy path (blocked) for the most obvious payload; it does not establish that the control is a canonicalization-based defense, which is what the design should guarantee for a file-serving endpoint whose whole job is to keep callers inside one directory.

title: SSRF via unrestricted `imageUrl` field on /profile/image/url
description: The /profile/image/url endpoint (handler lives in target-apps/juice-shop-blind/server.ts, outside this file) accepts a caller-supplied `imageUrl` field and performs a server-side HTTP fetch of that URL to populate the user's profile image. This test file demonstrates that the destination is fully attacker-controlled and unrestricted: a bare hostname with no scheme is accepted ('cataas.com/cat', line 101), a non-existent, unvalidated domain is likewise accepted and still redirects successfully (line 116), and — decisively — a URL pointing at 127.0.0.1/localhost on an arbitrary port is accepted and successfully fetched server-side by a locally spun-up mock HTTP server (lines 191-220), with the server confirmed to write the fetched content to disk and redirect to /profile. The mock-server block establishes a stand-in for an internal/attacker-controlled network endpoint (lines 152-182: authenticate to get a session, extract the resulting user id from the JWT payload, spin up a raw HTTP listener that returns attacker-defined responses, capture its port), then repeatedly proves the server-under-test will reach into that endpoint using a caller-chosen host/port with no allow-listing observed (lines 191, 195, 198, 211, 213, 215). There is no evidence anywhere in these tests of host/IP allow-listing, private-range blocking, or protocol restriction being enforced — every localhost URL variant tested succeeds. Because the server is willing to reach `http://localhost:<port>/...`, an attacker on the real deployment could substitute internal service addresses (metadata endpoints, internal admin APIs, other internal hosts/ports) as the `imageUrl` value to make the server issue requests on the attacker's behalf. The fallback behavior (line 191, 201-209) — storing the raw URL even on 404/empty-body — further shows the client fully controls a server-side-resolved resource locator with no destination validation gate.

description: The test intended to verify that anonymous (unauthenticated) callers are rejected from /profile/image/url is marked as skipped with the note 'FIXME runs into "socket hang up"'. A socket hang up during an automated test run typically indicates the server process is throwing an unhandled exception, crashing the connection, or otherwise failing to gracefully terminate the request when handling unauthenticated access to this endpoint — as opposed to returning a controlled error response (the JPG file-upload sibling test at line 62-72 correctly returns a handled 500 with an error message for the same anonymous scenario on /profile/image/file). If the underlying cause is an unhandled exception path in the URL-based upload handler when no user context is present, an attacker could exploit this to disrupt request handling or induce resource exhaustion/instability, and the lack of a passing regression test means this defect is not being verified or guarded against.

title: No evidence of size/rate limiting exercised for profile image URL fetch or file upload endpoints
description: Across all tests for both /profile/image/file and /profile/image/url, there is no test exercising a maximum file size, a request/content length cap on the fetched remote image, or any rate limiting on repeated calls to these endpoints. Since /profile/image/url causes the server to perform a synchronous outbound fetch and write the result to disk (as shown at lines 166, 176-178, 181-182, 211-220), and no test validates that arbitrarily large remote responses are rejected or capped, this endpoint is a plausible vector for memory/disk exhaustion if the upstream 'imageUrl' target returns a very large body. This is inferred only from the absence of such coverage in this test file; the actual control (if any) lives in server.ts and could not be confirmed from this file.

Mock server unconditionally returns the full fixed-size image buffer with a 200 status and Content-Type header, with no test asserting any rejection path for oversized bodies.

Test flow proceeds to POST /profile/image/url targeting the mock server, again with only the small fixed buffer as the response body, never testing an upper bound.
Server writes fetched remote content to disk with no test coverage of an upper bound on that content's size.

title: Unauthenticated challenge-state probing via /rest/repeat-notification with no differentiation between invalid, unsolved, and solved challenges
description: The test suite exercises GET /rest/repeat-notification with no authentication header/cookie set at all (lines 23-24, 30-31, 38-39), and in every case — no challenge parameter, an unsolved challenge name ('Retrieve Blueprint'), and a challenge explicitly solved just before the call ('Error Handling') — the only assertion made is that the HTTP status is 200. This confirms the endpoint accepts an arbitrary, caller-supplied 'challenge' query value without any authentication and without the test suite ever verifying that the server differentiates behavior/response based on whether that challenge name is valid, solved, or unsolved. Because the endpoint is publicly reachable and takes a free-form challenge identifier, an unauthenticated caller can use it to enumerate valid challenge names and (depending on server-side behavior not visible in this file) potentially infer global challenge solve-state, which the tests never assert is access-controlled or scoped. This is a design gap: the server never re-derives or restricts which challenge state a caller may probe, trusting the client-supplied name outright. Because the actual route handler lives outside this file, the finding is based on what this test file demonstrates is an acceptable/expected contract (200 for any input, no auth) rather than on handler code directly.

title: No rate-limiting coverage for repeated calls to /rest/repeat-notification
description: All three test cases invoke the GET /rest/repeat-notification endpoint without any authentication and without any test asserting throttling, rate limiting, or repeated-request handling. Given the endpoint's name ('repeat-notification') implies it can be invoked repeatedly to trigger notification logic, and no test in this suite exercises or asserts a limit on repeated invocation, this suggests (though cannot be confirmed from this file alone, since the handler is defined elsewhere) that the endpoint may be callable an unbounded number of times by an unauthenticated client, which could be abused to trigger repeated server-side work (e.g., notification dispatch) with no observed throttle.

title: GET /api/Recycles/:id returns recycle records (including other users' data) without any authentication or ownership check
description: The test 'Will GET existing recycle from this endpoint' issues a GET request to /api/Recycles/1 with no Authorization header at all (contrast with the POST, PUT and DELETE tests in the same file, which explicitly attach `authHeader`). The response is asserted to be status 200 and to contain an array of recycle records, each including UserId, AddressId, quantity, isPickup and date fields. This confirms that the underlying route handler for GET /api/Recycles/:id (in server.ts, not shown here) neither requires the caller to be authenticated nor scopes the lookup to the requesting user's own records — it returns whichever recycle rows match the numeric :id regardless of caller identity. Because recycle IDs are small sequential integers, any anonymous caller can enumerate IDs (1, 2, 3, ...) and harvest other users' UserId, home/pickup AddressId, quantity and scheduling data. This is a textbook BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) pattern: the endpoint performs a resource lookup by identifier without any authorization check on the result, and the design itself (an unauthenticated read path for what should be a private, per-user resource) is also an insecure-design defect — recycle pickup requests are business data tied to a specific user account, and the server never re-derives 'is this record mine' before returning it.

Server responds with HTTP 200 (not 401), indicating the route does not enforce authentication for this read path.
Response body data is asserted to be an array of recycle items, confirming multiple recycle records are returned from a single unauthenticated request.

Content-type header assertion confirms a full JSON payload was returned to the unauthenticated caller, not an error stub.

Earlier in the file, the first POST /api/Recycles call creates a recycle record, establishing the record that ID '1' will resolve to and demonstrating that IDs are assigned in a predictable, incrementing sequence.

Each returned item exposes UserId, AddressId, quantity, isPickup and date — sensitive per-user data — with no assertion or indication that the results are filtered to any particular authenticated caller, since there is none.

title: Sequential, enumerable recycle IDs combined with unbounded array response on GET /api/Recycles/:id enable mass enumeration/harvesting
description: The GET /api/Recycles/:id test shows the ID space is small sequential integers (created recycle 1 is fetched via literal '1'), and the endpoint returns an array of matching records rather than a single bounded record, with no pagination or rate limiting visible from the test's expectations. Combined with the missing authentication noted above, an attacker can script sequential requests (/api/Recycles/1, /2, /3, ...) to enumerate and scrape recycle/address data across the entire user base with no throttling asserted or implied by these tests. This compounds the access-control gap into a scalable data-harvesting / resource-consumption concern, since nothing in the observed contract limits request volume or result set size.

trace.description: Unauthenticated GET to a numeric, sequential resource identifier /api/Recycles/1.
Response returns an array (res.body.data) rather than a single bounded object, with no pagination parameters exercised or limited by the test.

Loop over res.body.data items with no upper bound asserted, indicating the endpoint can return an arbitrarily large set of records per sequential ID lookup, enabling scripted enumeration across many IDs without any observed rate limiting.

title: Open redirect via substring-based allow-list bypass (satisfyIndexOf)
description: The /redirect endpoint is protected by an allow-list intended to restrict the destinations a caller-supplied "to" parameter can send users to. The test at lines 101-110 deliberately crafts a request where the allow-listed string 'https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' is embedded as a query-string value inside an otherwise arbitrary path ('/score-board?satisfyIndexOf=...') and asserts that the request is still accepted and redirected (302 -> 200). The parameter name 'satisfyIndexOf' strongly indicates the underlying validation logic (outside this file, in the route handler) performs a substring match such as url.indexOf(allowedTarget) !== -1 or url.includes(allowedTarget) rather than parsing the URL and comparing the origin. Per the SSRF/open-redirect playbook, this is not a validation control: an attacker can place the allow-listed string anywhere in a URL they fully control, e.g. https://evil.attacker.example/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop, and the check will still pass, causing the server to issue a 302 redirect to the attacker's site. This enables classic open-redirect abuse (phishing, OAuth token theft, bypassing link-reputation filters) and demonstrates a design flaw: the server trusts client-supplied string containment instead of deriving/validating the actual destination origin.

trace.description: Test issues GET /redirect?to=/score-board?satisfyIndexOf=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop, exercising the caller-controlled 'to' query parameter that is handled by the redirect route (implemented outside this file, in server.ts).

The request explicitly disables auto-following redirects at first (redirects(1) here allows one hop), confirming the server itself issues the 302 to a URL where the allow-listed string only appears as a substring inside the query string of an unrelated path, not as the actual origin of the destination.
The supertest client builds the outbound GET request against the running app, carrying the full crafted 'to' value verbatim as the query string that the server-side route will read.

The 'to' value itself is a relative path ('/score-board') with a nested query parameter named 'satisfyIndexOf' whose value is the allow-listed URL string — this is the crafted payload whose only purpose is to make the allow-listed string appear as a substring of the overall value being checked, rather than being the value itself.

Assertion confirms the request succeeds (status 200 after following the redirect), proving the allow-list check accepted a URL because it merely contains the allow-listed string somewhere (parameter name 'satisfyIndexOf' hints at an indexOf/includes-based check) rather than validating the actual redirect target's origin — the exact weak-allowlist pattern that permits open redirect to attacker-controlled domains.

title: Unhandled exception leaks stack trace and internal error details to unauthenticated clients
description: When the /redirect endpoint is called without the required 'to' parameter, or with an unrecognized query parameter, the server throws an unhandled TypeError (apparently from calling .includes() on undefined) and responds with an HTML error page containing the application name, Express framework banner, the raw exception type ('TypeError'), the message fragment ('of undefined'), and an HTML-escaped fragment of the offending method call. This is confirmed by two separate tests (lines 70-79 and 81-90) that explicitly assert these details are present in a default 500 response. Exposing stack traces and internal error internals to any unauthenticated caller is a security misconfiguration: it discloses implementation details (framework, method names, code paths) that materially aid an attacker in further probing the application, and indicates the endpoint's input handling was never designed to validate/guard against missing or malformed parameters (an unguarded state precondition — insecure design), instead relying on an uncaught runtime exception to reject bad input.

Server responds with HTTP 500 instead of a controlled 4xx validation error, confirming the missing-parameter case is handled by an uncaught exception rather than explicit input validation.

The supertest chain completes the GET call against the running app, handing off control to the server-side handler with no 'to' parameter present, which is the precondition that triggers the later unguarded property access.

Response body is asserted to contain the application name and the Express error-page banner ('... (Express'), showing the internal framework identity and app metadata are disclosed as part of the leaked page.
Response body additionally contains the literal exception message fragment 'of undefined', exposing the exact runtime failure mode (calling a method on an undefined value) to the caller.

Response body is asserted to contain the raw TypeError text, the phrase 'of undefined', and the Express error-page banner including the application name — demonstrating the server returns full internal stack-trace/error detail to any anonymous client.

title: No evidence of security logging for blocked/attempted malicious redirect targets
description: The test suite exercises both a legitimate allow-list rejection path (406 response for an unrecognized 'to' target at lines 92-99) and the substring-based allow-list bypass (lines 101-110), but nothing in this file indicates that rejected or suspicious redirect attempts are logged, alerted on, or correlated for later incident investigation. Given that the redirect endpoint is a documented target for open-redirect/phishing abuse, the absence of any observable audit trail for blocked or unusual 'to' values (e.g., repeated 406s from the same client, or a request matching the substring-bypass pattern) would hinder detecting exploitation attempts. This is inferred from the absence of logging-related assertions across all tests in the file; the actual logging behavior lives in code outside this file and cannot be fully confirmed here.

The only observable trace of the rejection is the client-facing error message ('Unrecognized target URL for redirect: whatever'), suggesting the same information is not distinctly captured server-side for detection/alerting purposes.

title: Accounting-role authorization relies on spoofable client IP address
description: The test suite for /api/Quantitys/:id demonstrates that access for the 'accountant' role to GET and PUT specific quantity records is gated by an IP-address check rather than a genuine per-resource or role-based authorization decision. Normal accountant requests receive 403 ('blocked by IP filter'), but a skipped test explicitly documents that a request appearing to originate from a specific IP value ('123.456.789') is expected to succeed with 200 and even permits a data-changing PUT (quantity update) to go through. This reveals that the server's authorization decision for a sensitive internal-only pathway is derived from network-origin information (typically req.ip / X-Forwarded-For in Express apps sitting behind a proxy) rather than from a trusted, server-side identity/role claim tied to the resource. Client-supplied or proxy-derived IP values are commonly spoofable (especially if 'trust proxy' is misconfigured or the header is not stripped/re-set at the edge), allowing any authenticated accountant (or an attacker who compromises/guesses an accountant token) to bypass the IP restriction entirely by sending a forged X-Forwarded-For style header, gaining read and write access to quantity records that the design intends to keep restricted to an internal network segment.

title: Admin account reachable via known weak default password
description: Tests authenticate as the admin user using the hardcoded password 'admin123' and this login succeeds and is used to obtain a valid Bearer token with admin privileges. If this weak, guessable password is the actual default/seed credential for the admin account in the running application (as opposed to a test-only fixture unrelated to production data), it constitutes a weak-authentication / default-credential exposure: an attacker who is aware of the well-known default admin credential can authenticate as an administrator without any additional exploitation, then use the resulting token against any admin-gated endpoint (as these very tests do against /api/Quantitys).

title: Collection endpoint /api/Quantitys returns full data set without any pagination or size limiting exercised
description: The tests for GET /api/Quantitys (covering customer, admin, and accountant roles) only assert a 200 status code and never supply or validate any pagination, limit, or offset parameters. This suggests the underlying endpoint returns the entire quantity/inventory table in a single response for any authenticated caller, regardless of role. If the underlying table grows large, or if a caller scripts repeated calls to this unthrottled read endpoint, this can lead to excessive memory/CPU consumption on the server and is exploitable by any authenticated low-privilege user (customer role is explicitly allowed) to place unbounded load on the service.

Only the response status is validated (200); no bound on result size is asserted or implied, indicating the endpoint as tested returns an unbounded data set to any authenticated caller.

title: Unbounded, unpaginated product search results allow full catalog dump in a single request
description: The test suite explicitly documents and validates that the /rest/products/search endpoint returns the entire product catalog in one response whenever the `q` parameter is empty or omitted (tests at lines 53-65 and 67-79 assert that `searchRes.body.data.length` equals the full count returned by /api/Products). There is no pagination parameter, page size limit, or truncation being exercised or expected anywhere in this suite. Because `q` is attacker-controlled and unauthenticated (no auth header is set up before these requests), any caller can force the server to serialize and return the full product table on every request, and repeat this indefinitely with no rate limit visible in the tests. Tracing the full path: the test first independently fetches the unfiltered catalog via /api/Products (lines 54-58) to obtain a baseline count with no limit applied to that call either; it then issues the search request with an empty `q` (lines 60-61), receives a successful, unrestricted 200 JSON response (lines 62-63), and asserts that the search result size exactly equals the full, unbounded catalog size (line 64). The identical pattern is repeated for a request that omits `q` entirely (lines 67, 72, 74, 76, culminating in the equivalent assertion at line 78), confirming the defect is not incidental to one test but is the endpoint's established, repeated behavior: the server never derives or enforces an upper bound on result-set size or a required minimum query specificity, so as the catalog grows, each request becomes proportionally more expensive to compute and transmit, and it can be triggered at will without restriction.
