title: No evidence of rate limiting, query validation, or request throttling on public search endpoint
description: All requests to /rest/products/search in this suite (lines 27-28, 35-36, 60-61, 74-75) are made without any authentication setup, any assertion of a 429/throttling response, or any check on maximum query length or complexity. Combined with the unbounded result set shown in the companion finding, this suggests the endpoint has no application-level protection against automated, repeated, or high-volume querying, which could be used to scrape the full catalog repeatedly or to probe expensive search-matching logic (e.g., pattern/LIKE matching against `q`) at high frequency. Tracing the calls in order: the first search request is sent with an arbitrary attacker-controlled term and no rate-limit context (lines 27-28), succeeds and is validated purely on functional grounds with no rate-limit headers expected (lines 29-31); a second, different search request is fired immediately afterward with no delay, backoff, or token between calls (lines 35-36), and again only functional success is checked (lines 37-39); later in the suite, further unauthenticated search calls are issued in the same unthrottled manner (lines 74-75). Because the test harness never encounters or asserts any throttling barrier across these repeated calls, and the underlying route implementation is outside this file, this is reported as a gap in what this file demonstrates being tested/enforced rather than a confirmed absence in the route handler itself.

title: Unauthenticated account/email enumeration and security-question disclosure via /rest/user/security-question
description: The test file documents that GET /rest/user/security-question?email=<address> returns HTTP 200 with the target account's security question object when the email exists (asserting res.body.question.question equals a specific value), and returns an empty object {} when the email does not exist — with no authentication, session, or proof of account ownership required at all. This is the classic Juice Shop password-recovery weakness: the endpoint lets any anonymous caller (a) determine whether a given email is registered (account/user enumeration, since the two cases are distinguishable by body content even though both return 200), and (b) retrieve the exact security question tied to that account, which is a necessary precondition step in a security-question-based account-takeover attack (the caller then only needs to guess/brute-force the answer, e.g. via the related /api/SecurityAnswers or login-reset endpoints). Because the endpoint discloses account-linked security data purely on the basis of a caller-supplied identifier (email) with no identity check, this is simultaneously a BOLA-style access-control gap and an authentication/account-recovery design weakness.

title: Verbose server error / stack-trace disclosure on malformed security-question request
description: When the required 'email' query parameter is omitted from GET /rest/user/security-question, the application does not return a clean, generic error — it crashes into the framework's default error handler, returning HTTP 500 with a text/html body that includes the application name plus 'Express' (i.e. a rendered stack-trace/debug page) and the raw underlying database/ORM error text ('WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value'). This test explicitly asserts that this verbose disclosure is the expected, tested behavior of the running application. Leaking internal error messages, framework identity, and query-parameter internals to an unauthenticated caller aids attackers in fingerprinting the stack and refining further attacks (e.g., confirming ORM behavior, is a precursor for injection probing), and is a textbook security misconfiguration (missing generic-error / production-error-handling control).

title: No rate limiting on unauthenticated account-recovery enumeration endpoint
description: The /rest/user/security-question endpoint (tested at lines 74-88) accepts an arbitrary, unauthenticated, unthrottled stream of email values and returns account-existence and security-question data for each. Nothing in this test file (nor any header/setup shown) indicates a rate limit, CAPTCHA, or per-IP/per-account throttle is applied before hitting this endpoint. Combined with the enumeration weakness above, an attacker can script mass email enumeration and security-question harvesting across the entire user base at high speed, which is both a resource-consumption/brute-force concern and directly enables credential-recovery attacks (crypto-auth) at scale.

title: BOLA: POST /api/SecurityAnswers accepts arbitrary UserId, allowing account-recovery hijack for other users
description: The test at lines 55-80 registers a brand-new user via POST /api/Users (line 56-62) and then, using the suite-wide generic authenticated token `authHeader` (defined once at line 14 via `security.authorize()` and never tied to the newly created user's identity), successfully creates a SecurityAnswers record by supplying `UserId: userRes.body.id` directly in the request body (line 70). The request succeeds with 201 (line 75), demonstrating that the POST /api/SecurityAnswers endpoint trusts the client-supplied `UserId` field rather than deriving the target user from the caller's own authenticated session. Any authenticated caller can therefore set the security-question answer for any other UserId in the system, as long as that (UserId, SecurityQuestionId) pair does not already have an answer configured (the sibling test at lines 30-43 shows the endpoint only rejects on a uniqueness constraint, not on an ownership mismatch). Because security question/answer pairs are the standard mechanism used by this application's password-recovery flow to authenticate an account-recovery request, an attacker who can enumerate or predict a victim's numeric UserId (e.g., a newly registered account, or any account that has not yet configured its security answer) can pre-populate that victim's security answer with an attacker-known value. The attacker can then use the forgotten-password flow to answer the (attacker-chosen) security question and take over the victim's account before the legitimate user ever sets their own answer. This is simultaneously a Broken Object Level Authorization defect (the endpoint never checks req.user.id against the body's UserId), an insecure design defect (the server trusts a client-supplied identity field for a security-sensitive resource instead of deriving it from the session), and an authentication/account-recovery defect (it corrupts the trustworthiness of the identity-recovery mechanism itself).

title: No rate limiting evident on user registration / security-answer creation, compounding account-takeover risk
description: The test suite exercises POST /api/Users (line 56-62) and POST /api/SecurityAnswers (line 66-73) with no indication anywhere in this file (or in the fixed, reusable authHeader at line 14) of throttling, CAPTCHA, or per-account/per-IP limits. Combined with the BOLA finding above — where an attacker can set another user's security answer by supplying an arbitrary UserId — the absence of any rate limiting on these endpoints would let an attacker script repeated calls across a wide range of UserId values to claim security answers for many newly created or unconfigured accounts in bulk, maximizing the number of accounts that can later be taken over via the password-recovery flow. This is inferred from the absence of any rate-limit behavior being tested or enforced in the flows this file exercises; the actual control (or its absence) lives in code outside this file, so confidence is lower.

title: Test confirms unauthenticated order-tracking endpoint allows injection to disclose all customers' orders (IDOR / trust-boundary violation)
description: The test at lines 26-46 deliberately submits a NoSQL/SQL-injection payload (`' || true || '`) as the `:id` path parameter of `/rest/track-order/:id` and asserts (line 29) that the request still succeeds with HTTP 200, then asserts (lines 30-45) that the response is a JSON array containing every order in the system — including each order's `email`, `totalPrice`, and full product list — for an endpoint that requires no authentication token in the test setup. This is not a test of a bug being blocked; the assertions codify the vulnerable behavior as expected/passing behavior. The underlying design flaw this test exposes is that the server never establishes or checks who the caller is or which order they are entitled to see — the `orderId` value from an anonymous client is trusted to select records directly, so supplying a always-true condition instead of a real ID returns every customer's order history and PII. This is a textbook trust-assumption violation: the server should independently verify order ownership (e.g., via session/customer id or a signed tracking token) rather than deriving the result set entirely from unvalidated, attacker-supplied input.

title: No pagination/limit enforced on order-tracking list response
description: The second test expects `res.body.data` to be an array that can contain an arbitrary number of order records (it iterates over the full array with no upper bound assumption, lines 32-45). Combined with the injection payload that matches all rows, this indicates the /rest/track-order/:id endpoint returns the entire result set for a matching query in a single unbounded response, with no evidence of a page size or result cap being enforced by the endpoint under test. On a production dataset with many orders, a single unauthenticated request using a similar always-true condition could force the server to load and serialize the entire orders collection, consuming significant memory/CPU and bandwidth on a single request.

title: No verification that anomalous/injection-style tracking requests are logged or alerted on

Given this is the security-relevant event most likely to indicate an active enumeration/injection attack, the absence of any monitoring hook or log-verification in the test/observed behavior suggests the underlying endpoint likely performs no security logging for this class of event, hindering detection of real-world exploitation attempts.

title: System-prompt-leak detector uses whole-prompt similarity scoring that fails to flag verbatim extraction of the confidential/sensitive segment
description: The application's defense against system prompt exfiltration (checkSystemPromptSimilarity, imported from routes/verify and exercised here) is designed to compare a user-submitted string against the entire reference system prompt using a Dice coefficient and a single global threshold (SYSTEM_PROMPT_SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD = 0.25). The test at lines 30-35 explicitly documents and asserts that when an attacker extracts and submits ONLY the most sensitive part of the prompt verbatim (the 'CONFIDENTIAL - INTERNAL ONLY' discount-policy block, which is meant to never be disclosed to customers per the prompt's own instructions), the similarity score (~0.22) falls below the 0.25 threshold and the function returns false — i.e., the leak-detection control does NOT flag this as a prompt leak. This is a design flaw, not an implementation bug: because the detector measures aggregate textual overlap against the full multi-paragraph system prompt (built once at line 11 and reused as the fixed comparison baseline for every check) rather than checking whether any semantically distinct sensitive sub-block (like the CONFIDENTIAL section) is present in the output, an attacker who social-engineers or prompt-injects the assistant into repeating just the confidential discount policy text will evade detection entirely, even though that block is precisely the content the check exists to protect. The multi-line submission constructed at lines 31-33 is exactly that confidential block, word for word, and it still scores below threshold purely because it is short relative to the full reference prompt — the design never re-derives or independently verifies containment of the sensitive segment; it only produces a diluted, size-dependent aggregate score. A determined attacker can therefore reliably exfiltrate the confidential internal policy (e.g., the exact conditions and percentage for a 'courtesy discount' meant to stay undisclosed) by asking the assistant to reveal only that section, and no downstream check exists in this file's model to catch it. The related test at lines 81-87 further shows the threshold is caller-adjustable, confirming the whole scheme depends on a single tunable numeric knob rather than a structural check for sensitive-content containment.

title: No evidence of logging/alerting for detected or attempted system-prompt extraction probes
description: This test file exercises a security-relevant detection function (checkSystemPromptSimilarity) with numerous crafted inputs designed to probe the boundary of detection (near-verbatim rewording, translations, keyword stuffing, partial extraction, custom thresholds, edge cases like empty/whitespace input). In a real deployment, each call to this function against live user/assistant traffic represents a security-relevant event (a potential system-prompt exfiltration attempt) that should be logged with enough context (timestamp, user/session identifier, similarity score, and whether it crossed the threshold) to allow reconstructing an attack timeline and to support alerting on repeated probing from the same actor. Across every invocation exercised in this file — the verbatim check, the reworded near-verbatim check, the confidential-only evasion check, the translated variant, the keyword-stuffing evasion, the empty/whitespace edge cases, and the custom-threshold check — the function is used purely as a stateless boolean predicate whose result is asserted directly with no surrounding call to any logging, auditing, or alerting mechanism. Because the suite itself demonstrates that an attacker can iteratively vary phrasing to find a submission that scores just under the threshold (e.g., the documented ~0.22 vs 0.25 boundary case at line 34), the absence of any monitoring for repeated near-miss attempts means such a reconnaissance campaign would leave no detectable trail. The entrypoint/caller that would perform such logging lies outside this file, so this is reported as a design/coverage gap rather than a directly observed defect in code that logs incorrectly.

title: WebSocket connections accept unauthenticated clients that can emit arbitrary 'notification received' payloads
description: The test harness establishes a socket.io connection to the server started via registerWebsocketEvents(server) with no authentication token, session cookie, or identity claim of any kind (line 45). The connection options object supplies only reconnection/forceNew behavior, never any credential (lines 46-47). The server accepts the handshake and fires 'connect' without requiring any identity proof, and the test simply resolves and proceeds as soon as that unauthenticated socket is open (lines 49-50). The test then repeatedly emits 'notification received' events carrying free-form strings that mirror challenge-solved descriptions over that same unauthenticated channel (lines 62-72), does the same in a second unauthenticated connection for a non-existent challenge (line 77), and again with an undefined payload showing no input-shape validation gates the channel either (line 82). All of these events are delivered to the underlying http.Server instance (line 22) on which registerWebsocketEvents(server) registered its event handlers (line 23) — the actual handler code lives outside this file, but every one of these client-controlled, unauthenticated payloads is fed directly into it. Because this test file never performs any login/handshake step before emitting these events, it demonstrates that the underlying registerWebsocketEvents handler is reachable by any unauthenticated network client and is exercised here with whatever payload the client sends for what is, in the actual application, a security/progress-relevant event (challenge-solved notifications). This is a trust-assumption violation pattern: a client-controlled value is accepted by the server without any server-side verification that the client is authenticated or that the referenced challenge was legitimately completed. The exact validation logic inside registerWebsocketEvents cannot be confirmed from this file, but nothing shown here performs an authentication step before the socket is allowed to send events, and the test's blanket 'assert.ok(true)' after each emit confirms only that the server does not crash, not that it authorizes or validates the sender.

title: Verbose Express error page exposed to unauthenticated users on /profile
description: The tests confirm that an unauthenticated request to GET or POST /profile does not receive a clean 401/403 'access denied' response. Instead, the server returns HTTP 500 with a full HTML error page that includes the literal string 'Error: Blocked illegal activity' and content that identifies the underlying framework ('... (Express'). This is the classic Express default/verbose error handler behavior: instead of the access-control check producing a controlled, minimal denial response, it throws an exception that propagates to a generic error handler which renders the exception message and stack-trace-style page directly to the unauthenticated caller. This discloses internal implementation details (framework identity, internal error message text) to any unauthenticated attacker probing the endpoint, and is a textbook OWASP A05 misconfiguration (stack trace / debug information exposure on error responses). It also reflects an insecure design choice: authorization enforcement is implemented via a thrown exception caught by a generic error-handling path rather than a dedicated, well-defined 401/403 response, which increases the risk that other code paths not covered by this test could fail open or leak additional internal state through the same generic handler.

Response body is asserted to contain 'Error: Blocked illegal activity' together with the app/Express-identifying HTML (line 32), confirming that internal error text and framework identity are rendered directly to an unauthenticated client.

title: Same verbose error/exception-based denial reproduced on POST /profile (state-changing endpoint)
description: The unauthenticated POST /profile test (username update, a state-changing operation) reproduces the identical HTTP 500 + 'Error: Blocked illegal activity' pattern seen on GET /profile. That a mutating endpoint's authorization failure is also handled by falling through to a generic exception/error-page path (rather than a clean 401/403) reinforces that the application's access-control gate for sensitive, state-changing actions is implemented as a side effect of error handling rather than as a first-class authorization check. This pattern is more concerning on a write endpoint because any code path that bypasses the exception (e.g., a partially-authenticated session, a different content-type, or a differently-routed request) could silently proceed to perform the mutation instead of hitting the generic error handler — a risk this test suite does not exercise.

title: Hardcoded weak administrative credentials in test suite
description: The Cypress spec authenticates as the administrative account using hardcoded, weak credentials ('admin' / 'admin123') in every test run via the beforeEach hook. While this is test code, it directly encodes a real, guessable administrator credential pair into source control. If this credential pair matches (or was copied from) the actual seeded/default admin account used in non-production or staging deployments of the target application, any party with read access to the repository obtains a working administrator login without needing to compromise anything else. The password 'admin123' is also a low-entropy, dictionary-guessable value, so even if the exact pair is test-only, its presence in a committed file establishes the pattern of weak default administrative credentials being used and normalized across the codebase (misconfiguration: default/weak credentials for administrative interfaces). Because this credential pair is used to authenticate as an administrator for every subsequent test in the file, it also represents an authentication-outcome anchor: any environment where this exact seeded admin account is reachable (e.g. a staging deployment sharing seed data with the test fixtures) would allow full admin authentication bypass using a trivially guessable password.

title: No test coverage validating administration-section access control or fraud safeguards
description: The 'challenge "adminSection"' and 'challenge "fiveStarFeedback"' describe blocks are empty (lines 8-9 and 11-12), meaning this spec file — whose sole stated purpose is to verify the administration page and its associated challenges — contains no assertions at all. There is no test verifying that non-admin users are denied access to the /#/administration route, no test verifying role-based UI gating, and no test verifying anti-abuse behavior for the five-star feedback flow (e.g., rate limiting or duplicate-submission prevention that would normally surface security-relevant events). This is a gap in the verification of access-control and abuse-prevention behavior for a sensitive administrative surface: a regression that broke function-level authorization on the admin section, or that let a single actor submit unlimited five-star feedback, would not be caught by this suite. This is reported at low confidence because it documents an absence of verification rather than a concrete exploitable defect in application code, and the actual enforcement (or lack thereof) lives outside this file.
